item.title: Three More Women Say Josh Jacobs Physically Abused Them
item.author: Tom Ley
item.content:encoded: On Friday, the Hobart/Lawrence Police Department released a batch of records related to Packers running back Josh Jacobs's domestic violence arrest in May. The records reveal that while police were investigating the May incident, they were contacted by three other women who said Jacobs abused them in the past. One document describes a phone conversation a police investigator had with a woman who said she felt compelled to contact police after learning about the details of Jacobs's May arrest. According to the report, this woman told the investigator that she was abused by Jacobs in 2023 after meeting him in his house. She told police that she went to Jacobs's house after meeting him on Instagram. The woman claims that when she arrived at the house, Jacobs questioned whether she had come to have sex with him. When she said that wasn't the reason she came to the house, she says he became angry and slapped her across the face. The woman also told police that Jacobs grabbed her by the hair, pinned her to the bed, threw her off the bed, spit on her, grabbed her by the throat, and said, "I should kill you right now."The woman told the investigator that she did not contact the police at the time because she remained friends with Jacobs after the incident and was worried people wouldn't believe her.

item.title: It’s Sunday. Let’s celebrate some heroes.
item.author: Jeff Tiedrich
item.source: everyone is entitled to my own opinion
item.content:encoded: Yes, I know. Everything right now. But that doesn’t mean we can’t occasionally pause to celebrate the heroes within our midst.Today, let’s do just that.Sir Patrick Stewart passed away this week at the age of 86. During his life, he’d been a Shakespearean actor, a starship captain, and a role model, beloved by millions. But here’s another fun fact about Sir Pat: he fuckingDonny Convict. Check out this except from an interview Stewart did with the AV Club back in 2017.“You might say to me, ‘well, you’re not an American. What has it got to do with you?’ The fact is, when America sneezes, the world catches a cold. And America, I think, is on the edge of a very bad flu infection. And it’s because of the man who is in the White House. I do find, as time goes by, I find myself becoming increasingly anxious.”“I’m not a citizen,” he said. “However, there is, maybe it’s the only good thing, as the result of this election: I am now applying for citizenship. Because I want to be an American too.”He added, “All of my friends in Washington said, ‘There is one thing you can do. Fight, fight, oppose, oppose.’”Congratulations, Donny — you’re now an inspiration. Stand proud. No one every became a citizen just so they could vote against Joe Biden. You built that! (Full disclosure: in the interest of Responsible Journalism and Everything™, I asked Google’s janky, six-fingered plagiarism robot if Patrick Stewart ever did become a US citizen. Sadly, the answer was ‘no,’ for a number of reasons. I don’t care. Sir Patrick is still a hero.)Here’s another hero — actor Wil Wheaton, who played Ensign Crusher on Star Trek: The Next Generation.Stephen Miller, on behalf of Star Trek, and everyone who knew and loved him, keep my Captain’s name out of your fucking Nazi mouth. He despised you, and everything you stand for.Hang on, we should probably to do a quick fact check. Does Stephen Miller in fact have a ‘fucking Nazi mouth’?Yes — yes he does. And I would add to the mix.Look, I’m with Wil. Nosferatu needs to shut the fuck up. Whatever lessons he imagines he learned from watching Star Trek as a kid, he clearly got it wrong. There are no episodes where the fascist fuckwads are the guys. How does one watch Star Trek and come away with the conclusion that the racist oppressors are the icons? Not all heroes wear capes. Sometimes they stand in the audience and yell shit.I believe it was Jesus who so wisely counseled us in his Sermon on the Mount, ‘blessed are the hecklers, because they make the shit-gizzards we hate look like stupid dicks.’It’s not just Dear Leader bearing the brunt of it. Republicans coast to coast are getting an earful from their fed-up constituents. Ken Paxton: “Talk your friends. Talk to your family. Tell them the difference between me and James Talarico.”Audience member: “Paxton, you take bribes!”My god, is Ken Paxton the least-magnetic candidate, like, ever? He just stands there, farting tepid mouth-sounds out of his face-hole. He makes Couchfuck McGee seem like the most dynamic public speaker in the multiverse.Who is supposed to walk away from this sleepwalked drivel, inspired to vote?Can’t Paxton find himself a job where he can steal all the money he wants without having to bore people to death at the same time? Is that really too much to ask?I have no idea who this couple is, or where they were. I learned about it from opening my social feeds last night, and there was this clip, all over the place. All I know is that we need to gif that shit, pronto.Holy shit, that’s some nightmare fuel right here. Fucking terrifying.Folks, I’ve got one more hero for you. My very good friend Eliza Gilkyson has a new album coming out early next year.This week, she posted a song from the album, to both Facebook and YouTube. Please give it a listen. I promise you, ‘In America’ is the first single from my upcoming album, LIFELINE, to be released in Feb., and due to its political nature, Facebook is not allowing me to boost the song during election week. So they have totally held me back, and that’s where you come in. We are allowed to post it, just not boost it. So if you can post the song on any of your socials and let your friends know they can do the same, then we can defy the muzzle order and let this song find its way to other like-minded souls during this worrisome week ahead of us.Wouldn’t it be nice if we lived in a world where our tech-bro overlords didn’t tip the scales in favor of the fascists? What kind of un-American bullshit is ‘you can’t boost a political song before an election’? That’s unthinkable. What the fuck has happened to our country?What episode of Star Trek was Zuck watching when he came away with the notion that being a greedy, oligarchic piece of shit was the true way forward? Because I don’t remember that one.Oh, look. We’re down at the bottom of the post. You know what that means. It’s Daily Claudia time.Today, let’s revisit cocktail hour on the patio of the Coast Guard House in Narragansett, Rhode Island, on September 21, 2023.Have a great Sunday, everyone. here’s your daily reminder that I can be found on Blue Sky at this link.this is going to be my closing message for the foreseeable future: do what you need to do to keep sane. if that means you need to disengage with my daily posts for a while, I get it. this community of ours will still be here when you return.to all the people who have signed on in the days since the election, . settle in as we all try to deal with the shitfuckery that’s ahead of us.we are all in this together, and we are all here for each other.

item.title: Verifying my web archives with Playwright
item.author: Alex Chan
item.content:encoded:
To protect against link rot and disappearing content, I save local copies of web pages I like into my web archive.Ideally, this archive is completely self-contained. I want a local copy of each page’s HTML and all the assets it depends on (CSS, images, scripts, and so on). I don’t want my archived pages fetching resources from the original website, which could disappear at any time.Initially, I was verifying self-containedness by hand. I’d open each saved page in a web browser, and check the browser dev tools. I’d check the Console tab for errors and failed requests, and watch the Network tab for requests going out to the internet. That approach was tedious and error-prone, and I wanted something better.I now automate the process using Playwright, a testing framework that allows you to control web browsers. I open each page using Playwright, and check if it’s making external requests.Detecting external requests in PlaywrightWhen you open a page in Playwright, you can subscribe to events which tell you when the page issues a request.In this Python snippet, we start Playwright, start a WebKit browser, and open a new page. We tell the page to append external requests to a list, and then load . We see that makes two requests on page load: one for , and one for a JavaScript file. sync_playwright closingpwebkitlaunch closingbrowsernew_page pageon msg requestsappendmsg
pagegoto
print requestsIn a more complex scenario, we might use Playwright to interact with the page after loading – for example, clicking a button or filling in a form, and then we could see the requests triggered by each action.Once we have a list of requests made by the page, we can inspect the property to check if any of them were fetching from an external website. I wrote a function to carry out this check: Request str bool requrl original_url urllibparseurlsplitoriginal_url urllibparseurlsplitrequrl org_urlscheme req_urlscheme org_urlnetloc req_urlnetloc req_urlscheme assert_page_is_self_contained(ctx, url)I’ve wrapped these two steps in a function assert_page_is_self_contained(ctx, url), which is part of my chives utility library.The function takes a Playwright (or ) and a URL, then:Opens a new page in the browserLoads the URL in the pageChecks what happened when the page completes loadingIt throws an exception if there are any:Uncaught page exceptions or errorsConsole warnings or errorsRequests targeting external resourcesThe function tries to trigger important network requests that might be skipped on the initial page load. For example, it evaluates the body’s to force a synchronous reflow, which causes the browser to request any lazily loaded images or fonts that might otherwise be missed.Here’s an example which verifies a file from the working directory: sync_playwright closingpwebkitlaunch assert_page_is_self_containedbrowser urlfile_uriI originally passed a as the first argument, but changing the function to take a or lets it manage its own pages. It gets a fresh page for every verification, and closes it when it’s done. (The first time I ran this, I created a new page for every verification, and never closed them – my computer ground to a crawl as my script opened hundreds of browser tabs.)If you create a new context, you can emulate different browser settings, like location, locale, and window size. Here’s an example where we use contexts to test the same page in light/dark mode: sync_playwright closingpwebkitlaunch closingbrowsernew_contextcolor_scheme assert_page_is_self_containedlight_ctx urlfile_uri closingbrowsernew_contextcolor_scheme assert_page_is_self_containeddark_ctx urlfile_uriIn my web archive, I check every page in light/dark mode, and at 1×/2× pixel densities. It takes at least a second to run each verification, so I cache the results. As I save new pages, they’re added to a verification queue, and I’m warned of any missing assets.Unsurprisingly, the first run flagged many missing fonts and images, which I added to my local archive. Every saved page now passes cleanly.Browser is best-effort, but may still miss thingsEven with automated testing, it’s difficult to guarantee a completely self-contained archive. Different instances of a browser might load different assets, and a single page load might miss different variations:Responsive images – web pages can offer different sizes of an image, and the browser chooses a specific size based on the current window dimensionsAppearance settings – a browser might load different fonts or images depending on light/dark modeInteraction-dependent assets – a web page might have assets that are only required on hover or user actionYou can mitigate some of this by testing with multiple contexts or adding post-load interactions, but every step makes the process take longer. Fortunately, most of the pages I save are simple, blog-style pages where I’ve stripped out the JavaScript. For my specific use case, initial load verification is more than good enough.There are other projects where it could be useful to intercept and audit the requests made by a web page:Verifying your Content Security Policy (CSP). The CSP header restricts what resources can be loaded by a web page, and you could check that your configuration has the correct effect.Auditing login screens. You could check that sensitive pages don’t load any external scripts, which mitigates the risk of credential theft via a compromised third-party.Testing analytics and tracking. You could script user flows, like a shopping cart checkout, and confirm that tracking events fire correctly.I don’t do much front-end web development, but Playwright has become a key tool in my toolbox. I read a lot about people using AI agents and MCPs to interact with websites, but I prefer Playwright. It’s more fiddly and requires explicit instructions, but it’s constrained, deterministic, and I never have to worry about it doing something unexpected.

item.title: Halloween at Saturday Night Live
item.author: Miss Cellania
item.content:encoded: Going into the Halloween episode, everyone wondered whether the opening skit would features Donald Trump or David S. Pumpkins. The answer is: why not both? Ten years after debuting the character, Tom Hanks flew in just to be interrupted by a diatribe from the president and was forced to stand frozen for the rest of the speech. Hanks is a good sport. The real question now is: which one of these characters is scarier? I think we know the answer.

item.title: The Sunday Ramble - Free Agent Edition
item.author: bounce+2edd00.7bdc18-5mr68b7cb43ac2h04ai5=kill-the-newsletter.com@m.ghost.io
item.content:encoded: The mad dash that figures to be baseball's truncated offseason begins in earnest on Monday at 4 p.m. as that is the hour when all free agents will be eligible to negotiate with other teams. It seems like a perfect time to dust off the Ramble and rank the top 20 free agents. While the Royals, as usual, won't make a play for the top tier of free agents, this year's class is incredibly thin. In other words, it's Tarik Skubal at the top and then there's everyone else. That means the Royals could be—should be—in the hunt for several free agents that are on the list below.There are a handful of solid, and realistic, options on this list for the Royals. Later this week, I'll take a look at players outside my list of the top 20 that the Royals should be considering.We start, like every other free agent list you will see, with the undisputed heavyweight of the 2026-27 Free Agent Class. It looked like his walk year was going to be sunk when he hit the IL with elbow issues early in the season, but he dodged Tommy John surgery and opted for a NanoScope procedure. He made it back to the mound a month later and proved he was still The Man when it came to starting pitchers. The sky is the limit for the contact he will land. Left-handed, 30-years-old and the clear marquee player in an overall weak free agent class, the bidding will be fierce. I would imagine he'll go off the board as we close in on December 1.King missed considerable time in 2025 with a shoulder injury and a knee issue. He signed a three-year deal in San Diego with a couple of opt outs, which is why he’s here…King decided to take a $5 million buyout and passed up $28 million in 2027 and $30 million that would’ve been due to him in 2028. That’s a chunk of change he’s expecting to recoup on the market, obviously plus some extra. He features five pitches with some insane movement on his sweeper and change that make him difficult to barrel. A Statcast darling to be sure, which means he’s going to continue to get paid.He will be 32 in May and the number of starting pitchers that old who have received a four-year deal can be counted on one hand.Yeah, I have Rogers this high for a few reasons. He’s one of the younger starting pitching options on the market (he will be 29 next year) and he’s a strike-thrower. A rough start to his 2026 season skewed his numbers, but he rebounded to post up the best walk rate of his career and a 3.45 FIP against a 4.03 ERA. In other words, the back of the baseball card numbers may put off some people, but the metrics insist this guy is a quality arm. Put him on a team with a forward-looking pitching lab and watch him take off.He’s a guy the Royals should most definitely be checking on, but the competition for his services is likely to drive the price out of their comfort zone.Sato won the NPB Triple Crown, the first player to do it since Munetaka Murakami in 2022. You’ll remember the reluctance from MLB teams to pursue Murakami as there was some question how his contact skills would play in the majors. It turns out they were just fine. There’s a little more risk here in that Sato is an even more aggressive hitter, and there are questions about where he will play defensively, but he should do better than Murakami’s two-year deal with the White Sox.A corner infielder isn’t a fit, but I’m waiting for the days the Royals step up and play in this market.5 and 6) Randy Arozarena - LF & Seiya Suzuki - RFFull disclosure: I adore Randy Arozarena. The guy is a blast and, in his walk year, had the best offensive season of his career. He should get paid, but I don’t like the idea of handing out a long-term contract to a 32-year-old corner outfielder who is a defensive liability. While there’s an allure to right-handed pop, there should be an aversion to a long-term deal he will most certainly be seeking.The Royals desperately need help in left, but defensive limitations and what is certain to be a lofty price tag means Arozarena isn’t the guy here.Suzuki sure feels like Arozarena’s corner outfield free agent counterpart. You could probably put these guys in same slot when ranking free agents. (Which I sort of did!) Suzuki features more patience at the plate and better defense. In doing research for this edition of the newsletter I learned that Suzuki is one of four hitters to post an OPS+ of 125 or higher in each of the last four seasons. Not even Bobby Witt Jr. can make that claim. Impressive.Like Arozarena, he's 32 next year and there are some Statcast warnings that started bubbling up last summer, like a decline in exit velocity and barrel rate that ended up being the lowest of his major league career. Corner outfielders over 30 are scary.Given my admitted bias against relief pitchers, perhaps I have lost my mind for putting a setup guy this high on the list. Except when you’re bullpen mates with Mason Miller, you’re always going to be the eighth inning guy. Morejón is close to Miller on the filth-factor, tickling triple-digits and missing bats with regularlity. Plus, he’s just 28 years old. The top reliever on the market. Oh! There's also the possibility that a team could move him to the rotation. A four-pitch mix (four-seam, sinker, change and slider) makes him an option. Besides, if it doesn't work, the bullpen thing seems to be just fine.I generally think paying a reliever big bucks in free agency is folly, but if Morejón is looking at a four year deal, I’d be all over that. The Royals need velocity and swing and miss in their bullpen and the lefty would most definitely bring that.Other pitchers got the headlines this October, but I enjoyed the fact that Peralta was throwing meaningful innings in the World Series. You know the story: Traded by the Brewers to the Mets, he had a horrible first few months of the season. As in a 4.99 ERA and 4.45 FIP. Everything the Mets touch…yadda, yadda, yadda. Jettisoned to the Rays at the trade deadline, Peralta, under the tutelage of pitching coach Kyle Snyder and the other smart people in the organization, raised his arm angle, got more extension and drive in his delivery and worked exclusively from the stretch. He pitched to a 3.25 ERA and 3.93 FIP down the stretch. Are the changes sticky? It’s gonna cost a team to find out.That strong last couple of months, plus a solid World Series means his stock is on the ascent. He doesn’t pitch deep in games so you’d want a solid bullpen in place behind him. Until further notice, that eliminates the Royals. Lowe, who will be 32 next year, had the best all-around season of his career for the Pirates in 2026. Good timing. He’s always been an above-average bat with 30-home run pop while manning the keystone. The Pirates transformed his glovework and he became an elite defender up the middle last summer. It will probably take a three-year deal to rope him in and he will presumably be attached to a qualifying offer to boot.Second base is an interesting position in this class, something that is rarely said. Are the Royals set with Michael Massey? Both are Gold Glove finalists, if you’re into that sort of thing.A bat-first catcher with solid plate discipline will always get some free agent looks, as a savvy club will work to improve his framing. Not sure his pop times can improve, though. Jeffers missed time with a broken hamate bone and really ran out of steam at the end of the year.I expect the Twins to drop a qualifying offer here. That could be too tempting to pass.If you’re looking for a Proven Closer™ in this free agent class, Bednar is your guy. He’s racked up 146 saves over his career split between Pittsburgh and the Yankees. Apart from a weird season where he struggled with his command and the runs allowed in 2024 and missed time with an oblique injury, he’s been good for around 30 saves, a 2.25 ERA and 2.0 fWAR. He doesn’t have that closer flash but gets the job done.12) Jazz Chisholm Jr. - 2BA polarizing player to say the least, Chisholm has averaged nearly 4 fWAR over the last three seasons. He does it through a combination of decent offensive production, solid defense and some good baserunning. Yeah, he said he was going to go 50-50 in 2026, but he does have one 30/30 season under his belt. The power will take a dip when he leaves New Yankee Stadium, but he’s a solid everyday player who could fill out a lineup for a contender.A newly-minted World Champion, Bauers is an interesting case. For the first five years of his big league career, he was a below average hitter and defender. Just a guy. In 2025, he added on base percentage to his toolkit and became an above-average hitter for the first time in his career. This year, he unlocked power. The result? A career best offensive season where he hit .266/.389/.484, good for a 143 wRC+. Let’s say he’s peaking at the absolute best time. There’s some risk there, especially given that his future home lies as a designated hitter.How is it possible that Sonny Gray has pitched in 14 big league seasons? His strikeout rate tumbled in ’26, but he still managed to put up a 2.72 ERA, a 3.47 FIP and a 3.4 fWAR. Dip in punchouts aside, he’s been crazy consistent the last three seasons. He’s a workhorse, too, averaging 175 innings over the last four years. He declined his side of a $30 million mutual option to hit the open market.I’d be nervous at giving him a second year, but he’s a perfect short-term rotation piece for any team looking for innings from their rotation. In other words, he’s attractive to every single team in the majors.Holmes saw his season go sideways when he took a comebacker off his leg, which broke his fibula. He missed three months. When healthy, he’s a ground ball specialist two years removed from the bullpen. The bullpen to rotation jump in his mid thirties reminds me of Seth Lugo. Holmes could be an attractive option to pick up some innings and keep the ball on the ground at the back of a rotation, including the Royals.Happ has been a solid 3.0 fWAR kind of guy throughout his career, but experienced the roughest offensive season of his career in 2026, hitting .218/.326/.412 and a 107 wRC+. Bad timing for Happ but perhaps an opportunity for a club looking for a solid option in left. There’s been rumors of interest in Happ on the part of the Royals for the last couple of seasons. Expect those rumors to pick up steam over the next 30 days. He would certainly be an upgrade as a bounceback candidate.Another polarizing second baseman, but for a different reason. If this was 1977, a career .330 batting average would have you near the top of this list. Too bad for Arraez, we are heading into 2027. To his credit, he worked with Ron Washington for half a season in San Francisco and completely remade himself as a defender. He would be lower on this ranking but not for Wash. This will be his sixth different team since 2024.Shoulder problems and a Tommy John surgery limited Mahle to eight starts between 2023 and 2024. The shoulder barked again in 2025. That meant his first foray into free agency wasn’t as lucrative as he probably had hoped as he signed a one-year $10 million deal with the Giants. Like everyone in San Francisco, he underwhelmed, posting a 5.13 ERA and 4.38 FIP over 18 starts. Shipped to Atlanta at the trade deadline, he found his mojo. In eight starts he posted a 1.00 ERA and 3.32 FIP. He’s 32 and a constant IL risk, but the upside is there. A team deep in starters could take a look. That wouldn’t be the Royals.Mize was setting himself up for a big payday. He was having the best season of his career with personal best marks in strikeout rate (8.8 SO/9) and ERA (2.70) with a 2.58 FIP over 16 starts for the Tigers. He really stumbled after a trade to the Padres. He’ll be ok given that he’s a strike-thrower who will be will be 30 next season, he sould be attractive to the Royals as they seek to add depth to their rotation. Doesn't a guy named Casey belong in KC? (Sorry about that!)Gausman, who will be 36 next year, has been one of the more consistent starting pitchers this decade. While he's lost some velocity and his strikeout rate has declined while his ERA has gone up, the decline phase of his career has been relatively gentle. He's made some noise about retiring but could be tempted with a one-year deal. It wouldn't be a surprise to see him return to Toronto for a final lap. No shade on Gausman, but having him at 20 underscores how thin this free agent class is.

item.title: It won’t be over on Tuesday
item.author: 1axbudyce9lddieiyelq2dsneq4y7devwtlpz3@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
item.content:encoded: “I’m tired.” You’ve heard me say it before, but it's true.I’m tired of Trump’s attacks on democracy. His assault on the rule of law.I’m tired of the legacy media’s false equivalency and desire to please Trump.I’m tired of big law and business leaders doing nothing while democracy is attacked.But I’m also just tired, and I know many of you are feeling it too.I’ve done this work for over 30 years, and no midterm election has been this critical to the future of our country. It consumes my every waking hour.I have always worked long hours. But lately, those hours have been even longer.When we win one case, another one pops up. When we protect one voter, Republican operatives put 10 more at risk of losing their rights. When we win a case, the GOP appeals to the Supreme Court.Ever since Trump entered politics, I feel like Sisyphus — endlessly rolling a boulder to the top of a steep hill, only to watch it roll back down.It is not just the hours that have me drained. It is the emotional toll.I am not an optimist by nature, but over the last few weeks, hope has been ever harder to find than usual.But there is another thing about this election that is different.Every day, my inbox fills with messages from readers like you.I go live on YouTube almost nightly to answer your questions, but also because connecting with you directly gives me energy and hope. You tell me you’re tired too. You tell me to keep going.“We know it won't be over on Tuesday, and I'm reassured to know you'll be there,” Dean wrote.Kellee sent me this message on Friday morning: “Who knows if anyone will read this, but it feels good to send it. Thank you all for the work you are doing to help save our democracy. Keep the faith.”I read it, Kellee. I read all of them.I know you’ve been working long, hard hours, too. I see the photos you send me from protests, marching with your friends and neighbors to save democracy.Molly shared that she was on her way to the post office with her last batch of postcards to voters before the big day. “I’m proud to support your work,” she wrote.Just as you’ve been organizing in your communities, my law firm has spent the last year preparing for the worst-case scenarios in every district and state.We’ve planned for every scenario we can imagine. We’ve left no stone unturned, and I can feel the momentum is moving in our direction.But Dean is right: It won’t be over on Tuesday.These races will be close, and Trump and his lawyers will contest every last one. My team will be in court for as long as it takes, and Democracy Docket will be covering every twist and turn.Here’s what I’m asking of you for these final days:First, make your plan to vote and VOTE.Second, rally your community. Check in with the friends, family and neighbors who might need a reminder, a ride or a little encouragement.Third, share our work. We’ve taken down our paywall through the election so that everyone can get the facts. Send our coverage to someone who needs it. And if you can, please consider becoming a Premium member. Our members make it possible for Democracy Docket to keep covering every lawsuit and every challenge long after Tuesday.The work we have already done gives me hope for victory on Election Day, and in the long days and nights that will come after. I rest a little easier knowing that I have a powerful, hardworking pro-democracy community by my side.Thank you. Let’s finish this together.

item.title: Dad Embarasses Daughter
item.author: Miss Cellania
item.content:encoded: I'm pretty sure the dad was planning on following her in to school until she skedaddled out of the car so fast. It was at that moment that Dad realized he had crossed a point of no return in life. His daughter was no longer the little four year old he had brought in to see "Daddy's Work" while building the school. She was no longer the girl at the Elementary School drop-off ramp who asked if there was any way Dad could please walk with her all the way into her classroom because she wasn't sure if she could do it herself. There comes a point in a parent's life when they drop their child off at school one day, and then never drop them off at school again. This dad now knew that his daughter wished for that day to have come and gone already. This dad knew his days were over of asking his little girl if there was anything interesting going on that day at school. He knew. And his heart broke. Not in a way that would show outwardly. Just an internal realization of the inevitability of age. And then she turned and squeaked a tiny "bye". His world came back into focus. Tears sucked back into their tear ducts. And his heart was healed. He was still her dad, even if she was now a teenager. And who knows? Maybe there will still come one more day in the future where she... "accidentally" misses the bus.

item.title: How We Took Over ChatGPT Accounts
item.author: Simon Willison
item.content:encoded: Parameter Labs describe an exploit they found against ChatGPT's implementation of the artifacts pattern (OpenAI used to call this "Canvas" but it looks like the latest revision is called HTML previews), where interactive custom HTML apps are displayed in a sandboxed iframe.It's important that HTML in these stays tightly sandboxed to avoid untrusted code interacting with OpenAI APIs and accessing private data.Parameter found quite a complex attack chain. OpenAI use the MathLive JavaScript library as part of their graph support, and that library includes its own virtual keyboard, which can be triggered in the parent page via from the sandboxed iframe.That message receiving code uses , so anything that sends a message can add custom HTML to the parent - and there was no mechanism to prevent other sandboxed frames, including HTML preview frames, from calling that method.This meant untrusted code in an iframe could insert HTML, and while doesn't directly execute script elements it could be used to inject a new iframe sandbox restrictions.OpenAI’s CSP rules blocked inline scripts entirely, and only allowed script loading from a handful of domains, but one of those was YouTube - and the YouTube oEmbed endpoint could be used to reflect JavaScript back in a way that executed it.Once the attack had JavaScript execution on ChatGPT, it was trivial to fetch private user data from APIs and exfiltrate it via an image reference.The end result: you could create a ChatGPT share URL which, when visited by another signed-in user, could exfiltrate their private data or take actions on their behalf.OpenAI closed the hole and paid out a $5,000 bug bounty, which I think was a bit cheap for a vulnerability this serious.

item.title: datasette-llm 0.1a9
item.author: Simon Willison
item.content:encoded: I have some big upgrades to Datasette Agent in the pipeline, but in the meantime here's a tiny user experience improvement to the underlying plugin. It now picks up the default model used by LLM, which means you can start using Datasette Agent without needing to explicitly configure a default model:uvx --with datasette-agent datasette content.db --internal internal.db Previously you would also need to specify a model with -s plugins.datasette-agent.default_model gpt-6-astra.

item.title: Month in Review: Democracy & church-state separation
item.author: 010001a1927b2403-f6576f26-f011-466f-a19e-dfca4aeeba81-000000@amazonses.com
item.content:encoded:
I’m writing this from the road – from a tour bus, in fact – as I join some of the original Freedom Riders and their families on a get-out-the-vote journey through the South called The Ride. My role is to remind people about the important and less understood role that church-state separation plays in protecting our democratic ideals of freedom and equality for all. By the time you read this, we’ll have spent 10 days retracing the original 1961 Freedom Ride route from Washington, D.C., to New Orleans, visiting many historically Black colleges and universities (HBCUs) and speaking especially with many students along the way. I was honored that the organizers invited Americans United to join The Ride, and AU was excited to become an official partner and sponsor. Personally, I have treasured being able to get to know some of the original Freedom Riders and their family members – and to hear them tell their stories. Professionally, this has been an exceptional opportunity for Americans United to reach a predominantly young, Black, Christian audience, and to explore what about our work best connects with this group.
One helpful framework was explaining how the white Christian Nationalist agenda to destroy church-state separation is connected to so many of the attacks we’re witnessing on our democracy right now – restricting voting access, dismantling DEI programs throughout the federal government, rolling back reproductive freedom and LGBTQ+ equality, and infusing our government and public schools with one far-right version of Christianity. (You can watch a short video clip of one of my speeches here.) I wish you all could have heard the inspiring call to action from AU Board member the Rev. Traci Blackmon (she and her organization Faith Out Loud were key organizers of The Ride). She offered an optimistic message about the power of each person’s voice and issued a compelling call to participate in democracy. The Rev. Blackmon made sure I had the opportunity to speak at historic Ebenezer Baptist Church in Atlanta about AU’s fight against the misuse of religious freedom to discriminate. I will never forget the experience of being in the Rev. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr.’s home church and quoting him about the church not being the master or servant of the state but the conscience of the state on that hallowed ground. I posed the question, “How can the church do that if it’s merged with the state?”

item.title: Donald Trump Has Already Benefitted from “Spoiler” Candidates Aided by Republican Lawyers and More
item.author: Lisa Graves
item.content:encoded: With all the controversy swirling around the U.S. Senate race in Alaska, an important piece of context has been largely absent from the coverage of Democrat Mary Peltola’s bid to unseat Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan: Donald Trump has been the beneficiary of numerous “spoiler” candidates and initiatives aiding his political ambitions.This month, Trump directed the Justice Department to try to halt the election underway, citing Republican objections to the candidacy of Dan J. Sullivan, Jr., a potential spoiler to the GOP. But the Alaska Supreme Court already ruled that removing Dan J. Sullivan from the ballot would be unlawful. Plus, the ballot makes clear that Dan S. Sullivan is the “registered Republican” and the “incumbent,” while the other Dan Sullivan is not.Trump’s unprecedented intervention could determine whether his political party remains in control of the Senate and able to rubber stamp the operatives he wants installed as judges and government officials, like his lickspittle personal lawyer, Todd Blanche, who is now paid by us to act as the Attorney General of the United States.Long-standing DOJ rules and policies have prevented the use of prosecutorial power close to–and specifically before–elections to avoid government interference in the democratic process… until now. Under Trump, that restraint has effectively disappeared.Blanche’s selective use of prosecutorial power is also evinced by the way he has gone after Trump’s political targets, like James Comey, who, as FBI director, refused to swear a loyalty oath to Trump in 2017. Blanche is pursuing criminal charges against him for a third time, now accusing him of leaking national security information in 2016.Speaking of Russia, the hypocrisy is striking. Trump is hammering Peltola for purportedly “stacking” the race with a candidate who has the same name as her opponent to siphon off votes. But Trump himself sought to stack the deck against his 2016 political opponent Hillary Clinton by literally inviting Russia, a foreign adversary, to help him out. “Russia, if you’re listening,” Trump infamously declared, urging Moscow to find the 30,000 emails allegedly missing from Clinton’s private server. Russia went on to interfere in the election in numerous ways and helped Trump win.Afterward, his son-in-law Jared Kushner, with Kislyak’s help, even sought to set up a secret phone line with Russia at a diplomatic facility in DC to shield his communications with Vladimir Putin from the U.S. intelligence community. In the years since then, Trump has repeatedly acted like Putin’s stooge, destroying American foreign policy and alienating our nation’s closest strategic allies by acting in alignment with Putin’s interests. Todd Blanche has taken no action to investigate any of it.That’s not the only way Trump has benefited from spoilers in elections, even leaving aside his mysterious admissions about his billionaire buddy Elon Musk’s 2024 actions: “He knows those computers better than anybody. All those computers. Those vote-counting computers ... And we ended up winning Pennsylvania like in a landslide.” Blanche is not investigating that either.Among those helping her in 2024 was Jay Sekulow, a right-wing lawyer who represented Trump in his first impeachment trial. Sekulow is also known as one of the “four horsemen”–alongside Leonard Leo and two others–who helped get John Roberts and Samuel Alito installed on the U.S. Supreme Court. Does anyone seriously believe that Sekulow, a Trump loyalist, would help Stein if doing so didn’t benefit his man?Stein, like Dan J. Sullivan, had a right to run–even though her campaign was never designed to actually win the election. It was meant to draw votes away from Democrats. In 2024, she was especially focused on targeting Muslim Americans, many of whom were angry over the Biden administration’s aid to Israel in the war killing civilians in Gaza.Stein also paid $100,000 to a Republican-tied firm called “Accelevate,” led by Trent Pool, who, according to , was reportedly inside the Capitol with a Gadsden flag on January 6. And Stein was not Pool’s only 2024 client. His firm also received at least $10 million from the campaign of Robert F. Kennedy, Jr., who was running as an “independent” to siphon off “MAHA” moms from the Democratic Party. He eventually dropped out to endorse Trump–who rewarded him with a key cabinet position.In 2020, Kanye “Ye” West took off his red MAGA hat to announce an independent campaign for president. As with Stein and RFK, Jr., major Republican players worked to get him on the ballot, positioning him to draw some Black votes away from Biden/Harris. As the Daily Beast reported: West’s 2020 campaign “appears to have disguised potentially millions of dollars in services it received from a secretive network of Republican Party operatives, including advisers to the GOP elite and a managing partner at one of the top conservative political firms in the country.”Before Trump’s rise to power in 2016, billionaires Charles and David Koch were also busy promoting potential spoiler candidates to counter President Barack Obama, whom Trump had been assailing over his birth certificate since 2011. In 2011-2012, they used Tea Party events organized by the Koch-funded Americans for Prosperity to promote Herman Cain’s presidential campaign, which was run by one of the Kochs’ long-time operatives in Wisconsin, to potentially siphon away some Black voters. Years later, Cain backed Trump and remained an avid supporter until he died from Covid-19 in 2020.So, here we are in 2026, with Trump wielding the power of the U.S. Department of Justice to accuse a Democratic Senate candidate and her staff of taking a page from his own party’s playbook. Peltola, meanwhile, has denied being part of the ballot-stacking effort.Truth be told, the strategy of using candidates with similar names to draw votes away from opponents is hardly new in American politics. Both parties and their allies have employed variations of the vote syphoning tactic for decades. It’s not pretty, but it’s the way politics has been played repeatedly, and there’s no proof that any of what has been alleged–and denied–in the Alaska Senate race violates the law.But there have been criminal efforts to interfere in our elections–by Donald Trump. So let’s remember just who is pushing for a criminal investigation in Alaska: the felon president, the king of modern election interference and subversion.What I’m Reading or Rereading:Get the full receipts every Monday in The Cover-UpAccountability starts with the record. COURIER’s new Contradictions Tracker compares testimony to the Epstein files, with every source linked. Follow along every Monday in The Cover-Up.

item.title: Trump's Initial Attack on Free and Fair Midterms Has Been Effectively Thwarted
item.author: David Kurtz
item.content:encoded: Let me start by emphasizing that past returns are not at all indicative of future results.With that said, the federal courts have held their own so far through the pre-election phase of the Trump administration’s attack on free and fair elections. There’s still time for the Supreme Court to engage in mischief before Election Day, but there’s not much time. And that’s really the key thing.I’ve had my hair on fire about the federal interference in the California elections since the evening of Oct. 13 precisely because that was far enough out from the end of voting for real damage to be done — but not enough time to respond to mitigate that damage.What we couldn’t know then, but which now seems likely, is that the Trump DOJ’s effort — to use the Big Lie of rampant noncitizen votingas a pretext to assert federal power to change states’ election processes and procedures — was going to be largely limited to California. It’s the only place the Trump DOJ has gone to court to try to force the segregation of alleged noncitizen ballots and delay their counting — and it has so far lost, and decisively so.I still don’t understand why the administration focused on only one state or why that state was California. It’s possible this was just the last gasp of months of pre-election efforts by the Trump administration to skew the elections — or I’m just missing something that I will rue for a very long time. But in a series of district court wins and in two rulings by the 9th Circuit yesterday, the Trump administration’s interference in California has been confronted squarely.Even a late intervention from the Supreme Court in the California case (and the Trump DOJ hasn’t gone there yet as of Saturday morning) would have much less on-the-ground impact now because mail-in ballots have continued to be processed in the two weeks since it went to court. Once they’re processed, they can’t be linked to a particular voter, so they cannot be set aside. The batch of actionable ballots that could be segregated — which, honestly, wasn’t that big to begin with — continues to shrink.In short, the pro-democracy forces have nearly run out the clock on the worst of the pre-election interference attempts.But the pre-election phase is only Act I of this three-act play.Act II is Election Day itself, where all manner of mischief is possible in an intense 24 hours. The spread of early voting has helped to reduce the overall potential impact of Election Day sabotage, but there are still risks — and importantly, what happens on Election Day can set the stage for Act III.Act III is everything that happens post-election, from tallying the votes to challenging ballots already cast to recounts and certifications and ultimately election contests. It’s where close elections can be won or lost.The three acts aren’t entirely distinct. They overlap and play off of one another. Good legal strategies, whether offensive or defensive, try to set the stage in Act I for what will happen in Act III. What the Trump DOJ is doing in the Alaska Senate race right now — even though it’s inane — is an example of laying the groundwork during the pre-election phase for what could become post-election challenges if the race is close.What made the Big Lie of rampant noncitizen voting especially dangerous is that it was designed to create a pretext for post-election legal and political arguments as to why certain categories of already-cast ballots and perhaps entire election results should somehow be voided or disregarded.With two acts left to go, we’re by no means out of the woods yet. But Act I carried a particular risk that we’ve largely managed to dodge. Let’s talk about that next.The pre-election legal wrangling of Act I is particularly important because it is the phase most likely to result in changes to election processes and procedures nationwide.That was especially true given the Trump administration’s concerted effort to use the supposed threat of noncitizen voters to impose sweeping national impediments to voting, like interposing the U.S. Postal Service as a chokepoint for mail-in ballots or requiring election officials to set aside and not count mail-in ballots based on dubious lists of noncitizen voters.Any wins in court on those fronts would have potentially affected voters everywhere. Even a single win in one court would have buttressed subsequent efforts to make the same on-the-fly changes to processes and procedures in additional jurisdictions.Act I is different in that way. By the time you get to Acts II and III, the legal battles are being fought mostly on the margins: individual races that are close and where it’s worth contesting every single vote that has been cast. The constellation of tight races worth litigating in Act III is invariably smaller than the entire pre-election playing field was in Act I. So while Act III can determine the ultimate outcomes — who wins and who gets control of the House and Senate — the impact on voters everywhere is more circumscribed.We’re just nearing the end of Act I, and there’s still a long way to go. But the big, ugly attempted intrusions by the Trump administration have so far been repelled. And, while I say this guardedly, there’s just not much time left for the administration to parlay any wins it does manage in court over the next 72 hours into dramatic nationwide changes on the ground before Election Day.

item.title: This Week In Stupid: October 31 edition
item.author: Jeff Tiedrich
item.source: everyone is entitled to my own opinion
item.content:encoded: As another stupid week comes to a close here in America, let’s look back at the dumbest fucking shit that happened.Monday: make America think againDavram Steifler of the Good Liars: “What do you like so much about Donald Trump?”Cultist: “Everything. He does what he says.” Steifler: “The war in Ukraine, he said he was gonna end it on day one.” Cultist: “I don’t know that much about it. I didn’t hear him say it.” Steifler: “What policies do you think are gonna help Americans in the next couple years?” Cultist: “Not gonna talk about that cause I don’t really know that much.”Seriously, though — is this woman living a stress-free life, or what? While the rest of us are out here, punching ourselves in the face and hassling over just trying to survive in a world where we’re governed over by fascist fuckwads, this woman hasn’t a care in the world. She doesn’t know shit, and she doesn’t want to know shit. All she knows is what Dear Leader has told her is the True Way Forward.I swear, I’m almost kinda jealous.Tuesday: make America literate againI mean, if you’re a cultist, you don’t even have to sweat over stuff like .Folks, I swear to fuck, this ad is real. It was produced and paid for by the “Congressional Leadership Fund,” in support of some MAGAfied shit-kazoo named Brian Fitzpatrick, who is apparently running for reelection in some magical land of enchantment called I shit you not. Take a closer look.Again, it must be nice to be this serenely stupid. While the rest of us are out here, hassling over making sure every gets dotted and every gets crossed, Republicans aren’t even bothering to do the barest minimum. They just outsource everything to the nearest janky, six-fingered plagiarism robot, and no one even bothers to proofread the drek it shits out.No wonder our country is circling the drain right now. We’re being governed over, not just by fascist fuckwads, but by fascist fuckwads who are morons.Wednesday: make America completely lose its shit againHere’s a fun thing that no doubt has George Orwell churning in his urn. If you go to the Wikipedia page for Mike Waltz, the US Ambassador to the United Nations, it describes him as a ‘diplomat.’“And I’m the representative of the United States of America. BACK UP! Back up, Ambassador! Back away, this isn’t Havana. Do you understand who you’re dealing with? Back up!”Gentlemen, you can’t fight in here. This is the General Assembly.Dear Leader, of course, is too chickenshit to actually anyone who’s not a woman, so Drunk Dial Mike got shuffled over to the United Nations, because ? Skills — and anger management — are just as useful in the Donnverse as spelling is.Thursday: make America Germany again“To lie, so casually, so repeatedly, so comfortably. It’s genuinely so sociopathic. And they lied again and again and again, when everyone knows the truth.”Wait — Stephen Miller is bragging about himself, isn’t he?I’m so fucking exhausted by this asshole’s tiresome act. The lies. The projection. The over-the-top hysteria. The high-pitched caterwauling, delivered in a frequency that bats use to echolocate.Astonishing. The hands, the expressions, the tone, the projection… He should get a Daytime Emmy for his impersonation—if you can get those in prison.Seriously, we need to gif that shit for posterity’s sake.Friday: the further adventures of Some Fucking Idiot™On Friday, some fucking idiot had just one public appearance on his schedule — another pathetically tiny hate-rally in some shoebox of a high school gymnasium in who the fuck even cares where, these things are eternally interchangeable. The Fucking idiot just repeats the same shit over and over.Seriously, the fucking idiot once again ticked all the boxes. He did a racism.Trump on El-Sayed: I hope you send him back to where he came from.Abdul El-Sayed was born in Michigan, so sure — let’s send him back to exactly where he is right now. It makes perfect sense to me.Trump: Nobody knows DUMB has a B. I can’t believe it took me 9 years to figure it out.Yes, I believe this is true. I believe it took the fucking idiot nine years to learn to spell a word. That’s how fucking idiots roll.TRUMP: I looked at his ass and it was all muscle. I looked up and down his legs—very powerful.TRUMP: I did not marry my sister. I had two lovely -- I have one left. Elizabeth. She’s great. But I have not -- I never proposed to them. They’re beautiful, but I was never — I was never particularly attracted to either of them. It’s not my deal.Why do we need to know this? What’s the context? Why is the fucking idiot so compelled to assure us that he never fucked his sister? Is this one of those every-accusation-is-a-confession things? Wait, I don’t want to know. Oh, and the fucking idiot got heckled — because that’s a thing that now happens at every single one of the fucking idiot’s hate-rallies.After the hate-rally was over, the fucking idiot’s hair was so embarrassed by what had gone on that it tried to escape.But because the fucking idiot never takes questions from the press while doing hate-rallies, not one reporter had the opportunity to stand up and ask, ‘what the fuck is wrong with you?’How fucking idiotic is that?And now, let’s put a close to This Week in Stupid and reward ourselves with some Daily Claudia.Yesterday evening, as I was sitting by myself, having dinner at the bar of the Hudson Valley Steakhouse, a reader of these posts recognized me, and came up to offer her condolences. Thank you, . In honor of that, here’s another triptych from the Hudson Valley Steakhouse, on November 29, 2024.Have a non-stupid Saturday, everyone. I will never get used to being recognized in public. here’s your daily reminder that I can be found on Blue Sky at this link.this is going to be my closing message for the foreseeable future:practice self-care. do what you need to do to keep sane. if that means you need to disengage with my daily posts for a while, I get it. this community of ours will still be here when you return.to all the people who have signed on in the days since the election, . settle in as we all try to deal with the shitfuckery that’s ahead of us.we are all in this together, and we are all here for each other.

item.title: This TED-Ed Lesson is a Horror Story
item.author: Miss Cellania
item.content:encoded: You can tell this is a horror story because it features toothy green monsters and is narrated by a skeleton. But as an adult, you should also know that nothing good can come of going a long time without brushing your teeth. Your mother told you that if you didn't brush every day, your teeth would fall out. That really hit home when you turned six and your teeth fell out. But that second batch of teeth have to last a lifetime. Scientists can explain exactly what happens in your mouth to cause unbrushed teeth to fall out, and it's not pretty. Furthermore, rotten teeth and infected gums can affect the rest our bodies as well.

item.title: The only thing scarier than Halloween? Midterms. 🎃
item.author: bounce-mc.us1_388705.10708793-d186966748@mail155.sea81.mcsv.net
item.content:encoded: On a brilliantly sunny day in May, national correspondent Kiera Butler found herself eating quiche in the cheerful breakfast nook of a home high above the rolling farmland of Moscow, Idaho. Her host was Doug Wilson, a firebrand pastor, self-proclaimed Christian nationalist, and spiritual leader steering a rapidly growing empire. During her visit, Wilson, who is 73, was soft-spoken and friendly, reminiscing with his wife about when their now-grown kids were young. But behind that grandfatherly veneer lies a movement that preaches rigid patriarchy, strict discipline, and a deep disdain for progressive politics. “God has called men to be aggressive leaders,” Wilson says. “If they fail to follow through, then they are disobeying God.”, Butler and producer Steven Rascón go inside the homes of Wilson’s inner circle to show how fringe fundamentalist doctrines are quietly migrating from rural church pews into the heart of American national security policies pushed by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who counts Wilson as one of his spiritual advisers.

The seat is critical for both parties to have control of the Senate, but a Democratic victory could come with accusations of voter fraud in a race that has already been packed with racism and Islamophobia. The federal government has shown it has, and it looks like Detroit is of special interest as the Department of Justice is sending federal monitors there for. Accusations from the president and others could have a trickledown effect on trust in the other critical races on the ballot. Michigan is voting in a new governor, a new secretary of state, the entire state legislature and a slew of other key races. I'm also curious to see what Michiganders might expect from their election policy if either party. `

item.title: People Used to Drink Wine Made From Ground-Up Mummies. Now, Scientists Are Studying It
item.author: Becky Ferreira
item.content:encoded: Welcome back to the Abstract—and Happy Halloween! Here are the studies this week that smashed into Earth, put aliens on ice, drank mummy wine, and hugged it out.First, a century-old theory that comets enriched Earth with the stuff of life is upended by new models of ancient impacts. Then: the case for life in extraterrestrial sea ice, a Halloween-coded medieval concoction, and a scientific embrace.Carl Sagan eloquently said that we are all made of “star stuff,” but just how much of us is really comet vomit? This is a hotly debated question in science due to the popular theory that comets delivered essential ingredients for life to Earth during impacts more than four billion years ago, paving the way for the curious emergence of Earthlings.But scientists have thrown cold primordial water on this idea in a new study that challenges “the long-held assumption that cometary impacts played an important role in the origins of life on Earth.” By running more than 100,000 advanced simulations of comet impacts, the team found that key prebiotic molecules found in comets, such as hydrogen cyanide, would be smashed to smithereens during impacts with Earth’s ancient surface in most cases. Moreover, while Earth was pummeled by these snowballs during its youth—relatable!—this bombardment doesn’t neatly line up with the timeline of abiogenesis, the term of the origin of life. For these reasons, it’s much more likely that life assembled from earthly molecules that leaked out from our planet’s interior, according to the study. “The most probable timing of successful cometary impact is in the early Hadean…more than 100 [million years] earlier than the estimated emergence of the last universal common ancestor (LUCA) at 4.2 [billion years ago],” said researchers led by Richard Anslow of the University of Cambridge.“Taken together, the rapid decline in Earth’s cometary impact bombardment and the efficient destruction of fragile cometary organics indicate that the successful delivery of prebiotic feedstock molecules was an exceedingly rare event,” the team added. The researchers didn’t rule out the possibility altogether, but concluded that any impact that had a direct influence on abiogenesis would be an edge case. That said, comets might serve as prebiotic wellsprings on other planets, such as Mars, where key molecules might have faced better odds of survival upon impact due to the red planet's smaller mass and thin atmosphere.“Mars would have been the more favourable target for the cometary delivery of prebiotic feedstock molecules” which “strengthens the possibility that life could have emerged on Mars,” the study concluded. The tip of an alien icebergWhile we’re on the topic of prebiotic feedstock molecules—a household conversation, no doubt—let’s speculate about their accumulation on weird exoplanets. In a new study, scientists suggest that these molecules might build up in sea ice on a variety of extraterrestrial ocean worlds, providing a pathway to the emergence of aliens. “Water worlds with potential deep oceans are at the forefront of currently observable exoplanetary habitability,” said researchers led by Edouard Barrier of the University of Cambridge. “Here we outline a location where nutrients could be concentrated in sufficiently high quantities to make abiogenesis possible—at the interface between the open ocean and the surface ice shelf.” The team studied the dynamics of sea ice on Earth, and modelled how similar features might form on a range of different exoplanets, including hypothetical “Hycean” planets. These are worlds more massive than Earth, but smaller than Neptune, making them part of the “sub-Neptune” class of exoplanets. The results revealed mechanisms that “may plausibly provide concentrated chemical feedstock for prebiotic chemistry” on many of these exoplanets, suggesting they could be a substrate for the emergence of alien life. This “rich avenue of research…has the potential to significantly advance our understanding of aquaplanet habitability, and particularly to improve the prospects of abiogenesis on sub-Neptunes,” the team concluded. What a week for the prebiotic feedstock beat! Taken together, these studies point to multiple onramps for life on worlds like Earth, Mars, exotic sub-Neptunes, and more, upping odds that life exists elsewhere in the universe—regardless of whether we ever find it. To celebrate Halloween, here’s a trick a treat all wrapped up in one delightfully grotesque story about mummies. Roughly 700 years ago, someone had the interesting idea of grinding up parts of Egyptian mummies, mixing the residue with wine or other liquids, and prescribing it as a medicinal elixir for people to drink. This resulting product, known as , circulated in Arabic and European markets for centuries, but its exact composition and pharmacology remain unclear. You know what that means: It’s time to do science on the medieval mummy cocktails. Researchers analyzed historical products, mummified body parts, embalming residues, bandages, and two mummified skulls. The team discovered a wide range of formulas for this medicine, including one powdered product that appears to have been derived from a mummified head. The results demonstrate that “an apparently uninformative powdered material can be chemically linked to a specific mummified head,” said researchers co-led by Tim Berger and Amira Naimi of Marburg University. “This study shows that linking historical texts, material culture, molecular composition, and bioactivity, can open new routes for decoding historical medicines and reconstructing the material biographies of human remains and museum objects.”So if you are really committed to the spirit of this season, break out some to pair with your Halloween candy and witches’ brew. Bottoms up—or more accurately: mummified-heads up. What better way to close out this chilling spooky season than with the warm embrace of science? So come on, bring it in for a hug—or, in this case, roughly 15,000 of them. Hugging is an incredibly common form of affection among humans, and even some other animals, including Halloween favorites . But little is known about “how individual differences shape the remembrance of such experiences,” according to a new study.To fill this cuddly gap, scientists analyzed survey responses from 15,049 adult participants in the United Kingdom who were recruited in a public broadcasting campaign that included the BBC. The volunteers reported that their most memorable hugs were “for comfort, support, and understanding” and there was a noticeable gender split, as men were more likely to remember hugs that were “arousing” than women.“Regarding hugs, men have shown different lateralisation and arm crossing patterns when hugging other men compared to women,” said researchers led by Anna Lena Dueren of the University of Bristol. “Furthermore, women were found to experience a stress buffering effect of hugs that was absent in men.” And for anyone who considers themselves not a “hugger,” you are not alone. Plenty of participants expressed that they found hugs difficult or unpleasant. So whether you love bear hugs or cannot bear hugs, this study has something for you.Thanks for reading! See you next week.

item.title: The storm before the storm
item.author: 1axbilssfnjhmm40n6u442lrkqfv6jgx7vespv@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
item.content:encoded: The weekend before Election Day is usually one of my favorite times.The last campaign ads have shipped, field plans are finalized and Election Day preparations are in place. The fury of last-minute charges and countercharges subsides as candidates try to deliver a positive closing message.A seriousness settles over the electorate as election officials make final preparations for voting and vote counting.For a few quiet days, the fate of the election lies solely in the voters’ hands.I normally use the time to get organized and catch up on tasks I’ve set aside. I get some sleep, knowing that Tuesday will be a long night.It is the proverbial calm before the storm that is sure to come once the polls close and states begin the process of counting ballots and certifying results.This year, however, has been different. The weekend before Election Day has been anything but quiet. It has been the storm before the storm.Even with the warnings that Donald Trump would try to rig the election, and even knowing that Attorney General Todd Blanche would carry out Trump’s every whim, I did not expect it to be this bad.Over the last few weeks, we have witnessed a daily escalation in the government’s assault on free and fair elections. In the last few days, it has reached a level never before seen in this country.Trump’s Department of Justice is trying to force election officials to set aside, or segregate, ballots it claims are suspect, and it is threatening officials who refuse to comply. It is now using the threat of criminal investigation to intimidate political opponents and their supporters.On Friday, the DOJ admitted that federal agencies had contacted officials in five states, California, Nevada, Pennsylvania, New Jersey and Washington, about voters it claims are ineligible to vote in the midterms.The DOJ also revealed that it had sent letters to election officials in all 50 states, warning that they could face prison time if they do not preserve voting records for 22 months after the election.In Alaska, the DOJ has asked a federal judge to order election officials to segregate ballots based on which candidate a voter cast their ballot for. This is a lawsuit Donald Trump has said he ordered filed.It asserts powers the federal government does not possess. It tramples on the right of states to run their own elections and makes a mockery of the Constitution.Yet Trump’s loyal foot soldiers filed it, and they have been bobbing and weaving ever since to avoid a ruling on motions to dismiss their frivolous case.Now they have loudly announced a criminal investigation in the days leading up to the election.I am not going to bother pointing out the DOJ’s policy against this type of action. Nor will I dwell on the fact that the U.S. attorney seemed unable to articulate what the potential crime would be.Instead, I will only ask why so few are willing to speak out about what they know is happening.In the depths of the struggle for civil rights, Martin Luther King Jr. wrote that “the greatest tragedy of this period of social transition was not the strident clamor of the bad people, but the appalling silence of the good people.”Now, as we head into Election Day, the question is not whether good people remain. It is whether they will ever speak out.Instead, they prefer to act like nothing is really that different. This is just another election.Acknowledging the depth of the crisis would require large law firms to defend the rule of law instead of sitting on the sidelines. It would force corporate titans to speak out instead of cutting deals with Trump. It would make the legacy media confront how their fixation on both-sides coverage has damaged their reputation and failed their profession.Instead, they all pretend this is a normal election when it is anything but. Better to feign ignorance than to confirm their complicity.In the coming days, the storm will grow. Donald Trump will escalate his attacks even further. That is what he has done before.He may disrupt voting or demand more meritless lawsuits and baseless prosecutions. He might insist that ballots be seized and election certifications set aside. He might even try to declare some sort of national emergency.What he won’t be able to do is change people’s hearts and minds. He can try to rig the maps, suppress the vote and subvert the results, but he cannot change the fact that he and his party are deeply unpopular and that they will lose this election.I don’t know how big the blue wave will be or how many Republicans will be washed out when this storm finally breaks.What I am certain of is that once the election is over, we must stop the DOJ from being used as a tool of naked partisan aggression. And we must insist that more people who claim to be good speak out before the next storm arrives.

item.title: Saturday 80s Jam: How Will I Know – Whitney Houston
item.author: Schill
item.content:encoded: When Whitney Houston released “How Will I Know” in 1985, she was still in the early stages of what would become one of the most extraordinary careers in pop music. Her debut album had already produced “You Give Good Love,” but “How Will I Know” was the song that showed the world just how perfectly her enormous voice could fit into bright, energetic 1980s pop.Written by George Merrill, Shannon Rubicam, and Narada Michael Walden, the song was originally intended for another artist. Houston’s version transformed it into something much bigger. Produced by Michael Walden, the recording combined synthesizers, electronic drums, handclaps, keyboards, and a relentlessly upbeat rhythm that was almost impossible to sit still through.That was a major departure from the more serious image often associated with powerhouse vocalists.Houston could obviously sing a huge ballad, but “How Will I Know” demonstrated that she could also have fun.The song is essentially about romantic uncertainty. Houston is interested in someone but doesn’t know whether the feelings are mutual. Instead of treating that uncertainty as something dramatic and depressing, the song turns it into a burst of nervous energy.The production is a huge part of that feeling.The drums bounce along, the keyboards sparkle, the backing vocals reinforce the chorus, and Houston’s voice cuts through the arrangement with astonishing clarity. She doesn’t have to overpower the production. She simply sits perfectly on top of it.Directed by Brian Grant, the “How Will I Know” video was filled with bright colors, geometric sets, dancers, energetic choreography, and unmistakable mid-1980s fashion. It was tailor-made for MTV, which was rapidly becoming one of the most important promotional forces in popular music.Houston’s image in the video was youthful, stylish, and playful.She wasn’t being presented solely as a serious vocalist standing behind a microphone. She was a pop star.The song became Houston’s second number-one single on the Billboard Hot 100 and helped turn her debut album into a massive success. It also established a formula that would define much of her early career: combine an extraordinary voice with sophisticated pop production and make the result accessible to virtually anyone.“How Will I Know” is particularly impressive because Houston never sounds like she’s struggling to fit into the upbeat production.She sounds completely natural.Her vocal runs add personality without overwhelming the melody, while the chorus gives her plenty of room to show off the power that would eventually become her trademark.The song also captures something essential about 1980s pop. This was the decade when electronic production, MTV, fashion, dance music, and traditional vocal performances increasingly came together.“How Will I Know” sits right in the middle of that cultural shift.It sounds unmistakably like 1985, but its melody is strong enough that the song never feels trapped in its era.Most importantly, it helped establish Whitney Houston as something more than a promising new singer.She was becoming a superstar.Over the next several years, Houston would deliver enormous ballads, blockbuster movie songs, and some of the most recognizable recordings in popular music.But “How Will I Know” remains special because it captures her at the beginning of that journey.Young, energetic, impossibly talented, and surrounded by one of the decade’s most infectious productions, Whitney Houston turned a song about wondering whether someone liked her into a celebration of the excitement of not knowing.And the answer, judging by the success of the song, was pretty obvious.Everybody was going to know Whitney Houston.
