item.title: who’s on judge mathis today? #309
item.author: samantha irby
item.content:encoded: pauline from youngstown, ohio. pauline sashays into the courtroom in a black denim jacket over a chevron-striped collared shirt. her hair looks like—do y’all remember when prince’s hair that’s what pauline is giving. phyllis from youngstown, ohio. phyllis is wearing her hair in a tapered pixie cut dyed bozo red, and i am living. where are we, how are these divas so gorgeous, why is their hair so laid! phyllis is wearing a long denim skirt topped with a cowl-neck sweater made of black teddy bear fur, and not only does she have an accordion of truth™ in one hand, she also has an old school tape recorder in the other. okay, walter cronkite!!!!!!!! pauline says she and phyllis sang in a gospel group together. they sold dinners to raise money to promote their CD, but the plaintiff insists she paid for most of the supplies and claims the defendant split their profits with her married boyfriend instead promoting their CD, so she’s suing! $1333 (is this an angel number) filed: phyllis would like $2000 for harassment and defamation! pauline says that she has been singing since she was eight years old (greg: “professionally?” pauline: “no…?” greg: “oh, in the shower?”) and she loves to sing gospel music. she says phyllis enjoys singing gospel music, too, and she started a gospel group called faith2faith (i have no proof this is how she spells it, but i know deep down in my soul this is how she spells it) that she invited pauline and two other ladies to join. she says they were working on a CD and decided the best way to advertise that CD was fliers, which were going to cost $500. they had a meeting at which they decided that to raise money they were going to sell chicken and rib dinners. greg is like, “RIBS, TOO???” which is exactly what i just blurted out. pork ribs are what, six dollars a damn pound? please! unless god himself is barbecuing the one he yanked out of adam, i’ll see you in the vestibule with a paper plate of potato salad and some chicken wings.the faith2otherladies dropped out of the group, probably because they didn’t want to waste an entire saturday sweating over a pot of greens just to record their version of over an instrumental karaoke track that nobody was gonna buy. undeterred, phyllis and pauline decided they would carry on with the fundraiser and split the costs down the middle: phyllis would buy the ribs, pauline would be responsible for all the chicken, and they would split the sides. pauline says when they got to the grocery store phyllis couldn’t afford all the ribs they wanted to get, and of course she couldn’t! them shits are expensive!!!commercial break: i would run through a brick wall for pauline says she bought the ribs, chicken, macaroni and cheese, pasta salad, the cakes, the pies. greg says, “you got any left?” and……..does she? a church plate would really hit the spot right now (although she can keep the pasta salad, we really don’t play around with our digestive system like that). the judge asks phyllis for her side, and she says she’s been singing since she was years old and sang in the church choir, so i think that means god probably likes her better. this is a great time to remind you that i, too, grew up singing in the church choir, and considering how i turned out maybe phyllis should hold off on bragging.plot twist: phyllis says she has receipts for all the stuff she bought. pauline says that she, too, brought a receipt to court today, and when she gives it to the judge he scrunches his nose up and says, “three dollars??!?!?!?!!” um…did pauline mean to say she bought a chicken, or??? she says that the store wasn’t able to give her a receipt for the other stuff she bought, which is exactly what i’m going to say the next time i try to return a discount coffeemaker i copped from homegoods to crate & barrel for a refund of the full price. pauline says that after selling the dinners, phyllis and her boyfriend (maybe? he’s sitting in her witness chair, clad in a gorgeous canadian tuxedo that looks like it was made by karl kani, who wouldn’t wanna hit that in the name of the lord) said they made a profit of $400. the judge asks what they were going to do with the profits, and pauline says they were supposed to use that money to make flyers to advertise their upcoming “gospel explosion” concert. pauline says that never happened, that phyllis took the money from the dinner sales and split it with her “married boyfriend.” damn, i should’ve known a lady picked out his fly ass outfit!the judge keeps asking phyllis how much money she made off the dinners and phyllis keeps not answering him. he switches tactics and asks her if what she did make went toward promotion, and she gives him a receipt showing that she paid $300 for some radio ads. pauline interjects that she had no idea about the radio ads, and greg says that’s too bad because they’re even more effective than flyers. is that……………..true? maybe it’s because the only good radio station near me is WRKR 107.7 the rocker (i was driving earlier and they played styx and i almost ran my shit into oncoming traffic what a JAM), but is gonna hear that fucking ad? me and the nice ladies who work at my dentist’s office??? pauline is mad about the radio ads because she said she was out of the group by the time they ran but that seems like a pauline problem to me. if the purpose of the church plates was to make money for ads, and phyllis did indeed use the church plate money to pay for some ads, what’s the issue? greg agrees with me (should i go to law school?) and tells pauline that just because she left faith2faith after selling all those chickens2ribs, she’s not owed any money.greg wants to get into the harassment. pauline says that after this all went down phyllis started which is one of the most serious crimes you can commit against a black person. she says she filed a police report against her, and greg asks to see it because he says that’s not actually harassment and he wants to see exactly what pauline told the police. pauline says phyllis called her twenty times in one day and hands the judge a sheet of notebook paper that she says the officer wrote her case number down on. i’m fucking crying, because sometimes people roll up in here like perry mason with labeled evidence and crime scene photos and DNA results, and then other times people are like pauline. the paper looks like it came from the bottom of my jansport in 1996, folded with frayed edges that i’m trying to smooth out before mrs kellman comes around to collect the homework and sees that i am a slob. the judge is disgusted and turns to phyllis, asking, “ma’am, did you harass her?” and phyllis, of course, says she did not, so that’s the end of that. D- on pauline’s assignment.as for phyllis’s harassment countersuit, she says that pauline had her daughter make a myspace page to “slander [her] name,” saying that she likes to sleep with other women’s husbands (gasp!) and she’s forty-five years old (gasp2gasp!!!) and, most slanderous of all, she’s a pisces. greg says that maybe they weren’t talking about her but phyllis pulls a printed-out myspace profile™ out of her full accordion of truth™ and lo and behold there is her picture at the top. greg asks phyllis how she knows that pauline is behind the page and phyllis says, “because it has the rain coming down in the background just like [pauline’s] does” and this is the funniest shit i have ever seen in my life. you had your kid make a FAKE MYSPACE PAGE and that kid made the fake myspace page look EXACTLY LIKE YOUR PAGE??? incredible.phyllis says that pauline called her job and tried to get her fired, and when pauline denies it phyllis pulls out a letter her boss wrote. turns out her boss is the deacon of the church they attend, and he sent a letter detailing pauline’s harassment on the official church letterhead. i came to court with notebook paper with some pencil scribbles on it and my opponent has a notarized letter from god????? i’d have to kill myself on nationally syndicated television. oh, remember how phyllis had that tape recorder? she plays some nasty messages from pauline, in which she “this is pauline” omg, calling her all sorts of nasty names and threatening to fuck her up. she goes on and on with all these bleeped out insults, and greg starts laughing because he’s a messy bitch just like we are. after the recording ends he looks at pauline and says, “you’ve got a of praying to do.” phyllis gets $2000 for getting called an ugly bitch, which is amazing because i have been called that for free. pauline says she only said all that vile shit on her voicemail (at one point she screamed “you look like !!!!” which made me laugh but i did feel bad about it) because phyllis wouldn’t stop calling her. judge mathis says he believes her, and he’s awarding her $10 for her harassment claim. then he remembers that she also wanted half of what she spent on the groceries, so he rounds up $3.94 and adds two bucks to her total. [insert that 2 corinthians verse about god so you can go forth and do good work] did uncle greg say anything fucked up to anyone: “so the deacon is lying on you, too? girl, you’re going to hell!”

item.content:encoded: Inspired by qwenputer by Divyansh Agrawal, Drew Breunig baked a working emulator for a Nintendo Entertainment System 6502 CPU into the weights of Qwen3.5-4B. You can now play NES ROMs such as Super Mario Bros (very slowly) running inside Qwen!Read this article and any relevant source code: https://divagr.com/blog/qwenputer. Then explore if you could emulate the chip and ram in a Nintendo Entertainment System (as people do today with FPGAs in MISTRs) using this technique. If so, what size model would you have to build and if you could use smaller faster ones, could you get it to be at the standard clockspeed.I think we should build it! Just for fun. It's okay if it's not fast. We want to be able to have the weights, and a cli to run them that we can point at a ROM.

item.title: Let’s Talk About Alaska
item.author: Josh Marshall
item.source: Josh Marshall – TPM – Talking Points Memo
item.content:encoded: I was at the gym this afternoon when a press conference came on with the U.S. Attorney in Alaska floridly introducing a criminal investigation into this “Dan Sullivan” issue. One of my colleagues just noted that to do this, U.S. Attorney Michael Heyman “unrecused” himself from this case. “Unrecusal” is not a thing. He recused himself because he’s trying to get a judgeship from Alaska’s Republican senators Dan Sullivan and Lisa Murkowski. I note this simply for the comedic nature of this spectacle. This investigation is itself a corrupt abuse of power on three or four different grounds at once.Let me share some thoughts on this.I’ve heard a number of people say they’re “troubled” or “disturbed” or unhappy that this happened. All I can say is that I would really recommend that you toughen up because you simply won’t make it through the next few years, even under the best circumstances. There is no crime here and no possibility of a crime here. This is trolling. At worst, it’s a dirty trick. If it is a dirty trick, it is a special kind since it has been out in the open and has been a staple of Alaska political news for the better part of a year. Election officials in Alaska already took note of the possibility of confusion and added the word “incumbent” after Sen. Dan S. Sullivan’s name on the ballot, as well as “registered Republican” to make certain that no one can be confused as to who is who. State authorities are the only ones permitted to judge this question and arrive at a solution to it, if it requires one. They already have.

item.title: Royals Off-Season Report
item.author: SRS0=xjif=IU=mg-d0.substack.com=bounce+9ddca1.63af5d-misc=muneer.top@eforward.registrar-servers.com
item.content:encoded: Although the Royals season mercifully ended a few weeks ago, the 2026 major league season concluded this week with the Milwaukee Brewers winning their first World Series title in franchise history 4 games to 1 over the Tampa Bay Rays.The crowning of a World Series champion signifies the official start to the MLB off-season. With a lockout of the players looming on Dec. 1, the next few weeks are bound to be jammed full of MLB news. Some of it might even involve the Royals!This means that Alec Marsh’s time in the organization has come to an end. It really looked like he could be in the rotation for some time in 2024, but injuries derailed his career and he hasn’t pitched in over two years now. Alex Lange’s time with his hometown team did not go as either had hoped. He finished with a 6.75 ERA and 1.63 WHIP across 60 innings of work. I’m sure he’ll get another shot somewhere. Gonsolin had some decent years with the Dodgers before getting hurt, but this smacks of desperation. Then again, “desperate” might be the best word to describe the Royals starting pitching situation going into 2027.It’s been fairly quiet on the rumor front, but a few are starting to circulate around the Royals.Look, it’s not going to happen. The Royals aren’t going to trade Bobby Baseball. That said, if I’m Picollo and the Red Sox actually make this offer…I take it. Vinnie, Massey, and of course Bobby were consistently excellent, but Loftin? Really? His defense at third is better than at second, but I’m not sure it is Gold Glove caliber. Winners will be announced Sunday evening on ESPN.Beginning next Tuesday (11/3), teams can start signing free agents and making trades. Remember that is a process that sometimes lasts the entire three months of a normal off-season. With the impending lockout on Dec. 2nd, teams will have to cram all of their acquisitions into less than a month. It’s hard for me to fit my brain around the idea of signing some guy to a gazillion dollar contract when you don’t even know the rules the game is going to be played under next season. Will there be a salary cap? A salary floor? Will there even be a season in 2027?

item.title: Our Favorite Patrick Stewart Performances
item.author: Defector Staff
item.content:encoded: Following this week's news of Patrick Stewart's death, the Defector staff convened to remember some of our favorite performances by him.Patrick Stewart is one of our most recognizable forces in pop culture: the kind of star who could be identified just by his profile, a rare feat of notoriety in any era. Every bit of him is iconic, but it’s his voice that truly makes him the performer he was. It's only right, then, that he became a memorable voice actor in animated work.

item.title: ‘Wake Up Call:’ Fanfiction Writers and Readers React to AO3 Outage
item.author: Samantha Cole
item.content:encoded: In the wake of fanfiction repository Archive of Our Own (AO3) announcing a weeks-long security incident outage, readers and writers are reflecting on why the site is important to the fanfiction community, and how they’re coping with the downtime. , the Organization for Transformative Works (OTW), the non-profit organization that runs AO3, posted that the site was down for maintenance, eventually updating to say the site restoration will take around two weeks, but could take up to a month. OTW confirmed in an updated status report Friday morning that this outage is due to a security incident. Some have speculated that the outage is a result of the this week that led to several sites going down to update their security, but AO3 doesn’t use PHP. An OTW representative : “I can let you know that this is not related to the PHP security issue as the Archive uses Ruby on Rails.” A lot of people are grieving the loss of Kinktober, AO3’s annual group writing exercise where writers upload a chapter or fic every day throughout October based on a prompt of the day. (The prompts are horny, if that’s not clear.) Several of the writers and readers who reached out to me following the outage brought up the poor timing around Kinktober.One writer I spoke to who posts her writing and reads others’ writing on AO3, told me that she was in the middle of racing to finish a work that was deliberately timed to Kinktober and Halloween when the outage happened. She was hitting “next chapter” while reading a fic on Wednesday night when she got the message that the site was down for maintenance, “which I initially took as a sign from the universe to go to bed,” she said.“The outage hasn’t derailed my desire to write. If anything, I want to have more chapters ready to go so my readers can eat good once it’s over,” she said. Some writers are considering posting elsewhere while they wait for AO3 to return, but it’s not an ideal workaround. AO3 author who goes by Selkie Myth told me they’re moving to Space Battles, another fanfiction site, during the outage. “I'm shrugging and just posting on SB [Space Battles] while the site's down. Hopefully I'll remember to post the chapters over on AO3 once it's back up — the story is projected to end during the outage. I anticipate the same is true for a lot of other authors,” they said.Some people have said they’ll try in the meantime, but it’s a much more bare-bones website. Fanfiction site added a banner to its homepage welcoming AO3 refugees: “We’ve had a big influx of guests due to the AO3 outage. If you've been affected by the outage we're sorry to hear that and hope that they're able to get that fixed soon.” Wattpad, which many fanfiction writers and readers really, really hate for reasons I won’t get into here, “we're here to support you during this difficult time.” Overwhelmingly, the replies are from people telling Wattpad to go away.Another AO3 writer who goes by Ren told me she has two long works in progress right now with nowhere to post them. Posting elsewhere poses continuity and discovery problems, as some of these fanfiction works span chapters and hundreds of thousands of words of character and worldbuilding. “I could technically keep posting updates on sites like tumblr through the downtime, but both of these fics are quite long and I haven't been posting them anywhere other than AO3 — if I drop a new chapter for my 130k Pokemon Black and White fanfic on Tumblr completely out of context, people just now finding my work aren't going to be able to read the rest for a while :(“ she told me in an email. “I have seen other authors posting their gdocs and Ellipsus reader links in the meantime, but my draft files aren't exactly presentable... I will keep marinating but what will probably happen is my wips [works in progress] will just be on hiatus for a bit. My readers are used to hiatuses at least.” Another writer said she’s not considering posting elsewhere. “Wattpad can piss off,” she said. “But I may go back to fanfiction.net to save and physically print some of my favorite fics from way back in the day (the ancient/sacred texts, if you will) to ensure I have copies of those somewhere. This outage is a good reminder that things can vanish in the blink of an eye, whether a website crashes or is hacked or an author decides to suddenly delete their fic. If you love something, smash the kudos button, comment on it, bookmark it, subscribe, and consider downloading it. You never know.” A reader who emailed me following the outage said they’ve been enjoying getting into AO3 as a new fan. “I was a big fanfic skeptic, but that’s changed lately. I’ve found some truly excellent writers, and real creativity. The free nature of it in this increasingly horrifying stage of capitalism is refreshing,” they said.AO3 has said in status updates and to journalists that they don’t expect any data loss. Losing works would be devastating for writers and readers, but AO3 is more than just a repository for writing; it’s a community of people commenting and reacting to those stories. Selkie mentioned the rigorous tagging habits of AO3 members, where stories are tagged with sometimes dozens of fanfiction tropes, character names, content hints and warnings, and can constitute a language specific to the platform and its readers; “Crack Treated Seriously,” for example, means writing a silly premise with a straight face, while “Idiots in Love” is self explanatory. “To me, the more devastating thing would be to lose the comments and kudos on my fic. Technically I have them saved elsewhere because I get AO3 email alerts, but seeing them threaded in one place at the end of a chapter hits different,” a writer said. “Comments can turn an author’s entire day around and restore their will to live. I often reread them if I have writer’s block or a bad bout of imposter syndrome. They also turn the otherwise solitary act of writing into something communal. Seeing someone experience your story chapter by chapter is incredibly motivating and makes the writing process feel less isolating.” OTW is entirely volunteer-run, and people on social media and in speaking to them directly have said they hope AO3 users go easy on staff during this time. “So many people rely on AO3 as an outlet for creativity and escapism as the real world burns, myself included. It’s also important to remember that the site is run by volunteers,” that writer said. “The work they do to protect writers, fight censorship and safeguard freedom of expression is extremely important and necessary, especially right now. They deserve all the respect and patience in the world as they work to get the archive back up and running. Be kind.” Ren, echoing those sentiments, sent me a meme: “An additional sentiment I've seen is ‘ok so when AO3 comes back we're all going to tell our favorite authors how much we missed their work, right?’ which I hope catches on — I'm writing for niche fandoms and had to disable guest comments due to bot spam, so comments are few and far between as it is,” Ren said. “I do kind of hope that the extended outage serves as a sort of wake-up call to anyone who's been taking ao3 for granted lately. It certainly was for me.”

item.title: Manchester United And Michael Carrick Are Breaking New Ground In Organizational Dysfunction
item.author: Ray Ratto
item.content:encoded: There are few joys in sports that can truly exceed a game in which both coaches are in danger of getting fired, and no place does that game better than England. There are no distractions that can cause the fevered punditocracy to avert its eyes from the desperate hope that one (or, in the most orgiastic case, both) gets smoked right after the game. This is possible because a dissatisfying draw can enrage both fan bases equally, in the way that Giants-Commanders sickened the souls of football fans on this side of the ditch three weeks ago.But there is one scenario that trumps even that, and Americans will have it tomorrow morning at the breakfast hour: Manchester United at Chelsea. Two big clubs that are underachieving in their own specific ways, will face each other at 8:30 a.m. ET, and in deepest zombie hours on the West Coast. What makes it genuinely special for everyone is that no institution on earth, in any pursuit, does boss-in-trouble quite like Manchester United.Carrick got the full car wash a week ago after successive three-goal losses to Como (4-1) in the Champions League and Bournemouth (3-0) in the Prem. This extended a stretch of winless results that go back to United's Champions League win over Sabah of Azerbaijan, a newbie team that, on the European stage, qualifies not as minnows but something more on the order of plankton. The first loss was in Italy, in a very cool stadium that overlooks Lake Como, and which by definition is the coolest stadium in Europe because of it. The second was at home before—get this—an appreciative crowd that applauded Carrick when the team went for the postgame salute to the fans. They turned unanimously loud, profane, and ugly as soon as Carrick left the field.

item.title: Scientists Analyzed Thousands of Psychedelic Trips. They Found Something Disturbing
item.author: Becky Ferreira
item.content:encoded: Researchers have amassed a trove of more than 25,000 calls to a support hotline for people during and after psychedelic trips, making it “the largest dataset of psychedelic support interactions ever assembled—exceeding the combined sample sizes of all published psychedelic clinical trials by an order of magnitude,” according to a study published on Friday in .Despite the popularity of psychedelics as recreational drugs, and increasing interest in them as medically-prescribed therapeutic treatments, there is very little research about the effects of these substances outside of clinical settings with carefully-selected patients. That, scientists say, is limiting what we can learn about the effects of these drugs, because the vast majority of psychedelics are consumed by all kinds of people in homes, festivals, ceremonial gatherings, or other uncontrolled environments. The , a nonprofit founded in 2020, has filled this knowledge gap with its Psychedelic Support Line, which connects callers who are on bad trips, or who are seeking more information about psychedelics, with trained volunteers who offer confidential peer support. The team has now published a compendium of 25,419 anonymized interactions with 220 hotline volunteers that took place between April 2021 and February 2026. The database opens an unprecedented window into the experiences of people on psilocybin, ketamine, MDMA, LSD, ayahuasca, and even cannabis, which is not generally considered a psychedelic but can trigger similar effects, such as mild hallucinations. It’s a “treasure trove,” said Félix Schoeller, a senior research scientist at the Institute for Advanced Consciousness Studies, a California-based nonprofit, who led the study, in a call with 404 Media. “In general, we're really lacking any evidence and data beyond what exists in the underground world, if you will, for psychedelic therapy.” “There's different types of knowledge,” continued Schoeller, who is CEO of , a startup focused on novel experiential treatments for depression. “Some cultures and communities have been doing that for thousands of years. But there's a question about how to do this in a way that follows the principles of biomedical science.” The interactions included phone calls and text exchanges with hotline volunteers who provided support by talking through the experience or connecting callers with emergency services in the most urgent cases. About 40.2 percent of callers (10,208 interactions) were actively tripping, while 32.1 percent of callers reached out after they had tripped, a period known as “integration.” The rest of the calls fell into smaller categories, such as informational inquiries about certain substances, requests to prepare or buy drugs, or calls from “trip-sitters” assisting a person on psychedelics. Psilocybin was the most commonly reported substance (9,348 callers), followed by LSD (2,247callers), cannabis (2,004 callers), and ketamine (1,194 callers), and MDMA (682 callers), with ayahuasca and other drugs logging much smaller numbers. Surprisingly, callers who had used cannabis reported the highest distress rate—47.2 percent had bad experiences with the drug. Though cannabis has a reputation as a low-stakes substance, the study confirms that it can induce real distress in some cases that warrant consideration for harm reduction. The distress rates for the rest of the commonly used psychedelics were only slightly lower than cannabis, ranging between 40 to 42 percent.The study also revealed 43 rare but disturbing instances of “facilitator abuse,” including at remote retreats or ceremonial gatherings involving ayahuasca. In these cases, callers reported abuse from the people providing psychedelics, such as reports they had deliberately been given extra doses without consent. Those reports “provide the first quantitative documentation of this phenomenon in a community help-seeking sample,” according to the study. “The pattern of these reports—clustering in ceremonial settings involving plant medicines, presenting primarily as trauma-processing calls, and involving callers with elevated rates of prior PTSD diagnoses—suggests that even modest surveillance through existing peer support infrastructure can detect harm occurring in unregulated psychedelic settings.”Some calls also came from people who said they suffered from schizophrenia, or had taken multiple psychedelics, offering a rare glimpse of situations that could not be observed in clinical settings. “This kind of data can inform us on these topics in the context of legalizing these drugs and making them accessible,” said Schoeller. “I'm glad that there's this data that exists that people can look into to support or contradict the claims that they make as to how these things should be done.” The study also outlines several limitations, including its sample bias of people who are inclined to call a hotline in the first place—which is not representative of psychedelic consumers at large—as well as self-reported accounts of doses, among other factors that are impossible to verify.Despite the noisiness of the data, however, it contains helpful clues about avenues for future research. In Schoeller’s view, one of the most important revelations was that the success of a call was strongly linked to the perception that the hotline volunteer showed genuine care and empathy toward the caller. Using 2,777 postinteraction satisfaction surveys, the team found that the few negative experiences with the hotline tended to stem from feelings that the volunteer was dismissive, or didn’t seem to care about the caller. “My takeaway is that the number one thing that predicts whether a support call will not work” is “the volunteer being perceived as genuine,” Schoeller said. “That's something that, in many ways, poses a problem to the biomedical system of centralized hospitals. I'm not trying to be ideological in any way, but when you create a centralized institution where you throw everybody to a single place to get care” then “clinicians become burned out.”For this reason, Schoeller and his colleagues plan to follow up on the role of perceived care and empathy in treatment, and to emphasize this factor in guidance for community-based peer support for people in crisis due to psychedelics. It also reinforces the value of the Fireside Project’s hotline, which provides a safe and confidential service for people who might be reluctant to contact emergency services because of the criminalization of these substances or fear of incurring medical debt.“For many people, they have experiences with psychedelics, and they may not be required to go to the ER, but they still need someone to help them navigate the difficult experience,” Schoeller concluded. “The hotline can truly be a lifeline for them.”

item.title: Three-Body Orbits
item.author: Jason Kottke
item.content:encoded: There are no generalized solutions to the three-body problem. Say you have three planets orbiting each other: it’s impossible to calculate how they will move using Newton’s laws of motion and gravity.Unlike the two-body problem, the three-body problem has no general closed-form analytic solution. The differential equations that govern the motions of three gravitating bodies are not integrable and cannot be solved to give explicit formulas for the positions of the bodies as a function of time. For most initial conditions, the dynamical system for three orbiting bodies is chaotic, and the only way to predict their motions is to estimate them using numerical methods.The site even enables you to search for new stable solutions to the problem in your browser. This is what one of my unsuccessful tests looked like — two of the planets locked in a gravity death spiral while the other one peaces out in the other direction:

item.title: Darius Acuff Jr. Is A Problem, But Which Kind?
item.author: Patrick Redford
item.content:encoded: During the first quarter of Thursday's game between the equally winless Pelicans and Kings, Sacramento rookie Darius Acuff Jr. ran the length of the floor in transition and punched home a sweeping dunk past a late trail from Jeremiah Fears and a halfhearted contest from Trey Murphy III. It was an amazing play, which is why Acuff took a second to flex and mean-mug for the dozens of fans in New Orleans. It was also a live play, and as Acuff preened, the Pelicans ran back and Murphy got an easy dunk, after Acuff's absence forced Domantas Sabonis to abandon the paint.This sequence serves as a useful Rorschach test for the Acuff observer: Do you see Acuff's smooth athleticism, and his ability to produce not only tough but beautiful buckets? Or do you see an undersized guard whose lack of interest in the floor game is matched only by his inability to affect it? Both are totally valid reads of the most (and only) fascinating player on the worst team in basketball, although I think partisans of both positions would agree that Acuff's first five NBA games have been remarkable.Nobody in the league has attempted or missed more shots. No rookie has attempted as many shots in their first few games. Acuff sits snugly wedged between Steph Curry and Shai Gilgeous-Alexander on the usage leaderboard, with the sixth-highest rate in the NBA. It's both fantastic theater and an irresistible new front in the Real Hooper Wars; the Kings, in the meantime, are so bad that the question of any of it mattering will be entirely theoretical for a while. This leaves us all free to enjoy Acuff's game and use it as a plank from which to mount arguments about how basketball should work.

item.title: Poll-mageddon—Kansas Edition!
item.author: Josh Marshall
item.source: Josh Marshall – TPM – Talking Points Memo
item.content:encoded: WaPo published a fascinating piece this morning tied to their latest poll of Kansas. The headline, figurative if not literal, is that they came up with a result that shows incumbent Republican Sen. Roger Marshall not behind Adam Hamilton, but way behind. But they don’t buy their own result. What’s fascinating and laudable is that polls like this, this late in the cycle, often never get released or they get adjusted to bring them more into line with pollsters’ expectations or the consensus of other polls. But here the Post made the decision to release the poll as is and pull back the veil on all the internal details and decisions they made to get the poll as close to what they think is accurate as they could.Differential response has been the bane of pollsters for more than a decade. We know that no one answers the phone (or the text message) when pollsters get in touch anymore. The problem is that Republicans and Democrats “never” respond at slightly different rates. And even more specifically, the slice of usually disaffected voters that Donald Trump has repeatedly activated when he’s on the presidential ballot are the most poll-resistant of all. So a huge amount of what has happened in the polling industry over the last decade is pollsters trying to find ways to tweak numbers in some coherent way to adjust for getting too few of those poll-shy Trump voters. (And to be clear, this isn’t the old idea that they’re embarrassed to say they support Trump. They just don’t want to talk to pollsters.) Further complicating the issue is that that activation — and the polling misses tied to it — doesn’t seem to happen in midterm elections, based on 2018 and 2022.

item.title: Proton’s CEO Cancels AI ‘Re-Interviews’
item.author: Joseph Cox
item.content:encoded: On Friday, Andy Yen, the CEO of Proton, cancelled a series of nearly company-wide ‘re-interviews’ that would have forced employees to explain how they are using AI, with the clear intention that they may be fired if not using it enough in the eyes of Proton leadership, according to six current Proton employees and audio of an around two hour all-hands meeting obtained by 404 Media.The move came after 404 Media published an investigation on Thursday, which showed how Yen was aggressively pushing AI across Proton, in some cases despite security concerns from employees. In one exchange, an employee in the company’s security Slack channel urged Proton to at least take a few days to pentest newly written code before pushing it live. “That’s bullshit and loser thinking. Of course it’s possible to be fast and secure,” Yen wrote in the channel at the end of August. “Stop thinking always of how to be slower, and focus more on how to be faster.” Yen added, “stop lovingly handcrafting all our code and use AI more.”The re-interview cancellations likely don’t address the concerns of many Proton users, who are more focused on Proton’s deprioritization of security; many Proton users have blasted the company’s leadership on social media over the last 24 hours and explicitly called for Yen to resign.The investigation was based on conversations with eight current and one former Proton employees, Slack chats, meeting audio, and an AI manifesto written by the company’s CTO Bart Butler. It painted a picture of Proton that is very different to the public’s perception of a company carefully protecting privacy. Instead, Proton is barreling ahead with AI in large part to achieve more annual revenue. The investigation also found a culture of fear across Proton, where employees have genuine concerns about security or being asked to develop security-focused products with AI, but feel unable to voice them because Yen mocks or insults employees in front of everyone else.“I don’t think he will change anything, and I think the only reason we had this meeting is because he has a rebellion on his hands,” one employee told 404 Media after the all-hands meeting on Friday.Near the start of the meeting, Yen said, “I want to acknowledge myself, personally, that there was a communication failure on my part and there are many things that probably could and should have been communicated differently, and this is something that I’ll have to reflect on and improve over time. So I will do that.”“So what does that mean going forward? Going forward, I'm still going to push,” he added.Yen said leadership gathered in the last couple of days to talk about the re-interviews, and spoke to the Proton board too. “They’re closely monitoring the situation,” Yen said. (Proton is owned by the Proton Foundation, includes Yen, Sir Tim Berners Lee, Prof. Carissa Veliz, Dingchao Lu, and Antonio Gambardella.) After those discussions with leadership and the board, “We’ve decided to actually cancel the re-interviews,” Yen said. “Why? Well, I think actually in a, let’s say, unintentional way, they have actually already served their purpose.” As in, employees are now talking and learning about AI.Yen also mentioned “org changes,” and said that part of this is “redistributing talent across teams.” He said that the reorganization will happen next month, “but there will be no loss of jobs from AI.” Later in the call, Butler said Yen “needs to, and he has committed to, doing better” regarding how he communicates with his employees. “Using AI effectively and pragmatically does not mean that we’ve given up on security, or good architecture, or sound software engineering principles,” he added.“We fucked up, we know we fucked up,” Butler later said in response to an employee’s comments in the meeting.“Your old job is gone,” Butler’s AI manifesto, posted to Slack, told engineers, 404 Media reported on Thursday. He wrote that not embracing AI posed an “existential threat to the success of the mission itself.”Reactions to the re-interview cancellations were split across the Proton employees 404 Media spoke to. One said, “Some are happy as it’s progress. Others believe that this won’t change anything because there isn’t any consequence for Andy [Yen].” The employee added they “would have preferred real accountability from the leadership team.” They said they felt not much could have happened due to Yen having the majority of Proton’s shares.Another employee said, after Proton canceled the re-interviews, “They said in the next breath they want to continue pushing AI and that the things that were to be measured in the re-interviews would become a component of the performance reviews.”“They have said clearly the direction had not changed. As a Proton user that doesn’t reassure me,” the employee said. “As an employee, the re-interviews weren’t cancelled until this became public despite concerns raised by many of us. I think it goes beyond communication issues and growing pains.”“Right now, everything seems consistent with it being damage control,” they said. Another employee said they were “mostly happy with how this was addressed including by Andy [Yen].”Proton did not respond to a request for comment.After 404 Media published the investigation on Thursday, Yen . Users downvoted his response more than 1,200 times. Many Proton users on social media said they were cancelling their paid Proton plans.

item.title: College Football Enters Spooky Season
item.author: Ray Ratto
item.content:encoded: Saturday is Halloween, and the schedule is notably threadbare for showdown games; only two games this weekend are between nationally ranked teams, and a bunch more are showdowns involving 4-3 programs. So go ahead, dress up, go to a party, and absentmindedly house a bunch of Reese's peanut butter cups in your host's rec room while pretending not to watch Washington-Nebraska. There's no need to let the costume be the most embarrassing part of your day.As for the games: if you insist. Kentucky has the best record in the SEC for the first since ... uhh, ever? (Since 1977, actually.) The Wildcats' schedule down the stretch is unkind, but head coach Will Stein no doubt sent an aide to blow up a copy of the conference standings for display all over the campus, maybe covering all the basketball flyers. This is not likely to remain so, but a moment is still a moment.

item.title: Behind the Blog: Tech Support
item.author: Samantha Cole
item.content:encoded: This is Behind the Blog, where we share our behind-the-scenes thoughts about how a few of our top stories of the week came together. This week, we discuss customer service and Proton fallout.Since I wrote about ChatGPT turning me into tech support for people’s random problems, I have gotten many more AI-generated emails from people asking me to solve their tech support problems. So, mission accomplished I guess. I think and hope it was clear in the article, but I think this phenomenon is happening to a lot of journalists, not just us at 404 Media. A lot of the ChatGPT chats I saw told people to reach out to multiple journalists, and gave them contact info and instructions on how to do so. Some suggested that they reach out to lawyers or academic researchers as well, so I assume it’s all sorts of people who are getting this new type of spam. I have a really cluttered inbox in general and this new type of spam is annoying but doesn’t really upset me, I am an email maximizer—I sign up for every newsletter, every press release, I unsubscribe from nothing, etc. I do this because I sort of use my email as an archive I can search through, which comes in handy when I want to do a story like this one. I didn’t delete any of these bizarre emails and then over time I was able to go and search my inbox for various examples. I’m working on a story for next week about more and different types of AI spam I’ve been getting. I’ve always been interested in spam and internet “pollution,” how it’s created, and why it’s happening. So I do get a sick little thrill when I get more of these types of emails. I am still kind of losing it over the idea of a man issuing a press release because his chatbot agent wasn’t working so well. I got one yesterday where someone who lost their LinkedIn account emailed me and several other journalists, but also various police departments. And I got one from someone who ordered something from Amazon and apparently got the wrong thing in the mail. A few people suggested that I go through the process of trying to help some of the people who reach out, and then write about it. I’m thinking about it. Some of the problems I do think I could probably solve, some of them sound like simple misconfigurations or whatever that do not need to be adjudicated through a company’s tech support system. I’m not sure exactly how I feel about this phenomenon overall. I think big tech companies should have to have tech support that goes far beyond what they’re currently offering. And I don’t think they should be directed at me. But I do think more people are using ChatGPT as their interface for the internet, and, in the same way that if you Google me, I come up, I think I’m fine with ChatGPT recommending people who believe they have interesting stories reach out to me. The part I take issue with is ChatGPT doing it for minor tech support problems.It started with the piece before it. One person reached out to me about Proton re-interviewing employees about their AI use. They sent the email, I verified their identity, and we published that piece on Monday. It was quick.The following day, I woke up to messages from more Proton employees. Then I got more during the day. Then so many that I initially missed a couple of people who reached out. When this happens, you know there is something else going on. When close to ten people at a company have decided to reach out to you, entirely of their own volition, there is more to the story.Of course, turns out, there was a lot more. The main thing for me was the Slack chats. It’s one thing for an employee to say their boss is a bully (which is true, and what I was told), but it’s another to see the behavior itself.I’ve read a lot of Slack chats in my time. I’ve read a lot of Slack chats from CEOs. I’ve never seen ones quite like this. The closest parallel I can think of is when Jason and I covered Andrew Frame, the CEO of Citizen, and he was saying stuff like “FIND THIS FUCK.”As bad as the bullying is (and it is), for me the most important part was the impact Yen could have on security at Proton. That’s why I put the anecdote of Yen telling an engineer who wanted to pentest newly written code “that’s bullshit and loser thinking” at the top.There was a lot of other stuff that I either couldn’t verify at the time (like about specific movements in the company) or stuff I couldn’t quite fit in. But the vast majority of what I obtained is in the article. I do think the piece is especially interesting because it is an example of how a company culture may actually impact the very important thing the company is trying to offer: trust, security, privacy. A company’s culture can often be bad, wild, toxic (WeWork, the list goes on). But those didn’t really impact the end product in quite the same way. Here, employees are in fear of speaking up even when security is on the line.I’m keeping an eye on what is happening inside Proton at the moment, and am interested in what happens with the planned re-interviews in November. I’m also gonna think aloud a little bit about the influx of emails we’ve gotten from people finding us via ChatGPT and other chatbots, and try not to repeat Jason too much (and I totally agree with everything he’s said here and in the story). Around 2019 and into 2020, but as early as 2018 in the aftermath of , I started to really grapple with my own purpose as a journalist. People came to me looking for help restoring their accounts that were unfairly removed, restoring sources of critical income after platforms took them down without notice, getting funds back after financial platforms stole them, getting images and videos taken off the internet. I wanted to help, and to me at the time, helping meant blogging. It’s incredibly unfair and fucked up that to get any response from these platforms, people have to go to a journalist. We have bemoaned publicly and privately among ourselves here for years, long before 404 existed and certainly longer than chatbots and “GEO” existed, that platforms treat us as pro-bono tech support — often ignoring serious issues until the threat of bad press arises, at which point they quickly fix or scrub the problem ahead of publication and then act like it was a solve issue all along. But this is the dynamic they’ve created. It’s fucked! It’s also why I really hate when people say we’re “tech negative” when they’re only seeing the end result of a typically hair-tearing series of interactions with a platform or service. Go complain to Meta’s comms team about it, idk. Anyway, I started going to therapy around that point, totally overwhelmed by the desire to help people and my own need and sanity to not act as “tech support” for everyone who sent me a message. It was to the point when I felt like I couldn’t take a day off because someone might ask for help and I’d miss it. I ended up making a that I linked to in my OOO autoreply (and need to update probably) because a) I was going to the ER for totally unmanaged migraines during this time and b) I wasn’t equipped to handle some of these very serious, traumatizing situations and sometimes literal crimes people were reporting to me. It’s very good and cool when Youtube, for one recent example, restores people’s accounts after unfairly banning them, which after I contacted them for comment and then had a truly mind-numbing, multi-email with their comms person about how many licks it takes to get to the center of a lollipop. But that can't be the goal of writing a story. I've gotten a lot better at balancing the work and my own boundaries, and communicating these nuances to sources over the years.I think the ChatGPT spam Jason wrote about is the natural evolution of this fucked up dynamic between the press, platforms, and users, which the platforms themselves have fostered for years by being unresponsive and unaccountable to their own customers. The chatbots can see that reporting gets results, and it’s attempting to shortcut its way to that, which of course defeats its own purpose (bc if you’re sending me 500 AI-generated words with every other outlet on the planet cc’d I am sending you to spam). It’s an incredible honor to have someone share their story with me, someone they usually barely know but can trust to tell it fairly and unflinchingly. It’s almost always vulnerable. A lot of my best most “impactful” stories have come as a result of establishing relationships with sources that walk a very difficult line: this is a relationship but they’re sharing something deeply , like the fallout from nonconsensual sexual imagery spreading online or the ways losing a source of income or visibility affects their ability to thrive and survive. ChatGPT spam nullifies all of that, cuts out the real human connection and interaction required to do good journalism even when they have a point or a real case to make, and it’s very frustrating to see.

item.author: Jason Kottke

item.title: ‘The Devils’ Gets Its Due
item.author: Corey Atad
item.content:encoded: Aldous Huxley likened the exorcism of the prioress Jeanne des Anges to “a rape in a public lavatory.” It was this horrific description that director Ken Russell shared with production designer Derek Jarman before they set out to tell that story. Russell wanted to capture the spirit of Huxley’s nonfiction book, , about the 17th-century incident in which a convent of nuns claimed possession, exhibiting wild and lewd behavior, leading to the sorcery conviction and execution of the priest Urbain Grandier. For that 1971 adaptation, , Jarman took the assignment quite literally. Large, white tiles cover every inch of Loudun’s Ursuline convent in the film, from floor to wall to arched ceiling. Tiles, and iron bars. It’s a gorgeous set, photographed by cinematographer David Watkin in anamorphic widescreen grandeur, and immerses the audience in the suffocated, cloistered lives of the nuns. Its starkness is at once mesmerizing and maddening. It is the perfect place for a case of possession—or many—and a likely site for clinically staged abuse.This wasn’t the first time I’d seen the scene in question, which is somehow more and less disturbing than Huxley’s six words suggests. I first watched some 15 or 20 years ago, on a pirated copy. It was a film whose reputation preceded it, and I was a young guy, barely out of high school, titillated by its scandalous history. Even before it was originally released, was heavily cut to appease British censors. It was cut further still for its American release. Though it earned respectable sums at the U.K. box office, the lavish Warner Bros. production received a critical thrashing—Roger Ebert’s sarcastic review is a classic in the genre of getting it completely backward—and essentially buried thereafter, popping up on a couple of VHS releases in the ’80s, but never on DVD or Blu-ray. In the early 2000s, British film critic Mark Kermode rediscovered the censored footage, helping Russell put together a director’s cut that screened only once, off a DigiBeta tape. The copy I’d watched years ago was an earlier cut, likely the original theatrical version minus the most controversial scenes, but all that history had me primed for an outrageous film, and an outrageous film is very much what I got. Sister Jeanne’s exorcism—set in that white, tiled lavatory of a convent, molested by priests wielding giant syringes to perform forced enemas—was sensational, as was the rest of the film’s high-toned lunacy. Rampant nudity, violence, actors gesticulating wildly, saying things like, “They say they can stand up to the Church, but they can't stand up to this bitch.” A movie for sickos. I loved it, naturally, but I don’t think I took it very seriously.

item.title: DOJ Election Interference Turns Into Raw Thuggery
item.author: David Kurtz
item.content:encoded: I have the same mix of feelings that I did in the days leading up to Jan. 6, 2021: a queasy feeling that things are about to spiral out of control along with the recognition that it could end up just being a clown show.The Justice Department’s corrupt, heavy-handed, intimidation tactics of issuing grand jury subpoenas to election officials in California while launching a wave of new election-related subpoenas in Alaska is a level of thuggery we haven’t seen before and a grave threat.The only more direct and dramatic interference in free and fair elections would be blocking voter access to the polls, seizing ballots, and refusing to abide by the results of the election. Stay tuned, I guess?And yet there remains an unmistakable clownish quality to the whole endeavor, such as Attorney General Todd Blanche personally charging four misdemeanor cases in Nevada for alleged noncitizen voting, presumably because the top federal prosecutor in the state is implicated in the Trump U.S. attorney scheme and was disqualified.It is, as always, both/and.Trump DOJ Ignores Judges WarningIn California, the Trump DOJ reportedly made the decision to target election officials themselves with a new round of grand jury subpoenas, Bloomberg reports:Justice Department leadership directed top federal prosecutors in California to pursue criminal subpoenas of state and local officials regarding their roles administering allegedly illegal voting, according to two people familiar with the situation.This is different from earlier grand jury subpoenas in recent weeks that were directed at obtaining voting records to prosecute alleged noncitizen voting. The new subpoenas are going directly to election officials who are in the midst of counting votes and managing an election.The new subpoenas aren’t limited just to Los Angeles County: “All four U.S. attorneys in California were issuing subpoenas, according to a person familiar with the matter who insisted on anonymity to discuss an ongoing investigation,” the AP reported.The subpoenas come after acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter sent letters to election officials in every California county earlier this month warning that they faced potential criminal prosecution for counting the ballots of alleged noncitizen voters — an unprecedented interpretation of federal criminal law.Bill Essayli, the top federal prosecutor in Los Angeles, echoed those threats in court this week.U.S. District Judge David O. Carter warned from the bench Tuesday that DOJ’s threats against election officials needed to “cease immediately.”In his order rejecting the Trump DOJ’s request that he order Los Angeles County to segregate and not yet count alleged mail-in ballots from alleged noncitizen voters, Judge Carter warned DOJ again: “The court reiterates what it said yesterday: these threats must stop.”The next day came with word of the new round of subpoenas.Conflicting Reports on Timing of SubpoenasNot all of the reporting is consistent as to when subpoenas were issued and served. But it appears that some subpoenas of election workers went out as early as last week.“At least two employees of Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder’s office received grand jury subpoenas last week for a proceeding scheduled for Nov. 4, on the morning after the election,” the NYT reported.Three subpoenas to employees of the Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder were sent Oct. 21 and 24, according to the AP, which obtained copies of them:The subpoenas request any documents and communications related to letters sent in July and October by federal officials to state election officials outlining allegations of noncitizens on the state’s voter rolls. … They also seek any information about efforts to prevent noncitizen votes from being counted.Those subpoenas predate the new wave of subpoenas that reportedly began yesterday in all four federal district in California.Again, the focus of these latest subpoenas is different than a separate batch of prior subpoenas that focused on getting voting records in order to prosecute individual voters for allegedly being noncitizens. One such subpoena was received by Orange County election officials yesterday, adding to the confusion.Grand jury subpoenas days before the election is intimidation enough, but there was at least one extra twist: “Federal marshals served one county employee at home, despite having already served that employee at the registrar’s office and issuing a notification of counsel, according to officials familiar with the incident,” the NYT reports.“Threats and intimidation have no place in elections,” said Dean Logan, the top election official in Los Angeles County.Wave of Subpoenas in AlaskaFurther seizing on the NYT report that tied the candidacy of the Dan Sullivan to the Senate campaign of Mary Peltola, the Trump DOJ issued a wave of new subpoenas ostensibly to investigate what it claims is a conspiracy to deceive voters — but which is in reality a last-ditch effort to save a key incumbent Republican senator.“Federal prosecutors issued more than 40 grand jury subpoenas and record preservation notices to key targets by [Wednesday] evening, one of the officials said,” according to CNN, which reported that additional subpoenas were expected yesterday.There had already been a quiet federal investigation of the Sullivan candidacy before the NYT story, with some grand jury subpoenas issued and witnesses interviewed, CNN reported:The investigation had already roiled the US Attorney’s office in Alaska, one of the officials said, where some career prosecutors have balked at aspects of the probe and whether the effort broke federal law or simply represents electioneering dirty tricks.It seems clear now that the NYT report embarrassed officials at Main Justice since the newspaper story went farther than its own investigation had.In a move I’ve never seen before, the Alaska U.S. attorney Michael Heyman “un-recused” himself from the case after the NYT report at the urging of Main Justice, CNN reported. Heyman had previously recused himself early in the probe because he was in discussions with Sens. Dan Sullivan and Lisa Murkowski about being nominated for a federal judgeship.The prosecutor-in-chief made clear his intentions soon after the NYT story broke: “I think they should be prosecuted,” President Trump said. “To me, that’s voter fraud at the highest level.”Trump: Why Is MY Beak Dry?!?Special Weekend Morning MemoKeep an eye on your inbox for a special weekend edition of Morning Memo.With the campaigns chugging to the finish line and Trump election interference in full swing, Morning Memo will bring you the latest. Stay tuned …

item.title: Russia Is Coming Back To International Hockey
item.author: Barry Petchesky
item.content:encoded: Russia, which has been functionally banned from international hockey for more than four years, must be allowed to return to international events starting in December in Canada. That's the ruling today by the Court of Arbitration for Sport, the highest sport court in the land. But there's a whole lot still unsettled, including a looming shitshow at next year's World Championships.The International Ice Hockey Federation banned the Russian member association in February 2022, as did almost every other sport's Olympic federation following Russia's invasion of Ukraine. That war is still ongoing, but in July of this year the IOC lifted its blanket ban on Russian Olympic committees, and said that its recommendations to individual sport federations no longer apply. Ukraine is currently appealing that decision.(This is tricky business, and I'm glad it's not up to me to decide. Should individual athletes be punished for their government's actions? Or is a ban of Russia's prestigious hockey program more accurately a punishment of the country as a whole? But then, why Russia and not some other war-starting, international law-ignoring countries I could name and/or live in?)

item.title: Rudimentary Lathe comes out of retirement for the 3rd time
item.author: Jack Baty
item.content:encoded: I miss when a bunch of us weirdos overshared on our TiddlyWikis nearly every day. Most are gone or unmaintained now. Can we bring them back? I'll start: rudimentarylathe.orgNearly 5,000 notes going back to 2018, and man oh man, at least 4,800 of them are an embarrassment. I should keep this stuff to myself, but that horse left the barn long ago.We used to write "TiddlyMails" to each other (I don't think we actually called them that). I'd write a note that simply mentioned someone with their own wiki. They'd read it, and write a note on their wiki with a link back and a title something like: "Re: That thing you wrote". It was completely manual and done without pings or notifications of any kind. So fun!If you have a similar wiki, let me know. I'd love to visit!TiddlyWiki is more than 20 years old and still a miracle to me.

item.title: President Rottinghands McCankles cancels his remaining rallies. What a fucking loser.
item.author: Jeff Tiedrich
item.source: everyone is entitled to my own opinion
item.content:encoded: Yesterday evening, out of the clear blue and without warning, the White House abruptly announced that all of Dear Leader’s upcoming weekend rallies had been canceled — fuckity-bye, hit the bricks, sayonara — thereby depriving his remaining cultists the opportunity to sit uncomfortably on a folding chair in a thimble-sized gymnasium, and listen to Donny ramble incoherently for two entire hours about how he successfully pointed at the drawing of the camel, all while being drowned out by an endless series of hecklers.Reporter Jacob Bogage: “So you not going to Kansas has nothing to do with you being sick of traveling?”Donny: “Oh, you’re sick to ask that question. You are sick. Who are you with?”Bogage: Donny: “You are a sick guy. Reuters is terrible. Can you imagine? Look at this guy. He’s way out of shape. Look at how bent— he comes [makes accordion hands] he comes to me. ‘Sir, you’re not gonna go to Kansas.’ I’m not going to Kansan because he’s doing very well. We’re gonna do a tele-rally’ … but he says, ‘you’re not going to Kansas, sir, are you feeling well?’ You’ve been following me for two weeks. I feel perfect. You are disgusting. Put yourself in shape. You look like hell.”Wow, Dear Leader sure gets cranky when he’s got a full load in his diaper — and he didn’t even hear the question correctly. Did you catch that? The reporter asks Donny if he’s and Donny goes ballistic because all he hears is And he automatically explodes into some infantile rant about ‘I’m not sick, you’re sick’ — because he’s got the emotional maturity of a four-year-old.Maybe Donny needs to get his ears checked. Is this a piece of your brain, Donny?Dear Leader can’t hack it any more. He’s too old and tired and demented to be flying across the country every single goddamned day. Plus, he’s fed up. He loves the crowds — only this time around, there aren’t any crowds. All that remains are the die-hard, brain-deadest cultists — and there aren’t even enough of them left to fill the pint-sized high school gyms his flunkies are booking him into. How long before Donny has to open for a‘Oh Natty, you’re the only one who understands me.’ I think I just threw up in my own mouth a little.So now, if you’re a cultist and you need your Donny fix this weekend, you’re going to have to zoom in to some ‘tele-rally,’ and watch Dear Leader sitting behind the Resolute Desk, drooling all over himself as he gradually loses consciousness. It’ll be just like a real rally, except you won’t be able to smell the farts.Meanwhile, let’s go live to Republican National Headquarters for the GOP’s reaction to Donny having canceled his remaining rallies.“Sources say, though, that some Republican officials are relieved by the president’s decision to cancel those final two rallies. One top Republican official told my colleague Jeff Zeleny, quote, ‘thank God. He hasn’t moved the needle anywhere.’ And a second official, saying, quote, ‘everyone has seen the president who wants to see him.’”Boo fucking hoo, Republicans. Maybe it was a mistake to hitch your wagons to an increasingly-befuddled fascist who, thanks to an increasing fog of dementia and untreated tertiary syphilis, no longer has any idea which end is up.Reporter: “Have you heard that Lt. General Sylvia leaked classified information at the Pentagon?”Reporter: “I said, Lt. General Sylvia leaked classified information at the Pentagon.”Donny: “ got problems. gonna have big problems. did. We’re very much looking for leakers, and uh—gonna have big problems.”Surely, Donny can’t be this seriously misinformed, can he?Spoiler alert: yes he can be this misinformed. Remember, Donny’s daily intel briefing has been boiled to down to a single page of bullet points and burlesque photos from the 1940s.That’s the only thing that will hold Donny’s attention. So he hasn’t a fucking clue who Lt. General Sylvia is. All he hears is the name ‘Sylvia’ and away he goes, blithering about the retribution he’s going to inflict on some imaginary woman who doesn’t exist. I’m so old, I remember when Job Biden would occasionally stumble over someone’s name, and would have to correct himself. The press would have a field day, and start filling editorial pages with piece after piece about how Sleepy Joe was too old and icky and smelly do to his job, and how he needs to step down, right now, for the good of the country.Now we have an actual cognitively-collapsed president concocting fairy tales about strange generals, lying in ponds, distributing leaks — and not one worthless scribbler of the corporate-controlled press can be bothered to say one word about it.It’s so embarrassing to have a President of the United States who is an uninformed fool who has no fucking clue what’s going on inside his own government, and just makes shit up on the spot, based on what’s he’s But tell me once again how it was Joe Biden who was the real problem. That’s such an awesome story.I swear, I yam disgustipated. Fox News bobblehead: “Tom, why are you here this morning?”Tom: “Well, in the late 70s, I was a little too young to get involved and go to South America for the Jonestown Massacre. But this is as close as I’ll ever get, so that’s why I’m here.”Bobblehead: “Wait, the Jonestown Massacre?”Tom: “That’s right. There’s nothing like seeing a cult right up front, man.”Bobblehead: “Maybe this is not a Trump supporter [walks away dejectedly]And right there, that’s your problem for Fox news — and for all the wingnut media right now. When there are too few cultists in the crowd, it’s way too easy for any mischief-maker to walk up to the dude holding the microphone, and go Masterful job, bro. Norway will be in touch to let you know when you can pick up your Nobel Trolling Prize.[Oh, and that scream you just heard, that was me — because this is where I was in writing this post when I got the notification on my phone about Donny going ahead with the canceled rallies. I was this fucking close, man.]Well, it’s Friday — and we made it through another week in one piece. Let’s reward ourselves with some Daily Claudia and get out of here.Here are three photos off the same roll of film from the early 1990s. First, we have Ms Spouse setting up a slide for Katie, in our back yard.Second, Ms Spouse in a hotel room in Plymouth, MA.And lastly, Katie and her mom, on the beach in Plymouth.Have a great Friday, everyone. May you have better timing than me, when news is breaking.here’s your daily reminder that I can be found on Blue Sky at this link.this is going to be my closing message for the foreseeable future: do what you need to do to keep sane. if that means you need to disengage with my daily posts for a while, I get it. this community of ours will still be here when you return.to all the people who have signed on in the days since the election, . settle in as we all try to deal with the shitfuckery that’s ahead of us.we are all in this together, and we are all here for each other.
