item.title: Na, Na, Na, Na, Na, Na, Na, Na, Site Search!
item.author: Jason Kottke
item.content:encoded: After years in the making (or more accurately, years in the wanting), I finally figured out how I wanted to do search for KDO posts. I’ve been tinkering with this specific implementation since the beginning of the summer and it finally all came together. If you’re a member, please help me to kick the tires on this for a few days. (That link, as well as the search links below, will 404 for non-members for now.)Hopefully it’s pretty close and then I can open it up to everyone. I’ve been using it for the past week or two and it’s been really helpful so far, especially in surfacing older posts about topics I’m currently writing about or generally interested in. The tag pages are good for that too, but search can help hone in on specifics — like posts I’ve made about fascism or posts that link to McSweeney’s. Search also pulls in results from Quick Links, which aren’t included on tag pages. The rankings still need some work here and there (it’s not magic), but your searches will help calibrate things.For now, the search only looks at posts from 2014 to the present. You can search by keyword, describe what you remember (“the guy who walks in Japan”), or paste a link to find posts that link to it. Search is fuzzy-ish but it’s not an AI bot or anything like that so if you ramble on with a 25-word query, it’s probably not going to work that well. You can sort by best match or newest, search all posts or just Quick Links or main posts, and filter by time (past month, past 3 months, etc.)I’ll share more about how search works in a subsequent post. For now, kick the tires and let me know what you think in the comments or via email. As always, bug reports, comments, and suggestions are welcome.

item.title: Welcome to the offseason
item.author: bounce+2edd00.7bdc18-5mr68b7cb43ac2h04ai5=kill-the-newsletter.com@m.ghost.io
item.content:encoded: With the World Series over and the Milwaukee Brewers the rightful champions, it’s time to end my annual postseason sabbatical. After all this time, and as the cliché goes, I hope this edition of the newsletter finds you well.Even though we’re yet to November, I plan on pacing myself as much as possible to keep the newsletter productive during what is shaping up to be a lengthy lockout once the current CBA expires on December 1. When the owners lockout the players (an unnecessary move at this point in the process), the baseball world will grind to a halt. Sadly, we’ve seen this movie before, so we know the baseball desert that awaits. The Winter Meetings will be cancelled. There will be few or no negotiating sessions though the holidays. The urgency will return when we should have camps opening in February.It’s going to be a colder winter than usual. As for what I plan to do here, there will be some player profiles, some random (i.e. wrong) free agent guesses and, of course, I'll cover any news that happens over the next month ahead of the lockout. Along with the usual baseball foolishness. So hit that subscribe button if you haven't so we can make this offseason journey together.The first order now that the offseason is officially underway is for teams to massage their 40-man roster. There will probably be a flurry of activity ahead of the lockout and for now at least, it's business as usual. The Royals saw Jonathan India, Craig Kimbrel, Luke Maile and Josh Rojas officially become free agents on Thursday. On Monday, this quartet will be free to negotiate with the rest of the teams in the league. I can’t imagine a scenario where any of these guys will be back with the Royals.Late Thursday, word came down that Carlos Estévez will soon join them on the market as the Royals declined his $13 million club option. They’ll hand over $2 million instead as a buyout. Estévez recorded one out all year and gave up a walkoff grand slam. It wasn't what anyone was looking for.Tony Gonsolin, who signed a major league contract in August and also appeared in one game for the Royals, had his 2027 option picked up. His outing was in September against the White Sox where he looked good for two innings before the wheels came off in his third frame of work. Still, you could see some of that old magic that made him appealing to the Royals. For next season, the oft-injured pitcher will be officially on the books for $2.5 million, although there are reports he can earn up to $6 million in performance incentives. Once the Royals move their players off the 60-day IL, the Royals will have 38 players on the 40-man roster.What did you think of the postseason? Overall I thought it was fine, helped by the fact the Brewers and the Rays won their respective leagues. I also low-key enjoyed the fact that the higher seeded team won every matchup in every round. Underdogs are fun, but seeing good teams advance is satisfying. My only issue: The dominance of the Milwaukee nine removed any semblance of drama from these last couple of weeks. They are such a complete ballclub that this October felt akin to 1984 when the Detroit Tigers steamrolled to victory or 1989 when it was the Oakland A’s getting down to business after coming up short the year before. While nothing is ever certain in these playoffs, especially with the expanded format, but once the Brewers started throwing haymakers at the Dodgers in the NLCS, it all seemed settled.A couple of stray World Series thoughts as we process a long winter (and probably spring) ahead...I felt the similarities between the Brewers and the 2015 Royals in that both teams played a form of what I’ve taken to call Total Baseball in that they do just about everything right. Strong starting pitching? Check. A selfless move-the-line batting order? Uh-huh. A lockdown bullpen? For sure. Clutch hits, including home runs? Yep. Hell, both teams check the box with salt of the earth managers who are refreshingly honest.There was a moment in the dying moments of the NLCS where the broadcast was doing the obligatory crowd shots and found a woman who looked like she was about to pass out. It was a combination of stress and disbelief. It was the most relatable thing I saw all October, making me think of when I had to take a seat while in the upper tank at The K for Game Four of the 2014 ALCS. I seemed to have gotten a bit lightheaded. When something is unfolding in front of you that you never, ever thought would happen, it can hit hard. I sure she rallied and partied in an appropriate manner.As we know, winning a championship after suffering through years of heartache makes the moment all the sweeter.As a self-proclaimed broadcast geek, I have to wonder why American broadcasting networks hate their viewers so much. After a summer spent watching the World Cup on Univision to dodge the audio assault from Fox soccer announcers, I found myself regularly wondering if we really need nine innings (or more) of John Smoltz who was seemingly getting paid by the word? No, we don’t and I found myself often wishing he would just shut up. There are moments where he does bring up an interesting point or two regarding strategy and whatnot, but for the most part in this World Series he was shockingly unprepared. Fox does a huge disservice by having him on the broadcast. Maybe someday TBS will get the rights to the World Series and they can have Brian Anderson, Ron Darling and Jeff Francoeur on the call. Anderson, the Brewers TV guy when not on national assignments is a pro. Darling is part of the best booth in baseball for the Mets. And Frenchy is really, really good at providing commentary to the point that I wish we could’ve enticed him to stay in Kansas City at the end of his career.I’m not surprised the early television ratings for the World Series were, while down, better than expected. While the five games weren’t exactly what I would call crisp baseball, even casual fans can appreciate when the two best teams in the game face off for the championship. It also helps that both teams embraced the moment and seemed to just have fun playing the game.Speaking of the keep-the-line-moving mentality of the Milwaukee lineup, I’m going to be thinking about the fifth inning of Game Three for a long, long time. It was epic baseball, a symphony of exit velocity, launch angle and perfectly placed hits. In an October with close games and seemingly few extended rallies, this inning was unforgettable.I know newspapers are struggling for survival, but I can’t help but continue to be disappointed by the lack of baseball coverage provided by the Kansas City Star. It wasn’t difficult to come up with a local angle with Grain Valley’s Jacob Misiorowski and Park Hill’s Aaron Ashby both playing key rolls for the Brewers. They should’ve sent someone to cover this Series.Remember when we had Andy McCullough writing about the Royals at The Star? He had the World Series wrap for The Athletic. It is, as you would expect, exceptional.As McCullough points out, the Brewers have not had an easy road even though they’ve qualified for October in eight of the last nine seasons. They’ve made several trades along the way of key players including pitchers Josh Hader, Corbin Burnes, Devin Williams and Freddy Peralta. Not all of those deals yielded players who landed on their postseason roster. They filled the gaps through a strong international presence, outstanding scouting and exceptional drafts. It’s not an easy blueprint to replicate, but when you look at what Milwaukee General Manager Matt Arnold has done on the trade front, you have to wonder about how the Royals have failed to capitalize on peak return on some players they should’ve dealt. Missed opportunities equal missed postseasons.

item.title: Diehard Reds Blogger Spends His Office Hours Making Life Hell For Asylum Seekers
item.author: Chris Thompson
item.content:encoded: Judge Chadwick Dotson works out of the Charlotte Immigration Court, where he was appointed this past March. For a person to accept an appointment to the immigration court system—from the Trump administration, in the post-Minneapolis world—they have to be the person that you are imagining right now. In most ways, Dotson is exactly that. Prior to accepting this appointment—to a powerful position in one of the cruelest arms of the most blatantly criminal federal government in American history—Dotson was being sued as director of the Virginia Department of Corrections, where he was appointed by former Virginia Governor Glenn Youngkin. Before that, he was chairman of the Virginia Parole Board, also under Youngkin, where he ran an ostentatiously blunt and unyielding parole operation.All along, when he isn't doling out excessive punishment or denying asylum seekers, this immigration judge is something of a regular sports blogger.Dotson writes columns about the Cincinnati Reds, his favorite baseball team, for , under the byline Chad Dotson. On Oct. 6, a little over a week after the Reds wrapped up a disappointing 75-87 campaign, Dotson pondered whether it was time for fans to step away from the team. It was the 15th article that Dotson published for the magazine that season. He has co-written a book about the MLB team, and also has a Substack newsletter called The Riverfront, where he covers the Reds and other Cincinnati sports teams. (The Riverfront occasionally dabbles in movie coverage; in his year-end list for 2023, Dotson listed Killers of the Flower Moon and among his favorite films.) On April 22, Dotson was enjoying a surprising start from the Reds, who at the time were 16–8 and riding high atop the NL Central. "There is still room for improvement in this lineup. This team could get even better," he wrote. "In the meantime, I’m having fun."You can predict some of Dotson's performance as an immigration judge through his performance in his previous professional roles. When he is given the choice between more or less punishment, he opts for more. As director of the Virginia Department of Corrections, Dotson acted on an advisory opinion written by then-Virginia Attorney General Jason Miyares, who argued that the state could expand exclusions from sentence credits, beyond the written law, to prisoners who would otherwise benefit from those credits. That decision delayed the release of approximately 8,000 prisoners; Prison Legal News estimated that 560 of those prisoners had already been told that they were within a month of release. When the Virginia Supreme Court subsequently shot down Miyares's advisory opinion, Dotson's Department of Corrections delayed releasing the prisoners for another three months. A group of 53 state prisoners eventually filed a class-action lawsuit against Dotson and his predecessor, and won $1.6 million in a 2025 settlement. From the PLN article:

item.title: The Witch They Call Black Annis
item.author: Miss Cellania
item.content:encoded: Black Annis is an English witch who supposedly ate children, which is always a good story to keep your kids from wandering in the woods at night. A written account from 300 years ago said she lived in a cave, was raised by wolves, had sharp claws, and wore a skirt made from human skin. We know the specific area the legend came from, but where is the cave? Could the story of Black Annis come from that of a 15th-century nun named Agnes who lived alone outside her convent? A woman hermit was very unusual, but Agnes seems to have been respected and even revered. However, a couple of hundred years separated those stories, and intervening events may have changed the details greatly to fit new religious narratives. There are alternate theories on the origins of the legend, and Dr. Emily Zarka goes through them to judge their accuracy.

item.title: Apple Is Entering Its Slop Era
item.author: Matthew Gault
item.content:encoded: The once dominant company is struggling to find its feet in an AI-driven post-Tim Cook world. John Ternus — a 25 year veteran of the company with a track record of pushing harebrained hardware schemes like the and butterfly keyboard. With Ternus at the helm, I feel there’s a good chance Apple’s best days are behind it, that it will have to make do with less, that it’s déclassé. Apple, blindsided by AI and relying on crowdpleasing hardware gimmicks, is downwardly mobile. It’s in its slop era. The company that once asked consumers to is now releasing hardware that’s just like everything else on the market.Apple is not adjusting to this new position well. AI boosters agree that Siri AI is awful. Apple HomeView is a $300 Apple Watch meant to replace the family hearth. The iPhone Duo has only been out for a few days and all people can talk about is the cracks, yet Ternus is on the cover of Time Magazine this week holding the folding iPhone Duo and staring at the camera. “The other examples in the world felt kind of cheap and crappy,” . Many people holding cracked iPhone Duos this week are learning just what (not) cheap and crappy looks like.Flailing from crackgate, Apple announced the launch of a touch-screen laptop, an idea Steve Jobs extensively tested and ,” an idea Cook once compared to combining a toaster with a refrigerator. What’s next? What if the toaster-refigerator folded? Ternus has been trying to make an 18-inch foldable iPad . Maybe Apple will solve the screen cracking issues by then. Or maybe Ternus will continue to try to put .I have been waiting for this moment for more than a decade. I am relishing Apple’s recent trajectory more than I should. I confess I harbor a secret and petty grudge.In 2010, when Apple released the iPhone 4 I was working as a floor manager at a Banana Republic in Dallas. I was interested in smart phones, of course, but Dallas is an expensive city and the iPhone was a luxury. I made do . But the suit-wearing middle management retail psychopaths that were my coworkers saw my lack of an iPhone as a weakness. It was not, as they say now, On Brand.I had started at the store in the stock room, working my way up to manage the backroom before ascending to a coveted position on the sales floor. The other managers made it clear that a Razr was a “backroom” phone and someone in a prominent position on the floor needed to be seen using an iPhone.At first, I was not to buy an iPhone. The message came in the form of subtle and not so subtle bullying deployed over weeks.“Still using that old phone?” they’d say.“Didn’t you get a raise?” someone would ask a week later.“Try not to use that on the sales floor,” one co-worker told me, pointing at my Razr. “We’re trying to project a certain image here.”The social pressure had the opposite of its intended effect. I resisted. Eventually one of the friendlier managers pulled me aside. He told me that my colleagues thought it was weird that I didn't have an iPhone. He said I needed to buy one to fit in and he said the store could give me an advance on my paycheck to make it happen.Ever the contrarian and pissed I was experiencing high school style bullying as a full grown adult, I threw in with Google instead. I got an . My coworkers weren’t happy, but they stopped bringing up the iPhone. I’ve been an Android user ever since and studiously avoided Apple products until I broke down a few years ago and bought a Macbook Air. Time heals all wounds and Windows laptops are garbage. I’d even been considering changing from Android to iPhone because the privacy features are more robust. I’ve never been averse to a fast food meal either and maybe I’m a little more comfortable with Apple now that the cracks are starting to show in the foldable phone.

item.title: Listen to a Long-Lost Daft Punk Mix From 1997
item.author: Jason Kottke
item.content:encoded: A DJ named Ralph Lawson, who hosted a radio show called Trans Europe Express, found an incredible time capsule in his collection: an hour-long mixtape sent to him by Daft Punk in 1997, shortly after the release of their debut album, Homework. The tape was badly damaged, but he worked with a specialist to restore it and has put the whole mix up on Soundcloud.As I write this, the mix has been up for a little over a day and has just over 7000 plays. It’s unclear whether Lawson ever even played it on the show, so we could be among the first people, outside of Daft Punk themselves, to hear this mix in almost 30 years.

item.title: Ohio’s Jon Husted, object of Trump’s leering, is just an empty pair of pants
item.content:encoded: Jon Husted has a problem: People can’t seem to remember who he is. The former lieutenant governor of Ohio was appointed to be the state’s junior U.S. senator in 2025, after JD Vance became vice president. But Husted hasn’t much of an impression on the Buckeye State’s residents. In an August poll conducted by Emerson College, nearly four in 10 Ohio voters answered “unsure/never heard of” when asked their opinion of the Republican incumbent. Only 14% answered the same regarding his Democratic opponent, former Sen. Sherrod Brown. In fact, one in four voters in a Bowling Green State University poll even mistakenly identified Brown, a popular veteran of Ohio politics, as the incumbent. (In fact, Brown lost his seat to Ohio’s other Republican senator, Bernie Moreno, in 2024.)The Husted campaign has tried to spin his forgettability as an asset, hoping to trick voters into thinking of Brown as a failed incumbent, but it doesn’t seem to be working. Brown is pulling ahead in the most recent polls, riding a larger national turn away from the GOP. So Republicans turned to the one person who knows how to get a headline: Donald Trump.Bringing the president to campaign in Ohio has certainly helped to boost Husted’s name recognition, but at a painful cost. Now Husted has become the single most famous male victim of Trump’s relentless appetite for sexual harassment. The president’s public ogling of Husted started at a Youngstown rally on Oct. 12, when Trump delivered a monologue about how he’d “started examining [Husted’s] body” and had seen big hands and shoulders. Then he said the word “ass.” This caused a reaction of shock and laughter reaction in the crowd and also generated a lot of media attention. So Trump, like a narcissistic rat pushing the “applause” button, turned it into a running joke. At nearly every rally now, whether in Ohio or somewhere else, Trump raves about the 59-year-old Husted’s reputedly spectacular and muscular backside.Trump is famously a lifelong heterosexual, so many in the media and on the left are confused. They assume that latent homoerotic yearnings are burbling up, perhaps from the disinhibition that can occur among people who take regular tests for dementia, as does our president. But that’s unlikely, and not just because Husted actually possesses the softer derrière typical of a man his age. If genuine same-sex desire was behind Trump’s leering, the overtly homophobic crowds who populate MAGA rallies would be highly uncomfortable.Bringing Trump to campaign in Ohio has certainly boost Husted’s name recognition, but at a painful cost. Now he’s the single most famous male victim of Trump’s relentless appetite for sexual harassment.Instead, as videos show, they scream with the same laughter they produce when Trump goes on a racist tirade, encourages audience members to commit acts of violence or otherwise showcases his affinity for childish bullying, which remains his main and often sole selling point to his base. It’s a large-scale version of the infamous “Access Hollywood” tape, where Trump tried to impress the show’s host, Billy Bush, with braggadocious claims that he can grab women’s genitals and they have to put up with it. The MAGA crowd may not favor the term “sexual harassment,” but they get that’s what Trump is doing to Husted. He did the same bit with Nicki Minaj, making the rapper-turned-MAGA shill stand up and show off her backside to the crowd at a Michigan rally. As feminists like to remind folks, sexual harassment is about demonstrating power, not lust. Husted is far from the only man Trump ever catcalls. As the New York Times notes, Trump loves making a spectacle out of men’s looks, for the approval of hooting MAGA audiences who get a vicarious thrill from watching Trump say inappropriate things to fellow Republicans, who have no choice but to grin and pretend they enjoy it. It’s a continuation of the other ways Trump displays his dominance over Republicans with fancy job titles, such as senators and Cabinet officials, by expecting them to flatter him grotesquely on camera or to wear ill-fitting shoes he has “gifted” them. None of this should make us feel any sympathy for Husted or other Republicans, who could at any point grow an actual spine and reject Trump’s abuse. These people grovel for their failing leader in the vain hope that some of his celebrity stardust will rub off on them and boost their political ambitions. Husted is a classic example of the problem now facing Republicans. Like most in his party, he has nothing to offer voters, unless they’re hyper-rich capitalists seeking deregulation or massive tax cuts. He has no discernible charisma of his own, either. So all that’s left is leeching onto Trump and hoping his ability to speak to the lizard-brain impulses of bigots will rally enough voters to drag Husted’s empty pair of pants (and his mediocre ass) across the finish line. Like most in his party, Husted has nothing to offer voters, unless they’re hyper-rich capitalists seeking deregulation or tax cuts, and no discernible charisma. All that’s left is leeching onto Trump and hoping his ability to speak to the lizard-brain impulses of bigots can drag Husted’s empty pants across the line.What’s funny about all this is that Husted’s blandness is likely what landed him in the unfortunate spot of getting rhetorically goosed by Trump almost every night. By his own account, Trump knew very little about the Ohio Republican he was there to support at the Youngstown rally, but learned shortly beforehand that Husted played football in college. Trump, whose background is in reality TV, resorted to his tendency to reduce a person to a single defining trait that could fit on a chyron. So even though Husted’s gridiron career ended decades ago, Trump indulged in lame fantasies about how he thinks a football player should look like, complete with broad shoulders and well-defined glutes.Likely, it would have ended with one iteration if he hadn’t praised Husted’s ass, which elevated a pedestrian effort to define a candidate into the realm of attention-getting weirdness. But of course that remark got everyone’s attention, and Trump will reliably return to any bit, no matter how bizarre, as long as it draws eyeballs. So it was that Husted, who was on the verge of being relegated to “Former College Football Player” in the sprawling reality show cast of Trump’s political orbit, instead became the butt of Trump’s favorite new joke.It could be worse, of course. Trump has a similar bit he likes to trot out about Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, the Republican nominee for that state’s Senate seat. Except instead of being an imaginary muscleman like Husted, Trump has cast Paxton in the role of ugly loser. In nearly every speech where he mentions Paxton, Trump has to talk about how hideous the guy is and how poorly he supposedly dresses.With both of these GOP candidates, Trump’s oversimplified, theatrical descriptors don’t have much to do with reality. Whatever he once looked like, Husted doesn’t really have the athletic build Trump fantasizes about. Paxton is nobody’s idea of a handsome man, but it’s simply not true that he dresses poorly. There are many terrible things we could say about Paxton, but his wardrobe appears perfectly fine — especially compared to Trump, who seems to believe that wearing enormously oversized suits will hide his ever-expanding bulk. But these two guys are now characters in Trump’s world, where, as in reality TV shows, individual humans are stripped of all their complexities to be turned into broad, easily consumed caricatures.Whether he’s inviting the world to stare at these men’s allegedly spectacular rear end or daring them to smile while he calls them ugly, Trump is sending a message: He owns these people. He can define them in reductive, humiliating language, and they have been so hollowed out as human beings that they won’t even defend themselves. Normally, when a leader is both a lame duck and cratering in his approval polls, the way Donald Trump is now, that person’s party will start looking for ways to move on and forge a new identity. It’s a sign of how empty the Republican Party is that they seem incapable of doing that. They don’t just submit to Trump’s continued abuse, but even keep seeking it out. That must be a miserable experience, but clearly they feel that without him, they’re nothing at all. It’s tough to disagree.

item.title: Teach a Man to Phish
item.author: Dave Pell
item.source: NextDraft: The Day's Most Fascinating News
item.content:encoded: In the early days of the internet, tech industry folks were justifiably excited about the possibilities presented by the internet. What we weren’t really thinking about was the fact that the bad guys would have the same access to the tools as the good guys do. We’re not nearly as naive this time around, but we’re still creating massively powerful AI tools that will give the nefarious a new set of weapons to deploy, more quickly, more cheaply, and more maliciously. I’m not sure that AI is really going to destroy a large percentage of humanity, but the age of empowered hackers has already arrived. Tech has released the tools that most endanger the future of tech. But in this fight, we’re all in the ring. From individual phishing attempts made on your parents to major attacks on healthcare infrastructure, we’ve entered into a sort of war in which the same companies are essentially providing the weapons to all sides. DJ Patil, the nation’s first Chief Data Scientist, posted a good overview in LinkedIn. It’s mostly aimed at cybersecurity professionals, but anyone can (and should) get the gist. We Built for Peacetime. Prepare for Wartime: The AI Cybersecurity Reckoning Is Here. “Sustained, destructive, adaptive pressure used to require the resources of a state. It now requires a laptop, a few dollars of compute, and a model that does not get tired. When the price of relentless hostility falls to zero, you should expect relentless hostility from actors who could never have afforded it before — including some who want nothing from you but your absence. That is the new equilibrium: an environment in which someone is always trying to hurt you, and in which the tools you would use to fight back are themselves targets.” We came for the cute cat photos, we ended up in a war.+ “Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, said on Thursday that it had halted withdrawals after it was attacked by hackers who made off with more than $6 billion in digital coins, in what appears to be the biggest crypto heist in history.”If you look at traditional measures from the economy to polling to America’s role in the world, the first two years of Trump’s second term has been an abject failure. But those are probably not the measurements Trump and his family (and those who have fallen in line) are using. When you consider the pace at which the system has been corrupted, along with the financial gains of those who took advantage, it’s been a hell of a run. Noah Shachtman in the (Gift Article): Is This the End for Trump’s Princelings? Or Just the Start? “President Trump’s second term has ushered in a starkly different arrangement. Tariffs, prosecutions and regulations are all now subject to one man’s whims. Business leaders are being asked to underwrite government projects, such as the White House ballroom. The government assigns to itself a cut of private businesses. The White House bestows enterprises from oil fields to social media platforms on loyal allies. A coterie of top officials, their children and their gaggle of hangers-on move through the world like princelings. The rule of law can seem situational at best. It’s a throwback to an old style of governing, centered on a father figure who treats the nation like an extension of his household, and who dispenses resources and favors and jobs like a dad handing out candy to his kids. In an environment like this, fealty to the national patriarch can seem like the surest — in some cases only — way to get ahead.” (And plenty of people and companies are taking that way.) “Wealth can still buy political power, just as it did in the oligarchy’s previous iteration. The difference today is that a new gusher of cash has erupted and is flowing in the opposite direction. Political power, or even just proximity to it, is generating wealth to a degree unknown in modern American history.”+ In two years, American democracy has been turned into the plot of your average mob movie. Trump Erupted After Learning of Alina Habba’s $50 Million Deal. He wasn’t mad that his pardons are for sale. He was mad that he didn’t get a taste. “Angry about the scale of a contract signed by one of his former lawyers with the family of a wealthy pardon seeker, the president told allies he wanted some of the money to go to his future presidential library.” (In the business, we call this making her an offer she can’t refuse.)+ The tech market is looking dangerously shaky. What if things go really south and the bubble bursts? Guess who’s in charge of the bailout? (Gift Article): Can Democracy Survive the Next Financial Crash? “If the crash happens on Donald Trump’s watch, his administration would likely sidestep Congress entirely. A Trump bailout would proceed on whatever terms please the president and his allies, who would use it as a bonanza to enrich their favored companies and CEOs, even if they were the ones who caused the crisis to begin with.” So, yeah, the midterms are a pretty big deal.Here’s a lede that captures this moment in higher education: “A top administrator at Dartmouth College has resigned after a faculty committee found he used artificial intelligence to shape his writing, including in a guest column in The Washington Post on AI cheating.” Dartmouth Provost Santiago Schnell resigns following accusations he used artificial intelligence for writing. “The college paper, The Dartmouth, then ran other publications from Schnell through an AI detector. Writing that predated ChatGPT’s 2022 public release was found to be human-written, but high rates of AI use were detected in his recent writing.” One wonders whether that trend is at all uncommon. But wait, there’s more… “Schnell told the paper in an email last month that he uses AI for ‘language refinement, copyediting, improving clarity and organization and making writing processes more efficient.’ The paper ran the statement through an AI-detector and found it was AI-written.” (At this point, it probably makes more sense for journalists to talk to the AI directly…) This collection of weekend whats is going to be documentary themed. All three picks on Netflix are about the creative life, the love life, and, to some extent, the end of life. And all are, in their own way, very life-affirming. Martin Mull was a very successful musician, comedian, and actor. And none of those were even what he did best (or liked doing most). Who is Martin Mull? “Beloved for blurring performance and personal crisis, Maria Bamford unpacks the mental health journey behind her fearless comedy in this documentary.” Bamford is the comedian’s comedian. She once performed an entire show in her parents’ living room. Paralyzed by Hope: The Maria Bamford Story. And one from a few years ago: “Literary icon Joan Didion reflects on her remarkable career and personal struggles in this intimate documentary directed by her nephew, Griffin Dunne.” Joan Didion: The Center Will Not Hold. We could sure use Didion’s voice to add some context to what America is going through today. Another day, another top general squeezed out at the Pentagon. And, in this case, Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia is being referred for criminal prosecution because of possible leaks. General ousted by Hegseth referred for possible criminal prosecution, officials say. My first reaction to this story was that the administration probably wanted Sylvia out because his last name sounds female-ish. As per usual, the reality is more ridiculous than any joke you could come up with. “When asked by a reporter Thursday what proof the administration has that the general leaked classified information, President Donald Trump appeared unaware that Sylvia is a man. ‘She’s going to have big problems,’ he said. ‘Long-term problems.'” Plus, Hegseth Fires Top General After Laura Loomer Targets Him. From the party of strong defense to the party of Laura Loomer in the blink of an eye…+ The faux outrage about the Alaska Dan Sullivan(s) controversy is leading to some very real legal moves. “But there’s a long history of political operatives from both parties deploying the tactic — and largely getting away with it. ‘It’s a time-honored tradition,’ said Thomas Kahn, director of the Center for Congressional and Presidential Studies at American University. ‘It’s not a good practice,’ Kahn added, but ‘if trying to confuse voters was a crime, then every politician would be in jail.'” Three Bob Fergusons and two JFKs: A brief history of same-name ballot shenanigans.+ “All the research is driven by mounting concerns over the long-term brain health of contact-sport athletes. A study published on Wednesday used a statistical model to estimate that three in four former National Football League players who died between 2008 and 2023 most likely had signs of C.T.E. in their brains at death.” Can Scientists Make Football Safer? “A college football team in Utah is donning some curious caps this season. As part of their regular recovery routine, many Brigham Young University players are wearing headsets that shine near-infrared light onto their scalps — and up their noses.”+ “Patrick Stewart, who overcame a bleak childhood in England’s coal-mining country to find acclaim as a Shakespearean actor before making an unlikely career pivot in middle age that would bring him his greatest fame, playing a noble starship captain on the TV series ‘Star Trek: The Next Generation,’ died on Wednesday at his home in Los Angeles. He was 86.”+ A ship that was once celebrated as “the fastest passenger liner in the world, is scheduled to be sunk in the Gulf of Mexico in November, creating what will be the world’s largest artificial reef.” The name of the ship: The SS United States. (Sometimes, the metaphors just sink themselves…)

item.title: The real strategy of the DOJ’s Alaska lawsuit is more sinister
item.author: 1axblouew6p92pbpe56ydtxinvrtehldbz9oe7@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
item.content:encoded: A new batch of data on North Carolina mail ballot rejections arrived in my inbox late Monday. Mail ballots are getting flagged for rejection at a rate of nearly 6%, as of an Oct. 24 count. That’s almost 4,000 ballots so far. When ballot counting ends, the number will likely be significantly higher.While not all ballots with problems will ultimately be thrown out, they’re in limbo and essentially null until a voter takes action to resubmit or fix errors. It’s an extra hurdle to voting that many people don’t end up surmounting. What’s more, we can now definitively tie a majority of in two of the state’s largest counties — both Democratic strongholds — to a strict new rule, imposed by Republicans at the last minute, about sealing the inner envelope.If that wasn’t enough, the latest data revealed striking rejection rates in the double digits for some of North Carolina’s most rural counties where Black voters comprise a majority of the population. Those with lower internet access and fewer resources may have never gotten the memo that there’s an entirely new and arbitrary rule about ballot sealing. And now, it could cost them their vote.

item.title: At noon today, DOJ must reveal which states it pressured
item.author: 1axbwuejwrskfhlcmsabky17r6fy3l75ojcnab@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
item.content:encoded: Among DOJ’s objections was that the request covered communications from July 1 to the present. DOJ wanted to limit it to the last 30 days. That would have hidden what the agencies did in July, August and September.The question is why. What are they hiding? What threats have they made? What deals have they cut?I am not naive enough to think that one court order requiring an answer to one question will end Trump’s assault on free and fair elections. I know that even after this disclosure, much of this pressure campaign will remain secret.But it is an important step toward understanding the scope and scale of this scheme to corrupt the midterm vote count.Interestingly, in his order, Judge Boasberg offered DOJ and DHS a way out of answering this question, and out of the entire lawsuit. “Defendants may moot this process at any time,” he wrote, “by filing a notice indicating that they will not engage in the conduct sought to be enjoined in connection with the upcoming election.”In other words, if Trump and his cronies simply agree to stop threatening and coercing election officials and workers into not counting votes, the entire case will go away. Yet they will never accept this simple resolution.Trump wants the threats to continue. Indeed, he wants them to escalate. And they are escalating.According to The New York Times, DOJ has now served grand jury subpoenas on election workers in Los Angeles County, ordering them to appear with records on Nov. 4, the day after the election.The next step could well be search warrants and threats of indictment.We are in the midst of a constitutional crisis in which the federal government has weaponized itself against free and fair elections. It is using its vast array of tools and hiding the full extent of its actions from public view.We will have many more fights in the days and weeks ahead. I have no illusions about how hard this will be. A weaponized federal government is a dangerous adversary.But at noon today, at least part of that veil of secrecy will lift. We will learn which states DOJ and DHS have been pressuring in the dark, and I will share what we learn as soon as we can.We have to stand tall and fight back.

item.title: Sakura Tsuruta
item.author: Flow State
item.content:encoded: It’s Friday so we’re listening to something more upbeat. Today we’re listening to Sakura Tsuruta, a Japanese electronic musician from Tokyo. She studied classical piano growing up, and became interested in the therapeutic application of music in high school when her grandfather faced dementia. At Berklee College of Music she studied music therapy and electronic production; she thereafter worked at a hospice, using music in palliative care. That experience led her to start making music herself, in which she fuses her classical background and electronic production techniques. We’re starting with her 2024 LP, , a collection of eight tracks that combine driving bass lines, precise percussion, and melodic arpeggios and leads. We’re also playing her 2022 LP,

item.content:encoded: No big news or even original analysis in this post, just a general observation. I was just looking at the VoteHub Senate predictions. This is a relatively new entrant into the election modeling/forecasting world. They’re a bit more cautious than Nate Silver’s Silver Bulletin, seeing the most likely outcome as Democrats taking 52 seats versus 53. That’s probably actually technically the median result of running numerous modeling simulations. In any case, I was looking at the categories in which they place different races. For instance, they put Texas, as “Lean D”, so more likely to flip than Ohio, Maine and Iowa. I’m not sure that’s wrong. But it’s just wild to see.

item.title: Rest In Peace, Patrick Stewart (1940-2026)
item.author: Jason Kottke
item.content:encoded: He was largely considered an unknown when the “Star Trek” offer came along. At the invitation of a friend, a university professor, Mr. Stewart had been in Los Angeles conducting master classes on Shakespeare when, one evening, he gave a lecture and performed some bits of the plays in a program that was open to the public. A TV producer who was involved in developing a new “Star Trek” series happened to attend and soon persuaded Mr. Stewart to audition — even though, as Mr. Stewart later wrote, he knew “next to nothing” about the franchise.Surprised to get the part — the “Star Trek” creator, Gene Roddenberry, who was overseeing the new series, had not been keen to hire him at first — Mr. Stewart expected the project to be a short-term commitment. How, he remembered thinking, could the show possibly succeed with a middle-aged pacifist captain with a French name and a British accent?This is hard news to take, even though Stewart lived a full and fulfilling life. The Next Generation will always be my favorite Star Trek series and Picard my favorite captain. Stewart got off to a rough start on the series:So when he was on set shooting the show’s debut season and co-stars like Jonathan Frakes, Denise Crosby and Brent Spiner would tease him or ad-lib a joke or laugh when they flubbed their lines, it would low-key infuriate him.“I could be a severe bastard,” he writes. “My experiences at the Royal Shakespeare Company and the National Theatre had been intense and serious… On the TNG set, I grew angry with the conduct of my peers, and that’s when I called that meeting in which I lectured the cast for goofing off and responded to Denise Crosby’s, ‘We’ve got to have some fun sometimes, Patrick’ comment by saying, ‘We are not here, Denise, to have fun.’”“In retrospect,” Stewart continues, “everyone, me included, finds this story hilarious. But in the moment, when the cast erupted in hysterics at my pompous declaration, I didn’t handle it well. I didn’t enjoy being laughed at. I stormed off the set and into my trailer, slamming the door.”Q: There’s a passage where you say that, from your father, “I drew Picard’s stern, intimidating tendencies. But I like to think that my mother is in the captain too, in his moments of warmth and sensitivity.” Do you see Picard as your way of reconciling that conflict between your parents?A: Very much so, yes. Both Star Trek and therapy have been responsible for that. Having to open the doors into my childhood in order to be an actor became utterly intriguing to me in a way that it never had been before. And I regret that when I look back on some of the roles I played, what I might have brought to them if I just released myself a little bit more.

item.title: Second to none
item.author: bounce+2edd00.7bdc18-5mr68b7cb43ac2h04ai5=kill-the-newsletter.com@m.ghost.io
item.content:encoded: One Wisconsin man, waiting for a flight to Milwaukee, stood and gazed at the sign two gates away: Tampa. Another, splayed on the airport carpet, trying to wrangle his restless kids with an iPad showing the Packers game, said he had just come from there, had tried to rearrange his family’s schedule to stay for two, three more days. Because the Brewers, by then up 2-0 in the World Series, were on their way.This was in Nashville, Sunday afternoon. My wife and I were sitting at the gate in between, headed back to New York. All weekend, we had marveled at the preponderance of Brewers fans traipsing around town in jerseys, T-shirts, hats, talking about ticket prices and family members who ponied up, who skipped planned vacations to watch the franchise’s first World Series championship. In a city 564 miles from Milwaukee, everyone with any connection to Wisconsin was making sure to show it. And 725 miles from Tropicana Field, almost halfway there, they were thinking about Tampa, glancing toward it, itching to be there for their heroes’ increasingly imminent, some might say inevitable, coronation.When the moment arrived Wednesday night — the Brewers taking the game and the series over the Rays, 4-1 — thousands of fans in blue and yellow injected the road ballpark with the rapture of home. Thousands more were at American Family Field to jubilate together. The enthusiasm, the reach, of major-league baseball’s smallest city felt huge.The Brewers’ title was not sudden, not a surprise. It rode atop a swell of success that has been building since 2016, under David Stearns’ front office and then roaring on through Matt Arnold’s promotion from within. Eight postseason appearances, six division crowns, three NLCS appearances. An MVP, a Cy Young and another in the offing. Pride was there, with plenty of reason for it. But it was closely held, a targeted fire hose rather than a crashing wave, until this week.The impulse, mine and yours and the masses’, is to explain a newly observed phenomenon, to track that wave back to its origin. Their Triple-A affiliate is in Nashville, could that be … no the tie only dates to 2020. Were the Packers in town facing the Titans? Nope. Is this America’s team for dethroning the Dodgers? Are the 2026 Brewers the protagonists of a soaring sequel to Moneyball? Are they a blueprint being copied as they are celebrated?Is this how any team would feel on the cusp of its first championship? Is this what it looks like when the search for an explanation widens beyond logic, beyond words, and opens up into something that can only be described as an experience?The day it was agreed to back in December 2022, a three-way trade between the Braves, A’s and Brewers was called the Sean Murphy deal. The offshoot of the trade that redirected catcher William Contreras to the Brewers for speedster Esteury Ruiz was a noteworthy but secondary concern.History has perspective that headlines don’t. Last night, as Contreras hit, challenged and implored his way to World Series MVP honors, the Brewers forced the baseball world to look at them from a new angle. Because of money or media concentration or the happenstance of postseason results, the club with the most wins over the past three seasons has not been held in the regard that record would imply.Their championship and vengeful sweep of the Dodgers barrels the sport out of a particular type of tunnel vision. For years and years, as the postseason field expanded, “it was easy to see the playoffs as a crapshoot,” Matthew Trueblood wrote recently.“Then, Shohei Ohtani signed with the Dodgers and won it all twice in a row, and it was like the God particle had been discovered all over again,” Trueblood said. “That messy egalitarianism that seemed to have settled over the sport burned off like low-lying fog on an unseasonably warm autumn morning, and we all saw (or imagined, at least) the ugly truth: Only power matters; only money wins.”There was a time, not three years ago, when the Dodgers’ long run of excellence was still unvested. They were the best team in baseball, but that was valued on paper rather than in gold.Overnight, the Brewers have called for a new assessment. The season they just completed — 103 wins, with an 11-2 playoff mission completed against the best competition available — was second to none. In degree of dominance and difficulty, it compares favorably to every champ since the 2018 Red Sox. They are two regular season wins clear of the Dodgers in the very years of the supposed Ohtani dynasty, they have a World Series pennant headed to the rafters, a young team and booming farm system in tow.Is this Brewers team an underdog story with a happy ending or an adamant arrival of something else entirely?How, exactly, did you grow up? How did you fall in love? How did you get to where you are today? Do you really know? Was there a discrete, usable process involved? Or do you, in the grand tradition of the major religions, recount a singular story with the conviction of universal truth?The Brewers’ motto was everywhere in October: . But it’s a mantra, not an invitation. Milwaukee’s way lends itself to uncertainty. Under Stearns and Arnold, they have sustained winning teams on a middling ownership-imposed budgets by trading away a number of established stars (Corbin Burnes, Josh Hader, Devin Williams, Freddy Peralta) in favor of starter packs full of young, promising, unknown commodities. They fill out rosters by sifting for high-potential waiver claims and unheralded trade chips, not winning free agent bidding wars.In 2026, they wound up with three of the 30 most valuable players in baseball, and those players were 24 (Jacob Misiorowski), 26 (Brice Turang) and 22 (Jackson Chourio). Turang’s breakout last year was the only 4-WAR season among the group entering the spring. Two more 3-WAR hitters (Jake Bauers and Garrett Mitchell) had never even amassed 500 plate appearances in a single major-league season. The starting shortstop who batted .354 in the postseason (Cooper Pratt) had not yet glimpsed Triple-A.They gave rookie pitchers 80 starts, more than any other team in the sport. The oldest and least acclaimed of those arms, Robert Gasser, finished with the most starts and registered the best starting pitching performance of the World Series.Uncertainty, in such regular doses, is hard to distinguish from skepticism when viewed through a quantified lens.Over this decade-long ascent, the Brewers have persistently outfoxed wise and grounded projection systems. First, they did it under the professorial watch of Stearns and Craig Counsell. When Counsell took a larger contract for the rival Cubs, Arnold promoted Pat Murphy, grizzled motivator of men, the most football coach of baseball manager. He delights in the undershot projections, feeding them to his team like fuel to a fire.So many of them had felt like they were second-best, the second choice. And the ones who hadn’t? Well, Murphy made sure they would, as part of the collective unit that was less proven than the Dodgers, less appealing than the Cubs, less respected than they had earned.Projecting the Brewers to do all the things they did would have been malpractice. Not projecting all those things turned out to be wrong. Would you believe it if you didn’t see it?Belief is necessary. It’s the quotidian forward force, the gas in the combustion engine that carries you to work and the grocery store and back home again. Seeing, with thousands of others who waited and believed alongside you on the same warm nights, sitting in the same traffic, that’s transcendent. It’s the wind in your hair at sunset, driving 75 on a wide open highway. It's the thing you get up and start each day to reach.Throngs of Brewers fans took over Tropicana Field to see something bigger and less nebulous than overachievement. Like the outfield fences, the walls of collective understanding are arbitrarily drawn. Winning the World Series isn’t necessarily harder than winning 103 games or winning the division every year, but getting over that wall means something different. It’s a license for collective joy.It gets Christian Yelich jerseys packed in suitcases and Chourio jerseys purchased a size bigger than the kids need right now. It gets plane tickets booked and tattoos designed. It moves broadcasters and Cy Young winners to tears.No explanation is needed. ⚾️Jacob Misiorowski has found a perfect match. The woman who gave the broadcast a fantastic GIF-able facial expression …In addition to being the most football coach of baseball managers, Pat Murphy is the obvious choice for a hypothetical Reporters’ Favorite award.He even threw in an intentional mispronunciation of social media quip, which has a 100% chance of being quoted. “I’m not on social media, Twizzler or Instacart, whatever,” the AP has Murphy saying.I’m not accusing anyone of bias. I’m just noting the reality that Murphy is both constitutionally and topically perfect for the baseball media.Contreras’ older brother Willson, who has been openly affected by the hardship in their native country, was on hand wearing his brother’s jersey and tearfully celebrating with him on the field afterward.Joe Davis, the lead FOX play-by-play announcer, specializes in echos of baseball broadcasts past.When the Rays eventually came back to win in 12, he joined the linage of his predecessor, Joe Buck (who was adapting his own father’s call), when he yelled, “We’ll see you later tonight,” over the post-midnight walk-off knock.Davis’ flair for the cleverly deployed reference sometimes overshadows his original work, which tends toward the strong but subtle. But this is another area where time will crystallize the potency of the work. Last year, he punctuated the Dodgers’ epic Game 7 win with one I could see sticking for the ages: “To beat the champ, you gotta knock ‘em out.”“Unshakeable, unstoppable, and champions at last: The Milwaukee Brewers.”The part where I ask for your supportThis is a project by and for the passionate. It’s undertaken on mornings, nights and weekends. On trains and planes and holidays. Around the responsibilities of a full-time job.I recognize the building subscription creep, the proliferation of good writers operating independently and charging independently in an unforgiving industry. I don’t expect The Bandwagon to be your only destination for baseball writing, but I hope it makes your emotional investment more enriching.

item.title: Atlanta Took Golden State’s Lunch Money
item.author: Maitreyi Anantharaman
item.content:encoded: Five games into the Finals, it felt odd that we’d yet to watch the game where one team makes everything. The Atlanta Dream and Golden State Valkyries do both take great pride in their defenses, and their offenses do each have certain limitations. Golden State’s heavy diet of threes, for instance, leaves them prone to variance. But that means, you know, that the shooting numbers should vary—not be resolutely bad for two weeks.After Game 2, when the sludge of Game 1 appeared to carry over and the Dream tied the series, a reporter asked Valkyries head coach Natalie Nakase why she thought it had been such a struggle for these teams to score. Nakase didn’t take the question too seriously. “What’s our identity?” she said, panning the room, the impatient teacher in front of her class. “What? You guys should know this.”Two of the league’s top defenses, sure. Even so, the numbers were bad. The reporter pressed Nakase again.

item.title: Star Wars: The Radio Drama
item.author: Jason Kottke
item.content:encoded: Somehow I’d never heard of this before: NPR produced and aired radio dramatizations of the films in the original Star Wars trilogy. The first program was particularly popular, garnering NPR hundreds of thousands of new listeners. The original versions are available in full on The Internet Archive:All three programs contain elements of John Williams’ original soundtrack. Mark Hamill and Anthony Daniels reprised their movie roles for the first two radio programs and some other bold-faced names made appearances throughout: Billy Dee Williams as Lando Calrissian, John Lithgow as Yoda (??), Ed Begley Jr. as Boba Fett (???), David Alan Grier as a nameless X-wing fighter pilot, and Nia Vardalos.The radio programs were based on the original film scripts with some added scenes; from Open Culture:With science-fiction novelist Brian Daley brought on to add or restore scenes to the script of the original dialogue-light feature film, the story stretches out to thirteen episodes for a total runtime of six hours. The series thus stands as an early example of the expansion of the Star Wars universe that, in all kinds of media, has continued apace ever since.Daley adapted the script partly using material from earlier drafts of Lucas’s scripts, and restored several scenes cut from the final edit of the film, as well as adding original new scenes created specially for the audio version. The narrative of the first two episodes takes place entirely before the opening scene of the 1977 film, and expands the background to events leading up to the capture of the Tantive IV spacecraft above the planet Tatooine. Episode 1, largely based on cut scenes from the original, explores the life of Luke Skywalker on Tatooine. During the story, Luke’s skyhopper (a vehicle seen in the background in Luke’s garage during the film) is damaged during a desert race; Luke sees the distant Star Destroyer battle in the sky; and he is reunited with his childhood friend, Biggs Darklighter. Episode 2, made up of material written entirely by Daley, provides backstory to Princess Leia’s acquisition of the Death Star plans from agents of the Rebel Alliance on the planet Toprawa. In scenes set on the planet Alderaan, Leia discusses the plans with her father, Prestor Organa, and determines to go in search of Obi-Wan Kenobi.These versions, boldly called The Definitive Editions (Hope, Empire, Jedi), include opening scrolls and images taken from Star Wars comic books and trading cards:Yes, that’s a script turned into a movie turned into an audio drama turned into a, uh, quasi-cinematic Powerpoint? (via open culture)

item.title: Massive Fanfic Site Archive of Our Own Says It’s Going Down for 'Up to 4 Weeks'
item.author: Samantha Cole
item.content:encoded: Archive of Our Own (AO3), a massive repository for fanfiction and creative writing, might be down for as long as a month after going down for "maintenance" on Thursday.The Organization for Transformative Works (OTW), the non-profit organization that runs AO3, posted on its status page early Thursday morning that the site was down for maintenance. A few hours later, it updated the status to say that it was expected to take at least 12 hours. By Thursday afternoon, it said the site restoration will take around two weeks, but could take up to a month.“We are hopeful that we will be able to bring the site back up in a degraded state sooner. If that does happen, there may be times when the site has to be brought down temporarily until this is fully resolved. Please stay tuned for further info,” OTW wrote. A spokesperson for OTW told 404 Media Thursday night that there are no more updates at this time beyond what's on the status page. They did, however, say that they don't expect there to be data loss. Early Friday morning, OTW added an update to the status page: "First, no AO3 data has been deleted. All your works, bookmarks, kudos, etc., are safe," it says. "Second, while we currently don't believe that the user database was stolen, we are also unable to rule it out. The AO3 database contains account information that may include your username, email address, IP address, and a hashed version of your password." They say they use hashing techniques to protect password data, but recommend users change their passwords on any other sites where they use the same password as on AO3, as a precaution.It’s difficult to overstate the importance of AO3 to fan culture, fanfiction writers and readers, and its influence on internet culture in general. As of September, the open-source fanfic repository hosted over 18.4 million works spanning over 82,900 fandoms. This status update means AO3 is expected to be down during much of , most of new book release week, and on the cusp of the month formerly known as NaNoWriMo. If you were going as Ebony Dark'ness Dementia Raven Way for Halloween, you are in our thoughts. And if you have something to share about AO3’s extended shutdown and how it will affect the fanfic community, I'd love to hear from you: sam@404media.co.Updated to add OTW comment and Friday morning's status page update.

item.title: Ban The Headset Radio
item.author: Drew Magary
item.content:encoded: Drew Magary’s Thursday Afternoon NFL Dick Joke Jamboroo runs every Thursday at Defector during the NFL season. Got something you wanna contribute? . You can also read Drew over atIn case you missed it a week ago, The Athletic published this extremely detailedreport from Jourdan Rodrigue and Mike Sando on how NFL game-day communications work. I encourage you to read the entire thing in full, because it includes a lot of sweet tea, including stories about head coaches angrily firing their assistants over the headset (then changing their minds the next day) and, dearer to my heart, one assistant coach staying on the channel while he had to take a frantic piss. My kindred spirit.As with all things NFL, these communication systems are coordinated with near-military fuss. The graphic design in the story includes multiple ornate diagrams that outline how all of this shit works. We see how dozens of coaches on the sideline are talking with one another, on the field and up in the booth, during a game. We also see all of the tech crew workers behind the bench, wearing different-colored hats to signify which of them are in charge of keeping the radio channels private, which ones service the Microsoft tablets that players love to angrily smash on the ground, and such and such. All of these people are connected by a series of invisible lines so tangled, it looks like an old-timey phone switchboard when laid out on paper.

item.title: The election chaos is about to play out in three scary phases.
item.author: delivery_20261029100502.48141097.4768@bounce.slate.com
item.content:encoded:
The midterm elections are now underway across the country and as voters decide who should hold the levers of power in Washington, all eyes are on President Donald Trump. He’s spent the last decade baselessly questioning the integrity of U.S. elections—despite plenty of evidence finding they are safe and secure—with things coming to a violent head on Jan. 6, 2021. This year, as more and more polling is suggesting Democrats will sweep Republicans, even in solidly red districts, it raises the question: Will the president accept the results of critical House and Senate races, or won’t he? “I will, if they’re honest elections,” Trump ominously responded when asked this very question on Tuesday.
Since Trump began his second term, he’s been laying the groundwork to try to nationalize U.S. elections and go after “voter fraud” through executive action and lawsuits against states, though most of these efforts have been struck down in court. Yet, the Justice Department has not given up. In fact, in recent weeks the agency filed at least two more dubious election lawsuits against California and Alaska, plus a series of cases against immigrants for alleged noncitizen voting. The legal challenges suggest the administration is planning ahead this time around, planting lawsuits that might create a foothold in the courts for the GOP to seize on if the midterms don’t end up going their way.
To Charles Stewart III, a political scientist and professor at MIT who has spent decades studying American congressional politics, elections, and political development, the current situation created by Trump is a test of America’s democracy. “Not primarily because of fundamental shortcomings in American election administration, but because political actors associated with the Administration will attempt to delegitimize or overturn its work,” he wrote in a newly published paper, “The Day After: Threats and Guardrails in the 2026 Election.”
Stewart believes that Trump’s efforts to thwart this year’s midterms should be viewed in three distinct phases: Before Election Day, during the vote counting and certification process, and when the new Congress convenes on Jan. 3, 2027. In practice, this looks like Trump beginning to seed baseless claims that losing Republicans can make after Election Day: mail ballots are suspect, voter rolls are contaminated with noncitizens, slow ballot counts are evidence of fraud, and any Democratic victories in close races shouldn’t be accepted. After Election Day, the lawsuits begin, harkening back to the days and weeks following Trump’s 2020 loss to Joe Biden, and finally things might culminate at the Capitol, where lawmakers could be pressured not to certify election winners. I spoke with Stewart to understand how this framework can help us see important red flags in the hours immediately following Election Day, plus the chances that Trump incites yet another angry mob to take over the Capitol. And is there silver lining to hold on to? Here’s our conversation, lightly edited and condensed for clarity.Shirin Ali: In your paper, you drill down on the president’s efforts to undermine the midterms into three flashpoints: Before Election Day, during the vote counting and certification process, and when the new Congress convenes. Can you explain what each of these are? The ideas behind those flashpoints come from what we've seen the Trump administration working on in the second term: two executive orders, activities at the Justice Department and Homeland Security, actions that are beginning to nibble around the edges of the election administration process. Particularly before Election Day, putting pressures on mail voting, highlighted by the executive order from this past March that basically directed the U.S. Postal Service to create a new series of procedures for handling mail voting, marrying that together with directives to DHS to create these lists of citizens.
The second flashpoint has to do with pressures on election administration, especially election administrators and the institutions themselves. There, I think the pressures go beyond even what the administration has been doing. Certainly, a lot of the activity of the administration has been focused on the possibility that if election officials don't do what the administration wants, they will not only bring civil complaints against them, but they may very well bring criminal complaints against them. Then after Election Day, that's where we're thinking about getting the final count in. We shift into the formal process of canvassing the vote, certifying it, and making sure that we've named the winners. I'm thinking broadly about a potential replay of what happened after the 2020 election, where the Trump campaign lodged a number of lawsuits in battleground states like Wisconsin and Pennsylvania. I'm still anticipating, even more now, that coming true.
The final flashpoint is what happens when the 120th Congress convenes on Jan. 3, 2027, particularly the House. And there the question is whether there will be efforts to bar the seating of senators or members of the House who've been elected, specifically Democrats who would be the pivotal members of the two chambers that would flip control of the chamber to the Democrats. There's another obvious parallel with 2020, when there were efforts to deny the certification of the presidential election. How do the Justice Department’s lawsuits against California and Alaska fit into this? Those are kind of jumping the gun on the timeline that I had suspected, because they're really almost preempting post-election challenges and making them pre-election challenges. About a week ago I was saying, “Well, they've filed this lawsuit against California, it’s getting kind of close to the election. If there's just California, it's kind of a weak rule in terms of applying formal pressure on the states.” Then came Alaska, and this one makes me wonder what else the DOJ is going to do in the next week to bring early lawsuits against states and kind of do a shot across the bow.
The California lawsuit is the sort of thing that we that we've long expected the Trump administration to do, and in fact in the first administration, there were rumors that they were trying to put together a national voter database and merge it with immigration records to begin to go after states for having noncitizens on the rolls. This has been a long dream of the administration and people associated with the administration, and it's taken them basically a decade in order to act on it. It doesn't look like they've done a particularly sophisticated job, both in terms of the actual job of database matching or on the legal side.
The Alaska case seems to be the most frivolous election challenge that I can imagine, and in fact it's kind of orthogonal. It's unrelated to the things I had anticipated, because the lawsuit they're bringing is the sort of lawsuit that you would expect a candidate to bring. Really, it's up to Sen. Sullivan to bring these challenges under Alaska law and then potentially to bring a contest to the U.S. Senate. I only have to believe that the Alaska case is the classic case of pleasing an audience of one; Donald Trump wanted it and he got it. There's just no way in the world this is going to go forward. It's sort of like going after James Comey or going after the members of Congress who reminded service members they didn't have to follow illegal orders. It's really performative, to please the boss, and hard to take seriously, except the degree to which it's predictive of what we're likely to see after the election: the federal government putting the thumb on the scales of candidate-oriented post-election litigation. Next week, immediately after Election Day is over, what are you going to be watching for? I think there will be two things. One will be legitimate, and the other will be illegitimate. The legitimate thing is that we may very well see more losing candidates contest their elections and begin taking legal actions to try to save evidence, within the normal contest laws. Some of it may very well be performative to garner support from the administration or local political actors, but those are the ill-fated sorts of things that there's a legal framework for doing. Plus there's a legal framework for judges throwing these cases out, right? And that's the way it should happen.
What I think we need to be prepared for, and I don't think it's going to be widespread, are candidates supported by the administration going into court to attempt to impound voting machines and ballots and to remove them from where they're normally housed. Basically, a repeat of the Fulton County event a year ago where the FBI removed ballots. Those are the things I think we should anticipate, and I think that the Department of Justice may very well take matters into their own hands that are quasi-independent of the candidates themselves. For instance, the Alaska lawsuit was just something that the DOJ did because the president wanted it. That’s a disturbing thing that I think we need to be prepared for after the election because we've already seen it happen before the election. That is the DOJ just going into places they don't like and filing lawsuits. In your paper, you wrote, “The greatest danger is not that even a few challenges will succeed; it is that a small number of delayed certifications could matter greatly if control of either chamber is in doubt.” What did you mean by that? If you think about Jan. 6, 2021, in Congress and leading up to that, there was a whole lot of noise in the political system about whether the vice president could refuse to accept electors and whether Congress could impose their own view on what state electors they should accept, and all those sorts of things. In retrospect, traditional constitutional election lawyers had it right all along in terms of the law. The correct person was elected president, but the political ramifications of that whole episode and Jan. 6 itself were just catastrophic for American politics and certainly transformative in many ways. The law held, the right guy was elected president, but antidemocratic elements were energized and we had a riot at the Capitol.
A social movement has arisen in the country that makes millions of dollars based on stoking a view that elections in America are illegitimate. It's an extreme view, and a minority view even within the Republican Party at that level of extremity, but it's really been politically consequential over the last six years. I think we could be in an Act 2 of that, and that's what I'm getting at here. Imagine that this was a decade ago and we're coming into a Congress where the Democrats were going to take over the chamber and have about a 20-seat lead. You wouldn't have imagined anything major to come out of any contest, any seat. There might have been a couple of contests and it might have been highly politicized, but they would have been handled in the regular order.
Imagine right now if Democrats have that same margin of success. I think we have to assume there will be at least a few members of the House on the Republican side who will make a lot of hay around refusing their being seated, refusing to allow them to vote for the speaker, pressuring the clerk not to accept their certificates of election, those sorts of things. All of those would be illegitimate. The rules of the House are very clear about the clerk of the House accepting the properly given certificates of election for members of the House for the purpose of the roll-call vote at the beginning and electing the speaker. There is a very prescribed way of handling contests in the House of Representatives, and there is no legitimate, legal way for the current Congress to be the judge of those elections.
Now, one of the things I think will stoke the political fires, though, is the investigations into any contest that any member would want to bring in the 119th Congress. There will be pressures in the current Congress for House Speaker Mike Johnson to highly politicize those investigations, use them as opportunities to shine a spotlight on California and other states that are not cooperating with the administration over noncitizens on the rolls, for instance. Or on states with high levels of mail voting. It's going to unleash this political theater in hopes of blowing up regular procedures that are very clear, much more clear than the Electoral Count Act was in 2020, into something that looks like a rejection of this election. And the closer it is, the higher the stakes and the higher the temperature. Despite having serious concerns about what the Trump administration will do in the event Republicans lose control of Congress, you’re optimistic that the 2026 midterms will be resilient enough to withstand a Trump bashing. Why? It starts with the decentralized nature of election administration. When I've been asked about whether the Trump administration is going to be successful in overthrowing this election, I've generally responded with two words: —they've not been very good at what they've done; and there are just not enough lawyers left in the Department of Justice, or enough immigration agents, there's not enough of anything to take over the American electoral system. If it's a matter of mobilizing the federal government, there are more local election officials running elections than there's the capacity of the Trump administration to go after enough of them. That’s decentralization.
The second thing is that we continue to see evidence that the facts-based institutions of our electoral system continue to hold. That includes state and local election officials who are nothing if not careful about following the law. And there are the county boards of elections; we've seen general election boards stand by the canvassed results. There have been several states that have passed laws over the last few years reinforcing the notion that the certifications of elections at the local level are ministerial and that the proper place for conducting contests, if something is seen to be amiss, is in the court system, not in the election boards. Finally, I think we continue to see the courts holding to what the law is, holding to the precedents that have been established in the past about what do you do when someone contests the results of an election. There's established law there, and trial courts have, on the whole, held, and when they haven't, they've been admonished or overturned on appeal. It would be nice if we didn't have to say, “Well, at the end of the day, we're relying on the Alaska Supreme Court.” It would be much better if it didn't have to get that far, but we do still have a robust and independent judiciary that has been willing to stand up to nonsense.
