item.title: Building a multiplayer game world with autonomous Fable-class models
item.author: Simon Willison
item.content:encoded: Don't be put off by the clickbait headline, this piece by Jacob Sansbury describing how they are building Spawn is a fascinating exploration of the bleeding edge of what's possible with agentic engineering against frontier models.Spawn is a massively multiplayer gaming environment where players can use prompts (to the in-game agent, Savi) to modify the game world.I fired it up on my phone for a few minutes and was able to prompt a castle into existence, then a dragon, then ride the dragon to fly around that castle.By Jacob's telling, Spawn is now being developed autonomously by a swarm of Fable-powered agents costing over $3 million in tokens ("we spend 30x payroll on AI tokens").Our agents change the live code directly and ship to production hourly, so they read every error, bug report and metric themselves. About 60% of our work starts from a production error, a Savi bug report (Savi is the AI you build games with in Spawn), something odd in our logs, or a feature request.Savi files bugs herself. When a user hits one, or Savi hits one in the product, she files it. It goes straight to an agent that decides whether it's a real bug to fix, something we won't fix, or intentional design that needs a decision. Usually it becomes a change, delivered to that user within an hour, with a message in the same chat.A loop this tight only works if it never stops, so we treat an hour without a ship as a SEV-0, our most severe kind of incident. Unshipped changes pile up, and every problem already in production lasts longer. The feedback slows down too. An agent can only keep a few hours of work in its head, so shipping faster than that actually helps it stay coherent. [...]We can roll back a broken change in 30 seconds, exactly where it's broken and nowhere else. When a monitor or a log alert fires, it starts or wakes an agent that owns the incident, and we break things on purpose to test that those recovery paths work.My eyebrows raised at least a dozen times reading this. I have trouble imagining this style of development working on software with higher stakes for when something goes wrong, but for a game this appears to be working surprisingly well.Jacob says that Fable 5 (and then 5.1) was the model that made this level of autonomy possible. Opus 5.5 doesn't quite hack it for them, and when they tried GPT-6 Astra to apply fixes from a security review everything stopped working:Every feature had been disabled and marked to be turned on again once the security fixes were done. Astra had gone through our whole product and made the insecure things secure by turning them off.These kinds of extreme experiments are why I'm excited about game development as a substrate for exploring the edges of what today's coding agents can do.

item.title: Skye Blakely Ushers In The Next Era Of USA Gymnastics With Gold
item.author: Diana Moskovitz
item.content:encoded: My favorite moment from this year's World Gymnastics Championships was the second after Skye Blakely hit the final pose in her floor routine. For a second, she was all smiles, sass, and confidence, radiating exactly the energy her sport's judges want to see. Then the music ended, Blakely's muscles released, and the 21-year-old from Texas looked like she might cry. The performance was done and Blakely could once again be exactly who she was: a young woman who had just done something very difficult.That routine capped Blakely's first all-around gold medal, which was one of four medals Blakely brought home this week from the Netherlands—her gold joined a Team USA silver, as well as individual bronzes for herself on uneven bars and vault. A pair of Americans—Claire Pease and Reese Esponda—took individual gold and silver on the floor, respectively, in Rotterdam, while Pease also won silver on vault. On the men's side, Fred Richard won gold on the men's floor, making him the country's first gold medalist on that exercise since Paul Hamm in 2003.In other words, even if Simone Biles doesn't come back for the 2028 Olympic Games, women's gymnastics seems to be in good shape. In fact, Blakely's win meant the United States went a whopping without being home to the reigning women's all-around champion, as Biles had previously won the title in 2023 (at Worlds) and 2024 (the Paris Olympics). Even that requires an asterisk because at last year's Worlds, American Leanne Wong took home the all-around silver.

item.title: Don’t Follow the Early Vote! Except For This
item.author: Josh Marshall
item.source: Josh Marshall – TPM – Talking Points Memo
item.content:encoded: I jest, a bit, in the title. As I’ve told you several times, friends don’t let friends watch the early vote. But there’s one thing I want to point your attention to. I’ll explain in a moment why this leaves me mainly consistent. There’s one thing that seems to be showing up fairly consistently across the country and particularly in the Deep South. That is a high proportion of generally younger, non-regular Democratic voters. And they tend to be less white, relative to the rest of the electorate. In a number of Deep South states you’re seeing high turnout for non-regular Democratic voters which in states like Mississippi for instance means mostly Black voters.

item.title: Trump Is on an Absurd Collision Course With Yet Another Federal Judge
item.author: David Kurtz
item.content:encoded: Trump DOJ’s No. 3 Official in the Hot SeatA golf course in D.C. is the improbable venue for another significant Trump II showdown between the executive and judicial branches.Unlike, say, the Alien Enemies Act, Abrego Garcia, and immigrant habeas cases, where the actions that precipitated the conflict between the Trump administration and federal judges were unmistakably serious deprivations of liberty, the East Potomac Golf Course case has layers of absurdism, which we’ll get into below.My main reason for catching you up on this second-tier constitutional confrontation is to preview an important hearing in the case tomorrow, so that I can come back to this later without burdening you with a whole bunch of backstory.U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes had already ordered the Trump DOJ to show cause by yesterday why it should not be ordered to preserve all records in the case in what could only be interpreted as a prelude to her considering sanctions against government lawyers for allegedly misleading her. Reyes was particularly focused on the Trump DOJ’s failure to comply with her orders to provide sufficient notice of the surprise removal of hundreds of trees on the golf course over the Columbus Day weekend.But now Judge Reyes has a new bone to pick with the Trump DOJ.Judge Reyes has suspected that the mass tree removal over the holiday weekend was part of Trump’s plan to remake the historic golf course without congressional approval — but the administration and DOJ lawyers have denied it, repeatedly and emphatically.Then on Tuesday, on her own, Judge Reyes took judicial notice of a new Truth Social post by President Trump, in which he declared that the golf course will be closing on Nov. 15, and demanded to know why the Trump DOJ had previously told her otherwise:Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward told the Court on October 19 that “[w]ith regard to the November 15th date… there is no plan to close the course.” The Court ORDERS Defendants to clarify, as part of their response to the Court’s show-cause order from October 26, whether any plan exists to close East Potomac Golf Course on or around November 15, 2026. And, if so, how that can be reconciled with Associate AG Woodward’s representation to the Court.In her order, Reyes also scheduled a “status hearing” for Friday and ordered Woodward — who represented Trump’s co-defendants in the Mar-a-Lago case and Jan. 6 rioters — to appear at the hearing in person. The DOJ’s No. 3 personally handling cases is unheard of, let alone doing the president’s dirty work. Getting hauled into court for allegedly misleading a judge is beyond next level stuff.Yesterday, in his response to the court order, Woodward conceded that there is a plan to close the golf course, but he did not reconcile his prior statements to the contrary:The undersigned acknowledges the President has twice directed Interior and the National Park Service to close the park by November 15. Accordingly, Interior, acting through counsel, is working to develop a plan to implement that direction and will provide this Court with notice pursuant to the Court’s October 26, 2026, Order.That prompted another stern order from Judge Reyes ahead of tomorrow’s hearing, which she has now recast as a show cause hearing that is quite a bit broader than merely whether the Trump DOJ must preserve documents in the case:The Court ORDERS the Government to come prepared to state at the hearing: (1) whether it continues to maintain that there is no final agency action; (2) the dates and times at which President Trump “twice directed Interior and the National Park Service to close the park by November 15”; … and (3) the first date “Interior, acting through counsel” began “working to develop a plan to implement that direction,” id. Associate Attorney General Woodward remains ORDERED to appear at the hearing in person. The Court FURTHER ORDERS the attendance of at least one counsel from the Department of the Interior’s Office of the Solicitor with pre-existing experience on this case.Shortly thereafter, Woodward provided the court-required detailed notice of the administration’s plan to shut down the vast majority of East Potomac Park, including the golf course, even though the renovation plan at issue will not have been approved yet on the administration’s own timetable.The ostensible reason for closing the golf course before getting approval for the renovation is familiar: “significant safety hazards.” It’s similar to the pretext offered for the separate closure of the Kennedy Center, another D.C. public asset that Trump has tried to turn into a personal project. In this case, the public safety hazard is an allegedly “deteriorated sea wall that is currently crumbling into the Potomac River.”All of this is to tee up tomorrow’s show cause hearing for you. It’s admittedly an odd sideshow in the last week before Election Day. But it wouldn’t be Trump lawlessness without a heaping dose of absurdity.Trump DOJ Election Interference Watch: U.S. District Judge David O. Carter late yesterday rejected the Trump DOJ’s request to force Los Angeles County to segregate and not yet count mail-in ballots from alleged noncitizen voters. In a stirring opinion, Judge Carter repeatedly blasted the Trump administration’s interference in California’s election:Never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own Constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the Executive Branch. In bringing this lawsuit, the Executive would have this Court believe that it reigns as a sole sovereign. But California and its people are sovereign, too.: The Trump DOJ seized on a NYT investigation that tied the campaign of Mary Peltola to a scheme to add a second Dan Sullivan to the ballot. In a new filing by DOJ No. 3 official Stan Woodward, he withdrew his prior opposition to the Peltola campaign and the DSCC intervening in the DOJ lawsuit to block certification of the Senate election. Instead, Woodward said DOJ would use expedited discovery in the case to investigate the alleged “sprawling conspiracy to recruit and prop up a sham candidate for the purpose of deceiving Alaskan voters” and whether the Peltola campaign “attempted to deceive” the court. UCLA election law expert Rick Hasen assesses the legal implications of this whole mess.: Secretary of State Steve Hobbs told the Trump DOJ that its purported list of 400 alleged noncitizen voters contained actual U.S. citizens. In a letter, Hobbs said it would “irresponsible and illegal” to segregate and not yet count mail-in ballots from voters on the Trump DOJ list.SPLC Reveals Its Theory of the Case Against ItThe Southern Poverty Law Center has revealed in a new filing its theory of how the vindictive prosecution of it by the Trump administration came to be.The civil rights group alleges that the Trump DOJ — which has zeroed in on the SPLC’s former program of using white supremacists as paid informants against other white supremacists — was able to flip the SPLC’s own longest-tenured informant into a government informant against the SPLC because he had failed to pay income taxes for 30 years.The SPLC alleges that the flipped informant practically became a member of the prosecution team, with numerous meetings and 1,800 text messages between him and investigators over the last year. Identified in the filing as “F-9,” the informant also provided documents, reports, and four so-called “Intelligence Briefings” to investigators, the SPLC alleges:To be clear, F-9 should have been merely a in this case. But the government has treated him like part of the prosecutorial team itself, choosing to allow F-9 to decide which of the documents, recordings, and photographs in his possession he will produce, and how and when he will produce them. F-9 admitted that he has a “house full of documents,” some of which he has referenced plans to “shred.”The immediate purpose of the SPLC’s new filing was to obtain permission to subpoena the informant and obtain a court order for the informant to preserve the materials in his possession.Quote of the Day: Transformers Edition“The Arch is a generational national defense opportunity to mitigate these evolving threats. It will be utilized as a dual-purpose structure: a major national monument that also incorporates military utility to support Homeland defense.”—

item.title: The Rays Never Played A Home Game In The World Series
item.author: Ray Ratto
item.content:encoded: The Tampa Bay Rays have been dogged in their pursuit of excellence without extravagance, a process that is now two decades along and which has been hugely successful, provided your wall calendar is missing the months of October and November. They have mastered the technique of buying low, selling at an advantageous price, then rebuilding by buying low again so fully that they have convinced many of the league's other owners that theirs is the one true path. They have beaten baseball's mythical salary cap by staying below whatever it would be through simple discipline—as in, refusal to pay market-rate big-league salaries—and industry-leading player development. Good for them; they win a lot of ballgames most summers, and the owners meeting every winter. The ring for that must be enormous.But the Rays received a harsh education in this World Series, and not merely by being eradicated in five games by the Milwaukee Brewers. Other than the 12th inning of Game 4, the Rays left no footprint on the series; in every inning played before midnight in the Eastern Time Zone, they were the inferior team. They were overwhelmed by the Brewers' superior bullpen, the off-brand heroism of Cooper Pratt and Sal Frelick, and the more predictable heroism of William Contreras and Jackson Chourio. The difference between the best team in baseball and the best team in the American League was exactly as advertised.That's not the problem the Rays face today, though. There is little shame in losing as they did, because the Brewers were the better team when the series began as well as when it ended. Someone finishes second every year. We know this. We checked.

item.title: The Remarkable Serbian Election
item.author: Jason Kottke
item.content:encoded: I’ve been reading a bit about the recent election in Serbia and some of the details are fascinating. A student-led coalition toppled the 12-year corrupt reign of “the increasingly authoritarian leader” Aleksandar Vučić in recent elections. But in order to ensure voters and allies that this wasn’t a grab for power on the part of the students, the students ruled themselves out.Supporters had the votes, but they needed the losing side to stay. The strict rules were a promise: to those who had opposed running, that it would not turn the movement into a party; to voters, that the list was no party in disguise.No student may run: anyone enrolled in 2024/25, or with studies on hold, is excluded. The drafters wanted no suggestion that students were building political careers. Former members of the ruling coalition’s 20 parties are barred, and so are former officials of parliamentary opposition parties. That leaves doctors, academics, artists, former athletes and activists. Ordinary members of opposition parties were not barred, but almost none with a party past. The list is led by Ilija Srdanović, a cardiologist and professor in Novi Sad.The students’ list of 250 candidates is remarkable in itself. Comprising professors, scientists, doctors, workers, actors and activists, the candidates — most of whom had been unknown to the public — were selected through a lengthy sequence of scrutiny and interviews. University faculties proposed candidates, then reviewed nominees from across the country. After discussing the options, student assemblies made their choices. Thousands participated in this decision-making process — an extraordinary experiment in bringing direct democracy into mainstream politics.The established opposition, meanwhile, has been pushed aside, with many of its parties backing the student list. The student movement has turned the election into something like a referendum on the regime, captured in its slogan: “Serbia or the mafia.” Many assumed the students were too inexperienced or naïve for electoral politics. But with some polls putting support for the student list above 40 percent, the race appears to be tight.The students are coming for the machine. And, astonishingly, they might win.Super interesting, right? US electoral politics don’t work the same as Serbia’s, but I wonder if there’s a way to inject some aspect of the Student List into US elections?

item.title: Mahmoud Khalil On His Time In ICE Detention And The Existential Threat Facing Higher Education
item.author: Sarah Borus
item.content:encoded: I remember the pit in my stomach as I woke up to the texts telling me that Mahmoud Khalil had been kidnapped. I remember the terrifying 48 hours when we had no idea where he had been taken—just that the President wanted to make an example out of him. I remember crying on the phone to my dad, telling him I had lost all hope. It was difficult to relive, and in preparing for this interview, I wanted to do Mahmoud justice.Mahmoud was central to the community of activists at Columbia University. He was the person we looked to for calm and guidance in the midst of upheaval. When he was taken, we all felt his absence. We were mostly kids. We struggled not just with the question of how to push back against the intensity of encroaching fascism and the weight of the federal government's crackdown on free speech, but how to do so without Mahmoud. He knew the university rulebook front and back. He knew all of the administrators and had a friendly rapport with them (or so we thought). He would calm us down when it felt like everything was falling apart. All of a sudden, he was thousands of miles away at a detention center known for inadequate medical care, unsafe food and living conditions, and abusive tactics by guards. And we remained inside the gates of the place that had allowed it to happen, as the retired Homeland Security Secretary, former IDF intelligence officer, and war profiteers who made up the administration and board of trustees wrung their hands and told us they were powerless. Mahmoud’s book is a devastating and essential story of his time in ICE detention, his childhood in Syria, and his experience as a negotiator at Columbia. In typical Mahmoud fashion, he insists that there are people far braver than him, who have made more sacrifices than him. He wants you to know the stories of the men he was detained with. They too were separated from their families and held without any charge.

item.title: Finally, A Good Book About Men
item.author: Grace Byron
item.content:encoded: The past few months, I have experienced multiple male cab drivers trying to get my phone number to take me out on a date. One even stopped his car a few blocks away from my apartment. I have also had men yell "Nice tits" and make obscene gestures at me while driving away. I got a boob job a few years ago, so you could say I was asking for it, but the sheer volume of men who corner me in public would suggest that it’s more than an isolated incident. This kind of harassment is ubiquitous. Still, I love men. I would like them to do better because I do often enjoy their company. I know I have previously panned many books on reforming the coarser sex—you could say we are living in a crisis of bad books about the masculinity crisis. Thankfully, Jon Ronson's is a thoughtful, empathetic work of narrative journalism. His prose is rigorous. No adverb or adjective is wasted. Ronson is a sort of literary Louis Theroux, interested in the ideas and people at the fringes of society. He's explored a number of conspiracy theories, hosted multiple podcasts and radio shows, and wrote a book on cancellation and stigma called So You've Been Publicly Shamed. In , he follows two primary narrative strands: a man who is trying to lure women to his fortress in rural Connecticut, and a man who was shamed online for making video content that involved his kids. Through these stories, he wonders what a more positive version of masculinity could look like for future generations. He is neither proscriptive nor apolitical when considering the lonely destructive capacity of men without an outlet.

item.title: Manifestos, Fear, and ‘Loser Thinking’: Inside Proton’s AI Reckoning
item.author: Joseph Cox
item.content:encoded: Andy Yen, the CEO of Proton, had a message for an employee in the company’s security Slack channel who urged the company to at least take a few days to pentest newly written code before pushing it live. “That’s bullshit and loser thinking. Of course it’s possible to be fast and secure,” Yen wrote in the channel at the end of August. “Stop thinking always of how to be slower, and focus more on how to be faster.”In a follow-up message, Yen reiterated his point: “only losers think like that.” His ultimate message for the team was to “stop lovingly handcrafting all our code and use AI more.”That exchange was just one of many that showed how Yen and other company executives are aggressively pushing Proton towards AI. Proton is a Swiss company that famously makes the encrypted email service Proton Mail and a suite of privacy and security-focused products, including an encrypted drive service, an authenticator app, a password manager, and more.In the last few months, Yen set up an email address for employees to contact if they come across anything blocking adoption of AI at Proton, so leadership can “ruthlessly smash everything that stands in the way of AI velocity;” Proton installed software on workers’ computers that track how much AI code the company is generating; and Yen said this is the last year that Proton will hire engineers at all, and instead only hire people to build things with AI.That AI push came to head this week when Proton said it would re-interview staff about their use of AI, with the clear implication that those interviews, and employees’ willingness to embrace AI, could decide whether a worker is fired or not.404 Media spoke to eight current and one former Proton employees and reviewed Slack chats, meeting recordings, and an AI manifesto written by the company’s CTO. Our reporting reveals a culture of fear inside Proton, where many employees are hesitant to even mildly critique Yen’s views or discuss engineering problems. Workers describe an environment where employees have genuine concerns about security or being asked to develop security products with AI, but feel unable to voice them, lest Yen berates them in front of everyone or threatens their employment at the company.“The CEO is in full AI psychosis and has been for a while now,” one of the sources told 404 Media.Our reporting also paints a picture of Proton that is likely very different to the public’s perception of a company with a goal of carefully protecting privacy: one that in reality is barreling ahead with AI as quickly as possible so it can achieve the explicit goal of more annual revenue.“Due to insufficient velocity,” Proton is not on track to achieve its annual recurring revenue target by the end of the year, one internal document obtained by 404 Media reads. Proton’s year-over-year growth is also “far away from what the market today considers to be good,” and, “By all metrics that matter, we’re an underperforming company.”In response to detailed questions from 404 Media, a Proton spokesperson did not dispute any of our reporting or characterization of what’s happening inside of the company. “It’s clear that some people at Proton are unhappy with our direction, or misunderstand it, and many people are anxious,” they said. “In our determination to move fast, we have sometimes been too blunt or too slow in explaining ourselves to our people. We will work on that, as their questions are the ones we most need to answer.”Yen, a former CERN particle physicist, projects a measured approach in public, but internally he acts more like what one employee described as a “petulant child.” In May, Proton announced it was implementing post-quantum cryptography which should protect against future attacks from quantum computers. The work took years of effort, with one caveat that it would not work on older emails, only those written after the feature’s launch, at least for the moment. Yen was not happy that Proton was drawing attention to this limitation.In a Slack channel dedicated to thanking people for their work, Yen jumped in. “Get it fixed,” he wrote, referring to Proton’s Reddit post announcing the feature. “Now Reddit is pissed and we look worse than Tuta,” he added, referring to a Proton competitor. When employees explained to Yen the nuances of the encryption and why that was not immediately possible, Yen wrote, “I find this whole thing stupid. You cannot announce this in this way.”“Now we are left with two shitty choices. Deprioritize more important tasks for the business to re-encrypt old emails, or constantly get attacked online for not doing it. So maybe you can enlighten me on which of the two shitty choices we will take,” he wrote. “In the future there are two options. Either you guys are confident enough to not fuck this up, or you get my advice to make sure it is not fucked up,” he added. He then told a member of the team that made it to “go on Reddit.”“So go on there with your personal account and comment to set the record straight,” he wrote. “Perception is more important than truth, the truth doesn’t matter if you don’t win on perception.”One employee told 404 Media, “Whatever persona Andy [Yen] has out of Proton, he’s a straight up bully inside. He routinely breaks his little facade in Slack and calls people losers and stupid, often for stuff he’s paying them for.”Ever since launching Proton Mail in 2014 after the Snowden revelations, Proton has steadily introduced new products that make Proton more of a worksuite than a simple email provider. More recently, those products were focused around AI, with the launch of Lumo, a large language model (LLM) chatbot that the company says doesn’t log conversations or train on user data. In June, Proton of its chatbot.Up until this point, Yen’s public comments on AI were relatively tame. In an August interview with WIRED, he said Proton is “building AI features and AI tools, because I think if the privacy companies do not find a way to step in to build privacy-first AI, we are essentially ceding the future to tech companies that don’t have the best interests of users at heart,” and that the company was “capitalizing” on the backlash to corporatized, invasive AI from companies like Google. Last year, Yen and Proton were criticized for statements he made suggesting the Republican Party and Donald Trump would be harder on Big Tech than Democrats. Toward the end of August, Yen’s internal tone on AI shifted to having Proton use it as much as possible, and as quickly as possible, according to the Slack chats and multiple employees.“The train is coming, get onboard or get crushed. Don’t be the professional fax machine operator in the internet age,” he wrote to the security Slack channel. “I think by the end of this year most developers stop programming and start writing specs for tests that AI will code and run, to validate AI written code that humans will no longer be able to review. This will be the last year that we hire engineers, and starting next year we hire what we used to call product managers, to build things with AI.”AI is changing how cybersecurity works, with AI agents hacking into companies, and AI assisting in the discovery of gaping vulnerabilities in important code. Many companies across the privacy and security space are grappling with how to deal with AI, either in the development of their products or how to defend themselves against hackers who are using AI. Some may do this carefully. Others are trying to do it as quickly as possible for profit. This account of Proton’s own reckoning with AI provides an unprecedented insight into what is happening inside one security-focused company users especially trust. Initially, using AI was banned inside Proton, but the company has since approved AI for all sorts of use cases internally, including processing financial data, drafting customer-facing responses on Reddit and LinkedIn, and writing code “except when that source code contains information that would give immediate advantage to a competitor” or is related to “innovation or R&D [research and development],” according to an internal Proton document seen by 404 Media. Ninety percent of code at Proton in October was written by AI, the company’s CTO Bart Butler said in a meeting, according to audio 404 Media obtained. Much of that code is written with Anthropic’s Claude, multiple employees told 404 Media. And Yen tells employees in Slack chats to use Claude, too. “We are a tech company against Big Tech who are spending loads on Claude,” one employee told 404 Media.In the “bullshit and loser thinking” conversation, another employee pushed Yen for specifics on ensuring that AI-generated code was free of security issues. “AI won’t magically solve our problems, because security is low in our prioritization at present,” the engineer said. Yen didn’t respond directly, and went on to insult one of the other employees in front of the entire channel. The employee “is saying his usual bs of we can do it but we will be even slower than we are today and I’m saying only losers think like that,” Yen wrote, adding that workers should prompt “better.”“You have the models and the time every developer should be doing this and checking their code which they were doing before manually but now they can do faster with AI,” Yen added. (One employee stressed that engineers still strive to build in a secure way.) The second clear signal that Proton was going deep into AI for many employees happened when Butler, the CTO, published a self-described AI manifesto one Friday afternoon last month.“Your old job is gone,” the manifesto, posted to Slack, told engineers. It laid out a future for Proton that fully embraced AI, and said if the company did not do so, that posed an “existential threat to the success of the mission itself.”Butler said that Proton needs to change in three key ways: accept that an engineers’ job is now to help LLMs write better code, faster; that Proton needs to get to the point where most code is not reviewed by humans but by AI; and to more fundamentally change the company as a whole, and “commit, as an organization, to the transformation that the moment requires.”One Proton employee replied in Slack, “Perhaps scaring people with: We are in a new world. ‘Programming’ is dead [...] your old job is gone wasn’t really necessary on a Friday afternoon.”Butler replied, “It’s supposed to be provocative, because it needs to be. I suggest you read it, think about it over the weekend, and come with your questions to me on Monday rather than on Slack. Thanks!”An employee told 404 Media, “​​People were surprised and somewhat cringed out, since the document clearly exaggerates what you can do with LLMs today and doesn't address any of the problems you get in return for giving up your code base to the AI Jesus (e.g. AI cannot really maintain a large code base over time).” Another called it “ethically bankrupt.”Earlier this week, Proton sent the email to employees saying they would re-interview workers about how they use AI in their jobs. The tone was clear; you may lose your job because of these interviews, current employees told 404 Media. “These re-interviews are consequential,” the email read. Soon after, a senior employee spoke up in Slack to Yen about the re-interviewing process. He suggested instead that Proton detect who is falling behind and support them and enforce high quality training.Yen’s response was blunt: “Let’s put it this way, we already know more or less who is behind. If we were giving up on them, we would not bother with this process.”The employee replied, “That messaging is fear-based. Which is probably why I suspect there are dozens of other employees watching us talk about this live and except for [other employee] no one else is chiming in.”“People shouldn’t be scared to talk about this in public and to push back on you and leadership. A fear based culture feels like a cancer to me. It’s the opposite of engineering, you need to talk about things, even uncomfortable things,” they added. Yen eventually told the employee, in front of everyone: “If you are making the accusation that this is a financially driven decision and you don’t trust me when I tell you it’s not, then I think this might not be the place for you.”Only one other employee chimed in during that exchange: “It’s about the culture you instil, people don’t want to feel like they’re on a tightrope, and yes we understand you want to move fast but there needs to be a balance, people also need support, not everyone is the same.”“It was also faster for my parents to beat me until I ate my vegetables but I’m not sure it was healthy,” they added.The exchange with Yen was unusual not only in that someone was debating some of Yen’s ideas, but also that it directly referenced the culture of fear at Proton. “Whenever someone talks back to Andy it tends to be highlighted since very few people talk back to him,” one employee told 404 Media.Proton sources described that culture in various ways to 404 Media. One said, “People just shut up and get on with things.” Another added, “Most have just given up. Your expertise will be undermined, you will be told to do what the CEO wants, and there’s a decent chance you’ll be called all types of stupid in the process.” A third said there is “100%” a culture of fear, especially in the last few months. “Andy [Yen] tends to not communicate; when things are communicated, it is ‘this is happening.’ Views in which he doesn’t share, he can be hostile to and will shit on people in public chats. Like even for managers… which doesn’t look very prof[essional].” A fourth said, “Andy [Yen] truly seems to hate a lot of the people that work here.”In a meeting held after leadership sent the re-interview email, which 404 Media obtained audio of, Butler said that not everyone who received the email would in fact be re-interviewed. “So don’t freak out if you don’t receive an invite. Most of you will, but not all, just for logistical reasons and otherwise, or it’ll happen later.”“Nobody gets a pass from this, basically,” he said, referring to how Yen had already interviewed around 40 people, including Butler. Yen also re-interviewed Eamonn Maguire, the director of engineering for AI and machine learning, he said at another point. People who scored highly in those interviews are now being tasked with interviewing other Proton employees, Butler said.“You should not blow this off, okay? It's consequential. It's either that you are interviewing, fighting for your life, like in some sort of Hunger Games thing,” he continued. But, “it’s an opportunity and a risk, okay? If you haven’t done anything with AI and you haven’t thought about it, you haven’t changed how you work, and you’re in product design or engineering, well, now is the time. And if you have done things and you feel confident in it, that’s good too.” A speaker in the meeting also mentioned that some people may get promoted through the re-interviews.“I think we’ll see what the results say. But I urge you to take it seriously, but not freak out, I guess,” Butler said. “This isn’t a witch hunt,” he added. “It’s not a religion.”As for why this push for AI is happening around, “It’s because we ran out of time,” Butler said.“Perception is more important than truth, the truth doesn’t matter if you don’t win on perception.”Yen’s feverish desire for Proton to radically embrace AI can be explained, at least in part, by an internal Proton document laying out the company’s intention to make something it is calling a fast team of people who will try to make the company build at a much more rapid clip. The document says Proton is not on track to achieve its annual recurring revenue target by the end of the year because of “insufficient velocity.” The company’s year-over-year growth is “far away from what the market today considers to be good,” and, “By all metrics that matter, we’re an underperforming company.”Second, the document says Proton transitioning to an “AI-first company” requires additional time and effort before it will start to see efficiency gains. For around six months, Proton has been in an experimental phase with AI, but now the company is taking concrete steps to restructure the company around AI, according to meeting audio 404 Media obtained.Third, the document says Proton “suffered a catastrophic 6 hour downtime which showcased to the world (and to us) that Proton’s engineering is not actually reliable and resilient. We need to quickly remedy this problem, which will also increase workload because we need to pursue these reliability improvements simultaneously with shipping features ASAP to accelerate our growth rate.” That .Possible solutions to make the company faster are to move to the U.S. or China, the document says, which is “not an option for Proton unfortunately,” presumably referring to being headquartered in Switzerland for its strong privacy protections. Second is firing a lot of people and then rehiring, which Proton says is unrealistic because “we are based in Europe, where firing the wrong people is slow, and hiring the right people even slower.” The third is to “transform the company from within.”To solve some of these apparent problems, the document calls for the creation of an “elite fast team” which will demand a lot more work, including weekends. Being on the fast team offers a 30 percent increase to base salary, paid out as a monthly bonus; a company credit card employees can use to order food if working hard during weekends, upgrade a long haul flight work flight to business class, get a five star hotel when visiting another office, or take colleagues out to dinner for team building. “This program is not for everybody. It requires a certain drive and mental toughness. We expect it to be no more than 5-10% of the company. But for the ambitious, the young (or old), or those who are simply bored, come join the team that will re-found Proton for the future,” the document says. Yen also spoke in Slack chats about Proton being a “996 company,” referring to the culture of working from 9 a.m. to 9 p.m., six days a week, a practice that started in China and is becoming popular in Silicon Valley. The extra perks and money appear to be a move to get employees to work more than their contracted hours, which is harder to implement in Europe given its strong labor laws. “That’s bullshit and loser thinking. Of course it’s possible to be fast and secure.”In other settings where Yen is not present, employees and managers are more open about what is going on. In another meeting 404 Media obtained audio of, a Proton employee said they do not trust Andy’s judgement on highly technical choices. In another, even Butler said Yen doesn’t understand the technical points about the AI topics he is re-interviewing people on.“And for those of you maybe, oh, what the fuck does Andy know about anything technical? He doesn’t, and it’s not that technical,” Butler said. “But what this approach does do, is there’s nothing like a deadline to motivate people,” he said, referring to the re-interviews.When asked about Yen’s comments, whether there is a culture of fear in Proton, and may people be fired based on the re-interviews, a Proton spokesperson told 404 Media in an email, “Times of major change are scary, and the tech industry as a whole is contending with this transition. We have not always communicated our intentions as well as we could have, but Proton is committed to helping our colleagues retrain and reskill for the future.” On Wednesday, Yen started a new thread in the company’s Slack in an uncharacteristically calmer tone. “When thinking about Al, it's not really about the capabilities today, but what capabilities might be possible in the future, which is probably less distant than we think. We will need to transform our org, and doing so requires knowing who is using Al well, who is mis-using Al, or who hasn't used Al at all (don't be in this group),” he wrote. For much of the day, with the November re-interviews looming, almost nobody was working on actual work and standup meetings were cancelled, one employee said.One employee replied to Yen with Reddit posts from Proton users reacting to 404 Media’s article first breaking news of the re-interviews. “I'm paying a premium for this service and as such I demand that corners are not cut simply because some new technology of dubious means comes into existence. I want coders to understand their code. I want them to think about the problems they are trying to solve and come to those conclusions naturally. It will create a better product with reproducible results. If you want to replace some jobs replace the jobs of the people who thought this email was a good idea,” one of them pasted into Slack read.Yen, usually concerned with what people were saying on Reddit, didn’t respond.

item.title: Make no mistake about what the DOJ is doing
item.author: 1axb0hlhpcgirr5f8ame2x9omqpbfmjiqhvhlv@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
item.content:encoded: It is nearly certain to lose its frivolous case against Alaska over certification of the Senate election. And it is threatening to sue Washington State (and lose) in a copycat of the case it just lost in California.All this losing has not deterred the administration from escalating its attacks on our elections. To the contrary, each wave of defeats encourages Trump to propose an even more authoritarian response.It is this escalation in its war on voting that is so troubling.At no point in any of these cases have the DOJ or the White House reexamined their stance. Neither has even entertained the possibility that what they seek to do is illegal, unconstitutional and undemocratic.In the California ruling, the judge observed: “Never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own Constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the Executive Branch.”Instead of reflecting on these sobering words, the DOJ immediately filed an appeal.When I shared the news of this latest decision and the subsequent appeal, several allies assured me it would be fine because my legal team would prevail. While I appreciate the confidence, a democracy that counts on the federal government losing all of its election cases will not remain a democracy for long.It was one thing to defeat the likes of Rudy Giuliani and Sidney Powell in the aftermath of the 2020 election. It is quite another to pull off the same winning percentage when the Department of Justice is on the other side.Yet that is where we are once again for the 2026 midterm elections. And those willing to stand up and fight are largely on their own.Sadly, the legal profession, corporate leaders and legacy media have all failed us. They will risk nothing to ensure free and fair elections.The largest law firms stand on the sidelines and look the other way as these court fights play out. Corporate leaders are silent about the attacks on our elections. The legacy media is consumed with both-sides coverage and sanctimonious self-congratulation.The next few weeks are going to be difficult. The lies and threats will intensify.Trump will grow more desperate. DOJ will be further weaponized against Democrats and anyone else standing in Trump’s way.More cases will be filed. The DOJ will lose and appeal. All eyes will turn to the U.S. Supreme Court.I am used to this rhythm. It is my job and my obligation to do my part.But I am warning you now: this is unsustainable.Once this election is over, we must do more to protect democracy and free and fair elections.That means real reforms to how we protect voting rights and how we staff and run elections. The fate of our elections can no longer depend on pro-democracy forces winning every single case in court.We cannot afford to relive this in 2028 and beyond.

item.title: Pumpkins Should Have Gone Extinct
item.author: Miss Cellania
item.content:encoded: Plants that produce fruit want to be eaten, because that's how they disperse their seeds. Long, long ago, the ancient ancestor of pumpkins evolved to be eaten by megafauna like mastodons. They were too bitter and toxic for creatures like humans. Besides, they had a really hard rind. Only those large animals could open the fruit, tolerate the taste, and properly spread the undigested seeds around with some handy manure for fertilizer.Then around 12,000 years ago, humans wiped out the mastodons, giant sloths, mammoths, giant bears, and other animals that ate those proto-pumpkins. Those bitter pumpkins weren't appealing to other mammals, so how did they survive to today? They are an evolutionary anachronism, a species that should no longer exist. You might not be surprised to learn that it was because of humans, who do weird things. PBS Eons explains how we got pumpkins even though they should have died out thousands of years ago. (via Laughing Squid)

item.title: The Milwaukee Brewers Are The Obvious, Implausible Champions
item.author: Kathryn Xu
item.content:encoded: It is difficult to encapsulate the Milwaukee Brewers' first World Series victory, because for all the limiters and qualifiers that suggest they had done the implausible—the payroll, and the market size, and facing the Los Angeles Dodgers, and the "first World Series victory" of it all—they had, in all reality, done the very probable.The Brewers had the best regular-season record in Major League Baseball, with 103 wins. By many metrics, they had the best starting pitcher in baseball, with Jacob Misiorowski. They were rested coming into the World Series, and though no one could know this until the first game in Tampa, they were playing with a seven-game home-field advantage. They swept the Dodgers and then won the World Series in five; for good measure, they also nearly won the one game they lost. It is insulting to the broader picture that the Brewers failed to sweep. No team down 0-3 in the World Series has ever forced a Game 6. If the Tampa Bay Rays ever got close, it was in the manner of one of Zeno's paradoxes: closing in by halves to the possibility of making it an interesting series, and never getting there.However, it would be incorrect to state that the Brewers had done the very probable, because in an MLB postseason, achieving the very probable is very, very difficult. Even the best bullpen in baseball, never mind the third-best, will experience bad days. Hits dry up. Everyone makes an untimely error one time or another. Winning in baseball is one thing, but making it look totally controlled is hard work. Just ask the Los Angeles Dodgers, world-beaters for a decade or so, who failed to beat the world more times than not. On the most recent occasion they did, it required the intervention of several magicians, or at least Miguel Rojas and Andy Pages.

item.title: You Need a Pep Talk
item.author: Dave Pell
item.source: NextDraft: The Day's Most Fascinating News
item.content:encoded: Donald Trump loves to dance to at his rallies. But while his messaging attempts to empower young men, his administration is actually setting them up for some tough times. Like the YMCA, the MAGA movement promises an America that features “everything for young men to enjoy.” But that pleasure will come at a cost. In this newsletter, I’ve repeatedly warned about the damage that online sports (and everything else) betting, now made pervasive by the so-called prediction markets, is doing to young men in particular. While some states have tried to keep prediction markets from offering gambling inside their borders — the latest effort comes from Utah, where the state has brought criminal charges against Kalshi — the Trump administration has done everything it can to protect prediction markets from regulation. (If you can’t already surmise that this strategy is tied to Trump family investments, you really haven’t been paying attention for the last couple years.) While gambling attacks and addicts the minds of young men, RFK Jr is helping peptides have the same impact on their bodies. “Anti-vaccine Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy has unilaterally passed a rule that will allow specialty pharmacies to sell six specific peptide drugs, overruling scientists at the Food and Drug Administration. The peptides are popular among members of Kennedy’s Make America Health Again movement, and many prominent MAHA figures and Kennedy allies sell them.” Social media influencers are already pushing unproven and untested peptides on a generation of young people trying to turn themselves into Macho Macho men, which has led to editorials like this one in : Protect young people from the peptide boom.+ Other than being a health-damaging quack, why would RFK Jr overrule his own FDA to promote untested peptides? You don’t need a prediction market to answer that question. The FDA “essentially banned peptides in 2023 because of safety concerns. But an FDA committee met in July to review the evidence on peptides and recommend whether or not to take the highly unusual step of allowing pharmacies to dispense them absent scientific review. The committee was made up of new appointees who consulted with or were employed by companies that were interested in promoting or dispensing peptides.” Lobbyists insist that legalizing these compounds will eliminate “the unsafe gray and black markets.” But, as is the case with prediction market non-rules, it’s more about keeping certain companies and individuals in the black; even if that means a generation of young men are turned into guinea pigs. : The Peptide Rush Has Begun.On one hand, you have remarkably negative Trump poll numbers and a groundswell movement for change. On the other hand, you’ve got Elon Musk. And that other hand has a deep pocket. The with an obvious and clearly stated look at the bigger meaning of this election. The people vs. Elon Musk. “This is a culmination of the pernicious combination of the country’s increasingly extreme concentration of wealth and a half-century of U.S. Supreme Court rulings unleashing those riches on our politics. These twin troubles perpetuate each other: The superrich spend more and more to elect a government that, in turn, does more and more to make them richer. And the cycle repeats.” (Modern American politics comes down to hoping that your billionaires spend more than their billionaires.)+ Of course, financial power is only one of Musk’s levers of influence. Simon Shuster and Isaac Stanley-Becker in (Gift Article): How Elon Musk Turned on Ukraine. “In a series of posts on X over the weekend, he admitted to causing last week’s outages, and he lashed out at those who call for greater military aid to Ukraine. ‘I have nothing but UTTER CONTEMPT for the virtue-signaling evil warmongers who push for endless slaughter and offer no realistic solution to the conflict,’ Musk wrote. ‘May you burn in hell.'” (With Musk as arguably the most powerful person in the world, we just might.)May the best team win? Yes, it may. The Milwaukee Brewers brought home the organization’s first World Series title by being really good at baseball. They were great all season, and even better during the playoffs, especially their otherworldly bullpen. And they’re a damn likable team (I’m not just saying that because they beat the Dodgers, but I’m mostly saying it because of that). : At last, Milwaukee Brewers are World Series champions. “There is simply no facet of baseball and of winning games at which the Brewers do not excel. Only one team scored more runs. They ranked fifth in steals, first in walk rate. They led the majors in batting average and on-base percentage. They did not rely on homers but could go deep when needed and ranked seventh in average exit velocity. In run prevention, the Brewers ranked second in team ERA and second in strikeout rate. The team defense was in the top five to 10 in most leading metrics.” In addition to all that, they had the man upstairs on their side. In this case, I mean the man upstairs in the back row. Brewers dedicate World Series to Bob Uecker.+ : The Brewers Hid in Plain Sight. And the most familiar sight of the playoffs might have been Aaron Ashby, the Brewers’ reliever who pitched 18 scoreless innings without allowing a run.Don’t judge a man until you’ve walked 31,000 miles in his shoes. “It was the mid-1990s and Mr. Bushby was a paratrooper in the British Army, obsessed with endurance tests. He was trying to find the longest distance he could travel by foot, but none of his options felt challenging enough, maxing out at a few thousand miles. Then his father suggested in the card that he look into traversing the Bering Strait between Alaska and Russia when it froze in the winter — unlocking a path across four continents … ‘That was when I realized that that’s the kind of thing I’ve been looking for,’ he recalled in an interview. ‘Now we had the ultimate journey.’ Mr. Bushby flew to South America and started walking home. Nearly 28 years later, he’s almost done.” (Gift Article): After 28 Years Walking Across the Globe, He’s Almost Home. “Karl Bushby has walked 31,000 miles, crossing some of the world’s harshest landscapes. He plans to reach his mother’s house in England next week.” (When he hears what he’s missed, he’ll probably immediately go out for a walk…)Let the Chips Fall Where They May? “Mr. Huang has not received a defensive briefing, warnings sometimes given to Americans who are being targeted by foreign intelligence services, people briefed on the surveillance said.” (Gift Article): Nvidia Chief Seen as Target of Chinese Spy Plot. “A Chinese businesswoman who had a close relationship with Jensen Huang was found to be passing intelligence to Beijing. President Trump was briefed and took no action.” (So this is allowed to go on, but I can’t drive a Polestar?)+ “Less than 24 hours after losing Brazil’s presidential election, Flávio Bolsonaro appeared to vanish into a convoy of four dark cars. After pulling away from his home in Brasília on Monday evening, the vehicles split in different directions, leaving journalists and authorities scrambling to determine which one carried Bolsonaro. By the next afternoon, the former presidential candidate’s allies were telling reporters he had already reached Florida.” (Gift Article): How Bolsonaro Fled Brazil: Decoys, a Private Jet and a Friend in the White House.+ Watch, and Listen to, Your Six? “Some hosts and many guests argue that the United States was defeated in Afghanistan because our presidents and generals, more concerned with politics and optics than the realities of the battlefield, imposed crippling restrictions on Special Operations. Freed from constraints, they say, the lethal raiding machine that Team 6 was a part of — with its exquisite training, cutting-edge technology and overwhelming firepower — might have simply killed its way to victory.” A very interesting piece on why some vets think America is losing wars — it’s an argument that has a lot of influence on the current administration. (Gift Article): They Were the Military’s ‘Quiet Professionals.’ Now They’re Talking. Meanwhile, we’re in a war right now, and Hegseth just fired another top general.+ After Trump made the demand on social media, “Republican Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy has ordered an investigation into the Democratic candidate running for the U.S. Senate in the state after revelations that her campaign appeared to be involved in recruiting another candidate with the same name as Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan.”+ AI fears hammer Google parent’s stock, erasing $500 billion in value. Google is mostly getting stung financially because a lot of ad space goes away (for now) when it answers so many search results with AI. But everyone knows there’s a correction coming. Will Google’s bad day be the trigger? In other tech news, DoorDash to acquire Instacart for $17B. (If they had used Dashpass, they could have closed the deal for $16.9B…)+ However the midterms play out, there’s no denying that Trump has become much less accomplished when it comes to being terrible. “Many Republicans, and even some in Trump’s orbit, don’t quite get it. What has happened, they ask, to the instincts of the man who authored two of the most improbable victories in American political history? Trump’s superpower was his intuitive understanding of what motivated his supporters. Many Republicans privately tell me that he’s lost that feel. Trump now lives, they think, in a gilded bubble, palling around with billionaires, oblivious to—and, even worse, uncaring about—the problems facing so many voters.” (Gift Article): Trump Is Closing From Behind. (I guess that explains why he keeps talking about people’s asses…)

item.title: Senators Demand Meta Answer for 'Pervert Glasses' Following 404 Media Investigation
item.author: Samantha Cole
item.content:encoded: Oregon Senator Ron Wyden and Massachusetts Senator Edward Markey sent a letter to Meta on Wednesday demanding the company answer for the privacy concerns its smart glasses pose to the public. The letter cites 404 Media’s October 2025 investigation into how people use Meta’s smart glasses to harass massage parlor workers. That investigation found Instagram accounts with hundreds of thousands of followers and millions of views uploaded videos filmed with Meta’s Ray-Ban glasses, where men entered massage parlors across the country and solicited the workers for sex work. The “Meta’s own disclosures confirm that imagery processed through its glasses’ visual AI features may be retained and used to train AI systems, including with the assistance of human reviewers,” the letter says. “Using intimate imagery for AI development is itself an invasion of privacy when the people depicted have not consented to that use, as is inherently the case for most bystanders captured by Meta’s glasses. Retaining that material for AI development, thereby extending the period during which it can be accessed, disclosed, or misused, exploits people’s highly sensitive information for Meta’s commercial benefit.”Research revealed how Meta’s platforms encourage an ecosystem of abusive, harassing content from pickup artists and influencers who use Meta’s smart glasses to capture interactions with people minding their own business in public or at their workplaces, who might not even know they’re being filmed. In a January report by the BBC, a woman who was recorded with the glasses said she was “bombarded” with phone calls because her phone number was posted with the video, and men who had seen the video stalked her at work., more than 70 people sued Meta, claiming that their intimate images and videos were exposed to workers hired by the company to label the data for AI. In March, Swedish journalists reported that Kenyan data labelers were viewing and annotating uncensored footage from Meta’s smart glasses, including sexual and violent content; Meta ended its contract with those workers less than two months later. These are labor conditions that groups like the Data Labelers Association in Kenya are , and for the people whose images are in the videos and photos, it’s an obvious violation of their privacy. People have also been to disable the light that indicates they’re recording for years Meta has about the difference between AI glasses you wear on your face and an iPhone for a long time. Now, these senators want the tech giant to answer for themselves. In the letter, Wyden and Markey demand answers about what safeguards, if any, Meta has in place to prevent the nonconsensual “capture, disclosure, or processing of sensitive and intimate imagery,” whether Meta specifically evaluated the potential for its glasses “to facilitate voyeurism, nonconsensual intimate image capture, or similar privacy invasions,” what imagery it uses for AI training, and whether people can request their biometric and other data captured by its glasses be deleted, along with several more questions about the glasses’ safety and design.“The reported disclosure of intimate footage to contractors for the purpose of AI training is particularly disturbing. Human review to fulfill a service knowingly requested by the person depicted is one thing; exposing unsuspecting individuals’ intimate moments to strangers for AI training is quite another,” Wyden and Markey wrote. “The individuals whose naked bodies, sexual activity, and other private moments have reportedly been captured by Meta glasses did not knowingly agree to having those images shared with strangers, much less for the purpose of improving Meta’s commercial AI systems. That disclosure and processing is an invasion of privacy, regardless of whether the footage is subsequently published or misused.” In the last few weeks, for quietly changing its privacy policies for business accounts and granting itself permission to scrape user’s content and connected websites to develop its AI products. Meta has been pushing its smart glasses over the years with ads featuring A-list celebrities, including Chris Pratt, Chris Hemsworth, and Kris Jenner (all three in ), from K-pop group BLACKPINK, and most recently, . Guerrilla ad makers have countered with their own ads around the world, and people have started calling the smart glasses "pervert glasses" in response to these widespread invasions of privacy they've come to represent. In August, Meta to add facial recognition and highlight reel features to its smart glasses.

item.title: Jeremiah Chiu (Interview)
item.author: Flow State
item.content:encoded: Today we’re listening to Jeremiah Chiu, a Taiwanese-American synthesist and composer from Chicago. He took up piano and violin at age five, and went on to play keys in bands (pop punk), leading to an interest in synths. Now based in Los Angeles, Chiu creates fascinating synth compositions, often on interesting instruments. His 2023 album, , was made at the Vintage Synthesizer Museum in Los Angeles. He’s a member of the electro-jazz quintet SML, contributing modular synths to the group’s virtuosic live improvisations (see example on YouTube), or their “five-person dialogues” as he called them. On his new album, , he mixes arpeggiated synth with drum machines, acoustic drums (by Booker Stardrum and Ben Lumsdaine), viola (Marta Sofia Honer), saxophone (Patrick Shiroishi), and more. “A large part of the studio process is experimenting by taking improvisations or other performances and using them as material for new pieces,” he told us. “I also use these samples to re-synthesize things – i.e. as a carrier voice for a vocoder or as an envelope follower or any other idiosyncratic way of taking one thing and using it to transform something else.” A conversation with Jeremiah follows the streaming links.What’s your earliest memory of music?It was very cute. I remember my parents and I would call my grandparents on holidays or to occasionally catch up – I must have been 3 or 4 – and at the end of each call I would sing Stevie Wonder’s “I Just Called to Say I Love You” to them. Because of that, the song has a permanent spot in my memory and life. As a teenager, I remember learning this song to cover in my pop punk band. Maybe it’s time I do a version.What was your first instrument and how did you get started with synths?I started playing piano and violin at age five or so. I took private lessons on both instruments and eventually joined the junior high orchestra as well as a regional youth orchestra in the Chicagoland area. In high school, I decided not to continue playing in orchestra. It’s something I regret now, but at the time, I started learning guitar and bass and wanted to hang out with my peers in punk bands – a pretty normal desire for a highschooler in the suburbs, I assume.Near the end of high school, all of the friends I had were in bands and equally into punk, emo, and rave culture. Chicago House and Detroit Techno were hugely inspirational and analog (vintage) synthesizers were cheap and plentiful. We were playing in emo punk bands – starting to incorporate synths – and also learning how to beatmatch drum machines to tracks on a turntable. At the time, you could buy a synth (something like a Roland Juno-106) for $100. It provided us with the opportunity to try out a bunch of different synthesizers and sell and trade them easily. A friend, Mike Bingaman, lent me his MC-505 Groovebox and that really got me interested in sequencing, programming synths, and connecting the instruments to each other through MIDI and CV/Gate.In retrospect, it was a unique experience to have so many teenagers in a community that was really open to a lot of music and art.What were your first recordings like? What did you use to make them?My sister had this Casio WK-1200 that wasn’t being used. It sat in our dining room, next to the kitchen. When my parents would be fixing dinner, I would sit on that thing and make songs. It had the ability to record up to six parts using internal sounds. So I learned to make a drum part, bass part, chords, and lead parts. It really taught me how to put parts of a song together. I also spent a lot of time making mixtapes by recording snippets of radio onto boombox that had a record function. I still work like this quite a bit, except I use live performance as my “radio.”Once I was in bands, we – like so many people – had a Tascam 4-track recorder and a single microphone. We learned how to record parts and bus them down to single tracks to add more tracks. From there, the evolution went a bit like this: a 16-track minidisc recorder, a Fostex digital recorder, a Compaq computer with Cubase controlled by a 12-track MIDI console, a Pro Tools MBox with that goofy dongle. All of the early recording experiments were done on cassette tape or CD.What early artists/albums were most influential to you finding your own sound?Isotope 217, Tortoise, and the whole “post rock” Chicago scene were and still are huge influences. I’m grateful and honestly in disbelief that I call a lot of those people friends and collaborators now. Beyond the sound of the albums and music, the proliferation of different groups within a community reminded me of other thriving music scenes, like ‘70s Dusseldorf, Cologne, and Berlin scenes and ‘80s downtown New York scenes.I love looking at liner notes and personnel on albums and seeing a rotating cast of similar characters – especially when those relationships traverse mediums. In particular, I remember being in art school and finding out that Steve Reich and Sol Lewitt were close friends. Moments like that blew my mind because I grew up in a culture where everything seemed to have a defined boundary. Music was Genre, Art was Movements. But the actuality was much more fluid, hybrid, and boundaryless.Ultimately, the goal is to participate in, and support a thriving artistic community where artists can come together, be in dialogue with each other and contribute positively to our understanding and experience of the world.What was your studio setup for ? What instruments/gear/software did you use to make it?I work in Ableton. All of the contributors on the album recorded remotely and then I edited and arranged the material. More than once, a drum take would get resampled or sliced and it would form an entirely new track. For me, a large part of the studio process is experimenting by taking improvisations or other performances and using them as material for new pieces. I also use these samples to re-synthesize things – i.e. as a carrier voice for a vocoder or as an envelope follower or any other idiosyncratic way of taking one thing and using it to transform something else.In my modular rig, I have several samplers and oscillators that I use to create percussion and melody. The samplers are all routed via my mixer’s aux send, so at any given moment, I can sample something and work with that.Only recently have I started to incorporate software synths as a way to work out some of the compositions in MIDI before recording them again with analog synthesizers. On this record, I used my modular synth rig, Roland gear (101, 202, 303, 606, 808), Moog Matriarch, and a few sample-based organs or pads that I made. Beyond that, Marta Sofia Honer (viola), Marquis Hill (trumpet), Patrick Shiroishi (saxophone), Ben Lumsdaine (drums), Booker Stardrum (drums), Takako Minekawa (voice & field recordings), and Will Miller (EVI) all contributed to the album.How did your experience with SML affect your solo work?SML has been a great experience in listening and making intentional moves. Josh (in SML) has talked about it as being a mode of self-producing, or live producing. I think what he means is that when we’re playing live, it’s all improvised, but since it’s a performance, we’re balancing risk-taking with intentionality. Every sound each of us brings to the table is a part of a five-person dialogue. However, each of us has the opportunity to shift the conversation as it’s moving, because we all respond.In my solo work, I improvise a lot in performances. This is usually done with live-sampling and sequencing. With sequencers in my modular rig, I often have a sequence sequencing a sequence. To clarify, instead of sending a sequencer a steady clock pulse, I’m sending it a rhythmic sequence. This starts to articulate and move the sequence I’ve written in ways that are unexpected and forces me to listen, adjust, and react. What I’m interested in is having some volatility in the performance. An opportunity to have things go awry that force me to be present.With my previous solo album, , it felt very close to how SML currently operates. It was collection of improvisations that was then edited down into an album. With I intentionally swung the pendulum in the other direction. Instead of build the record based on improvisations, I wanted to compose some pieces from the ground up. Some of the songs were still born out of an improvisation, but I challenged myself to explore the album in a way that I hadn’t been doing with my other groups (SML, Marta Sofia Honer duo, and Jeff Parker Expansion Trio).You’re also a graphic designer and educator. What are some examples, if any, of your work in those disciplines affecting your music, or vice versa?When people ask if there’s overlap between my art, design, and music practice, I always talk about the vocabulary as a way to understand how similar they are. In all of the creative fields, we can talk about composition, narrative, contrast, tensions, rhythmic, dynamics, etc… While we generally pin art and design towards a more visual realm, and music to be more sonic, I don’t really separate them that way. When I make an album, I always approach it like a film, or narrative work. I’m thinking about the pacing from the beginning to the end. I’m thinking about the tension and release and the changes between songs as opportunities to carry a listener through a series of ideas tethered to one larger concept.In a more direct example, some years ago I was commissioned by The Getty Center in LA to create a score for a player piano as part of their performance, Pianographs. The player piano score rolls vertically across the face of the piano as the music is played. Holes punched in the paper scroll activate notes. Because the scroll was such a visual part of the performance, my approach to the composition was to compose the score by drawing images and words onto the scroll. I was less worried about the exact harmony, melody, or counterpoint, and more interested in hearing how these images and text came to life through sound.Name an underrated artist from the past 50 years.I’m not sure if Franco Battiato classifies as underrated as he became one of Italy’s most famous singers. However, his early experimental records , , , etc. are all so incredible, and I’m always surprised that they’re not more widely recognized by today’s selectors. Go listen to them!What are you working on next?I feel so grateful to have the support of International Anthem and to be collaborating with so many incredible artists in our wonderful community. In the coming year, I’m continuing the work with SML, Marta, and Jeff Parker in hopes that one or more of those will finish another album. At this very moment, I’m about to send this interview off and record on an amazing track for Marquis Hill.
