item.title: Forgotten Band: Icicle Works
item.author: Schill
item.content:encoded: There are plenty of forgotten bands from the 1980s that make you wonder how they ever disappeared. Then there are bands like The Icicle Works, where the question becomes even more frustrating:How did a band this good have only one song that everybody remembers?If you were listening to alternative radio in the early 1980s, you probably remember “Whisper to a Scream (Birds Fly).” It was catchy, energetic and just strange enough to stand apart from the endless parade of synth-heavy new wave that was filling radio stations.The song was a legitimate hit.And that’s a shame, because The Icicle Works had a much more interesting story than their one familiar song suggests.They came from Liverpool, England, created a sound that mixed post-punk, new wave, progressive rock and straight-up pop, and produced several albums that deserve far more attention than they receive today.They were never quite weird enough to be completely underground and never quite commercial enough to become superstars.That awkward middle ground is where a lot of forgotten bands ended up.From Liverpool to the WorldThe Icicle Works were formed in Liverpool in the early 1980s by singer, guitarist and songwriter Ian McNabb.McNabb was the creative force behind the band, and his songwriting immediately separated The Icicle Works from many of their contemporaries.The band wasn’t interested in simply copying the synth-pop formula.There were keyboards and electronic textures, but there were also jangly guitars, driving rhythms and surprisingly ambitious arrangements.The music could sound bright and upbeat while still having a slightly melancholy edge.That combination fit perfectly into the early-1980s British alternative scene.Liverpool already had a remarkable musical history, and The Icicle Works became part of another generation of musicians trying to figure out what came after punk.The answer, for them, was to take the energy of punk and combine it with ambitious pop songwriting.The song that changed everything was “Whisper to a Scream (Birds Fly).”The title alone sounded like something you’d find printed on an early-’80s import single.The song itself was even better.It started with a distinctive rhythmic pulse before opening into jangling guitars and McNabb’s urgent vocals.It was catchy without sounding disposable.The song eventually became a significant hit in the United States, reaching the Top 40, and suddenly The Icicle Works had an opportunity to become much bigger.For a brief moment, they looked like they might be one of the British bands capable of breaking through in America.That didn’t quite happen.Which is a shame, because they had the songs.The band’s 1984 debut album, , is where anyone rediscovering the group should start.It’s much more than a vehicle for “Whisper to a Scream.”The album demonstrates just how adventurous McNabb could be as a songwriter.There are atmospheric passages, energetic guitar-driven songs, electronic touches and big melodic choruses.The band could shift from moody to explosive without losing its identity.It’s very much an early-’80s record, but it doesn’t feel trapped in the decade.That’s an important distinction.A lot of new wave records now sound like museum pieces.The Icicle Works still sounds like a band.They Were More Than New WaveCalling The Icicle Works a new wave band isn’t necessarily wrong, but it’s incomplete.They had too many different influences.There were progressive-rock ideas.There was folk and psychedelic influence.There were enormous pop melodies.McNabb wasn’t afraid to experiment with song structures either.That made the band difficult to categorize.And once again, that’s probably part of the reason they never became huge.The 1980s music industry loved easy descriptions.The Icicle Works could fit into several of those categories without completely belonging to any of them.The band continued with albums including and If You Want to Defeat Your Enemy Sing His Song.The latter title alone should tell you something about McNabb.He wasn’t exactly thinking in terms of three-minute radio formulas.The albums continued to demonstrate that the band had plenty of ideas beyond their biggest American hit.There were moments of experimentation alongside straightforward pop-rock.Unfortunately, the commercial momentum wasn’t enough to turn The Icicle Works into a household name.They became one of those bands that had a recognizable song without becoming a recognizable band.That’s a particularly strange form of musical fame.The Icicle Works benefited from MTV during the era when British bands were flooding American television.The visual presentation of “Whisper to a Scream” helped the song stand out.But MTV also created an interesting problem.It could make a song famous much faster than it could make an entire catalog famous.A viewer might see the video, remember the chorus, and move on to the next band.That’s essentially what happened.The Icicle Works became associated with one song.The rest of the catalog disappeared behind it.Ian McNabb Never Really StoppedOne of the biggest misconceptions about forgotten bands is that they disappeared because they had nothing left to say.That wasn’t the case with Ian McNabb.After The Icicle Works’ original run, McNabb continued recording and performing, including solo work and later incarnations of the band.He remained an active musician while The Icicle Works became increasingly associated with nostalgia for the 1980s.That’s another reason the group is worth rediscovering.They’re not simply a historical curiosity.There is a substantial body of music behind the one song most people remember.The Icicle Works suffered from terrible timing.They arrived during an extraordinary period in British music.There were so many great bands that even genuinely talented groups could get lost.You had The Cure, New Order, The Smiths, Echo & the Bunnymen, Simple Minds, U2, Tears for Fears, The Psychedelic Furs, The English Beat, The Church and dozens of others competing for attention.That’s a ridiculous amount of competition.A band could have a hit and still disappear from the larger cultural memory.The Icicle Works did exactly that.They became a footnote in a decade packed with musical stories.The Great Thing About Rediscovering ThemThe Icicle Works are one of those bands where the rediscovery process is genuinely rewarding.You start with “Whisper to a Scream.”You think, “Oh yeah, I remember this.”Then you listen to the first album.Wait a minute. These guys were actually really good.And there are more songs.More ambitious arrangements.More of Ian McNabb’s excellent songwriting.That’s the fun of forgotten bands.You’re not discovering some obscure group that nobody liked.You’re discovering a band that was good enough to have been much bigger but got lost in the shuffle.They Deserve More Than One SongThe Icicle Works aren’t completely forgotten.Their biggest song still turns up on ’80s playlists, radio retrospectives and new wave compilations.But the band behind that song deserves to be remembered.They weren’t a one-hit novelty.They weren’t simply another synth-pop act.They were a talented Liverpool band with a distinctive sound, a gifted songwriter and a willingness to experiment.“Whisper to a Scream” may have been their ticket into the mainstream, but it shouldn’t be the end of the journey.If that’s the only Icicle Works song you know, you’ve heard the introduction.Now listen to the albums.Because once you do, you’ll probably have the same reaction that happens with so many forgotten bands:“How the hell did I forget these guys?”And that might be the best reason of all to bring The Icicle Works back into the conversation.They don’t need nostalgia.They just need somebody to press play.

item.title: The Terror
item.author: Miss Cellania
item.content:encoded: 1963. Directed by Roger Korman, starring Jack Nicholson and Boris Karloff. From IMDB:France, 18th century. Lieutenant Andre Duvalier has been accidentally separated from his regiment. He is wandering near the coast when he sees a young woman. He asks the road to Coldon, where he hopes to rejoin his regiment. But the woman doesn't answer, doesn't even greet him and walks away. Eventually she takes him to the sea, where she disappears in rough water. Andre loses conscience when he is trying to following her, and is attacked by a bird. He awakes in a house with an old woman and a numb man. She claims to never have seen the woman. After he leaves, he sees her again and when trying to follow her is saved by a man from certain death. He learns that to help the girl, he must go to castle of Baron Van Leppe. When he arrives, Andre sees the woman looking from a window. Baron Van Leppe is old and seems reluctant to let André in however. He claims there's no woman in the castle, but shows André a painting which does indeed portray her. Andre learns that she is the baroness, who died twenty years ago.

item.title: Quoting Ted Sanders
item.author: Simon Willison
item.content:encoded: In general, LLM performance is incredibly multidimensional. There's no guarantee of a fixed ordering where the model that is best at math is also the model that's best at jokes. Despite that complexity, much of the variation in performance is explained by just a single variable: model size. In general, models that are bigger will (a) be more performant / reliable, (b) cost more per token, and (c) have better recall of esoteric facts. As you note, our models are ordered:Luna < Terra < Sol < Astra[...] These days, version number signifies a few things at once: the order of release, the relationship to other releases, and the magnitude of improvement. So something like 6.1 would indicate it was launched after 5.6, may share some similarities to other 6.1 models in terms of training data / personality (which is why it's not 5.7), and isn't a giant enough leap to merit the headlines and expectations that would come with a 7.— Ted Sanders, explaining OpenAI's model naming conventions

item.title: A Nuclear Bomb in the Mariana Trench
item.author: Miss Cellania
item.content:encoded: We've done underground nuclear tests, and we've done underwater nuclear tests. We found out that they work, and they did some nasty environmental damage. But what if we were to take those tests to an even deeper, more remote location, like, say, the Mariana Trench? And let's make it a big bomb, like the Tsar Bomba! That's the question in the latest episode of What If? from Randall Monroe and Henry Reich. They take these questions seriously, so we find out what would happen. However, the world's largest nuclear bomb is no match for the deepest part of the ocean. That's not very fun, so our guys came up with a new scenario in which the bomb is equivalent to the Chicxulub impactor (which is fun to Google). That gives us results more in line with what we expect from the What If? series.

item.title: The shark I’m watching most closely
item.author: 1axb2nr7dk2hqyxwmzzjlx1yw9qgeh3szdp1nn@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
item.content:encoded: We are six days away from the midterms, and Donald Trump’s unprecedented attacks on free and fair elections are continuing to escalate. Many of you have asked what to watch for and what to expect next.A colleague of mine once coined the phrase “shark closest to the boat” to help focus on the most immediate threats. It doesn’t mean it is the only concern, but it is the most immediate.Here is my guide to the sharks closest to the boat carrying our democracy in these troubled waters:The Department of Justice’s lawsuit blocking ballot counting in California is the shark closest to the boat. This is the shark from “Jaws,” and it threatens to sink our democracy if we don’t call up Captain Quint.And yes, we’re going to need a bigger boat. Especially because the DOJ has already spread this playbook to Washington State, where the DOJ demanded that the state set aside ballots from more than 400 voters it claims are noncitizens. No matter where you live, your vote is not safe.I am certainly concerned about this shark. My legal team is already running from the beaches into the water to fight back.U.S. District Judge David Carter is expected to issue a ruling today. The DOJ will likely lose. But that will not be the end of this shark. The department will take this case to the Supreme Court, where I am certain this shark will meet its end.This is a frivolous case, but be warned: The shark is still circling the boat.As a reminder, Trump’s DOJ is suing to block certification of the Senate election if Democrat Mary Peltola wins. The DOJ’s argument is baseless and weak. This case never should have been filed in the first place.But that doesn’t mean we should rest easy. Trump is invested in this case because he is determined to steal the Senate. He claims that he’s the one who gave the go-ahead for the DOJ to file.My law firm has moved to intervene on behalf of Peltola’s campaign and the DSCC. The DOJ must respond to the motion to dismiss by tomorrow. I expect we will see the last of this shark soon enough.The DOJ has been threatening state election officials who are simply doing their jobs. They warned election officials they could face criminal prosecution over noncitizen voting, and as we get closer to the election, those threats are only ramping up.On behalf of the DSCC, DCCC, DGA and Nevada Democratic Party, as well as Sen. Schumer and Rep. Jeffries, my law firm sued to stop these threats. Trump and the DOJ are clearly using intimidation to dictate who can vote and how elections are run. We will not let them win.This is a pretty big shark that should unsettle all of us. Right now, this shark is a little further off the coastline, but it’s moving fast and picking up speed. We need to keep an eye out.There is a shark keeping a low profile on the ocean floor. That shark is red state officials colluding with the DOJ and Trump to subvert the election results in their states.In some states, that looks like willingly handing over voter data. In others, it’s delaying mail ballots. As early voting starts, that could be welcoming federal agents at polling locations.While this shark hides from view of the public, we need to be aware of it and keep our eyes peeled. It could make the difference between a Democratic or Republican victory.This is the great white shark haunting our elections. We have not seen it yet, but the sea shanties worry us. This is the shark we fear the most.If ballot seizures happen, it will be in the days following the election. The Tina Peters of the world — MAGA election clerks colluding with Trump — will mobilize and cause mayhem at the local level. Republican governors like Ron DeSantis and Greg Abbott will likely not stop them.I worry because our attention will be divided. We will be fighting a lot of battles on a lot of different fronts. The sharks will attack before we see them.But that does not mean we are not ready to fight back.When the sharks attacked in 2020, I won 64 out of 65 cases. And we will win again.The sharks may be circling, but they are no match for us.

item.title: The Vivek Trainwreck—How Performative Bad Personness is Roiling Ohio
item.author: Josh Marshall
item.source: Josh Marshall – TPM – Talking Points Memo
item.content:encoded: Axios reports on a new private GOP poll conducted in the aftermath of Vivek Ramaswamy’s decision to run his ad questioning his opponent’s having been raped by her stepfather when she was 12. It shows Ramaswamy falling to 8 points behind Amy Acton compared to 2 points behind in a poll conducted by the same pollster a month ago. The poll found that 86% of respondents had heard of the ad and by a 2 to 1 margin those said the ad made them more likely to vote for Acton.Ramaswamy has always been an especially Trumpy character in the sense of leaning — both in his actions and how he his actions — into transgressive verging on sociopathic behavior as a signifier of Republicanness or Trumpiness. Indeed, when he released this ad he said explicitly that he was sending a message that he was ready to break rules and conventions in the context of Ohio politics just as Trump had at the federal level. All of this comes under the headline of being, as the phrase goes, “extremely online” and shaped by the aesthetics, mores and instincts of online trolling.That’s a remarkable and a remarkably frank expression of MAGA politics and aesthetics. The problem, however, is that Ramaswamy is not Donald Trump. What’s most notable about this episode is that lots of fellow Republicans appear to have warned him not to do this — not because of some subjective sense of decency but because it seemed so obviously self-destructive. I’ve thought from the beginning that this ad might not only backfire on Ramaswamy but possibly pull down the whole ticket. Ohio has very Trumpy demographics. It’s the kind of state where, if there’s going to be a GOP-underestimating polling error, you’d expect it to be particularly pronounced. Sherrod Brown — who, remember, is a semi-incumbent — has had a very steady if modest lead for months. He’s currently about three points ahead on average. So this ad, a performance of bad personhood, could end up making a difference in that race too.

item.title: The Moving Image Archive
item.author: Jason Kottke
item.content:encoded: The Moving Image Archive is a collection of over 120,000 clips from almost 2300 archival films drawn from public domain collections. The internet is full of forgotten films, and this archive is a growing library of that collection. When synthetic footage can now fabricate the past, preserving verifiable history matters more than ever before.A few things I found while poking around:Story of a City: New York (1946). “This 1946 film explains the historical and economic forces behind New York City’s growth into one of the world’s largest cities and its vital relationship to the rest of the United States.”Alice In Wonderland (1915). “This tinted, 42-minute cut of the 1915 silent fantasy film Alice in Wonderland, based on Lewis Carroll’s work, is available with a synchronized soundtrack sourced from an early vinyl recording or as a silent version.”Apollo 11 — 30th Anniversary (1999). “Marking the 30th anniversary of Apollo 11, the film combines mission footage with later interviews featuring Neil Armstrong, Buzz Aldrin, and Michael Collins.”Story of Television (1956). “Story of Television traces the development of television from early experiments in transmitting images across distance to RCA’s electronic systems, which improved picture quality and expanded broadcasting nationwide.”A is for Atom (1953). “This animated film explains atoms as the fundamental building blocks of matter, identifying elements by the number of protons.”Space Shuttle: A Remarkable Flying Machine (1981). “This 1981 NASA film documents Columbia’s maiden space shuttle mission, from its April 12 launch at Kennedy Space Center through onboard tests conducted by astronauts John Young and Robert Crippen to its successful April 14 landing on Rogers Dry Lake in California.”

item.title: Freshly Humiliated Flavio Bolsonaro Scurries Off To Miami
item.author: Patrick Redford
item.content:encoded: Three short weeks after he appeared to be on the cusp of assuming the presidency of Brazil and turbocharging the fascist revival movement started by his cadaverous father Jair, Flavio Bolsonaro is now a fugitive from the Brazilian justice system. Having been humiliated by an octogenarian in Brazil's presidential election, he was unable to gin up any support for an election theft, and was thus forced to choose between handing over his passport or scampering off to Miami like so many failed dictators before him.Bolsonaro will no longer get to see through his family's dream of evangelicizing Brazil and turning the full force of its military inward. Instead he will be browsing the aisles of Publix and begging a different, much stupider octogenarian for the scraps of his dwindling mercy.How did the younger Bolsonaro get here? His journey to Florida began with the collapse of the powerful bank, Banco Master, just over a year ago. That collapse resulted in the world learning about all the corrupt schemes the bank was doing, and also how intertwined it was with the Bolsonaro family. Incredibly, Flavio hitting up the now-jailed Banco Master owner for money to finance a Jim Caviezel–led biopic of his tubercular father is at the center of his corruption case. Flavio's best and perhaps only chance of avoiding jail time hinged on his family's ability to win Brazil's 2026 presidential election.

item.title: Why Donald Trump Wants To Replace American History With Big Statues Of Famous People
item.author: John Garrison Marks
item.content:encoded: As the nation marked its 250th anniversary this summer, Donald Trump could not stop posting AI-generated images of himself alongside George Washington. In one, Trump and Washington ride horses through a bucolic landscape, the sun setting in the distance. In another, Trump saves Washington from falling off a cliff; this one is styled as a movie poster for a time-traveling buddy-cop film. These are in addition to the very real images of Washington’s and Trump’s faces hanging side by side on massive banners outside the Department of Interior building.More than any others, though, Trump posted images of him and George Washington in the proposed White House ballroom. There's one in which Trump holds rolled up architectural plans (in an already-completed ballroom) while pointing out some distant feature to George. In another, they both stand in the ballroom, staring directly at the camera; even from the front, you can tell they’ve both adopted Trump’s signature ass-out posture. There are at least fivedifferentversions of this particular scene.Trump’s insistence on posting images of himself alongside George Washington offers the perfect distillation of how he thinks about history. For him, history is synonymous with celebrity—and there could be no higher honor for our historical VIPs to be feted in Trump’s glimmering new ballroom. Unwilling, for obvious reasons, to wait for history’s judgment, Trump uses AI to place himself alongside the past’s most famous figures.

item.title: The Line Between Young And Dumb Is A Thin One For The Flyers
item.author: Barry Petchesky
item.content:encoded: It has been a trying start to the season for the Philadelphia Flyers, who were a surprise playoff team last year with one of the league's youngest rosters. Their impact players are still basically all 25 and younger, so some growing pains were to be expected. But things started brutally on Day 1 and haven't gotten much better: At 3-7-4 they are last in the East, despite having played more games than anyone else.The young fellas are mostly getting their goals—Trevor Zegras, Matvei Michkov, and Porter Martone are top three on the team in points; Denver Barkey, in his first full season, is still scuffling a bit—but there's more to NHL success than scoring. That's the message head coach Rick Tocchet is trying to drill into his charges. Even a slightly better record in overtimes (0-4, only one of those reaching a shootout) would have the Flyers sitting a little prettier, but they are proving less than adept at protecting the puck. Yes, a scoring chance looks very appealing at 3-on-3, but the Flyers' skaters are acting like they've forgotten that the puck can go the other way.Consider Tuesday night at home against Columbus. The Blue Jackets jumped out to a 3-0 lead, but Philly dominated the rest of regulation and roared back to tie the game with 11 seconds left. Then, in overtime, Michkov got stripped soon after entering the attacking zone, something that can't happen as the trailer. Cole Sillinger and Zach Werenski went the other way on the juiciest 2-on-0 you'll see see (until 30 seconds later), and only a nifty Dan Vladar stop kept the game alive.

item.title: The Trump DOJ’s OTHER Scheme to Interfere in the Midterm Elections
item.author: David Kurtz
item.content:encoded: The Retribution: Election Interference EditionThe Trump DOJ’s unprecedented moves to stop ballot-counting and election certification are its most direct interference in the midterms — but it’s also bootstrapping in its long-running scheme of retribution against Trump foes in service of partisan campaign narratives while voting is underway.By timing prosecutions and overt investigative steps to maximize their pre-election impact, the Trump DOJ is not merely ignoring long-standing department policy about avoiding the public impression of election meddling. It’s actively abusing the powers of the federal government by using federal law enforcement for partisan ends. It’s happening broadly under the auspices of DOJ, but Department of Homeland Security law enforcement components are also involved.I had intended to write about this dynamic this morning anyway, and then the NYT and WaPo each published versions of the same story. I’d recommend both of them. Here are the recent cases most directly tied to complementing and reinforcing Trump campaign rhetoric while voting is underway:: The Trump DOJ tried to indict the star witness of the Jan. 6 Committee yesterday — exactly one week before Election Day — but was rebuffed by a D.C. grand jury.2 FBI agents in Hunter Biden case: The first inkling of the no-true bill in the Hutchinson case came during a raucous hearing on concerns about a highly politicized and problematic new prosecution of two FBI agents involved in the Hunter Biden investigation. The flimsy case was thrown together on orders from FBI Director Kash Patel and was perceived inside the bureau as a political “witch hunt,” a key FBI witness testified yesterday. The case was first charged on Friday.: The Oct. 5 timing of Trump II’s criminal case against former FBI Director James Comey — which was unsealed this week at Comey’s request — seems to have been driven at least by an expiring statute of limitations, not solely the election. But they’re not mutually exclusive, of course. Like in the case against the FBI agents above, DOJ proceeded to file charges against Comey without a grand jury indictment.: The Oct. 12 HSI raid on the private D.C. residence of a sitting Democratic member of Congress, who also is a Black woman of Somali heritage, managed to be brazen retribution and to mirror President Trump’s persistent racist targeting of Black women and Somali Americans.Virginia state Sen. L. Louise Lucas (D): On Oct. 14, the Trump DOJ indicted the President pro tempore of the Virginia Senate on allegations that her family set up an illegal marijuana business. Attorney General Todd Blanche and Patel held a press conference announcing the indictment.: The FBI yesterday raided the Beverly Hill mansion of billionaire and former Democratic donor Stephen Cloobeck, reportedly a close associate of former Rep. Eric Swalwell. The NYT reports that the raid came as part of an ongoing investigation into sexual misconduct allegations.The key is timing. Even where there might arguably be properly predicated investigations and prosecutions, the decision to proceed in high profile public ways before the election is a — notwithstanding Blanche’s feeble protests to the contrary.A great visualization from the WaPo of the abuse of federal law enforcement in service of GOP election rhetoric around the Big Lie of rampant noncitizen voting:Awaiting Ruling in CA Election Case …As I reported late yesterday, U.S. District Judge David O. Carter of Los Angeles said he will rule today on the Trump DOJ’s request for a TRO to segregate and not yet count ballots from a list of some 20,000 alleged noncitizen voters.During a 3 1/2-hour hearing on the TRO, Judge Carter appeared likely to kick the core of the case past Election Day, thereby thwarting the Trump DOJ and minimizing the worst impacts of its effort to interfere in the election.Bill Essayli Disqualified AGAINFor the second time, a federal judge has found that Bill Essayli is unlawfully serving as the top federal prosecutor in Los Angeles. Essayli was slotted into the role as part of the broader Trump scheme to install loyalists as federal prosecutors in blue states, bypassing the Senate and defying federal law.Essayli was previously disqualified by U.S. District Judge J. Michael Seabright of Hawaii from handling certain criminal cases as acting U.S. attorney because he overstayed his term in that role. Essayli was allowed to stay on as first assistant U.S. attorney and assumed all the duties of a regular U.S. attorney.But subsequent appeals court decisions in others cases have more thoroughly blocked the workaround that President Trump and the DOJ used to install Essayli, so in a new ruling Judge Seabright tightened his previous decision even more. The most immediate impact will be to keep Essayli from managing or overseeing attorneys in the specific criminal cases where his appointment was challenged. Seabright gave Essayli a chance to appeal before the ruling goes into effect.Ironically, Essayli personally argued the administration’s side in the California election case on the same day Seabright found him to be unlawfully serving.The Ongoing Coverup of the Alex Pretti KillingAs Morning Memo first reported two weeks ago, despite what publicly looked like a breakthrough in July, the Trump administration has continued to stonewall Minnesota authorities trying to investigate the three ICE shootings during Operation Metro Surge.Yesterday, the parents of Alex Pretti, one of the two U.S. citizens killed by ICE in January, held a press conference deploring the Trump DOJ’s conduct since the shooting of their son.“Our son was murdered. We all saw it. And the lack of cooperation is baffling, it’s disappointing and reprehensible,” his father said.A Confounding Read: DOGE EditionWired: A 28-Year-Old DOGE Operative Gutted USAID. HR Had No Record of Him Working There

item.title: GitHub Octoverse 2026
item.author: Simon Willison
item.content:encoded: I'm at GitHub Universe today (GitHub gave me a free ticket through their "GitHub Stars" program). EVP Jay Parikh just announced this year's Octoverse report, and highlighted these numbers in particular:This is a pretty stark representation of the impact of agentic engineering on GitHub. In 2026, merged pull requests tripled in less than a year to 220 million per month. Commits more than tripled to 7.38 billion per month, with most of that increase in the second half of this year. New repository rate doubled this year, to 30.3 million per month.The report includes new numbers by industry, and breaks out numbers for repositories that involve "interoperability or reverse engineering". The methodology section includes notes about how they did this: Top countries by pushes to public repositories, adjusted by profile location. Pushes from each country were summed across the Octoverse year. To adjust for biases caused by VPN usage, LLM classification was used to extract the ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 code from the profiles of GitHub users who contributed pushes during this period [...]. Public repositories created 2022 to 2026 were sorted into NAICS sectors by a fine-tuned multilingual embedding model using name, description, topics, and README, from random samples per year. [...]. Counts public repositories created each year whose name, description, topics, or README mention interoperability or reverse engineering, or related terms, such as clean room implementation, drop-in replacement, or protocol re-implementation.

item.title: Some Theories About That Nude Scene In ‘You Can See Everything’
item.author: Israel Daramola
item.content:encoded: is the movie event of the fall. Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s documentary has proved to be a potent mixture of zeitgeisty cultural insight and its own discourse-generating machine about the value and nature of documentary filmmaking. The screenings have been sold out, and everyone wants to discuss and argue about each scene in minute detail. It is a testament to the film that even given a three-hour runtime, basically every moment feels like it could be ripped out and discussed as though it were the skeleton key for the entire premise. But there is one particular scene that I can’t let go of, and that I really feel needs to be examined at length in order to unearth certain truths about the film and the participants involved. That is the scene in which Billy Evans, Elizabeth Holmes’s partner and the father of her two children, shows hog.Obviously, I am not alone in wanting to discuss this scene, which occurs when Evans decides to shower in front of the filmmakers.It has inspired much conversation, including with Oppenheim himself, who confirmed that the scene was Billy’s idea and that he just did it in front of the cameras, no prodding or even discussion necessary beforehand. But this raises the obvious question: Why? What was the thought process here? And what does it say about Billy in general? We are only left to speculate and theorize. Please understand that this is purely for the sake of journalism. Theory No. 1: Billy is proud of his penis and wants to show it off.

item.title: The Limbo Plays
item.author: bounce+2edd00.7bdc18-5mr68b7cb43ac2h04ai5=kill-the-newsletter.com@m.ghost.io
item.content:encoded: It started to feel familiar in the 11th inning. A first baseman drew a walk. A pinch-runner took his place, then stole second. The Rays, down 3-0 and staring down the end, got a whiff of what could be.World Series Game 4 chanted the words itself, really. Broadcaster Joe Davis just identified the apparition that was summoned: Dave Roberts, the 2004 Red Sox, David Ortiz, the only comeback from down 3-0 in baseball history. This runner — Jorge Mateo, in for Yandy Diaz — didn’t end up scoring. But like the first chapter of that Red Sox comeback, this game ended in a 12th-inning walk-off that preserved the seeds of Rays hope and Brewers doubt.The Game 4 moments that were and weren’t to be are suspended in a reality between Good and Bad, History and Forgotten, Something and Nothing.The vast majority end up in the bin of Nothing, tossed out with the loser’s championship T-shirts. As detailed by Sarah Langs, the Rays are just the 11th team out of 44 in MLB postseason history to even force a Game 5 after going down 3-0. Only four of those came in the World Series, and none have successfully extended it to a Game 6. The 2024 Yankees avoided a sweep, with Anthony Volpe hitting a pivotal homer in Game 4, only to succumb to the Dodgers in Game 5. Prior to that, the last World Series team down 3-0 to even win Game 4 was in 1970.For now, the tension is in our blindness. We don’t if the plays that riveted us late last night and early this morning are Big Papis or little Volpes. Rays fans have to hold onto them, hoping they last. Brewers fans have to live with them, willing them to go away.While they mean the most and the least to us, let’s rank the plays from World Series Game 4 that could turn the most pungent with time.8. Rays let a Jake Bauers foul pop-up drop, but strike him out — top of the 10th inningIt feels like the Brewers have been feasting off their opponents’ mistakes, growing more powerful with each slip-up. When Liam Hicks and Junior Caminero stumbled into a classic blooper reel drop, it gave the Brewers an extra opportunity with a full count and two outs in the 10th. Imminent doom, a Bauers homer, felt like the only outcome that could follow. But it didn’t.This was one of four times after reaching the 2-2 deadlock that the Brewers left a man on base, and one of two times Bauers made the third out.7. Chandler Simpson catches Garrett Mitchell’s fly ball at the wall — top 9thSimpson’s grab was visually pleasing, but ultimately was never really precarious for the Rays despite the elevated tenor of the broadcast. Still, if Simpson’s outfield chops had been at his dreadful 2025 levels, the runner taking off from first might very well have scored.6. Junior Caminero dodges David Hamilton’s tag, scores on his errant throw — bottom 4thThe earliest entrant into limbo gave the Rays a 2-1 lead. Jonny DeLuca’s grounder and Caminero’s, uh, unconventional baserunning decision put Brewers third baseman David Hamilton in bind set to fast forward. Surprised to have the opportunity for a tag play, he went after Caminero but missed, then botched the throw to first in his haste to secure an out.Hamilton rectified the score with a homer the following inning, limiting the mistake’s memory potential.5. Jonny DeLuca singles in the tying run off Shane Drohan — bottom 12thUp in the count 1-2 against the least imposing hitter he had faced thus far, Brewers rookie pitcher Shane Drohan needed this. He made an OK pitch — cutter, 90 mph, bending to the outside corner. It just wasn’t sharp enough. DeLuca poked at it and made solid contact up the middle, at which point the game was tied, there were still no outs and the un-double-uppable Simpson coming to the plate. Drohan’s surprise cameo felt cooked.4. Brewers manager Pat Murphy pulls Aaron Ashby — bottom 11thDrohan, a rookie lefty who had pitched once in the past month before entering a World Series-clinching save situation, didn’t have it. Probably was never primed to have it in that moment.The Brewers got to Drohan by being aggressive earlier in the game. Murphy went to closer Trevor Megill in the eighth inning to neutralize the threat of Yandy Diaz, a right-hander, with two outs and no one on base. After just that one out, he turned to Ashby to start the ninth inning against left-handed hitter Jonathan Aranda, relying on the flamethrowing lefty’s ability to stretch multiple innings if needed.Ashby did, carving through 2 1/3 perfect innings. But eventually Murphy reached the limit of his comfort zone with a pitcher he wants available for whatever may come next.“The velo was down quite a bit,” Murphy told reporters afterward. “We can tell when Ashby’s ball doesn’t have the same movement and the same finish. So it was time.”Having burned through his usual leverage options, Murphy went to Antonio Senzatela, then summoned Drohan after Senzatela had faced four batters, getting two outs and falling victim to a play still to come on the list.I don’t know if Ashby was good for five more outs. And Murphy couldn’t have known that Cooper Pratt was about to smash the biggest homer of his life, that a potential finish line was approaching. The options remaining were such, and Ashby’s October dominance is at such historic levels, that the decision will raise an eyebrow or two for as long as it lives on.3. Ben Williamson chops a walk-off single over first base — bottom 12thCalled off the bench, the last bat available to Rays manager Kevin Cash had to make contact, at the bare minimum. And he did.2. Cooper Pratt caught stealing by a whisker — top 9thAndrew Vaughn is this game’s man who wasn’t there. A dangerous hitter relegated to bench duty by Bauers’s breakout, Vaughn was pinch-hitting when Pratt took off for second.The throw and tag were a sort of combination miracle, with catcher Liam Hicks’ ball tailing just into the path of Pratt’s sliding glove, trailing behind his body. He was safe but for the cosmic grace of a baseball god that wanted more baseball.Yet the same speed that allowed for the steal might have allowed Pratt to score without it. Vaughn is a strong contact hitter. Even though his power is superior against lefty pitchers — he was facing right-handed Rays closer Bryan Baker — Vaughn struck out only 17.7% of the time against righties this year and batted .285. He also reached base at a .369 clip against right-handers. The chances of a ball in play, or a free pass to second, were pretty good.Wasting Vaughn’s appearance, which ended immediately without an official at-bat, was a missed opportunity.1. Caminero reaches on a bounced throw from Joey Ortiz that Bauers can’t pick — bottom 12thErrors are like a toothache. You can’t resist prodding, checking if it still hurts. Yep, it does.This one was charged to Ortiz, a superlative defender who fielded a bounding grounder cautiously against the lumbering Caminero, then threw a one-hopper that Bauers couldn’t handle at first. It ended Senzatela’s outing, put a runner on and set off the spiral that took the Brewers from championship clinch to sphincter clenched."There's no excuse," Ortiz said postgame. "Not one at all. I should make that play every (bleeping) time.”You could easily debit the mistake to Bauers, mentally. It might be an in-between hop, but it was a one-hop throw on line, with the runner nowhere near the bag. It was the sort of split-second mistake the Brewers usually churn into runs. It’s the sort of split-second mistake that can last forever, or fade into nothing by Friday. Until then, it’s a raw nerve. ⚾️The part where I ask for your supportThis is a project by and for the passionate. It’s undertaken on mornings, nights and weekends. On trains and planes and holidays. Around the responsibilities of a full-time job.I recognize the building subscription creep, the proliferation of good writers operating independently and charging independently in an unforgiving industry. I don’t expect The Bandwagon to be your only destination for baseball writing, but I hope it makes your emotional investment more enriching.

item.title: The Cheesecake Factory aesthetic won’t save MAGA
item.content:encoded: As soon as former president Barack Obama described Donald Trump’s aesthetic assault on the White House as “looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory,” the current president did what he does best: seethe. Ever since Obama’s weekend joke at an Ohio rally, Trump has been complaining non-stop. On Sunday, he posted on Truth Social that Obama was “a grossly incompetent President” and accused him of “campaigning for a Muslim Brotherhood Jihadist.” The following day, he told reporters that Obama is “not a smart guy.”At a campaign rally to shore up Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith’s fledgling re-election bid in Mississippi, Trump chewed on his grievance even more. After calling the Cheesecake Factory a “successful company,” he launched into a confusing defense of his garish White House redecoration. “A guy like Obama,” he said, “doesn’t understand the White House has to be clean, pristine, beautiful.”There are a lot of words for what Trump has done to the White House, but “clean,” “pristine” and “beautiful” are not among them. The president has covered every corner of the Oval Office with cheap-looking gold-paint and elaborate carvings. The once-stately decor now has a cluttered and claustrophobic feel — an embarrassing departure from the dignified appearance that all modern presidents, regardless of party, adhered to, which had a simplicity meant to reflect the sober responsibilities of the citizen-leader. But to understand why Trump clings to words like “clean” to describe his chaotic and overwhelming design impulses, it helps to look at how authoritarian movements like MAGA relate to kitsch. As I wrote in 2019 about Hallmark films, schmaltz creates a safe space the right can escape to — a cavern where they can wallow in fake feelings and nostalgia, without having to face complex realities that might challenge them. What makes something “clean” or “pristine,” then, isn’t actual clean lines or even a lack of clutter. It’s a conformist fantasy where everyone is white and straight and knows their place in the social pecking order. For Trump in particular, “clean” and “pristine” are racially charged words, building on his long history of equating whiteness with purity and diversity with disorder. Trump and his fellow MAGA leaders are engaging in performative outrage over Obama’s comments. On Monday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, whose net worth hovers around $600 million, ventured to a Cheesecake Factory in suburban Maryland, where he participated in a photoshoot. It was just the latest in a series of MAGA’s long list of kitsch-related tantrums, which have seen them feign enthusiasm for middlebrow corporate products as evidence of their identity as “real” Americans, unlike those snooty Democrats with their fancy mustards. This schtick has worked plenty of times to rally the MAGA base because, in this world, “elitism” has nothing to do with money or status. Instead, it’s a code word for the racialized paranoias that unite small-minded white people across the class divide. Just last year, MAGA propagandists got a huge boost when another restaurant chain, Cracker Barrel, tried to change its logo from the overly busy image of a man leaning on a barrel to something more minimalist — or, one might say, “clean” and “pristine.” This update was spun as a subterranean assault on white culture, an effort to smuggle in those “elite” and urbane values into the restaurants cornpone comforts, a place Fox News Grandpa used to feel safe from having to hear hip-hop music in the parking lot. This time around, my sense is that the Cracker Barrel Panic of 2025 cannot be remade into a Cheesecake Factory October Surprise that will save the Republicans in this midterm cycle. I’m a Cheesecake Factory virgin, but my gracious Bluesky followers and old-fashioned internet research revealed that the restaurant’s marketing is a lot different from the white-bread Christian brunch vibe that Bessent and other MAGA leaders seem to assume it must have. Apparently, it’s a deliberate, self-aware camp rather than dime-store kitsch, appealing to a younger, more modern audience that doesn’t take itself seriously. The Cheesecake Factory is supposed to be silly, which is why its fans don’t think its look is appropriate for the White House. Its famously long and decadent menu is also part of the joke. But at the same time, it reflects the expanding tastes of a diversifying nation, borrowing flavors from all over the world.It’s not just that the Cheesecake Factory’s wonton chips and chicken shawarma appeal to a different crowd than the chicken-and-gravy offerings at Cracker Barrel. The distinction is a sign of the way that middle America is moving on in general from the rigidly white, rural and suburban conformity so valorized by the Trump administration. The president and his acolytes, particularly during his second term, have been explicit about narrowing their view of what a “great” America should look like. The administration puts out a steady stream of propaganda envisioning a country composed solely of Aryan-looking nuclear families dressed in old-fashioned clothes. But it’s not clear if this has much appeal beyond some elderly white conservatives at Trump rallies, nostalgic for childhoods spent watching “Leave It To Beaver,” or the small number of bitter young men who let social media tell them it was easier to get a wife in the bygone days.After his narrow win in 2024, Trump and his aides like Stephen Miller convinced themselves that the result was a resounding victory for his fascist fantasy. The president’s rapidly plummeting approval ratings, though, tell a different story: He mostly won because swing voters have short memories and thought he might make good on his promise to bring down prices. Instead, they got more inflation. Likewise, Trump and Miller thought they won on a “no more tamales” platform. But as it turns out, Americans just want those tamales to be a little more affordable. In fact, Trump’s policies are now even threatening to take away free chips and salsa. In the process, we’re learning that, for most Americans in 2026, this traditional Tex-Mex appetizer is considered as all-American as, well, cheesecake.During the 2024 campaign, Trump’s love of kitsch mostly endeared him to his voters, who saw themselves in his corny preferences for the musical “Cats” or faux-baroque interior design. The president may be rich, but he connected with his fans in their shared resentment of smarter tastes, which require the very curiosity and intellectual engagement that the president fears. Instead, as Sam Adler-Bell wrote in New York magazine at the time, they craved the “As the popularity of Bad Bunny at the Super Bowl reminded us, the escapist fantasies of authoritarians don’t appeal to most Americans. It was just easier for some to look the other way when there wasn’t a war in Iran, rapidly rising gas prices and paramilitary troops grabbing grandmothers off the street. In good times, kitsch feels like harmless fluff, making its long history of being used for fascist propaganda easier to ignore. But when the president is more worried about redecorating the White House in his schmaltzy self-image than he is about the real struggles of Americans, the kitsch stops being so funny.Love it or hate it, the Cheesecake Factory cannot save the MAGA movement — no matter how many Cabinet officials get photographed in front of it.

item.title: Everybody hates Pat McAfee
item.content:encoded: here’s an election next week, which means that you and I are currently being bombarded, ceaselessly, with unwanted voices. Here’s one such voice that, alas, we cannot vote out of office come Tuesday:That’s ESPN commentator and one-man pandemic Pat McAfee. If you’re unfamiliar with McAfee’s work, I envy you. No seriously, if I could trade bodies with you right now, I’d do it in a heartbeat. I don’t even care if you’re 85 and dying of gonorrhea, I’d still do it. That’s just how much I can’t stand Pat McAfee.Article continues below this adAnd I’m hardly alone. The clip you see up above is McAfee’s response to the harassment (NOTE: term used with ultimate generosity) he endured before co-hosting “College GameDay” for the four-letter live from the Salt Lake City campus of the University of Utah this past Saturday. McAfee is a known quantity to college football fans by now. They know that he’s the former Indianapolis Colts punter who abruptly retired from pro football to take a job for the chauvinist liberation front that is Barstool Sports. They know that McAfee parlayed his Barstool gig into a high-profile radio show where he paid Steelers QB and emotional cancer Aaron Rodgers literal millions of dollars to come on the air with him to muse at length about the dangers of getting vaccinated. And they know that ESPN, desperate to appeal to teenage gambling addicts, scooped up McAfee to become the de facto face of their network, now to the tune of $60 million a year.They also know that McAfee absolutely, unequivocally sucks.That’s why, prior to McAfee’s arrival in SLC on Saturday, a few Utah students made a short video of Utes fans doing their best McAfee impressions, which the university found harmless enough to post to its Instagram account (since deleted). I cannot stress how gentle of a ribbing McAfee gets in this video. Even Mitt Romney thinks these kids could have gone in harder on him. But McAfee himself found the video incredibly distressing, so much so that he told his studio bros afterward that he feared for his life going into the belly of the beast!Article continues below this ad“The university puts that out? Like as I’m about to go out and do an infomercial for the place? And then I’m walking in front of thousands of these people. This is how the university feels about it? It’s an uncomfortable feeling … I thought to myself, has anything, like, really scary happened at a college gathering in the state of Utah recently?”McAfee there is referring to the late Charlie Kirk, who was fatally shot while on stage at a campus event at Utah Valley University over a year ago. For reference, the UVU campus is located some 40 miles away from Salt Lake. So why would McAfee instantly think of Kirk getting killed right after a handful of mean and nasty college kids taunted him for always taking his shirt off? Well it’s because, like Kirk, McAfee is a self-absorbed asshole.Article continues below this adAnd even more galling than McAfee’s inability to tolerate low-ABV jokes from a bunch of Utahns is the fact that ESPN took his security risk comments at face value:“The safety and security of our on-air team, crew and fans is paramount at ‘College GameDay.’ We are committed to ensuring a safe environment, and given the very real threats that members of our team face, we take issues involving their safety seriously. We support Pat and recognize the very real and valid concerns he has around safety and security.”According to a report in Front Office Sports, the network apparently feared for McAfee’s safety on the road immediately after Kirk had been shot dead, and the FBI even advised McAfee to wear a bulletproof vest afterward. Although one supposes that McAfee would have simply torn that vest off while on the air to brandish a couple of “guns” of his own.But even if McAfee was justified to feel skittish about appearing in public crowds, it’s pretty telling how ESPN responded to his concerns with such an outlandish show of force. Because what’s so valid about this man’s safety concerns compared with the concerns of the women he works with, or the women he’s endangered? Are they more valid than the VERY real safety concerns of “GameDay” field reporter Holly Rowe, who was the subject of an AI-generated video of University of Texas head coach Steve Sarkisian punching her in the face ... a video that future fifth-round pick Arch Manning openly laughed about at an official UT presser? Or Mary Kate Cornett, that Ole Miss freshman? After McAfee slandered her on the air to an oblivious Adam Schefter, Cornett’s home was swatted, with armed police knocking down her door. Were either Cornett or Rowe afforded the institutional, DEFCON 1 level response that McAfee got from ESPN (and from the University of Utah!)? Of course they didn’t. That’s because they’re women, and because ESPN didn’t pay either of them $60 million a year to be professionally unfunny 20 hours a day. Even in Donald Trump’s America, the injustice on display is blinding.Article continues below this adThere will be no consequences for McAfee from all this. “College GameDay” has enjoyed record ratings since he joined the program (I’d argue this is because college football, not Pat McAfee, is more popular than ever), and ESPN already stood by McAfee in the wake of the Cornett scandal. As far as that network is concerned, there’s big money to be had in cheap trolling. It’s why they pay Stephen A. Smith millions of dollars a year too, after all.And so, you and I must bear witness to yet another unremarkable man in Pat McAfee failing upward while also clumsily making a martyr of himself. This whiny tank top will never be held accountable for his worst offenses, and he’ll always be shielded by the empty suits working above him. The whole thing is an insult to my intelligence and yours. And I already get my intelligence insulted on a daily basis in this country. Do I really need it from ESPN, too? I’m just trying to watch some football without some wildly self-absorbed, MAGA-coded jackass constantly trying to reach through the TV to suck my brains out. And yet ESPN can’t even afford me, or a handful of clever kids in Utah, that basic courtesy. So I hope that every other “GameDay” crowd from here on out makes Pat McAfee even more uncomfortable than he already is. After all, it’s only fair to return the favor. Article continues below this adHearst, the parent company of SFGATE, owns 18% of ESPN.

item.title: Everything Is Content
item.author: Mark Asch
item.content:encoded: Given that we’re all being filmed and filming ourselves all the time, how can it be exploitative to put someone on camera? The two movies this fall directed by Lance Oppenheim, and (which he co-directed with Nathan Fielder), explore voluntary surveillance and the ethics of non-fiction. Together, they share an interest in the violence and vulnerability of seeing and being seen in a sickly recursive popular culture.Oppenheim was precocious: His first feature-length film, , with an executive-producer credit from Darren Aronofsky, premiered at Sundance on January 26, 2020, Oppenheim’s 24th birthday. He was fresh out of Harvard, where he studied under the film diarist Ross McElwee. At a time when consumers were buying new, smaller cameras and making home movies, McElwee turned his life into a sprawling documentary project, interweaving personal milestones with larger social concerns across, such as his masterpiece, the 1985 New South dating odyssey , and 1993’s , about the death of his father and the birth of his son. By the time Oppenheim met him, McElwee was at work on , his most recent film, which draws from his many hours of footage of his son from his birth to his tragic early death, and in which McElwee expresses remorse over casting his family as characters that he misinterpreted.In one way or another, Oppenheim’s films also live with the consequences of throwing people into the spotlight. The feature-length documentaries he made in his 20s, , , and the three-part HBO series , were about aging and loneliness: retirees in The Villages, a sprawling community in Florida, spending their golden years indulging in precarious hedonism; compulsive sperm donors; the Lear-like elderly “king” of a Texas Renaissance Faire, and the children and employees vying to inherit it, should he ever step down. Oppenheim’s subjects are all, in one way or another, , but they’re fully integrated into a uniquely heightened aesthetic scheme. Intense conversations occur in tight, frame-filling closeups, under stylized lighting and with faces tinted in aggressive color grading that strains against accepted notions of verisimilitude, as if these people are offering up their lives to the camera and losing control of the narrative. Shot-reverse shot setups suggest the conventional camera coverage and editing rhythms of a narrative film; no moment of these characters’ lives is so abject that it isn’t being filmed with an audience in mind.

item.title: Connor Hellebuyck Is A Devil
item.author: Lauren Theisen
item.content:encoded: Connor Hellebuyck was in purgatory, and now he's living it up in Hell. It sounds like he preferred both to Winnipeg. After 11 seasons with the Jets, the three-time Vezina-winning goalie played his first game for another NHL team, earning a win for the New Jersey Devils in Dallas on Tuesday night.Hellebuyck got to the States by forcing his way out of Manitoba, and the 33-year-old's status as the President's favorite player, a playoff choker, and a possible tender-in-decline as he comes off his worst season since the beginning of his career all serve to temper the excitement of his move to Jersey. But goalie was a hole that the Devils desperately needed filled, and the modest package they sent in return—basically the 20-goal scorer Dawson Mercer and the kid they drafted 12th overall this year, Alexander Command—means they should be a better team right away.The pressure is certainly on Jersey to show some real improvement. After a promising first-round playoff win over the Rangers in 2023—their first series win since advancing to the Stanley Cup Final in 2012—a mix of injuries and plateaued youngsters have kept the Devils from making any real noise. It was supposed to be a new era for Jersey when Jack Hughes and his fellow kids broke out, but so far the team's most important players have yet to prove they can lead a contender. However, there are reasons to be optimistic about their depth, if not their top-end talent. Raiding Nashville for the all-around solid Luke Evangelista, who's still got a high ceiling at just 24, was perhaps my favorite move of the offseason, while another winger, rookie Amadeus Lombardi, is one of my top newcomers to watch for reasons that are only about 80 percent related to his name. (His siblings are Symphony and Ulysses, by the way.) The most glaring weakness has been in goal, with Jacob Markström failing to be the answer in the last two seasons. So the buyck stops here.

item.title: Paleovirology: How HIV Started a Century Before Anyone Noticed
item.author: Jason Kottke
item.content:encoded: I’ve been vaguely aware for awhile that researchers had traced the origins of HIV/AIDS back to Sub-Saharan Africa. But I didn’t know the whole story, which turns out to be really fascinating.For decades, one man was blamed for bringing AIDS to America. But the “Patient Zero” story was wrong. This is the story of how genetic detective work traced HIV’s true origins — from chimpanzees in Central Africa to a global pandemic — and how science unraveled one of the biggest myths in modern medicine.Disappointingly, they didn’t list any of their sources for the video. I poked around a little and found a book called The Origins of AIDS that a Science magazine review called:Extensively referenced, the well-written book reads like a detective story, while at the same time providing a didactic introduction to epidemiology and evolutionary genetics. As far as the origins of AIDS are concerned, unless some completely new evidence emerges, it will be difficult to come up with a better explanation than Pepin’s.The YouTube comments are worth a read too, filled with remarks from those who lived through the early years of the pandemic or knew someone who did (or someone who didn’t).Had a gay uncle who lived in San Francisco in the 80s and 90s. He would get so upset when he talked about HIV/AIDS. He lost so many friends to the virus. When I went to visit him in the 2000s, we visited 27 graves over the course of a weekend and laid flowers. Rest in peace to all those young people.I worked in blood banking at Cedars -Sinai Medical Center in Los Angeles. It was policy to freeze blood samples from patients that expired due an unknown cause. Once the HIV test was approved the samples were tested and some were reactive to it. The samples were collected over decades, going back to the 1950s.I have family who were foreign hospital workers in the now-DRC in the 1970s, where what we call AIDS was known as the Slims because of how the patients wasted away and died. People on the ground knew there was something going around, but they didn’t have the resources to figure it out.

item.title: Objection, your honor
item.author: Jason Koebler
item.content:encoded: You've probably heard, at this point, about the big changes coming to Meta's AI scraping terms for business accounts. Nieman Lab had that scoop, and since then, small businesses, journalists, and artists using Meta products like Instagram have been raising the alarm. But if you're in the EU or UK, you might be in luck and can object to that use of your data, as some users have pointed out.Earlier this month, Meta updated its commercial terms of use for business accounts to allow it to “use any content from such domains, web pages, or URLs to provide, develop, improve, research, train, and maintain the integrity of” Meta’s products. Many artists and small business owners that rely on Instagram and Facebook are livid at Meta granting itself permission to use their content, including from websites simply connected to their Meta accounts, to train AI. But for users in the United Kingdom and European Union, for now, there’s a way to object.Meta in its , and Nieman Lab first reported on the change. The update was originally set to go into effect on October 30, but following backlash, Meta changed the effective date to November 20. Adding to the confusion, Meta then removed the word “train” from a list of allowed use cases, , and limited those uses to “advertising and business products,” where previously it said that data would be used for all Meta products. Those terms still allow Meta plenty of leeway for scraping users’ data to develop its products, however.Several users based in the UK and EU have explained how to object on Instagram. On mobile: by clicking the three lines on their account, going to the privacy center, and clicking “object,” which goes to a form that asks users to write why they are objecting to their data being used. They received an email from Meta saying their objections were approved. On the podcast this week, we talk Flock CEO’s leaked police conference audio and Sam’s piece about Marissa Mayer’s latest meltdown. Subscribe wherever you get your pods. The New York Times has an antisocial aversion to linking: Another day, another the-New-York-Times-isn’t-linking controversy. The specifics here almost don’t matter because this happens seemingly every day, but basically the New York Times investigation about chemical plant polluters under the Trump administration was covered in much the same way by Hunterbrook, a news outlet fused with a hedge fund. The article—which led the Sunday print edition—uses similar photos, some of the same sources, and covers similar ground to Hunterbrook’s earlier investigation from February, with no acknowledgment or link whatsoever. After the cofounder of Hunterbrook rightfully ranted about this on X, the added an acknowledgment (but no link!!!) toward the bottom of the story. Puck’s Dylan Byers has a good rundown about what happened, which includes parts of a three-paragraph ’ spokesperson statement explaining at length why they don’t think they have to link. This is extremely antisocial, deranged behavior and it’s ridiculous that the is still getting away with this. Bottom line: I’m sure the was already working on this story, what with their massive newsroom. Even so, they got beat, and they should link. Journalism awards need to stop looking the other way when big outlets do this. This has happened to us many times and it actually does matter for smaller outlets and links are free. Let’s try them!TIL that a gigantic military ship, the SS United, is going to be purposefully sunk to be turned into an “artificial reef.” Scuba divers seem quite excited. I didn’t really know that this was a thing that was done, but maybe I’m a rube.Ransomware scam mitigation scammer: A company that promised to help victims of ransomware (for a fee) was indicted by the feds, according to ProPublica and a Department of Justice affidavit. The original investigation that led to this was published by ProPublica back in 2019 but is still worth a read; there are so many of these companies that prey on victims of cyberattacks, sextortion campaigns, etc.CIA whistleblower John Kirakou is doing sponcon for Kalshi, writing “I spent 15 years at the CIA trying to figure out what was going to happen next in the world. Now Kalshi is finding new ways to put a price on those predictions. This partnership between Kalshi and S&P Dow Jones Indices is fascinating.” C’mon, man. A Roblox scraper has been grabbing more than a hundred gigabytes of data from a 3D modeling community, including more than 60 GB of adult content from a section of the site called “SmutBase.” “We don't think Roblox set out to collect adult content, and we have no evidence that any of it reached a model or a product. The scrapes were likely automated. But that is exactly the problem: as far as our logs show, nobody checked. A crawler working for a company whose platform tens of millions of children use was pointed at an adult site, and it took explicit models without telling them apart from anything else,” Open3DLabs wrote in a blog post about the scraping. “For a company being sued by several US states over child safety, ‘our AI team bulk-downloaded an adult site without looking’ is not a good position to be in.”

item.title: Another Israel Election Update—Fractured Electorate Absurdity Edition
item.author: Josh Marshall
item.source: Josh Marshall – TPM – Talking Points Memo
item.content:encoded: This is the weekly, free edition of The Backchannel. If you’d like to receive the free edition of The Backchannel in your inbox, you can subscribe here.Here’s a brief follow up on yesterday’s Israeli election now that the actual vote count and results are coming into view. We began with exit polls suggesting that the “change” bloc had secured slightly more seats than the Netanyahu bloc — 52 to 50 seats — with the two Arab parties getting a historically high 18 or 19 seats. Then the exits started to shift to the Netanyahu bloc and Likud officials were claiming he had been dramatically underestimated and would get upwards of 60 seat and perhaps even a majority. The actual results were lopsided in Netanyahu’s direction but as they’ve been counted they’ve trended down. Now with 86% of the vote counted it’s down to 53 seats Netanyahu bloc, 48 for the “change” bloc and 19 for the two Arab parties. If the trend continues, the Netanyahu bloc might fall one or two seats lower but I have no insight whether the votes that remain will continue that downward trend.

item.title: The Colts Are Holding A Fire Sale, And You’re Invited!
item.author: Drew Magary
item.content:encoded: The NFL trade deadline is two weeks from now, but Indianapolis Colts owner Carlie Irsay-Gordon has no interest in waiting that long to blow up her team. At some point during her team’s loss in Minnesota on Sunday, Irsay-Gordon probably wrote “Fuck this” into her notebook, and WHOA HEY. There goes longtime general manager Chris Ballard out the door, followed shortly thereafter by perennial All-Pro guard Quenton Nelson (to Seattle for a 2027 third-rounder and 2028 fifth-rounder), followed immediately by DT DeForest Buckner (to San Francisco for a 2027 fourth-round pick). Suddenly we got ourselves a big ol’ trade party! Which other Colts will get uprooted, and will other middling franchises will now commence fire sales of their own? Folks, Arif and I revel in all of those possibilities on this week’s episode of https://art19.com/shows/the-distraction/episodes/d2c042fd-ed58-4bf5-8afe-8cad45944dae Of course, there’s plenty more to talk about. Arif and I lead off the podcast with a story about Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed giving our podcast an 11th-hour stiffarm. From there, we segue into talking about the undefeated Vikings, who don’t even respect themselves at this point. We also try to sort out why the Houston Texans’ seemingly all-world defense has fallen off a cliff, we speculate on a potentially lingering cold war between Ravens QB Lamar Jackson and his team’s upper management, and we preview a fairly attractive Week 8 slate. As always, there is ZERO talk of gambling, fantasy football, or any of that other tedious bullshit. This is , where we only care about the good stuff.

item.title: If You're In the UK or EU, Here's How to Object to Meta's AI Training
item.author: Samantha Cole
item.content:encoded: Earlier this month, Meta updated its commercial terms of use for business accounts to allow it to “use any content from such domains, web pages, or URLs to provide, develop, improve, research, train, and maintain the integrity of” Meta’s products. Many artists and small business owners that rely on Instagram and Facebook are livid at Meta granting itself permission to use their content, including from websites simply connected to their Meta accounts, to train AI. But for users in the United Kingdom and European Union, for now, there’s a way to object.Meta in its , and Nieman Lab first reported on the change. The update was originally set to go into effect on October 30, but following backlash, Meta changed the effective date to November 20. Adding to the confusion, Meta then removed the word “train” from a list of allowed use cases, , and limited those uses to “advertising and business products,” where previously it said that data would be used for all Meta products. Those terms still allow Meta plenty of leeway for scraping users’ data to develop its products, however.EU users’ personal data rights are governed by the General Data Protection Regulation and the AI Act. , which became enforceable in 2018, requires explicit consent to use personal data. This includes the right to object to one’s data being used. The AI Act, which went into effect in 2024, dictates how AI companies can use personal data, and how people can opt in or out, that they can withdraw consent at any time. The UK has its own . The European Commission : “The GDPR rules only apply to personal data about individuals; they do not govern data about companies or any other legal entities. However, information in relation to companies may constitute personal data where it allows the identification of a natural person.” Several users based in the UK and EU have explained how to object on Instagram. Instagram a walkthrough of how they did it on mobile: by clicking the three lines on their account, going to the privacy center, and clicking “object,” which goes to a form that asks users to write why they are objecting to their data being used. They received an email from Meta saying their objection was approved. Instagram user jenniqueart posted a similar walkthrough with the same results. My Meta accounts are based in the US, but using a VPN to locate my IP address in London, I could see options in my Meta privacy settings that would let me object to the use of my information by Meta AI. To get there on desktop with a VPN on, I went to my account , clicked “Submit a privacy rights request” at the bottom, selected Instagram, clicked “How can I object to the processing of my information?” and got to a page where I could choose to object to the use of my information for Meta AI or third parties, which were two separate options.When my location is based in the US, these options don't appear.When I clicked through the option to “object to the use of my information for Meta AI,” however, it returned an error page that said “This form is only available to people in certain regions.” GDPR is meant to apply to wherever someone is located at the time, but since this objection applies to the preferences of one account, it might be based on where the account was created. I tried again located in Belgium and got the same results. I’ve asked Meta to clarify. As many have already pointed out in the comments on UK and EU users who’ve posted walkthroughs, these objection steps aren’t available to people outside of those countries, and as Meta continuously changes its platform, these steps might not work for everyone always. Unless something changes before November 20, the rest of us are screwed.

item.title: Unsatisfied With Employing Just One Evil Kicker, Chiefs Sign Justin Tucker
item.author: Tom Ley
item.content:encoded: The Kansas City Chiefs have found themselves in a pickle. Their longtime kicker, Harrison Butker, kind of sucks. He has missed five of his 16 field goal attempts so far this season, including two in Sunday's 20-3 loss to the Seahawks. This scenario, in which a once-reliable kicker stops being useful, is one teams deal with all the time, and it comes with a relatively easy solution: You cut the guy and sign one of the many unemployed kickers floating around the league's margins. Butker isn't just any kicker, though. He's also a conservative freak and a misogynist, which means that the Chiefs could make themselves far less odious by cutting him. You can't just let someone that awful and despised walk out the door without replacing at least some of what he brings to the table, though. Which brings us to today's news: The Chiefs have signed Justin Tucker to the practice squad.According to ESPN, Tucker has been signed to Kansas City's practice squad to "serve as insurance" to Butker. The message the Chiefs are sending to their struggling kicker is clear: You think we can't find a guy who is even more of an awful person than you are? Think again.Tucker, who turns 37 next month, has been out of the NFL since 2025. The Ravens released him that spring after 16 massage therapists from eight different spas in the Baltimore area accused Tucker of sexual misconduct. The Baltimore Banner published multiplestories in which massage therapists who worked at these spas described Tucker exposing his erect penis, brushing his fingers against their thighs, and leaving ejaculate on the massage table. Tucker received a 10-game suspension for violating the NFL's personal conduct policy, which he served last season.
