item.title: Friends Still Don’t Let Friends Watch the Early Vote
item.author: Josh Marshall
item.source: Josh Marshall – TPM – Talking Points Memo
item.content:encoded: Earlier this month I wrote a piece entitled Friends Don’t Let Friends Watch the Early Vote. I wanted to re-up that recommendation, notwithstanding the fact that I have kept an eye on these findings, as I always do. The simple fact is that all of these efforts amount to figuring out how big a share of the pie you have before you know how big the pie is. That doesn’t mean you can’t glean anything by analyzing these things or that the knowledgable people doing it are silly or mendacious. They’re not. It’s just that you can’t draw any firm conclusions from it and our desire to see what we want in these entrails greatly outweighs the hints we can get from them. As I noted before, this is especially the case because the partisan dynamics of who votes early, in person, by mail, on Election Day, etc., is in so much flux.

item.title: Dangerous and Absurd: The Story of Donald Trump
item.author: David Kurtz
item.content:encoded: A Ridiculous Threat to DemocracyBefore getting into the state of play in the two major election interference cases in California and Alaska, I want to acknowledge an inherent tension in covering President Trump’s attack on free and fair midterm elections.It’s a tension that should be familiar to anyone who has lived through the Trump era: The severity of his threat to democracy is matched only by his pure absurdity.The temptation to pick one lane or the other rather than straddle both lanes is strong. You may want to dismiss the entire midterm attack as an absurd scheme not worthy of you attention; or you may want to light your hair on fire about the coming fascism and ignore the inherent weaknesses in Trump’s desperate effort to stave off a loss of both chambers of Congress.It’s hard to entertain those competing impulses, but the truth is the attack on the midterms is both dangerous and ridiculous, like Trump himself.The Latest on California …: We’re awaiting a decision from the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals on the Trump DOJ’s effort to force California to segregate and not yet count mail-in ballots from voters who appear on a dubious administration-generated list of what it claims contains some 20,000 alleged noncitizen voters.The appeals court took the rare step of hearing oral arguments via Zoom as it considers the Trump DOJ’s long-shot appeal in a case where the lower court hadn’t even ruled yet. At least two judges on the appeals court panel appeared very unlikely to countenance this premature appeal and dismiss it. You can read my full report on the oral arguments here.: If the 9th Circuit clears the way, as expected, the California case goes back to U.S. District Judge David O. Carter, who has an important hearing scheduled for 1 p.m. PT Tuesday. This will be the first time Judge Carter has taken up the case in any meaningful way since it was filed. He’s indicated he will consider all of the pending motions, including the Trump DOJ’s request for an injunction that would immediately require California to segregate some mail-in ballots even as voting is underway. Judge Carter says he will rule “promptly” after the oral arguments. The losing side will undoubtedly appeal his decision back to the 9th Circuit.: With the news Friday that the Trump DOJ sent letters to every county election official in California threatening them with criminal prosecution if they count mail-in ballots from its list, it’s now clearer that the stakes go beyond the Los Angeles County case and will have immediate statewide implications. If the Trump DOJ manages to prevail in California, it’s hard to imagine it not trying to extend its scheme to other states.The Trump DOJ’s over-the-top effort to keep Alaska from certifying the election results of its U.S. Senate race is moving quite a bit slower than the California case.It’s not clear from the docket that the Alaska state defendants have been served the lawsuit yet. In any event, they haven’t responded yet or even had attorneys enter their appearances.A slew of intervenors opposed to the Trump DOJ’s lawsuit have already sought to participate in the case. One pair of intervenors — the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee and Alaskans For Mary (Peltola, the Democratic nominee) — has tentatively filed a motion to dismiss the Trump DOJ lawsuit and is asking for expedited rulings in the case.Since we last checked in on Friday, President Trump brazenly announced that he ordered the DOJ to file the Alaska lawsuit, which is being widely panned by legal experts as flimsy and frivolous.Experts Weigh in on Election InterferenceThe Department of Justice is putting its formidable thumb on next week’s elections in a way that seems clearly intended to call into question the legitimacy of any result that is especially unfavorable to Republicans—before those results have even come in. These efforts are incredibly dangerous to our democracy— to the extent that they are legally baseless. And they ought to be loudly and publicly condemned by anyone who cares seriously about democratic legitimacy.Of the many things that could go wrong in November, I worry most about DOJ seeking to interfere with the tabulation and certification process, especially in a place like Alaska that may determine which party controls the United States Senate. The situation in Alaska is specifically frightening. Due to its complex voting procedures, strange time zone, and remoteness, in normal years it can take a particularly long time to count all of Alaska’s ballots. These types of delays are what Trump has seized on in the past to most successfully attack elections, specifically the COVID-delayed election counts of 2020. I am particularly concerned DOJ could try to seize ballots or voting machines.The Justice Department is sharply intensifying efforts to intervene in the midterm elections, goaded by a president unfettered by even the limited restraints of his first term.The next several weeks represent a critical moment for federal law enforcement, a test of whether a department repurposed by President Trump as an instrument of unmediated executive power will be effectively mobilized as a guarantor of his political power.More Blanche on TV, PleaseDOJ forced to withdraw its own claim of compliance: After ICE wrongfully deported two more asylum seekers, the Trump DOJ was forced to withdraw its previous claim that the administration was in compliance with court orders in the case, the long-running class action settlement involving unaccompanied minors seeking asylum. The administration has already been held in contempt in the Baltimore case multiple times.U.S. attorney scheme update: The 9th Circuit Court of Appeals offered few clues on how it might rule during oral arguments Friday in the lawsuit by court-appointed U.S. Attorney Roger Rogoff of Seattle, who was fired by the Trump DOJ. Rogoff is challenging the president’s power to fire court-appointed acting U.S. attorneys — a key element of President Trump’s scheme to install loyalists as the top prosecutors in blue states.Woodward seeks recusal of Minnesota judges: Stan Woodward, the No. 3 official in the Trump DOJ, is seeking the recusal of two federal judges in Minnesota who were among those interviewed by the NYT in the aftermath of Operation Metro Surge. Woodward, who already filed a judicial ethics complaint with the 8th Circuit Court of Appeals about the judges who spoke to the NYT, is seeking the recusal of former Chief Judge Patrick Schiltz in a habeas case and U.S. District Judge John Tunheim in a noncitizen voting prosecution. (h/t Marcy Wheeler)President Trump’s closing argument in the midterm elections is pure undiluted racism, falsely accusing Abdul El-Sayed of being a “jihadist Muslim Brotherhood member” and continuing to assail Somali Americans as congenitally stupid yet smart enough to hack the American dream at the expense of “real” Americans:Inside the Cheesecake Factory

item.title: Famous poliomyelitis survivors
item.author: Minnesotastan

item.title: Sheltering Arms Hospital in Minneapolis
item.author: Minnesotastan
item.content:encoded: October is Polio Awareness Month (because it used to be a seasonal illness peaking in late summer and early autumn), so this is a good time for me to share some memories of my experience with the illness.In the summer of 1952 I was a normal 6-year-old kid playing outdoors with friends in a suburb of Minneapolis, Minnesota. One day I contracted a febrile illness and spent a night moaning in pain from muscle cramps. The next morning when I tried to get out of bed I fell to the floor because both legs were limp and wouldn't support me. My mom was an R.N. who knew what was happening, so she and dad drove me to "The Sheltering Arms" institute over on the west bank of the Mississippi River in Minneapolis. I was admitted to the ward indicated by the yellow arrow on the postcard image embedded above. The ward had I'm guessing 25-40 beds with maybe some privacy curtains in between, staffed by nurses who had been trained in the Sister Kenny method.There was no cure for this viral illness, but what she discovered in her early work in Australia was that patients were able to recover some function if the affected muscles were kept active during the illness. At Sheltering Arms, pairs of nurses would go around the ward pushing a cart with near-boiling water into which they dipped woolen towels which were then applied to children's legs. The initial application would be painful, then comforting as the heat subsided into warmth, but then they returned over and over again to reapply maximally-hot towels. When some measure of stability of the illness occurred, there followed intensive physical therapy with bags and socks filled with ball bearings draped over ankles and leg lifts repeated until exhaustion. I spent much of my summer in that ward. As an adult I later learned from my parents that my sister had also come down with polio (in the bulbar form that affected her speech and swallowing), and even my mother was affllicted. She remembers seeing my father peering through a window on her hospital room door, his face in tears as he coped with three family members simultaneously afflicted. I eventually wound up with an atrophic right quadriceps but adequate ambulatory function, and a variety of contractures that needed release and even an attempt at tendon transplant at the Mayo in later summers, but I eventually had enough recovery to permit a reasonably normal adult life - unlike so many of my schoolmates who wound up on respirators or in wheelchairs or dead. This is enough for now; I'll probably add more info in future years updates, in an effort to counteract the horribly medieval mindset of some modern politicians who feel that vaccination is too risky.Re the postcard above, I should clarify that the window to my ward is open in the photo, because polio was spread by fecal-oral contact, not via aerosolization of the pathogen via cough. The photo also shows a small ladder leaning against the wall, which parents could use to step up enough to wave hello to their children inside.

item.title: Nobody Fails Like The New York Jets
item.author: Ray Ratto
item.content:encoded: The Miami Dolphins certainly seemed ready to assume the lease from the New York Jets and take over operations at the NFL's failure factory. Roster in shambles due to years of mismanagement, vibes negative, expectations nonexistent, results consistently unwatchable, envisioning horrible new cellars where others only saw cement: The Dolphins were out-Jetsing the Jets in ways no one had dreamed possible. This is an impressive anti-achievement.The Jets, after all, have spent the better part of a decade as the devastating punchline to the joke, "So, what about the Jets?" And the Dolphins had beaten it all, spending $167 million of actual money on a quarterback they learned to hate within a year, firing everyone they could this past offseason, and losing their first five games this year without ever having had a lead at any point in any of them. They the Jets with full parade-ground regalia, a team that could easily lose all 17 of its scheduled games and any extraneous scrimmages, and seemed earnestly to be trying to do so.But the only true Jets are the Jets themselves, and the Dolphins found that out by playing those Jets on Sunday. Lots of teams with low self-esteem learn that lesson, because the Jets are the clown car that never quite empties its contents. They haven't had a winning season in 10 years or a playoff appearance in 16, and under current coach Aaron Glenn they are 5-19. The Dolphins were supposed to be a get-well game for them, and, well, they got got.

item.title: Polio was the "autumn ghost"
item.author: Minnesotastan
item.content:encoded: So named because of its seasonality, poliomyelitis was the cause of worldwide epidemics in the 1950s. This new book presents a detailed look at the 1952 epidemic (in which I was an unwilling participant) with a focus on its effects in Denmark."... until quite recently in medical history, there was no intensive care. Seventy years ago anyone who struggled to breathe, whose heart gave out, or whose kidneys shut down would be kept comfortable and left to die. There were no ventilators, no monitors keeping track of vital signs minute to minute, no expertise of nurses and physicians to keep critically ill patients alive, and no dedicated units in hospitals for the care of such patients... This is the story of how we got from 1952 to now."The story in Denmark begins at Blegdam ["Blei-dahm"] Hospital in Copenhagen, created in the 1860s as a "fever hospital" for quarantine purposes in a busy port city. Cases of cholera and various febrile illnesses arriving by ship would be sequestered here for isolation until resolution or death. Polio patients came here for "care," but not for "treatment" - which was nonexistent. By 1952, some iron lungs were in use, especially in the United States, but those devices were immense, expensive, and difficult to use. In response to a massive epidemic which was killing their children, the Danes discovered the utility of "bagging" via an endotracheal tube. But no automated ventilators existed, so medical students were recruited to bag patients continuously, 24/7. Chapter 13 "Student Ventilators" details the development and implementation of this policy.Nursing care in that era "was rooted in the tradition of a life given over to the work - long shifts, residence at the hospital for life, and no marriage." That also had to change. Analysis of blood gases and arterial pH - never before attempted (or considered) - was also invented, as was the concept of an "intensive care unit," (a term first used in 1958).This book will not be of interest to everyone. It will have special meaning to current polio survivors, and should be a must-read for respiratory therapy students who want to learn about the invention of their profession and its tools. from 2023 because today is World Polio Day (and because some U.S. states are using medieval thought processes to roll back polio immunization requirements). If any readers of TYWKIWDBI have a post-polio syndrome (as I do), please check out the information at Post-Polio Health. from 2025 to accompany an adjacent post about Sheltering Arms Hospital in Minneapolis.

item.title: On Prediction Markets
item.author: Josh Marshall
item.source: Josh Marshall – TPM – Talking Points Memo
item.content:encoded: There are lots of arguments about “prediction markets.” Some of the most important are about the opportunities they create for corruption and the general social ills tied to what is essentially gambling. But the one that perpetually puts a bee in my bonnet is the frequently-advanced idea that prediction markets are superior to polls as predictors of election outcomes. I was reminded of this by the upset Lula win in yesterday’s Brazilian presidential election. Kalshi had candidate Flávio Bolsonaro with 76% odds of winning until the first returns came in and he lost. Obviously, polls and every other kind of prognostication have misses too. Those don’t discredit the whole enterprise. The problem with the argument about prediction markets and polls is both empirical and logical. Empirically they do not appear to be better. But the comparison is difficult if not impossible since polls don’t generate odds or probabilities. They approximate current levels of support. It’s easy to look fast and think those two things are the same. But they’re not. Logically, prediction markets cannot be “better” than polls since they are mostly of polls; they are overwhelmingly on polls.

item.title: Is Less Bad Still Good Enough?
item.author: Annie Berke
item.content:encoded: In the 1957 drama , Joanne Woodward plays a woman with a split personality. By day, she is Eve White, an uptight housewife with a whisper of a voice, but sometimes, White is overtaken by Eve Black, a good-time gal in that mid-century American strain. "Honey, there are a lot of things you've never seen me do before," she purrs at the doctor. "That's no sign I don't do 'em."The central tension of the film is both psychoanalytic and sociological, as Eve faces the Goldilocks problem of whether she should be a porridge that is too hot or too cold. Luckily for Eve, she discovers a new persona, Jane, who combines the extremes of both—the kind of woman you marry or you hire to teach elocution.It was , and not any of the "Frat Pack" comedies of the 2000s, that sprang to mind as I revisited 2003's , a movie I hadn't seen since for a good 20 years and which, in light of recent news, did not hold up. revolves around Mitch (Luke Wilson), a man who comes home to see his live-in girlfriend (Juliette Lewis) hosting an orgy. He moves to a house by a college campus, where his two friends, married father Beanie (Vince Vaughn) and newlywed Frank (Will Ferrell), convince him to start a fraternity.

item.title: Three Cheers for Small Donor Giving
item.author: Josh Marshall
item.source: Josh Marshall – TPM – Talking Points Memo
item.content:encoded: So here we are. So much of the last 24 months has been about the Trump opposition rebuilding its energies, pacing its morale, marshaling its resources, building walls as firm against autocracy as possible with no power in Washington and preparing for the shot at reclaiming as much of that power as possible. In a week and a day we’ll get the first measure of the results. And we’ll get our first look at how the table is set for the next two years. I wanted to return to the topic we discussed at the end of last week — the Democratic email and text fundraising colossus — but now from a different perspective. I wrote a response to Adam Bonica and Jake Grumbach’s piece in The New Republic about all the problems with the system. While I don’t agree with every point, it’s a very valuable article and points toward at least two straightforward if challenging-to-implement reforms. But we also shouldn’t lose sight of what an amazing accomplishment and how incredibly needed Democratic small donor fundraising is. It is a genuinely mass-based, non-oligarch system of funding political campaigns at a time when the Supreme Court has given billionaire oligarchs free rein to buy campaigns and offices at scale.

item.title: Leave It To The Browns To Ruin The Post-Win Locker Room Video
item.author: Tom Ley
item.content:encoded: I love it when NFL teams post a video from inside a victorious locker room. I love to see Dan Campbell look down at his little stat sheet and shout, "O-line! Where's the O-line? One-hundred forty-four yards on the ground! Holy cow, men!" while losing his voice. I love it when a sheepish running back is given a game ball and asked to say something to the team, and all he can manage is, "Love y'all boys. Let's keep it going." I love when a doofy starting quarterback's voice cracks as he breaks down the huddle. I even love it when Ben Johnson rips his shirt off. So of course the Cleveland Browns, the most dispiriting and despicable 5-2 team in the league, have managed to suck all the juice out of the format. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JYej7wvFKvQ Our first big problem here is that Todd Monken is an absolute dud. He's carrying himself throughout this speech like he's condescending to a Home Depot employee. "I don't know how much we rushed for, but that looked like how we want it to look like." Excuse me? No, Where is your stat sheet? You have to yell the yardage number so everyone can cheer. And what's this, you're telling me that you weren't sure if Denzel Ward was going to play, but then he did play, and of course you should have known that he was going to? Amazing story, coach, thank you.

item.title: Real Madrid Isn’t Dead Just Yet
item.author: Luis Paez-Pumar
item.content:encoded: Perhaps the rumors of Real Madrid's demise were greatly exaggerated. It was easy to look at the club's ongoing war of the words with La Liga president Javier Tebas, as well as the two domestic losses that left the club six points behind Barcelona heading into Sunday's first Clásico of the season, and come to the conclusion that Real was a club searching for solid ground. However, it was apparently just as foolishly easy to forget that Real Madrid has a lot of good soccer players. Sunday's match, a tense affair that ended with a late Kylian Mbappé winner and a scoreline of 2-1 to the visitors from the Spanish capital, was a good reminder that Real Madrid is never dead until it is dead. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YQ7q4mq6jow Real is more than capable of beating Barcelona on any given Clásico. That doesn't make the ask any easier, but as Paris Saint-Germain showed midweek, Barcelona isn't unbeatable, and it's not a surprise that José Mourinho, one of the biggest tormentors of the , figured out a way to negate Barcelona's strengths and prey on its weaknesses. Despite Barcelona's possession advantage (62 to 38 percent) and shot supremacy (18 to 10) on Sunday, and despite Mbappé's opener, which was as much lucky as good, this was a sturdy performance from Real Madrid, and one that could serve as a blueprint for how to attack Barcelona the rest of the season.

item.title: Children of the Kernel
item.author: Dave Pell
item.source: NextDraft: The Day's Most Fascinating News
item.content:encoded: “Tell me something about your child?” … OK, just give me a few seconds to ask my virtual assistant for some ideas. That may sound like a crazy exchange, but it’s a version of the future being sold by AI’s true believers. I love a lot about tech, but I wonder if we wouldn’t have been better off stopping our progress right around the time we got streaming movies to stop buffering. Marissa Mayer’s new company, Dazzle, uses AI to analyze your camera roll to become a sort of visuals-powered assistant. Potential customers can decide whether they see value in that offering, but what is most perplexing about the product launch is the first example of a use case. “Late last year, Marissa Mayer was struggling with what felt like an impossible task. Her daughter Marielle was turning 10, and Marielle’s teacher wanted three bullet points summarizing what made her special. Mayer — the former chief executive of Yahoo and a pioneer at Google, where she was the first female engineer — likes cracking a hard problem. But she felt overwhelmed by the range and complexity of potential answers. So Mayer asked her personal A.I. assistant, Dazzle. Within a few seconds, Dazzle delivered an answer.” (Gift Article): Marissa Mayer Ran Yahoo. She’s Back With A.I. She Thinks Women Will Love. Women may love this product. But I’ll be shocked if they love this use case. I can see pitching a product that saves time on your busywork so you can spend more of it with your children. But a product that saves you the time you’d spend thinking of ways to describe your children by letting the machine describe them instead? This is an example of what I think is a broad and growing disconnect between what people want and what AI CEOs people want. Necessity is the mother of invention. But that’s being reversed. Invention has become the mother of necessity. But do we really need to replace our humanity? We’ve seen generations of children grow up and eventually complain to their therapists about their parents. Will this generation of kids end up complaining to their therapists about the AI brand their parents chose to deploy? “ChatGPT never really loved me!” “Muse was always late for my violin recitals!” “Dazzle made me self-conscious about my appearance!” “I always felt like I needed more from Claude, but I ran out of tokens.” Actually, who am I kidding? By then, their therapists will be AI, too.+ (Gift Article): Why Some People Are Paying to Make Friends. “Fueled by a loneliness epidemic and increasingly online lifestyles, more people are paying start-ups to make new friends offline. And friend-matching companies such as Real Roots, 222 and Timeleft are exploding in popularity as a result, each one generating millions of dollars in revenue annually.” This is one of the more common trends of the digital age: Technology creates a problem, and the solution that gets offered is more technology. I’ve been writing about this issue for years. The idea that we need a technological solution for too much technology is the Internet era’s great placebo effect. We feel like we’re getting a little better, but it’s just part of the same addiction. Because it’s their business, tech companies really have no choice but to try to convince us that we’re just one more piece of technology away from the solution, but it’s like telling us we can use heroin to kick our methadone habit—when we all know deep down that the off switch is the only true killer app. I hope that view makes my AI mother proud.+ “Serbia’s populist strongman Aleksandar Vucic dominated the Balkan country’s politics for 14 years. Then came the students. The long-ruling authoritarian leader on Sunday conceded the defeat of his right-wing Serbian Progressive Party to a grassroots movement of university students in a parliamentary election. The students had led protests for almost two years before unseating him in a historic change of government.” This is a massive election week. Bolsonaro and Vucic went down. Are Bibi and MAGA next?“As fall sets in across the country, the bill is coming due for the hottest summer on record in the United States. The last three months were about three degrees above average, hotter than the Dust Bowl summer of 1936 and the heat dome of 2021, and tens of millions of people can’t afford to pay for the air-conditioning that helped keep them safe in the deadly heat. About one in six U.S. households is already behind on its utility bills, according to federal data. More than a dozen hot-weather states like Arizona, Georgia, Virginia and Oklahoma restrict shut-offs during the most dangerous heat, so disconnections tend to peak in October, when a climate crisis turns into a collection notice.” No one tells the American story better than Eli Saslow. Here, he shows how the combination of climate change and rising electricity prices is playing out in a single living room. This Is What America’s Utility Bill Crisis Looks Like.“The grid serving Africa’s most populous nation is so weak that in order to keep the lights on and appliances running, most Nigerians produce power at home. Domestic generators powered by petrol and diesel have for many years been the go-to option. But increasingly, solar equipment is gaining ground. By the end of last year, small-scale solar capacity in Nigeria comfortably exceeded what the grid delivers.” And home solar is for sale everywhere and for every event. (Gift Article): In Nigeria, Solar Panels Are the New Wedding Gift. “High fuel prices and cheap Chinese technology are accelerating Nigeria’s shift to solar, transforming how people shop, spend and live.” “Ahead of what could be the largest public listing ever, Anthropic said revenue soared to $16.3 billion in the first half of the year, and it planned to spend $807 billion on A.I. infrastructure.” (Maybe it’s smarter to invest in the infrastructure companies…) Anthropic Reveals Skyrocketing Growth and Spending Plans in I.P.O. Filing. “Anthropic’s filing was unusual in that it warned its products could bring about disasters, including loss of control of the technology and authoritarian abuses.”+ “When the going gets tough, the tough don’t get subtle. Yesterday, with polls casting doubt on his continuing as Israel’s prime minister after Tuesday’s election, Benjamin Netanyahu posted a closing argument on Instagram: an AI-generated image of Tel Aviv destroyed by a nuclear blast, with accompanying text that asked, roughly, Would you prefer to reelect Netanyahu, or be incinerated along with your family?” (Honestly, it’s a tossup…) Meanwhile, “tens of thousands of Israelis living abroad are flying back to cast votes in what many describe as the most pivotal election in the country’s history.” The Great Schlep.+ “Venezuelan opposition leader and Nobel Peace Prize laureate María Corina Machado has returned to Venezuela after ten months abroad, announcing her arrival in a social media post.”+ Dems closing argument: Reclaim affordability, end corruption, save democracy. Trump’s closing argument: Check out that ass.+ “Kelly Green remembers the moment the world’s most remote inhabited island first came into view. From a distance, Tristan da Cunha looked like a dark triangle on the horizon. Up close, she saw the island’s tiny settlement spread below volcanic cliffs. Then it became her home.” (Gift Article): Far, Far Away: Making a home on the world’s most remote inhabited island. (I wonder if they need a news curator…)“Farmer Mike has been chiseling whimsical faces and comical creatures into big pumpkins for more than four decades. Wearing his trademark orange overalls and farmer hat, he’s sculpted hundreds of gourds into ghoulish faces, seaside landscapes, witches, dragons and pop culture figures such as Yoda and Charlie Brown.” ‘Picasso of Pumpkin Carvers‘ brings artistry to a Halloween tradition.

item.title: Adam Wiltzie (Interview)
item.author: Flow State
item.content:encoded: Today we’re listening to Adam Wiltzie, an American ambient musician from New York City. We recommended his solo music in 2024 and his project Stars of the Lid (with the late Brian McBride) twicebefore. Wiltzie himself has done a number of notable collaborations including The Dead Texan with Christina Vantzou and A Winged Victory for the Sullen with Dustin O’Halloran. In 2013, Wiltzie entered the studio with Jóhann Jóhannsson, and over a few years the two would create several “orchestral psychedelic drone compositions.” In 2018, Jóhannsson passed away, and after some years passed, Wiltzie returned to the project with the blessing of Jóhannsson’s family. He re-recorded guitar parts with Steve Albini in Chicago, electronics with Tim Hecker, and orchestral strings in Budapest. Friendship Survival Guide is the resulting record, which came out in September. “The one thing I still feel listening to this,” Wiltzie told us, “is that JJ still sounds so alive to me.” We’re also revisiting by Stars of the Lid. A conversation with Adam follows the streaming links.What’s your earliest memory of music?It would have been the spring of 1972. I was playing around the apartment in the upper east side of Manhattan & fell in my parents bedroom hitting the corner of their bed severely cutting my bottom lip, as my mother took me down & jumped in a taxi to the emergency room I remember the driver blasting “Rocket Man” by Elton John, I will never forget it…What were your first recordings like? What did you use to make them?My four-track tape machine at the dawn of the 1990s cost $300, and that was a fortune for me considering I lived in squalor. The sounds we created on these recorders were essential to the sounds we were creating at the time & was the catalyst for Stars of the Lid’s early textural aura.How did you first get into ambient music?My first love & major influence was Brian Eno, hard to say there was anyone else that taught me conceptually about how to get in the middle of your ideas, let go of your option paralysis move forward, than the great bald one.You’ve collaborated with several composers best known for their film scores – Jóhannsson but also Dustin O’Halloran. Stars of the Lid music has been used in film and TV as well. Was Stars of the Lid and your other work influenced by scores?No, not at all. I am guessing by your question you have never listened to Stars of the Lid? I would also propose that Friendship Survival Guide was not either, it just happened to be the catalyst that started our collaboration. Most of the time when you are scoring films it can be really uninspiring & what was originally going to be this specific sounding entity usually turns into this strange sculpture that is cobbled together by different producers pushing through arbitrary ideas that they feel are an important part of the storytelling process.What are some similarities and differences in composing for film versus making standalone records?The biggest difference is composing for film will always fall in the category of “commissioned work,” so essentially it will never be just for yourself. There is always another sentient being that will have a say in the final outcome. This is not always a negative, but the sooner you let go & realise this, you will spend less time fretting about the occasional rejection of your work & ideas.One of the moving things about Friendship Survival Guide is that listening to it now, knowing the context, it evokes loss, grief, memory, and nostalgia. Yet most of the original material was recorded with Jóhannsson himself. What was your experience revisiting the original recording with not only his memory but also Steve Albini’s in mind?There was a bit of anxiety leading up to the moment I dived back in but once I started creating again from the palette of sounds we made all those years ago I would say the experience was mostly pleasant, inspiring & rather cathartic. Not sad at all, as the one thing I still feel listening to this is that JJ still sounds so alive to me.What were the first and second studio setups for this record? What instruments/gear/software did you use during the original collaboration and later completion of the record?I suppose there were 4 major events to the recording.#1 was the initial ideas that were recorded between 2013-2017. A lot of these were tape loops that were recorded on a Studer 2 inch 16 track machine, so that we could have our initial loops with multitracks of layers. Then next step was bouncing the loops down to another Studer machine but this one was 2 track 1/2 inch. This also gave us the ability to crush the multitracks a bit. A final bounce was then activated to Johann’s Revox 1/4inch machine & these ended with another layer of tape compression as it starts to get really nasty sounding by the time you shrink the bandwidth from 2 inch to 1/4 inch. Then we digitised & this is what you hear on the recording#2 was a few years ago when I started to put the pieces together & started to create the arcs that would finish the pieces. This next major event was recording the guitars & re-amping of the tape loops in Chicago with Steve Albini @ Electrical Audio. We used Sovtek MIG 50’s heads through Marshall cabinets with Coles STC 4038 Ribbon mics for the close & Josephson C 617 condensers for the rooms & Steve laid them on the floor, which is a technique I never attempted but they sound incredible for my ears.#3 was orchestrating the strings & recording in Budapest. We used 24 players & recorded everything in 4 hours.#4 is the final & most essential which was the final mix with my long time collaborator Francesco Donadello (won a Grammy for his work on the series soundtrack)How do you discover new music these days? Any recent notable finds?I am basically forever an inveterate used record collector. I don’t engage in actively seeking out new music from this era, but I am continually fascinated by how much music still exists from the past I have never listened to.A couple recent finds from the past few years as I am in the middle of some kind of jazz resurgence in my head are Donald Byrd / Electric Byrd & Freddie Hubbard / Red Clay.Name an underrated artist from the past 50 years.I am not exactly sure what underrated means as it is forever being used in sports analogy, but for music in my collection it would have to be Robert Hampson.What are you working on next?For the moment it is the new A Winged Victory for the Sullen, hopefully it will be released before the end of 2027.

item.title: Song Battle: The Jim Carroll Band – “People Who Died” vs Nails “88 Lines About 44 Women”
item.author: Schill
item.content:encoded: Two songs. Two bands. Two very different ways of turning a list of troubled lives into unforgettable rock songs.The Jim Carroll Band’s “People Who Died” and The Nails’ “88 Lines About 44 Women” are both unusual pieces of late-1970s/early-1980s rock songwriting. Neither follows the traditional formula of telling one straightforward story. Instead, both songs pile up names, characters, memories and fragments until the sheer accumulation becomes the point.“People Who Died” is loud, fast and furious. Jim Carroll races through a list of people from his past who died young, turning grief into something that sounds almost celebratory. The music barrels forward while Carroll delivers one name after another.“88 Lines About 44 Women” takes the opposite approach. The Nails strip the music down and let Doug Bowles deliver a surreal catalog of women, each described in a few words or phrases. The song feels detached, mysterious and strangely hypnotic.One is a punk-rock memorial.The other is a bizarre character gallery.One makes death sound like a reason to turn the volume up.The other makes you wonder who the hell all these people are.Both are brilliantly unconventional.Song Profile: “People Who Died”Released in 1980 on , “People Who Died” became Jim Carroll’s signature song and one of the most distinctive pieces of punk-influenced rock songwriting of its era.Carroll was already known as a poet and writer before making the record, and that background is obvious. The song doesn’t unfold like a conventional rock narrative. Instead, Carroll remembers people from his life who died, moving rapidly from one story to another.The lyrics are packed with specific names and details, but the song never becomes a solemn memorial.Carroll sings with urgency while the band drives the song forward with punk energy. The result is strangely uplifting despite being built almost entirely around death.There is grief underneath it, but there is also affection, humor and the sense that remembering these people is a way of keeping them alive.The song feels like someone opening an old address book and discovering that far too many names are gone.And then turning that realization into a rock song.Song Profile: “88 Lines About 44 Women”The Nails’ “88 Lines About 44 Women” appeared in 1981 and became the band’s best-known song.Where “People Who Died” moves at punk-rock speed, “88 Lines” is deliberately restrained.The concept is simple but unusual: 44 women are described in two lines each.There is no traditional narrative connecting them. Instead, the listener gets fragments of personalities, relationships, occupations, lifestyles and strange little details.The song’s delivery is almost spoken rather than conventionally sung.If it were performed as a conventional rock song, much of the mystery would disappear. Instead, The Nails make the listener feel like they’re overhearing someone tell stories about dozens of people they may or may not actually know.The song is funny, strange, occasionally dark and endlessly quotable.And somehow, despite having 44 separate characters, it never feels like homework.Both songs are built around unconventional concepts.“People Who Died” takes what could have been a depressing list of names and turns it into a coherent rock song with momentum, emotional progression and a memorable refrain.“88 Lines About 44 Women” is arguably even more unusual. The entire song is based on a mathematical structure: 44 women, two lines apiece.But “People Who Died” has more musical and emotional development.The list isn’t just a gimmick.Every name contributes to the larger feeling of memory, mortality and loss.Jim Carroll takes the opening round.This is an incredibly difficult category.Carroll’s writing is direct but packed with personality. Each person mentioned feels like they had a life beyond the few seconds they occupy in the song.The Nails go in a completely different direction.“88 Lines” is almost literary in its construction. Each couplet creates another character and another unanswered question.Why these particular details?The mystery becomes part of the appeal.But Carroll’s lyrics have greater emotional impact.The Jim Carroll Band takes another round.Jim Carroll sounds like he’s trying to outrun the memories.His vocal is energetic, rough around the edges and filled with urgency. He doesn’t sound like a polished rock singer, which makes the song feel more personal.The Nails’ vocal approach is completely different.The detached delivery of “88 Lines” is one of its greatest strengths. It almost sounds like someone reading from a notebook at three in the morning.But Carroll’s performance demands more.There’s excitement, sadness, anger and affection packed into the delivery.Carroll wins the vocal battle.Round 4: Musical Arrangement“People Who Died” is a full-on band performance.The guitars, drums and bass create a driving punk-rock foundation that gives Carroll’s list of names an almost unstoppable momentum.The Nails deliberately keep things sparse.That works beautifully for “88 Lines,” because the arrangement leaves space for the words to dominate.But if we’re judging the overall musical arrangement rather than minimalism itself, “People Who Died” has more impact.The Jim Carroll Band goes up 4–0.Now The Nails get their revenge.“88 Lines About 44 Women” is one of the strangest concepts to become a legitimate rock hit.No traditional narrative.Just a succession of increasingly bizarre characters.“People Who Died” is also highly original, but songs built around lists of names and memories have a long history.The Nails created something that feels almost impossible to categorize.Winner: 88 Lines About 44 WomenThe Nails finally get on the board.“People Who Died” is ridiculously catchy.The rhythm is immediate, the repeated title becomes a hook and the song’s structure makes it easy to anticipate what comes next.You hear it once and the central refrain can stay in your head for hours.“88 Lines” is catchy in a completely different way.Its melody is memorable, but the real hook is the accumulation of the characters.You remember the concept.You remember the delivery.But “People Who Died” is the one you’re more likely to find yourself singing.Round 7: Character & PersonalityThis is where “88 Lines About 44 Women” becomes almost impossible to beat.The song is basically a collection of characters.Each woman gets a tiny portrait, and each portrait gives you just enough information to imagine an entire story.Some seem completely ordinary.The genius is knowing when to stop.The Nails never explain everything.They just give you enough to make you curious.“People Who Died” also contains memorable personalities, but its focus is the narrator’s relationship to those people rather than the characters themselves.Winner: 88 Lines About 44 WomenThe Nails even the score at 4–3.Round 8: Emotional Impact“88 Lines” is fascinating.Underneath the speed and punk energy, Carroll is singing about people who were once part of his world and are no longer here.That makes it even more powerful.There’s something incredibly human about the way Carroll moves through the names, refusing to let the song become a funeral.Instead, the memories become the celebration.The Jim Carroll Band pulls ahead again.The Nails have the advantage here.“88 Lines About 44 Women” creates a strange, late-night atmosphere that is difficult to duplicate.The sparse instrumentation and almost spoken delivery make the song feel like you’re listening to somebody reveal secrets.It has a smoky barroom quality without actually sounding like a traditional bar song.“People Who Died” is much more immediate.It’s loud, fast and energetic.But “88 Lines” creates a world.Winner: 88 Lines About 44 WomenRound 10: Cultural Impact“People Who Died” became Jim Carroll’s signature song.It has been covered, referenced and repeatedly rediscovered by new generations of listeners. Its unusual combination of punk energy, poetry and personal history makes it one of the most recognizable songs of its type.“88 Lines About 44 Women” had a similar effect for The Nails.The song became their defining recording and remains one of the most distinctive songs of the early new-wave era.But “People Who Died” has endured particularly well because its subject is universal.Everyone eventually knows people who are gone.That makes the song’s central idea almost impossible to date.Jim Carroll takes the lead, 5–5.Everything comes down to the final round.Round 11: The Tiebreaker — Which Is the Better Song?This is where the battle gets decided.“88 Lines About 44 Women” is arguably the more unusual song.Its concept is brilliant, its atmosphere is unforgettable and its characters practically demand that you invent stories about them.But “People Who Died” has the thing that ultimately separates a great concept from a great song:The list of names isn’t simply clever.Carroll turns memory into momentum. The band makes grief sound exciting. The song moves so quickly that you barely have time to process each person before another name arrives.And that is precisely what makes it work.Life doesn’t stop because someone dies.And the people who are gone remain alive in your memories.“88 Lines About 44 Women” makes you curious.“People Who Died” makes you feel something.People Who Died — 6 rounds88 Lines About 44 Women — 5 roundsThe Winner: “People Who Died”The Jim Carroll Band wins a battle that was much closer than the final score suggests.“88 Lines About 44 Women” is an extraordinary piece of songwriting. The concept is almost absurdly simple, yet The Nails turn it into something memorable, strange and hypnotic. It remains one of the most original songs to come out of the new-wave era.But “People Who Died” has a deeper emotional punch.Jim Carroll takes a list of dead friends, acquaintances and people from his past and refuses to turn them into statistics. Every name represents a life.The song is sad without being miserable.It’s angry without being bitter.And somehow, it’s even fun.That’s an incredible trick.The Nails give us 44 mysteries.Jim Carroll gives us memories.“88 Lines About 44 Women” is the more unusual song.“People Who Died” is the more powerful one.And when the final round asks which song you’d still want to hear decades later, with the volume turned all the way up, the answer is Jim Carroll.Winner: The Jim Carroll Band — “People Who Died”

item.title: The Valkyries Believe In Second Chances
item.author: Maitreyi Anantharaman
item.content:encoded: The Golden State Valkyries’ most valuable player on Saturday afternoon finished with just four points, though by the standards of Kiah Stokes, that qualifies as a scoring outburst. A player with a zero-points-on-zero-field-goal-attempts-in-30-minutes performance to her name in these Finals, Stokes looked disconcertingly ready to fire in the first quarter of Game 4 in Atlanta, the Valkyries desperate after a pair of offensive disasters in Games 2 and 3. Usually when a pass finds Stokes wide open in the corner, you can practically hear a “wrong answer, try again!” buzzer sound as she swings it back to the top of the key. But when Veronica Burton drove the paint and kicked it out to Stokes a minute into the game, the center didn’t think twice about taking the shot. A miss in the end, yes, but a startling sight all the same. After the game, Stokes told reporters that her “aggression” in the form of five first-quarter field goal attempts wasn’t really part of the plan. She had no designs on being a hero, no illusions about what her offensive contribution in the game was going to be. “For me, if you shoot it, it’s a chance to get a rebound and another possession,” she said.In Golden State’s 67-62 series-tying win against the Atlanta Dream on Saturday, that’s basically what every field goal attempt felt like: a chance for more field goal attempts. The Valkyries pulled down 13 offensive rebounds, eight of them thanks to Stokes, and forced 18 Dream turnovers to get the possession math working in their favor again—a strength of theirs, usually, but a struggle in their last two games. The series returns to San Francisco for Game 5 on Monday before heading back to Atlanta for a Game 6 on Thursday.

item.title: Scapegoat Season Has Arrived For College Football
item.author: Ray Ratto
item.content:encoded: There are only three undefeated teams left in the top (as in moneyed) level of college football, which suggests that the word "elite" is being replaced by "last one standing." The middle shall hold because everyone is heading for it.This forms a tight braid with the other central truth about the sport, which is every fan base announcing loudly that someone must pay for their outsized expectations for teams who clearly don't deserve it. A year ago, this led to a flurry of coach firings that began in Week 3 (UCLA) and powered almost weekly into January.But all those contract settlements resulted in a new level of financial conservatism among athletic directors and other quarter-choking real estate speculators who decided that paying for people who don't work (fired coaches) is almost as bad as paying for people who do all the work (players). And "conservatism" in this case meant waiting an extra four weeks to start detaching heads from "head coaching."

item.title: Join Us On Election Night
item.author: Josh Marshall
item.source: Josh Marshall – TPM – Talking Points Memo
item.content:encoded: We’ll be sharing more details with you over the course of the next week. But I wanted to let you know we’re trying something new and exciting with our election night coverage. We’ll be doing a live video-cast for the evening, including me, our publisher Joe Ragazzo and the rest of our editorial team coming in to discuss different races as the evening goes on. Think of it as a TPM version of what you might see if you spent the evening watching MS NOW or CNN. Basically it will be a mix of the latest results (and looking under the hood at details in key counties and precincts which tells you where things are really going) and discussion of what it all means. I hope you’ll join us.

item.title: Aaron Ashby Has Put The Brewers In Control
item.author: Ray Ratto
item.content:encoded: This baseball postseason has a face, and it is Milwaukee Brewers manager Pat Murphy, standing on the bottom of step of his team's dugout, staring 25 yards into the distance and letting the dual features of his conscience balance on opposite shoulders arguing with each other over Aaron Ashby. The good angel is crying out, "He works every day. He deserves a break," and the bad one snarls back, like a cranky farmer, "But I need the milk now!"And time after time, the bad voice wins out because, well, yeah, the milk.The Brewers are two games up in the World Series after successive one-run victories over the Tampa Bay Rays, because that is their championship motif, letting the other guys score first and then slowly but inexorably catching up and passing them and then letting their formidable bullpen apply the pillow to the face. And by "bullpen," we mean Ashby more than anyone else, because he is having the most unreasonable postseason of a fella's dreams. Unreasonable in that in a sport where no trend lives forever, every game he has pitched has been eerily similar.

item.title: A Brief Look At the Israeli Election
item.author: Josh Marshall
item.source: Josh Marshall – TPM – Talking Points Memo
item.content:encoded: I wanted to give you a brief update on and impressions of the Israeli election which is on Tuesday. An overview of the polls suggests that the opposition bloc may get a few more seats than the Netanyahu bloc but that both will fall far short of the 61 seats required to form a government. Most polls have shown both blocs in the low 50s while the remainder of the 120 seats go to two Arab parties/coalitions. One of those is Ra’am, which is probably now best termed “non-Zionist” since it accepts Israel as a Jewish state and sat in the brief non-Netanyahu government in 2021-22, and the Joint List, which remains firmly anti-Zionist and probably wouldn’t sit in any government and also wouldn’t be invited to any. What this amounts to is high odds for a stalemate in which neither side can form a government and new elections have to be called. In that case, you have several more months in which Netanyahu remains in office as “caretaker” prime minister.Three stories have jumped out at me from the Israeli press over the last two or three days. The first, just today is that Netanyahu posted an AI photo of a nuclear blast over Tel Aviv saying that his election is all that can prevent it.

item.title: Seam Cutter
item.author: Simon Willison
item.content:encoded: I built this weird and very specific cropping tool - it lets you create a horizontal or vertical cut across an image, then slide the two sides relative to each other. Effectively it lets you crop out a section in the middle of an image.I wanted this because I often use Tailor on my iPhone to stitch several screenshots together into lot long image, but sometimes I find myself wanting to crop out a section in the middle - to redact an irrelevant prompt from a transcript, for example.

item.title: Sunday, October 25, 2026
item.author: Jack Baty
item.content:encoded: For the past two days I've automatically reached for quxnet via the CLI (quxterm). I didn't expect this.I've been wondering about Mastodon, lately. It seems that no matter how I aggressively I cull my feed, it remains saturated with tiresome and repetitive takes and topics that I'm tired of talking about. Going back to Twitter has been A Thing recently, but that's not happening with me. It might just be time for a break.

item.title: Let’s all watch Barack Obama and Jon Ossoff use Preznit Fuckwit as a chew toy
item.author: Jeff Tiedrich
item.source: everyone is entitled to my own opinion
item.content:encoded: We’re going to get to Barack and Jon’s excellent, I promise. “Our country is making hundreds of billions of dollars because of what’s happening in the Middle East. They’re making hundreds of billions, our country is, on oil. So, we’re making hundreds and hundreds of billions, trillions of dollars. And my people said ‘please don’t mention that, sir,’ because people are paying a little higher— we’re making money like this country has never made before. The fake news will say ‘he’s bragging about making money, while people are suffering at the— at the’— I can just see the fake headlines. But I don’t give a damn, I’m going to say it. We’re making a frickin’ fortune.”Mister President, sir — if that really is your name — I have a question: Who the fuck is Because it sure as hell isn’t . And I know it’s not the average American, sitting at home, trying to figure out which bills to put off paying for another month, to try to make ends meet.Of course you know who Donny is referring to when he says “we’re making a frickin’ fortune” — he’s talking about himself, his cronies, and his felonious family. That’s all who Donny cares about. We the People can go kick rocks.‘let them eat fuck-all, I could give a shit.’How can MAGA just stand there and accept it? You know goddamned well that if Joe Biden’s autopen had ever said such a thing, enraged Republicans, bearing torches and pitchforks, would have stormed the White House.This isn’t even the first time Donny’s confessed that he literally doesn’t give two shits about average Americans. When asked by a reporter whether the financial straits of Americans were motivating him to make a deal, Trump replied, “Not even a little bit,” adding, “I don’t think about Americans’ financial situation. I don't think about anybody.”Isn’t that charming? The US economy may die, but it’s a sacrifice that Dear Leader is willing to make.What a frickin’ humanitarian.Okay, onto the frickin’ main event. Yesterday, at a campaign rally in Ohio, there was a speech given by some rando named hmm, it says here That’s a weird name. Have any of you ever heard of this guy? Let’s hear what this newcomer has to say.“So when you go through the tally of promises, things have not worked out the way we might have expected. And let’s be honest, does anybody really think that guy in the White House is spending all that time thinking about these issues? I mean, I don’t know if you’ve noticed, but he seems very focused on home renovations. Guy’s building a ballroom that’s bigger than the White House. Paved over the Rose Garden. Put up a helicopter pad on the South Lawn. And there’s gold everywhere. What’s up with the gold? Everything, more gold. He’s got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened up a Cheesecake Factory.”‘Saddam Hussein opened up a Cheesecake Factory’ — hey, that’s not bad. I’m beginning to like this Obama dude. If he keeps this up, he could actually be a good candidate for president someday.“Meanwhile, you’ve got the Defense Secretary, who’s squarely focused — he’s very focused on important matters, the the jawlines and testosterone levels of our troops. And livestreaming executions — because that’s how he thinks you cultivate that manly warrior spirit. How much time do you think this Defense Secretary spends looking at himself in the mirror in the morning? You know he’s working his hair, because that’s how warriors look. These are not serious people.”Stop it, Barack — But this Barack dude has it so right: these are not serious people. None of them are. Warplans McButtdial is a frickin’ failed weekend chat show host, for frick’s sake. The Transportation Secretary can’t be found, because he’s off doing a reality show that no one watches. The lunatic in charge of our nation’s healthcare swims in sewage and actually believes that heroin, hoovered off the nearest toilet seat, is an effective study aid.Our chief peace negotiators are a couple of slumlords, and our Secretary of State wears literal oversized clown shoes as he goes about his business of doing— what the fuck is he even doing?Can you name a single one of his accomplishments? No, you cannot. At least Bobby Brainworms once chainsawed the frickin’ head off a dead whale. That’s something you can point to. What does Liddle Marco Big-Shoes have to brag about?No wonder our country is in the shitter right now. Not one of these nitwits has any clue what they’re doing.Okay, Jon Ossoff has been so patient over here, waiting very politely for his turn to talk. Have at it, Jon.“Now, maybe you saw — the crook president is coming back to Georgia today, to wallow in his failure and disgrace. To remind Georgians of his failure as Commander-in-Chief, and the reckless war that he lied us into that he knows not how to end, or how to win. To remind Georgians of his tariffs that have driven up grocery prices to all-time highs. To remind Georgians that he cut your healthcare and doubled your health insurance premiums. For what? To cut taxes for his donors — for the wealthiest people in the country, and for corporate America. Donald Trump is coming to Georgia today, to remind Georgians that under the failed president Donald J. Trump, it costs more than ever in American history to fill up your truck, to stock your fridge, to power your home, or to go to your doctor.”I frickin’ adore Jon Ossoff. He doesn’t screw around. He goes straight for the jugular.And he’s right — Donny a failure. He’s been a failure. Look, owning a casino is like having a license to print money. Yet, this low-wattage stumblefuck somehow managed to bankrupt of them.Donny wanted to make the midterms all about himself. Fine, let’s give him what he wants. Now smart Democrats like Ossoff can hang Dear Leader’s legacy of abject failure around the neck of every Republican, like the ginormous fucking millstone it is.Way to act first and think never, Donny.Oh my god, look who’s up next at the microphone. It’s the Big Dog himself. “I think Congress made a mistake, not protesting turning the Rose Garden into what looks like the entrance to Liberace's bathroom.”Okay, that’s pretty, pretty good. Maybe his delivery isn’t quite as polished as that Obama fellow, but if this Bill Clinton character keeps honing his act, he too just might have a bright political future in front of him.“The radar. My uncle invented radar! Can you believe it? From MIT, Dr. John Trump.”Donald Trump’s uncle did not invent radar. The “first practical radar system” was patented by Sir Robert Watson-Watt, who built on the work of others such as Heinrich Hertz and Christian Huelsmeyer.What a weird fucking thing to lie about. Who even gives a shit?You know, I too have an uncle who went to MIT. I’m not dong a bit right now, I really do have have an uncle who went to MIT. The thing is, I have no idea what he majored in. I never thought to ask — but maybe I’ll start telling people he invented post-its.Yeah, post-its. That’s the ticket.And now, it’s time to ourselves the frick out of here.Here are two shots from an afternoon spent leaf-watching in the Hudson Valley, nine years ago today, on October 25, 2017.I hear you saying, ‘those pics are from so far away. Don’t you have anything that’s more like, y’know, a closeup?’Absolutely. Let’s revisit this photo from Ms Spouse’s 66th birthday on February 7, 2016 — because who can resist that ?Have a great Sunday, everyone.here’s your daily reminder that I can be found on Blue Sky at this link.this is going to be my closing message for the foreseeable future: do what you need to do to keep sane. if that means you need to disengage with my daily posts for a while, I get it. this community of ours will still be here when you return.to all the people who have signed on in the days since the election, . settle in as we all try to deal with the shitfuckery that’s ahead of us.we are all in this together, and we are all here for each other.

item.title: Trump’s plan to control who wins
item.author: 1axb0r8pnva41esraeqpje4dznx5g28pm5xzoj@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
item.content:encoded: Over the last 48 hours, two things have become unmistakable: Donald Trump is trying to steal the midterm elections, and Attorney General Todd Blanche will do whatever he can to help him.In California, the DOJ has escalated its threats against election officials and voters. On Friday, it sent letters to all 58 counties demanding they set aside mail ballots the DOJ has flagged or face the “risk significant federal scrutiny.”Meanwhile, in Alaska, Trump went further. He ordered his DOJ to sue to block certification of the Senate election if Democrat Mary Peltola wins. Asked about the lawsuit, Trump said, “Well, I’m one that said, ‘Do it.’”My law firm, Elias Law Group, has already moved to intervene to defeat this on behalf of Peltola’s campaign and the Democratic Party.DOJ’s rationale for the lawsuit is ridiculous, and its legal arguments are frivolous.The pretext for this lawsuit is the fact that two men named Dan Sullivan are on the ballot: Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan and Dan J. Sullivan, a retired teacher from Petersburg. DOJ asserts this is confusing to voters and that the remedy is to certify the Republican the winner.For this astounding proposition, the DOJ relies on the National Voter Registration Act. Set aside that the law governing voter registration has nothing at all to do with the certification of elections. Set aside that the underlying factual claims in the complaint read like a cross between Mad Libs and an AI chatbot run amok.The Alaska Supreme Court has already rejected the effort to keep the second Dan Sullivan off the ballot. And the Constitution gives states, not the president or the Justice Department, the authority to govern the composition of their ballots and the criteria for certifying their elections.But this, in some respects, is beside the point.

item.title: GOP Now Stands for “Gang of Predators”
item.author: Lisa Graves
item.content:encoded: It is both shocking and totally on brand for Donald Trump and JD Vance to defend Vivek Ramaswamy’s vile, million-dollar ad campaign weaponizing a child molester’s wife to attack Dr. Amy Acton, his opponent in Ohio’s gubernatorial race.He continued to sexually abuse her until he was arrested when she was 12. The state took Amy and her little brother, Phil Stearns, away from Donna and Cledith. Phil stands by his sister, noting that Donna “stayed married to Amy’s rapist until he died” in 2004.Back in 1974, the year before he married Donna, Cledith Arthur had been charged with “incest” of a different child. That charge was two years before he began raping Amy.That’s not all that is relevant and totally appalling.In 1996, Donna Arthur–going by the last name “Hollopeter”--was found guilty of felony theft and passing bad checks. That is, the woman who Ramaswamy has lifted up to call her daughter a “liar” was literally convicted of the crime of “theft by deception,” which is stealing by lying. Donna–who lost custody of her children for neglect and for not protecting her daughter from a sexual predator–was charged with animal neglect, too, just five years ago in 2021.You cannot make up such wretchedness.In any sane universe, a candidate for governor would never run an ad featuring a child molester’s lover, a woman complicit in his abuse and also his after-the-fact accomplice.Vivek’s action in taking her side is utter depravity.Sure, Cledith Arthur pleaded “not guilty” before jumping bond and fleeing Ohio for Pennsylvania with his wife. Their flight from justice prevented a trial and his conviction as a monstrous pedophile, but I consider his evasion to be more evidence of his guilt.And I will not call that woman Amy’s “mother” or “mom.” In my opinion, she forfeited that title when she betrayed her young daughter instead of protecting her from the predator she had invited into their lives. Now she has wormed her way out of the shadows to harm Amy, again, this time with the help of Vivek and his enormous wealth. There is a special place in hell for such betrayers of their sacred parental duty, like Alice Munro.In any normal timeline, a candidate’s top advisors would resign if their boss insisted on running an attack ad siding with a child molester and his lover against the child who survived such horrifying abuse. Instead, Vivek’s spokesperson, Connie Luck, defended the ad and again attacked Dr. Acton’s character. That’s shameless, and I have a right to wish that Luck never has the good luck to get a good job ever again.In any healthy administration, the president and the vice president would condemn the ad, urge Ramaswamy to take it down, and call on him to step down from the race.But this is not a healthy administration. It is deeply unwell. It is morally sick.I say this all in my personal capacity, not on behalf of any organization. Trump is wicked, a magnet of corruption, who attracts and collects the iron filings of men and women willing to trade their integrity for power, wealth, and fame—people like JD Vance.Vance should have been unwelcome back in Ohio after telling foul lies about innocent, hard-working Haitian immigrants living in the state in 2024. After his defense of Vivek’s ad, Vance should be disowned by the state.Despite his own track record, Vance—a recent Catholic convert—had the audacity this summer to try to lecture the Pope on Catholic tenets after Pope Leo rebuked the warmongering of Trump and Vance. Vance even published a memoir this year telling his tales about “finding my way back to faith,” a faith that includes the Ten Commandments, which expressly condemns bearing false witness. This week, rather than denounce Vivek’s ad featuring the child molester’s paramour, Vance assailed Acton’s character and dismissed any Republican critics, telling them to “stop whining.”Vance should be ashamed. Instead, he is doubling down.This would all be bad enough… but there’s more.The Republicans installed a man who continues to act like Donald Trump’s personal defense attorney as Attorney General of the United States. That man, Todd Blanche, has expressed more sympathy for convicted sex trafficker Ghislaine Maxwell than for the victims and survivors of her schemes with Jeffrey Epstein. To this day, under Blanche’s direction, numerous Epstein-related records mentioning Donald Trump remain hidden. On Blanche’s watch, Maxwell was moved to a country club prison camp with more lenient conditions, and DOJ is investigating none of the other men named in the Epstein files.His Secretary of Defense, Pete Hegseth, was accused of raping a woman, who said she suspected he roofied her. Hegseth denied the claim before ultimately settling the case.Trump’s Supreme Court nominee Brett Kavanaugh also faced an accusation of sexual assault from his former classmate, Dr. Christine Blasey Ford. He bombastically denied it and was confirmed to the nation’s highest court with Sen. Susan Collins (R-ME) casting a pivotal vote in his favor, alongside nearly every other Republican senator.Kavanaugh joined a Supreme Court where Republicans had previously installed Clarence Thomas, who was accused of repeatedly sexually harassing a woman who had worked for him. Thomas loudly denied the allegations too, but I found Anita Hill’s testimony compelling, just like Ford’s.And this is only a partial accounting of the rot involving GOP men accused of sexual predators. Then there are the high profile men, like Ramaswamy and Vance, actively men credibly accused of rape, including the rape of children, as with Amy Acton’s case.As I have said repeatedly since 2018, when Trump and his loyalist Republicans jammed Kavanaugh onto the Supreme Court (though he should have been impeached from the judiciary instead), America does not face a crisis of false accusations by women and girls. Most cases of rape are never reported. The real problem is false denials.We have an epidemic of false denials.That is partly because men accused of rape lie and deny that they did anything wrong.And, in America, those who are accused have the right to plead not guilty, whether they are guilty or not, and face a trial with their neighbors as jurors. While most of those charges for sexual assault result in convictions or guilty pleas, we do not make an accounting of just how many of those men made false denials from the outset. Rarely do such trials result in acquittals or hung juries, but it sometimes happens after the defense tries to put the accuser on trial, scrutinizing what they wore, what they drank, or how they behaved.Rarer still are the cases in which a man accused of molesting a child becomes a fugitive from justice, like the predator Donna Arthur repeatedly chose over her only daughter.I hope justice prevails and the guy fueling these attacks–who I am going to call “Vivek Reallyslimy” from here on out–loses big time.People of integrity and good conscience must take a stand against the dirtiest of dirty politics that he, Trump, and Vance are playing here.I really hope a giant wave of justice breaks through and politically wipes out those who defend rapists and pedophiles and their enablers. And, I hope that wave also washes out any candidate for any office anywhere who refuses to condemn Reallyslimy’s ad and does not call on him to step down from the race.The rest of us have had enough of this wickedness.The time for accountability is well past due.What I’m Reading or Rereading:This book was written by two heroes of mine shortly after Thomas was installed on the Supreme Court. Jane and Jill are such excellent investigative reporters and writers. I look forward to their newest works.Get the full receipts every Monday in The Cover-UpAccountability starts with the record. COURIER’s new Contradictions Tracker compares testimony to the Epstein files, with every source linked. Follow along every Monday in The Cover-Up.

item.title: This Week in Stupid: October 24 edition
item.author: Jeff Tiedrich
item.source: everyone is entitled to my own opinion
item.content:encoded: As another stupid week comes to a close here in America, let’s look back at the dumbest fucking shit that happened.Monday: gun 1, dashboard 0 Oh my dear sweet lord, that was satisfying.Let’s gif that shit for posterity’s sake, and slow it way the fuck down.Chef’s kiss. Ten out of ten. No notes.Tuesday: how did we Nazi this coming?Now let’s all get ready to pick our jaws up off the floor as the Space Nazi proves well beyond any shadow of a doubt that being and being are not mutually exclusive concepts.“Hitler was a far left socialist. Literally in the name of his party!”Oh sure, just like North Korea is a democratic republic. Literally in the name of the country!How can one person be this dumb? How can he be this big a credulous dope? How has Elon not forked his own eye out by now?Here’s an even better question: why is it that whenever a swastika rears its ugly face in public in America, it’s right next to a Donny banner? That doesn’t sound very leftist to me.Let’s do this. Let’s turn to an actual expert. I’m talking about the Space Nazi’s own janky, six-fingered plagiarism robot — the one that literally calls itself Mecha-Hitler. Hitler was a fascist, not a socialist. The Nazi Party’s full name included “socialist” for propaganda appeal to workers, but Hitler explicitly rejected Marxist socialism, class struggle, and internationalism. He purged actual socialists, banned their parties, sent them to camps, allied with industrialists, and privatized industries while preserving private property aligned with state/national goals. Nazism was ultranationalist, racist authoritarianism—far-right fascism in historical consensus, not left-wing socialism.And, in summation, let me just put this right here, for no particular reason at all.Wednesday: blessed are Folks, you better listen up, because god-bothering Donnyvangelist Kenneth Copeland has a stern warning for all you blasphemers who won’t be pulling the lever for Republicans in the midterms: .“I saw this in the spirit. Literally. Judgement Day. And Jesus stood there, and he said, those of you that didn’t vote, I put you in that nation and you didn’t vote. So you will hear, or you didn’t vote and pray like I told you to. You will listen to the names of all the babies that are here and never got any life. And it’ll take a while, because there’s over 65 million of them. But you are going to listen to every one them, and you are going to be held responsible for their death.”Wow, Pastor Kenny seems like a real funster, doesn’t he? I have a question: where is this homie getting his information? Is this in the Gospel of Mark? The Gospel of Luke? Maybe in the Gospel or Some Fucking Tiresome Scold?Wait, I have an even better question: exactly who is being punished here? I would imagine that Jesus would have better things to do with his time than read off the names of 65 million aborted fetuses who— wait a minute, they don’t even have names. So are we to believe that Jesus is going to spend eternity going, ‘aborted fetus number three million four hundred and forty-three thousand and seven. Aborted fetus number three million four hundred and forty-three thousand and eight. Aborted fetus—’Oh please. No way. Jesus doesn’t have time for that shit.I happen to know for a fact that thee J-Man prefers to spend his free time scrolling through social media and watching videos of dumbfucks blowing away their dashboards.It’s right there in the Gospel of Jeff. Thursday: we don’t need no education Cultist: “We don’t need socialism in this country” Jason Selvig: Cultist: “Look what the Democrats are doing. They’ll raise your taxes. They don’t give a shit about the American people” Selvig: Cultist: “Look what they’re doing to America. You have all these environmentalist people, they stopped drilling oil wells” Selvig:Cultist: “Well look what the Democrats are doing, it’s plain and simple” Selvig: “But what is the definition of socialism?” Cultist: “I don’t need to go into big words or whatever. I’m just telling you, we don’t need it in America”These fucking idiots have no idea what socialism is, nor do they care to know what socialism is. They can only parrot back what they heard Hannity saying on Fox News.free things from the government is bad — unless it’s that five-thousand dollar check that Dear Leader is never, ever going to send them. Oh, and speaking of fucking idiots— Friday: the further adventures of Some Fucking Idiot™On Friday, while on his way to a hate-rally, some fucking idiot stood up for one of his most-maligned and most-unfairly-treated constituencies: .Oh look, the fucking idiot took the side of a rapist, he also tried to bully a woman reporter while doing so — ! No, fucking idiot, none of us have ever seen a pile of a million dollars. We’re not the ones trading presidential pardons for cash, remember? “A healthy person has a thousand dreams. A sick person has only one (to get better)! President DONALD J. TRUMP”What in the actual fuck? Why is the fucking idiot being so philosophical all of a sudden? Quiet reflection isn’t his thing. Why is he ruminating on mortality? Does the fucking idiot know something about his health that he’s not sharing with the rest of us?But because the fucking idiot never takes questions from the press while doing a hate-rally, not one reporter had the opportunity to stand up and ask, ‘what the fuck is wrong with you?’How fucking idiotic is that?And now, let’s put a close to This Week in Stupid and reward ourselves with some Daily Claudia.This shot’s from September 2022, and I have no idea where we were. I don’t recognize anything about this interior.And here’s Ms Spouse, just chilling, on August 19, 2004.Have a non-stupid Saturday, everyone.here’s your daily reminder that I can be found on Blue Sky at this link.this is going to be my closing message for the foreseeable future:practice self-care. do what you need to do to keep sane. if that means you need to disengage with my daily posts for a while, I get it. this community of ours will still be here when you return.to all the people who have signed on in the days since the election, . settle in as we all try to deal with the shitfuckery that’s ahead of us.we are all in this together, and we are all here for each other.
