item.content:encoded: Heather Cox Richardson is one of today’s unlikeliest social media stars. The Boston College historian has been teaching and writing about 19th-century America, Reconstruction, and the Civil War for decades. But it was only in 2019 that her work took off when she began writing her daily newsletter, , a no-nonsense analysis of the news through the lens of US history. The newsletter became one of the most popular on Substack. And today, Richardson has millions of loyal fans who rely on her to make sense of American politics and provide a little sanity and democratic reassurance, even as she herself is concerned about the direction of the country today. “I’m worried about where we’re going. Just don’t even start me,” Richardson tells host Al Letson. “But I am heartened in this moment by the number of people who are rediscovering that they do have agency to change the future. And of course, that’s always been the story of our democracy.”, which first aired in June, Richardson doles out some advice for the Democrats if they take back power in the midterm elections, the decades-long failure to hold corrupt American leaders accountable, the still-resonant death of Reconstruction, and what she sees as the tragic hypocrisy of Thomas Jefferson.

item.title: Too many people are afraid to say this
item.author: 1axb8bim5scxqfqc0unl8nq7xy37ldasxih5sz@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
item.content:encoded: Too many people know the truth but are afraid to say it. I will.We are in a constitutional crisis.I don’t mean this in the general sense of Donald Trump flouting the law or violating norms. I mean specifically that, with only days before the midterm elections, Trump is using the power of the federal government to threaten states, intimidate election officials and disenfranchise voters.This is most obvious in California, where his Department of Justice demanded that state election officials set aside ballots from 20,000 voters the Trump administration claims to believe are noncitizens.When the election officials refused, the DOJ sued. Then it threatened criminal prosecution. Trump said the election officials in California “will all go to jail for a long period of time.”This week, Attorney General Todd Blanche refused to commit to respecting state election results. He made clear that the DOJ would interfere in the elections or their certification if it deems it necessary. The U.S. Constitution bars such conduct, but Trump doesn’t care, and neither do his government lawyers.Blanche also made clear that the DOJ is poised to sue other states on similar grounds.Over the last two years, legacy media outlets have done everything they can to normalize Trump’s threats and attacks on democracy.When he says he wants Republicans to take over the voting in blue cities, they dismiss it as mere rhetoric. When he claims the power to control ballot counting, they excuse it as politics. When he says he wants to rig elections, they insist both sides use heated words.I’ve been here before. In 2020, I was called an alarmist when I said Trump would never concede. When I defeated Trump and his allies in court, I was told he was simply letting the process play out.For a while, many of my critics grew quiet. But then came the Biden era, Merrick Garland and a belief that we could return to normalcy. What I saw as MAGA regrouping, others hailed as a new era of civility and norms.

item.title: Saturday 80s Jam: Faith – George Michael
item.author: Schill
item.content:encoded: When George Michael released “Faith” in 1987, he was already one of the biggest pop stars on the planet. But the song represented something much more significant than another hit single. It was the moment Michael stepped completely out of the shadow of Wham! and established himself as a solo artist with his own identity, sound, and image.The title track from his debut solo album, , was almost deceptively simple. Built around a stripped-down acoustic guitar riff, handclaps, percussion, and Michael’s confident vocal, the song sounded dramatically different from the polished synth-pop that had helped make Wham! famous.Michael wanted to move in a more mature musical direction, drawing on rockabilly, early rock ‘n’ roll, soul, and R&B. “Faith” combined those influences into something that sounded both retro and completely suited to 1987.The opening is particularly memorable. The church-organ sound fades into the guitar riff before Michael enters, creating an unusual mixture of gospel imagery and rock ‘n’ roll swagger. The song then settles into a deceptively relaxed groove.Michael wasn’t simply singing about romantic faith. The song is also about independence and refusing to remain trapped in a relationship that isn’t working.That attitude was reflected in the video, which became one of the most recognizable pieces of MTV-era imagery. Michael appeared in leather, sunglasses, blue jeans, and a leather jacket, playing guitar in front of a jukebox.The image was a complete transformation from the carefully coordinated pop-star presentation associated with Wham!The transformation worked.“Faith” became a massive commercial success, reaching number one on the Billboard Hot 100 in the United States. The album became one of the biggest-selling records of the decade, eventually earning Michael the Grammy Award for Album of the Year.The song itself became one of the defining singles of 1987.What made it particularly impressive was how little it actually needed. There wasn’t a giant synthesizer arrangement or an enormous chorus. The hook came from the rhythm, the guitar, Michael’s personality, and the confidence of the performance.He sounded completely in control.That confidence was important because “Faith” arrived during one of the most significant transitions of Michael’s career. Wham! had been enormously successful, but remaining part of a duo would always make it difficult for Michael to establish exactly who he was as an artist.With , he didn’t simply continue what Wham! had started.The song also demonstrated Michael’s extraordinary ability to move between musical styles. He could write sophisticated pop songs, soulful ballads, dance tracks, and more stripped-down rock-influenced material without sounding like he was simply copying someone else.“Faith” became the perfect introduction to that new version of George Michael.More than anything, the song is memorable because it feels effortless. The guitar riff is simple. The arrangement is relatively sparse. The rhythm is straightforward.But getting simplicity to sound this good is difficult.Every element is in exactly the right place.The result was a song that managed to sound retro, modern, sexy, playful, and confident all at once.Nearly four decades later, “Faith” remains one of George Michael’s defining recordings. It marked the beginning of one of the most successful solo careers of the late 1980s and proved that Michael was capable of becoming something beyond the pop star audiences already knew.Wham! had made George Michael famous.“Faith” made it clear that George Michael didn’t need Wham! anymore.

item.title: Follow Up About Political Giving
item.author: Josh Marshall
item.source: Josh Marshall – TPM – Talking Points Memo
item.content:encoded: Following my morning post about the Democratic political contribution infrastructure, I had a number of TPM Readers write in saying, in so many words, No! You’re wrong. People are totally burnt out about the annoying emails. I want to point out that I said the same thing, how abusive and stupid and annoying the avalanche of emails is. What I noted is a sort of admission against interest, which is that the haul from online small donor giving keeps rising. So at least at the aggregate level, effective burnout, actually seeing contributions decline, is not something we’re seeing. It may be around the corner. And we can and should do better. But on this acid test, the money keeps rolling in. And that’s clearly a big reason why it continues.

item.content:encoded: Kimi K3.1 Pro landed on the Kimi API today - it's not yet open weights, but Moonshot promise "Full model weights will be released by Nov 4, 2026".They're also offering a "Highspeed" version that's 2-3x faster, at twice the price (except for input token cache hits, which are priced the same).The US dollar pricing is $2.00/million tokens for input and $10/million for output - the same as GPT-6.1 Sol and half the price of Claude Opus 5.5.Moonshot's own benchmarks show Kimi as approximately level with Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra - beating them on a few benchmarks, coming close on others.Artificial Analysis scored Kimi at 55 - ahead of Claude Fable 5.1, GPT-6 Astra, and Gemini 4 Argon (all at 53) and behind only Claude Opus 5.5 (58).This is the first time a (soon-to-be) open weight model has scored this highly against the frontier.llm openai endpoint \ https://api.moonshot.ai/v1 \ --key kimi \ -m kimi-k3.1-pro \ "Generate an SVG of a pelican riding a bicycle" \ --responses \ -o reasoning_effort low \ > kimi-k3.1-pro-pelican-low.stdout.txt \ 2> kimi-k3.1-pro-pelican-low.stderr.txt can run prompts against any OpenAI-compatible endpoint but doesn't log the results, hence the extra options to save stdout and stderr (the reasoning trace).Here are the pelicans I got for Kimi K3.1 Pro on the three reasoning levels it supports - low, medium, and max. item.title: Now Is The Time For Hysteria
item.author: Ray Ratto
item.content:encoded: We had ourselves the hell week of all hell weeks last Saturday. And in the aftermath, the top of the sport is upside down and everyone sounds incoherent—babbling and whining about which teams are good and which are bad, in tones you can otherwise only find from Old Testament prophets. Is Florida secretly good? Is Texas truly a tire fire? Is it going to come out that Cooper Manning never even showed Arch a football before college? Why can't Notre Dame close? Why would Oregon bench Dylan Raiola, just to play him in the fourth quarter against his former school? How did we end up with a first-ranked Miami? These are the questions left to us in the wake of some near-unprecedented football mayhem. The two directions left to go from here are either set the universal order right or make shit go even more left. I know what I choose.After the pyro-spectacular of last weekend, with all those ranked teams either losing outright or barely escaping defeat, something needed to be done to restore normalcy. And so Maryland fired head coach Mike Locksley on Tuesday. Locksley is most recently noted for having guided the Terps to 12 consecutive conference losses, seven of the last eight by double digits, and the most recent coming against Rutgers. The last and decisive one was just a seven-point loss, but it may as well have been 49 when you apply the added "You lost to RUTGERS?" metric.

item.title: James Dolan Finds Innovative New Way To Be Cruel And Cheap
item.author: Samer Kalaf
item.content:encoded: Most owners of sports teams are wise enough to understand that their reputations will never be better than when their teams are winning. If they're fortunate enough to see that team capture a championship, they know that it's easy image rehabilitation. Just show some basic appreciation, sprinkle it around to everyone in the organization, and try not to say much aside from "We did it" and "Thank you." That way, the public will momentarily forget how you made your money off predatory mortgages or whatever.James Dolan has chosen a different path. Since June, when the New York Knicks won their first title in 53 years, the owner has done his best to make the victory lap as unpleasant as possible for all involved. At the championship ceremony, in a juiceless and mercifully short speech, Dolan took swipes at New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and—for some reason—Knicks fans under the age of 53. He brought back notable creep Isiah Thomas, and appointed him to the team's board of directors. He scheduled a fundraiser for Republican gubernatorial candidate Bruce Blakeman right before a Knicks preseason game, and has sued magazine for reporting on the invasive surveillance technology he uses at Madison Square Garden. He's also played hardball in contract talks with the very stars who won a championship. It's rare to have a title-winning team begin its subsequent season on such a sour note.But wait, there's more: According to Joe Vardon of The Athletic, the Knicks' pregame ceremony ahead of Tuesday's season opener was a bit more ceremonial than it appeared. Team president Leon Rose opened a box to show off his sparkly championship ring, but nobody on the coaching staff did, because their boxes were empty. They didn't have rings yet, and it was still unclear who would actually receive one. From the article:

That’s in part because this is a big article and in a several different articles bundled into one, some parts of which I agree with more than others. The basic gist is that you have a Democratic consulting industry based on profit maximization which is burning through Democratic Party patience, commitment, money rather than cultivating them for the long haul. That expresses itself through high-pressure, doomy fundraising asks and by SuperPACs, fundraising vendors, consultants, etc. who spend a huge amount of fundraising dollars on fundraising itself. item.title: Trump DOJ Plays Dirty Pool In California Election Case
item.author: David Kurtz
item.content:encoded: In its attack on the midterm elections in California, the Trump DOJ has taken an extraordinary new step that exemplifies how far off the rails it has gone under Trump II.I mentioned yesterday that the Trump DOJ was seeking an immediate ruling on its emergency application for a temporary restraining order to force Los Angeles County to segregate and not count certain alleged noncitizen ballots. As I noted then, the Trump DOJ request for a ruling from the court by noon yesterday came the judge in the case had already set a hearing on the TRO application for next Tuesday.They appeared to have settled that.But by the end of the day yesterday, the Trump DOJ appealed what it claimed was the lack of a ruling from the judge, making the astounding assertion his “silence” amounted to a “constructive denial” of its application for a TRO.It’s hard to convey to non-lawyers how wacky this is — on so many levels — but let’s start with the claim that the judge had been silent.U.S. District Judge David O. Carter was assigned the case just before noon Wednesday morning. About four hours later, he granted an already-pending request from the Trump DOJ to exceed the court’s page limit for its legal memorandum in support of its TRO application. A couple of hours after that, the Trump DOJ formally filed its TRO application.Sometime after 6:14 p.m. PT, when the the Trump DOJ filed its TRO application, Judge Carter issued an order setting a hearing on the TRO application for Tuesday, Oct. 27 at 1 p.m. ET.At 8:57 p.m. PT, the Trump DOJ for the first time asked for an expedited ruling by noon PT on Oct. 22. By then, Judge Carter had already set a hearing for next Tuesday.Noon yesterday came and went without any new ruling from Carter so before the end of the day, the Trump DOJ moved to appeal the case on spurious constructive denial grounds.How the Trump DOJ construes Judge Carter setting a hearing on its TRO as “silence” is mystifying.But it actually gets worse.In its notice of appeal to Judge Carter, the Trump DOJ outlines the sequence of events leading up to what it deems his “constructive denial” but that he had already scheduled a hearing on the TRO. (The appeal isn’t showing up yet on the Ninth Circuit docket so I can’t confirm whether the Trump DOJ played hide the ball with the appeals court on this, too.)There’s more to say on this, but first here’s a timeline I put together of the key filings and court orders to help orient you:(Derived from the court docket as it appears on Pacer; exact times from Courtlistener): Trump DOJ files its lawsuit against California: Trump DOJ files a motion to exceed the page limit in its application for a TRO, which it attaches as an exhibit: The case is assigned to U.S. District Judge John W. Holcomb: The case is reassigned to U.S. District Judge David O. Carter, a Clinton appointed, because it’s related to an existing case he’s already hearing. (This was a win for California, which had sought the move, and a loss for the Trump DOJ, which had sought assignment to a Trump appointee overseeing a different case that it argued was more related.): Just four hours after being assigned the case, Judge Carter grants the Trump DOJ’s motion to exceed the page limit in its application for a TRO (exact time the order was issued is unclear): Judge Carter schedules a hearing on the Trump DOJ’s application for a TRO for Tuesday, Oct. 27 at 1 p.m. PT: Trump DOJ files its request for an expedited ruling on its application for a TRO by noon PT on Oct. 22: Trump DOJ notifies Judge Carter that it is appealing his failure to rule on its application for a TRO by noon, claiming “the Court’s silence is a constructive denial”Bad DOJ Lawyering All the Way DownThe Trump DOJ’s “constructive denial” argument is the most egregious, but it’s not its only questionable conduct in the case:Five days elapsed after it filed its lawsuit and before it first sought a TRO. Under these circumstances, that delay doesn’t convey the sense of extreme urgency that the Trump DOJ is now insisting the case deserves.It didn’t ask for an expedited ruling in its initial TRO application either (although it was arguably implied by the nature of the filing ).It didn’t engage at all with Judge Carter’s order scheduling a hearing for next Tuesday.It’s a helluva way to greet a judge who’s been on what is a big, national, high-profile case for all of 28 hours.“To say this is irregular is an understatement,” writes election law expert Rick Hasen. “I’m not aware of any case where a party, much less the DOJ, sought to appeal a district court’s failure to quickly enough schedule a hearing on a TRO when a hearing had already been set.”This morning, the Trump DOJ filed a new application for a preliminary injunction (as opposed to a temporary restraining order), trying to take another bite at the apple of getting an immediate ruling from Judge Carter.Don’t Lose the Forest for the TreesAll of the above procedural wrangling in the California case is only of note because it is part of the Trump administration’s unprecedented attack on the midterm elections. I’ve mostly tried to avoid getting down into the nitty gritty of civil procedure in this case, but the latest Trump DOJ moves are too egregious to ignore, especially given the context.For my earlier big picture overviews of the case, you can pick from:Trump DOJ Sues to Block Certification of Alaska Senate ElectionWithin a few hours of Attorney General Todd Blanche denying that he had any plan to block state’s from certifying the results of the midterms elections, his Justice Department filed a new lawsuit to block Alaska from certifying the U.S. Senate election there — one of the key races that will decide control of the upper chamber.The Trump DOJ is jumping in before Election Day to try to salvage the re-election of Sen. Dan S. Sullivan (R), who is facing former Rep. Mary Peltola (D) and a spoiler candidacy by the similarly named Dan J. Sullivan.“The sole purpose of his candidacy is to benefit the Peltola campaign by reducing the number of votes for Senator Sullivan,” the Trump DOJ claims in its lawsuit.It’s not at all clear that DOJ has a proper legal basis to bring such a lawsuit, and what it’s seeking in court is disturbingly vague and open-ended: prevent Alaska election officials from certifying the results of the Senate election “pending an investigation to determine whether votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan were meant to be cast for Senator Sullivan.”How it would be determined that ballots were mistakenly cast for the wrong Dan Sullivan is not clear, either.The lawsuit is signed by Stanley Woodward, Jr., the No. 3 official at DOJ.

item.title: Ramaswamy’s ad exposes MAGA’s obsession with parental estrangement
item.content:encoded: As soon as Vivek Ramaswamy released an ad celebrating a woman accused of backing a fugitive rapist, the widespread assumption among the pundit class was that it would backfire on him. Ohio’s Republican gubernatorial candidate is falling behind in the polls against his Democratic opponent, Dr. Amy Acton, in a race that threatens to turn long-red Ohio blue.In a move reeking of desperation, Ramaswamy’s campaign ran a spot featuring Acton’s elderly mother, Donna Arthur, calling her daughter a “liar” and suggesting she suffers from severe mental illness. But it took almost no time at all before the record was widely corrected, with extensive media reports showing the facts in black-and-white: In 1978, Arthur sided with her husband, Cledith, when he was charged with raping his 12-year-old stepdaughter Amy. Acton has not seen her mother since the Arthurs fled Ohio in an effort to evade justice nearly five decades ago. Her brother confirmed what both Acton and court records show, calling the Ramaswamy campaign “despicable.” The news that the GOP nominee was championing an abusive mother over her daughter quickly became the media narrative, leading to multiple predictions that the ad would backfire on Ramaswamy.And yet MAGA leaders, including President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance, are doubling down on the ad. At a Wednesday campaign event in Cincinnati, Vance praised Ramaswamy for his “audacity to run a TV commercial which calls it out like it is,” despite there being no evidence that Acton lied about her rape and ample evidence — such as fleeing the state — that the Arthurs did. On Wednesday, Trump defended the ad, saying, “It’s very unusual for a mother to hate her daughter, but I don’t think that has anything to do with Vivek.”The president escalated his rhetoric on Thursday, posting on Truth Social, “let everyone listen to the mother of a defective, dishonest, and incapable Candidate.” In Iowa on Thursday, Trump went further, calling Ramaswamy “lucky” to have this situation to exploit, and that he should thank “God” for the favor. The reason is grim political strategy. With Trump’s approval ratings hitting record new lows by the day, Republicans feel their only hope to eke out victories in close midterm races is to juice MAGA turnout. Demonizing an adolescent rape victim is a likely two-fold play; it could energize the same people who are currently attacking Jane Doe, the Cornell gang rape accuser.But the framing of Ramaswamy’s ad also suggests there is another audience his campaign has in mind: aging MAGA voters who are obsessively angry about the phenomenon of parental estrangement. As I documented in an extensive 2024 report, right-wing media frequently runs scare stories about adult children who cut off their parents, a phenomenon that gets blamed on therapists, progressive ideology and social decay supposedly producing selfish children — but never the parents themselves. Just this year alone, Fox News has run multiple stories blaming “cutoff culture,” “social contagion,” “social media” and “ungrateful” children for parental estrangement. Earlier this month, the conservative National Review castigated children who go no-contact for being too poisoned by left-wing ideology to return their parents’ allegedly unconditional love. In September, the Wall Street Journal called it an “epidemic” and quoted supposed experts who claim children suffer from “self-delusion,” “diminished skill for tough conversations” and ““No one is reckoning with the question of what is happening in a lot of families that makes kids feel like they would be better off going low- or no-contact,” explained Joshua Stein, a political researcher who has spent years tracking parental estrangement forums. Instead, there’s an “online ecosystem of estrangement experts,” who often work through right-wing media, “selling services and stories appeal to that audience by first assuring them that it’s not their fault.”“This is the same underlying politics of grievance at the heart of the American right,” he told me, noting that the Acton situation, while an extreme example, is not unusual. “Donna Arthur is a symptom of the moral psychology of right-wing reactionary politics,” Stein said, noting that for the “reactionary right,” the concept of respect “is one-directional.”“Donna Arthur is a symptom of the moral psychology of right-wing reactionary politics,” Stein said, noting that for the “reactionary right,” the concept of respect “is one-directional.” In this view, “authority figures are entitled to respect, regardless of conduct,” and that “respect includes deferring to the authority,” which all too often results in making excuses for child abuse. While none of the estranged adult children who spoke to Salon in 2024 had endured sexual violence, many described how right-wing politics were deeply intertwined with parents being controlling, cruel and abusive. Some spoke of being severely beaten. Others had parents who wanted to dictate their romantic lives. One woman was pushed into a bad marriage at an early age. Another man described how his parents ran off girlfriends for being the “wrong” race or religion. A woman reported being denied medical care for religious reasons. Another woman, who is biracial, said her white mother made racist comments to her. In online forums for estranged parents, which tend to lean conservative, Stein found that children’s stories of mistreatment were regularly dismissed. “The driving narrative of children exaggerating trauma is central to reactionary politics of estrangement,” he explained, noting that Ramaswamy’s ad featuring Acton’s mother is “a manifestation” of this “reasoning under its worst conditions.” Ramaswamy, Trump, Vance and their advisers are all notorious for being constantly online, and they are almost certainly aware that the topic of parental estrangement is a driving concern with many MAGA voters, some of whom have experienced estrangement or distancing from their own children, family members or friends, and are outraged at the thought of facing social consequences for their reactionary views. Much of the online response in right-wing spaces suggests this read on the GOP base is accurate enough. On social media, plenty of GOP voters have defended Arthur and denounced Acton. Many of them appear to be elderly.“Because of the estrangement factor,” one Daily Wire commenter wrote, “I believe the mom.” Many concurred.“So telling the truth is a horrible thing. Mothers know their kids better than anybody,” one person posted on Facebook in response to a local news post about the ad. “NOT all daughters are good daughters EITHER,” agreed one. “Our mothers know us best!!” added another. To be clear, these attitudes are not the norm among Americans generally, and pollsters haven’t had a chance to gauge if Ramaswamy’s ad has boomeranged. But if the goal is to energize Republican voters who may feel demoralized this cycle, the strategy makes more sense. There’s a widespread sense of grievance on the right over feeling rejected for their political views, which manifests in everything from Republicans complaining that liberals won’t date them to a woman at a rally for Byron Donalds, Florida’s GOP nominee for governor, demanding that the law force her “petty” daughter to stay in contact.The Donna Arthur ad was designed to stoke that very sense of entitlement and persuade conservatives to use their vote to punish liberal family members and neighbors for shunning them. It may not be enough to overcome the disgust that Ramaswamy stirred up in voters who have a healthier attitude about family and boundaries. Still, from the party that gave us “Haitians eat pets” and “LGBTQ kids poop in litter boxes,” there really is no move too morally depraved, if they think they can get votes with it.

item.title: Boom, there it is: Todd Blanche won’t rule out trying to steal the midterms
item.author: Jeff Tiedrich
item.source: everyone is entitled to my own opinion
item.content:encoded: Here’s a super fun story from the early days of Dear Leader’s Fucked-Up States of America. After getting his bloated ass handed to him in the 2020 presidential election, Donny went running to Attorney General William Barr, his hand-picked goon at the Department of Justice, and he was all ‘we gotta do something about this election.’Barr sighed, looked at Donny, and replied, ‘eat an entire bag of dicks, pal. “We” ain’t gotta do shit.’ And then he resigned.Billy Bee was an asshole, but he had no desire to be a criminal.Reporter: “Is there any scenario in which the Department of Justice would try to block states from certifying the election?”Attorney General Todd Blanche: “Yes, of course. It is not DOJ’s intention to improperly interfere with elections or the state certification process, but ...”And there it is, folks — the head of the Department of What Used To Be Justice will not rule out meddling in the upcoming midterms.You have to love how the Toddinator pretends that if he has no choice but to step in and attempt to halt the certification process, it’s because he to. Y’know, for the good of the county.Look, a man’s gotta do what a man’s gotta do, am I right?“There was this misperception that there's this ‘separation’ and ‘independence’ between the Department of Justice and the White House and everybody likes to accuse me of not suffering from independence. I don’t. I work for President Trump.”You keep telling yourself that, honcho, but guess what: BZZT! WRONG ANSWER!That’s not how this works. That’s not how any of this works.You know, I’m so old that I remember all the way back to June 27, 2016. That was the day that former president Bill Clinton — who at that point had been out of office for — and then-Attorney-General Loretta Lynch just happened to run into each other, completely by chance, on the tarmac of the Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport.All hell broke loose. The entire wingnut outrage-industrial complex shat one massive brick. Breach of ethics! Breach of ethics! All because two old friends happened to run into each other, and shot the breeze for half an hour.Shut the fuck up, James Comey. You’ve done more to damage our democracy than any random airport meetup did.Fast forward twenty years, and these same sacred guardians of the media can’t be bothered to utter one word when a corrupt president appoints his personal criminal lawyer to be attorney general, and orders him to do his bidding.Hey, do any of you assholes care to say anything at all about Toddy and Donny sitting in a tree, c-o-l-l-u-d-i-n-g?Yes, it’s going to be one nightmarish mess — but when all is said and done, Donny’s just going to be on the losing end of a shitload of poorly-written lawsuits, just as he was in 2024.None of these Donnyverse fucknozzles have any respect for the offices they hold.Let me it for you. Basically, in the Pentagon are two globes that were used by Gen. Dwight D. Eisenhower during World War II. You know, national historical treasures. Official curators at the Pentagon were all ‘well okay if you must, but these globes are priceless artifacts and fragile as fuck, so let us arrange for professional conservators to move them’ — but Piss-Drunk Pete, because he’s basically a child, started screaming DON’T CARE HOW, I WANT IT NOW, and dispatched a couple of complete randos to fork them globes over to his office, like, RIGHT NOW.Of course you will absolutely guess what happened next. The randos dropped one of the globes, and broke the shit out of it.I’m not even sure where ‘destroying a national treasure’ goes, on a scale of ‘butt-dialing classified war plans to a reporter’ to ‘starting an unwinnable war that fucks the entire world’s economy straight into the shitter’ — but holy moly, these incompetent numbskulls can’t do right.That was Donny and his diaper nurse, once again shitting out nonsense in the middle of the night. Oh look, Donny wants you to know that his beloved Epstein Reflecting Pool is ‘85% full.’Of course, it’s all nonsense. The Pool hasn’t been ‘broken since 1922.’ That was the year it was . And he’s still blaming imaginary vandals for his own clowntastic screw-up. And who even knows what the fuck Donny is blithering about when he blames dead grass on ‘a large, and very inappropriate, phrase’?Shut up, Donny. a large and very inappropriate phrase.But Donny wants a cookie, for taking months to fix the thing he broke for absolutely no reason at all. Natty, could you please give this idiot his cookie, and put him to bed? We’re all tired and we really could use some peace and quiet.Let me leave you with this dollop of .“You might have known, you might have seen yesterday, we had a little debate. Or, I had a debate, and he just pointed at me and said, ‘well, he’s a Muslim.’”“His cadence during this was so much like Obama’s, and I love it.”Holy shit, they’re right. El-Sayed have the cadences — and vocal range — of Barack Obama. How had I never noticed it before? I don’t know if El-Sayed is doing this on purpose, or if it’s just a random coincidence, it’s effective. No wonder we love this guy so much. Not only does he says the right things, he says them just as that other guy we love would have. Take a listen. You can’t un-hear it.Well, it’s Friday — and we made it through another week in one piece. Let’s reward ourselves with some Daily Claudia and get out of here.Here are a couple of pics from December 1983, taken by Ms Spouse’s bestie Mandi, in Mandi’s Greenwich Village apartment.Have a great Friday, everyone. here’s your daily reminder that I can be found on Blue Sky at this link.this is going to be my closing message for the foreseeable future: do what you need to do to keep sane. if that means you need to disengage with my daily posts for a while, I get it. this community of ours will still be here when you return.to all the people who have signed on in the days since the election, . settle in as we all try to deal with the shitfuckery that’s ahead of us.we are all in this together, and we are all here for each other.

item.title: Showing the Receipts
item.author: Dave Pell
item.source: NextDraft: The Day's Most Fascinating News
item.content:encoded: You may not be keeping the receipts on your retail purchases, but retailers are definitely keeping the receipts on you. Journalists have requested the dossier McDonald’s has on them, and the reports have come back at over 500 pages (more if you wanted fries with that). You may be able to hide that trip to the donut shop from your family, but you aren’t going to be able to hide it from the host of retailers collecting, sharing, marketing and selling your information. It’s enough to make your eyes glaze over. As Christian Schneider explains in the (Gift Article): You’re in a Toxic Relationship With Your Retailers. “With every purchase, you are entering into a lifelong relationship with a needy lover who is never willing to set you free. Every product you buy is added to your curriculum vitae.” This is hardly a new story. So why focus on it now? Because we are moving into an era where people are starting to use AI agents (or computerized personal assistants) to take over many tasks, including making purchases. What the most sophisticated data brokers have collected about you is nothing compared to the amount of personal, financial, and behavioral information people are willingly handing over because, apparently, shopping online and having items delivered directly to your doorstep seems too hard. And if you’re sharing your contact list with your agent, you’re probably sharing some of my data, too. All this personal information is being surrendered without a fight to the very companies that have shown us, time and time again, that they will take as much of our data as they can and use it against us if it means increasing shareholder value. Definitely something to muse on. Or if that seems like too much work, maybe you can have Muse muse on it for you. It probably already knows you’re musing anyway. Even if you’ve surrendered, there’s still an ongoing fight between retailers and agentic AI companies. “Meta, Google, OpenAI, and others have all introduced some version of agentic shopping tools that promise to make buying things even easier than it already is. Demos show AI agents that can seamlessly book flights and hotels, browse billions of products to find the right one, and secure tickets to sporting events on a human’s behalf. But as AI companies — and their users — are finding out, buying things requires that the other party is willing to sell them in the first place.” (Gift Article): AI agents are ready to shop. Some retailers are wary. Maybe you should be wary, too. After all, ultimately, you’re the product. There’s an ongoing battle to see which companies get to own you. Don’t sell yourself for nothing.At this point, the two world leaders running America (and, in some cases, beyond) agree that they want to betray our ally, Ukraine to the benefit of their ally, Russia. They’re just not in total agreement as to how to execute that betrayal, which leads us to an incredible lede like this one from the : “President Trump called Elon Musk on Wednesday and asked him to lift restrictions on a military-grade version of Starlink in Ukraine that the SpaceX chief had throttled, U.S. officials said. Some U.S. and Ukrainian officials said the system was working more normally on Thursday, after Trump and Musk spoke, but wasn’t restored to full functionality. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Friday ‘the speed has not been restored.’ ‘I’ve heard it was fixed but if it’s not I’ll speak to him,’ Trump told reporters Friday, referring to Musk.”+ Obviously, Musk has way too much power for an unelected (not to mention unsavory, untoward, unkind, and increasingly, unAmerican) citizen. And he’s spending bigly to make sure things stay that way. “Elon Musk gave another $76 million to boost Republicans in the first two weeks of October, bringing his total giving this cycle to more than $442 million.”“Pasa and Yoyo, two female chimpanzees, are best friends. They spend their afternoons lounging together in the warm grass of the Ngamba Island Chimpanzee Sanctuary in Uganda, grooming and sharing food. Sometimes they even try to escape the grounds together. They are also less likely to steal food from each other, according to the results of a new experiment that pitted friendship against pineapple slices.” (Gift Article): Chimps Steal Less Often From Their Friends, Even When Offered Pineapple. “The discovery may hint at the roots of human norms around fairness and friendship.” (Either that, or Yoyo’s not that into pineapple.) You undoubtedly know the name, Edmund Hillary. But there’s a good chance you don’t know Tenzing Norgay. Yet, the two men arrived at the top of Everest at the same moment. In fact, only Tenzing’s photo was taken up there. See the story you may have missed in the excellent Tenzing on Apple TV. (And then check out some minidocs on Tenzing on YouTube. The true story is even more amazing than some elements of the movie.)+ “For decades, we’ve explained corporate corruption as a problem of bad actors, moral weakness, or isolated scandals. But that story doesn’t match reality. Again and again, companies founded with strong ideals drift toward short-term thinking, extractive behavior, and mission abandonment—often despite the best intentions of the people inside them. Incorruptible argues that this failure is not primarily ethical. It is structural.” Eric Ries is famous in the tech world for his book on lean startups. Hopefully, his latest book gets as much attention. Incorruptible: Why Good Companies Go Bad… and How Great Companies Stay Great. Or, how we went from “” to this: Finns Are Seething After Google Illegally Toppled 250,000 Trees for a Data Center.+ Anne Applebaum in : What the U.S. Is Really Doing in Venezuela. “Searching for a model or a reference point, I asked Hausmann how he would describe it. ‘A coalition of two kleptocracies,’ he said.”+ Speaking of election-related efforts: “Israel has launched a campaign of collective punishment against Palestinians in Hebron after gunmen killed two Israeli soldiers and injured three near a checkpoint outside the city. Benjamin Netanyahu announced a siege on Hebron and neighbouring Halhul and said residents of the gunmen’s home neighbourhoods would all be forced out. He promised mass demolitions of homes.” (The Israeli election is in 3 days.)+ “It’s quite a feat, in this numb and debased era, to create a political advertisement so shocking and indecent that people from across the political spectrum feel the need to denounce it. The Ohio gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy, who has long fashioned himself as a kind of Donald Trump 2.0 — younger and brainier but just as brash — has managed it.” It’s sickening. It involves a childhood sexual assault suffered by his opponent. Trump is for it. Vance has defended it. Is this the bottom? (And if it isn’t, is there one?) Michelle Goldberg: The Meaning of the Republican War Over Ramaswamy’s Vile Ad.+ “For six years, I lived in China and observed how Chinese companies became global leaders, in part because American firms brought them better technology and management. In Arizona, I saw how Taiwanese engineers are training American workers to build some of the most complex technologies in the world … And guess what? TSMC engineers and their families are having a great time. In interviews, they marveled at their new lives in the Sunbelt: the large homes, the friendly community, the opportunities for their kids.” The Factory Outside Phoenix That Could Save American Manufacturing.

item.title: Quxnet.net
item.author: Jack Baty
item.content:encoded: Remember when I said that I was done signing up for every new service that comes along? Yeah, me too. But...Quxnet has everything. Boards, mail, photo galleries, links, blogs, an RSS reader, and more. It looks super-retro cool, which adds to the vibe. I don't know what I want out of it yet, but if it can remain "A private network with old internet manners." then I can see it becoming a fun new place to hang out.There are still fewer than 1,000 people there, so naturally things are cordial and sufficiently nerdy and polite. I hope it stays polite, but I worry that with popularity comes conflicting views from people who "We" don't agree with, and once the finger-pointing starts, things tend to go south. I hope it doesn't happen that way.But for now it's clever, fun, nerdy, and new, so I'm in. https://quxnet.net/u/jbaty.

item.title: We sued Trump to protect the midterms
item.author: 1axbj896dj3844z3caxmgigkvex2u5bfsbfk5v@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
item.content:encoded: Earlier this week, my law firm and I filed a lawsuit to stop Donald Trump’s latest power grab and protect the midterm elections.We are suing on behalf of the DSCC, the DCCC, the DGA, Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer, House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, the Nevada State Democratic Party and a California voter who became a naturalized citizen 20 years ago and has voted ever since.Republicans know they are losing.Trump’s approval rating is plummeting. The GOP’s money advantage may buy more ads, but it cannot convince the American people that Trump hasn’t betrayed them.House Republicans have given up on holding the majority, and Senate Democrats are poised to do what, until recently, was viewed as impossible: win the majority.In a final, desperate effort, Trump has turned his administration into a voter suppression war machine.He started with extreme gerrymandering. He tried to co-opt the U.S. Postal Service to take control of mail voting. He sued more than 30 states to seize their voter rolls. He begged the Senate GOP to pass the SAVE America Act.All those efforts failed.Courts blocked the Postal Service scheme. All 26 courts that ruled on Trump’s voter roll lawsuits threw them out. Congress never passed his disenfranchisement bill.Now he is escalating his attacks on our elections and the people who run them. He is asserting powers he does not have and trampling on the constitutional role of the states.Earlier this week, I called it a constitutional crisis. Now I am fighting back.

item.title: Djrum
item.author: Flow State
item.content:encoded: It’s Friday so we’re listening to something more upbeat. Today we’re listening to Djrum, an English electronic musician and DJ. It’s pronounced “drum.” We recommended Djrum’s album last year, which ended up landing on our best of 2025 list. Djrum is a talented producer but he’s an even more talented DJ. His all-vinyl sets are marathons of eclecticism, of which there are several examples on YouTube, the standout being the Tower Bridge show he did with Fabric in 2021. Last week he released a record, which he recorded on vinyl and then lightly edited and overdubbed. The 82-minute journey is all over the place, “from orchestral breakcore to field recordings, and from spaced-out jungle to the nastiest bass rumblings,” as wrote in Pitchfork. We’re also giving another listen afterward.

item.title: First of its kind: A World Series preview
item.author: bounce+2edd00.7bdc18-5mr68b7cb43ac2h04ai5=kill-the-newsletter.com@m.ghost.io
item.content:encoded: The matchup of the Milwaukee Brewers and Tampa Bay Rays guarantees a Fall Classic first. Over the next week or so, baseball will deliver unto one of these franchises and fanbases its first World Series celebration.“First” is one of the best words you can encounter in sports, and “place in the standings” might be its least intriguing application. Like a third-base coach touching his nose or tapping his belt, “first” is an indicator signal for a fun fact about to be delivered.Entry level versions follow the “first … since …” format. The thing has been done before, but perhaps the time elapsed or the last team/player to accomplish it makes it interesting. A pitcher throwing a compete game would be the first complete game since Yoshinobu Yamamoto in 2025. Yeah, not that interesting. A champion clinching in its home ballpark would be the first since 2022 and only the second since 2013. OK, weird.Relentlessly deployed Brewers fireman Aaron Ashby might have a shot at a fun one, if the series cooperates: First pitcher to pitch in seven games of a World Series since Brandon Morrow in 2017, or first pitcher to in seven games of a World Series since Darold Knowles in 1974. That would be something!But for this preview, I wanted to aim higher, to true beacons of novelty, of revelation, of “I Was There” momentous occasions.Here are nine firsts that have never happened in the World Series, ranked by likelihood they happen in Brewers-Rays, starting with the most likely.Some firsts tell us about the conditions of the game. The challenge system is making its World Series debut after a positive and pretty seamless introduction to major-league gameplay.The top of the first inning of Game 1 will feature William Contreras behind the dish for the Brewers — the most prolific head-tapper of both the regular season (by a healthy margin) and the postseason. There’s a good chance this seal is broken in expedient fashion.From there, the question becomes how adrenaline and stakes and heightened strategic instructions play on the biggest stage. Already, we’ve seen a significant postseason shift toward saving challenges for catchers. In the regular season, catchers around MLB challenged 5,559 calls to hitters’ 4,765, a 1.17 catcher/batter ratio. In the postseason, that ratio is 1.55.And with these two teams, the change has looked even more extreme. Brewers have challenged 20 calls, while their batters have challenged 7. And the Rays catchers have challenged 12 calls, while all their hitters have made like Yandy Diaz and refrained from tapping even once (an infinite ratio, if you’re doing the math).Any close call in a big spot will now have an extra layer of drama: To challenge, or not to challenge?Some firsts tell us about freakish human achievement. Aroldis Chapman threw the fastest World Series pitch on record (pitch tracking dates to 2008), back in 2016. It was a 103.2 mph fastball on 0-2 that Coco Crisp actually made contact with, grounding out to second base.Brewers starter and presumptive NL Cy Young Jacob Misiorowski has thrown 100 pitches faster than that one this season, including 28 that broke the 104 mph threshold. This is an excitable young man, in a good way.His way of saying “Welcome to the NLDS” was chucking 104.8 mph on the first pitch.He actually broke 104 mph in Game 1 of both the NLDS and the NLCS. The Brewers sweep of the Dodgers means he will be on 11 days rest when he takes the mound for Game 1. Of the World Series. He’s going to throw the ball real fast.First game to end in 13, 15, 16, or 17 inningsOther firsts tell us about the possibility a die could be mistakenly manufactured with seven dots on one side.Two different World Series marathons involving the Dodgers have stretched to 18 innings in recent memory, but no games have concluded in several relatively normal-sounding spans before that. Frankly, I would be pro extra-inning scrambling without extreme sleep deprivation. Rooting for this. Let’s see Chad Patrick or Steven Matz or some other very regular pitching contributors from the regular season summoned into high-pressure action, why not?With the zombie runner excised from postseason competition, more aggressive pitcher usage, and a lower scoring environment ruling the day, a long (but not that long) extra-innings game is probably in the cards for the near future. But we’ve already dropped from “near certainty” to a statistical improbability.Yoshinobu Yamamoto is not walking through that door. Last season’s complete game was an adrenaline shot straight to the heart for starting pitching junkies, providing the headline for a series that included a lot of good starter performances. The Dodgers and Blue Jays combined for seven starts of six frames or more.The Brewers’ innings leader this October is the aforementioned Aaron Ashby, a reliever. Manager Pat Murphy has not been inclined to push his uniformly young starters — Misiorowski, Logan Henderson, Robert Gasser — and doesn’t seem likely to alter that stance with veteran Dustin May, the fourth starter. If a Milwaukee arm sees the seventh, it’s probably because he’s doing something historic (more on that later).The Rays, on the other hand, are rolling a pretty traditional starting rotation and trusting their guys. I’ve lost track of whether that’s a zig or a zag from the club that popularized the opener (wait for it …) eight years ago. Drew Rasmussen is averaging seven innings a start this month. His 21 innings pitched are 4 1/3 innings clear of second place, his teammate Freddy Peralta. But Peralta, an icon of the five-and-dive modern approach, being the second-most-likely candidate is also a recession indicator for starters working deep.Probably, , at least one starter will have a good night and keep this rather unappealing first at bay. But the bullpen phone is always right there, waiting to ring.First walk-off walk (or walk-off hit by pitch)No World Series game has ever ended with a bases-loaded walk or a plunking, which I found a little surprising.There have been 63 walk-off endings in Fall Classic games. There have been 23 plate appearances across 15 games meeting the conditions to produce a walk-off walk — home team with the bases loaded, ninth inning or later, tie game. In any given 23 plate appearances, even in special conditions, you’d expect to see a walk or a hit by pitch.The MLB walk rate with the bases loaded was 7.3% in 2026, below the overall 8.9% walk rate, as you would hope, but not by a lot. That gap has been consistent in recent years. Only include high-leverage spots within that sample … like a tie game in the ninth or later would be … and the walk rate ticks down even further to 6.7%. I looked at the last five years for a bigger sample: Combining walk rate and hit-by-pitch rate in high-leverage, bases loaded situations and you’re looking at a 9.8% free pass rate.It speaks to something about the extreme pressure of that moment, perhaps on both sides of the equation, that we have count information on 21 of the 23 World Series at-bats in this scenario, and none of them have even reached three balls. No one on the mound wants to be the pitching equivalent of Bill Buckner, and everyone in the batter’s box wants to be the latest version of Luis Gonzalez or Freddie Freeman.This requires a special brew of circumstances to come to fruition: just seven games since 2000 have played out this way. But if it comes up, Milwaukee been steadfast in taking walks this postseason, and in working the count to register three true outcomes across the board. Jake Bauers, he of the multiple 12-pitch at-bats, is running a 20.6% walk rate in the playoffs, and Brice Turang isn’t far behind.Where a walk will do, a walk-off into history is in play.First 20-strikeout game (by a team)Dodgers pitchers struck out 19 Red Sox batters in Game 3 of the 2018 World Series … but that was in 18 innings. The high-water mark in a nine-inning game remain’s Bob Gibson’s 17-K masterpiece in 1968.But combination whiff-fests are inching closer. The Dodgers struck out 16 in 2020, the Blue Jays struck out 15 last year. The Brewers struck out 20 White Sox batters on Opening Day this year, in a nine-inning game, and also struck out 20 A’s in a 12-inning game in June.Less than two weeks ago, the Guardians logged 21 strikeouts against the White Sox in ALDS Game 5.(This first would have ranked higher if the White Sox were involved, clearly.)First World Series with all games decided by one runIf I’m being honest, this postseason has been relatively short on riveting series and moments. Maybe the best series was the Brewers’ white-knuckle game of chicken with the Padres. Three of those games were one-run affairs, while the fourth and final game was a two-run Brewers win.The Rays took two of their three games against the Yankees by one run, and the Brewers' dethroning of the Dodgers had its thrills, but both teams have spent much of the month feeling in control. Maybe — here’s hoping — that produces a less controlled environment this week.It’s not totally implausible. A few Fall Classics have come close. In 1972, six of the seven games were decided by the narrowest of margins as the A’s prevailed over the Reds. And in shorter series, five of six were one-run battles when Atlanta beat Cleveland in 1995. Four of five has happened twice (1915, 1974), while three of four happened once, in 1950.First walk-off bunt without an error involvedThere has been a walk-off bunt, two actually. The most recent was in 1969, when a Mets sacrifice bunt turned into a throwing error and a run and a win. An earlier similar instance came in 1914.This first is about the bunt winning the game on its own merits. (For the record, there has also not been a late-inning go-ahead bunt of any sort other than the previously mentioned, error-empowered two.)Bunts are a little bit back in vogue, because athleticism is fun, speed is fun, and it’s hard to score. Look under every rock, right? The Rays and Brewers look under every rock. These two teams led MLB in bunt hits in 2026, with the Rays first at 49 and the Brewers second at 32.It doesn’t have to be a bunt single necessarily. A wicked fielder’s choice gone awry could work. But even for teams with some small ball tendencies, this doesn’t happen very often. This is a claustrophobic tale of agile underdog excellence, like a gnat escaping a tiny, windowless room by zipping around a man with a flyswatter, dizzying him to the point he falls and knocks himself out while opening the door handle.His stature has leveled up significantly since that moment (Turang was the fifth-best position player in baseball this year, full stop, by FanGraphs WAR), so I don’t think he’d be to bunt in that situation. But is there a part of him that would be interested in testing Caminero, the Rays third baseman whose defense graded out ahead of only other six corner infielders this year?This season, the defense-first Rays shortstop Walls bunted in the tying run in what has to be considered an unusual bunting situation — runners on second and third, no one out, 10th inning — against the Yankees in April.Add in Simpson’s “any bunt could just be a hit” speed, Mullins’ proclivity for surprise bunts and Hamilton’s bench bat positioning for the Brewers, and the possibility exists. More than in any other recent series, that’s for sure.First 20-strikeout game (by a pitcher)Self-explanatory, really. The 20-strikeout game (in nine innings) is less common than a perfect game, more exquisite than a four-homer night. Only four pitchers have done it (Roger Clemens did it twice). Gibson’s 17-strikeout World Series shutout in 1968 is the all-time record in a postseason game. That’s one of only seven playoff games where a pitcher got to 15.It’s not happening. But if it did … would Jacob Misiorowski not be the candidate? He just finished off a season with a 37.9 K%, the second-best rate by a qualified starter in a full season, behind Gerrit Cole’s 2019. He doesn’t really give up runs. He is amply rested, 24 years old and hyped.Maybe there’s no such thing as a candidate for this before he’s on the mound, throwing the game of his life, of all our lives. Maybe there’s a first time for everything. ⚾️

item.title: The Legal System Is Taking Another Shot at Forcing Trump to Tell the Truth About January 6
Trump is making one more play to screw with the midterms
item.author: delivery_20261022061102.48033472.15032@bounce.slate.com
item.content:encoded:
California being the Trump administration’s target should come as no surprise. Outgoing Gov. Gavin Newsom has been a constant critic of President Donald Trump. California is also the only Democrat-controlled state that successfully countered Trump’s mid-decade redistricting push, with voters there overwhelmingly passing a proposition to adopt new voting maps that could net up to five new Democrat-leaning House seats. The Trump administration unsuccessfully tried to convince the Supreme Court to ban California from using its new maps because they were “tainted by an unconstitutional racial gerrymander.” Clearly still salty about that matter, among others, the administration seems to have been cooking up a new way to attack California.
Over the summer, Homeland Security sent California’s Secretary of State Shirley Weber a letter alleging that nearly 200,000 registered voters in California might be noncitizens (numerous secretaries of state received similar letters). But the letters included allegations alone, no evidence or data verifying DHS’s claims, which Weber said she flagged and asked to see, to no avail. Fast-forward to Oct. 13, when Weber, along with Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder and County Clerk Dean Logan received another letter, this time from the DOJ— before Election Day—asking them to review a list of over 20,000 individuals suspected of being noncitizens who were sent a vote-by-mail ballot for the November election.
DOJ wanted both Weber and Logan to direct election officials across the state to “segregate” submitted ballots from voters whose citizenship could not “immediately be verified,” refrain from sending ballots to any more people on its list of 20,000 suspected noncitizens “until we confirm their citizenship status,” and “if a ballot for any individual on the list has been returned, instruct the appropriate elections official to not verify the signature and/or tabulate the ballot until citizenship can be determined.”
Weber and Logan were given approximately 48 hours to respond to the DOJ’s letter. And like clockwork, on Oct. 15 the DOJ filed a lawsuit asking a judge to issue a restraining order to prevent California election officials from processing ballots for any individual on its list of purported noncitizen voters. Never mind the fact that asking California to remove even a single name from its voter rolls at this point is a direct violation of the National Voter Registration Act, which established a 90-day “quiet period” before an election. This provision is meant to prevent states from doing exactly what the Trump administration is asking for: mass removals of voters too close to a federal election, which can cause confusion and prevent voters from fixing any registration issues with enough time left to cast their ballots.
Weber called this out in responding to the DOJ’s Oct. 13 letter. She cited the NVRA and the unlawful ask being put on her and election officials across California. “With less than three weeks before the election, you are demanding unprecedented measures that threaten thousands of Californians’ right to vote, based on unverifiable information or methodology that you still fail to explain or provide,” she said. Weber also went after DOJ’s list of 20,000 purported noncitizens registered to vote in California, reiterating that she requested the underlying data and methodology months ago in order to attempt to verify the federal government’s claims. As it stands, the DOJ's list effectively failed to “be of any investigative use.”
On Tuesday, a Los Angeles County election official responded in court to the DOJ’s lawsuit. She called the DOJ's demands potentially "catastrophic" and said they could end up halting all ballot counting, in person or by mail. She also revealed that election officials looked at a sample of 200 people on the federal government’s list and found that about 43 percent of them had a voter registration canceled, 71 percent had never actually cast a ballot, and nearly 40 percent indicated they U.S. citizens.
This would not be the first time the Trump administration’s alleged noncitizen voting lists were found to be inaccurate. Last month, the Trump administration admitted that a list of nearly 16,000 purported noncitizen voters it flagged for Nevada election officials was wholly inaccurate. After Nevada Deputy Attorney General Greg D. Ott attempted to verify DHS’s claims, he found that every single person on DHS’s list was actually a lawful U.S. citizen. And since Trump retook the presidency, his DOJ has sued 30 states and D.C. to get access to their unredacted voter rolls. Twenty-six of those lawsuits were dismissed by federal judges, half of whom were appointed by Republican presidents, including by Trump himself.
None of this matters to the Trump administration because its goal isn’t actually to weed out voter fraud, but to accomplish two things. First, these efforts seed doubt in America’s electoral process that could convince some voters to distrust the system to the point where they won’t bother casting a ballot. Second, these sham lawsuits give the administration a foothold in the courtroom in the event that a state’s election results are not satisfactory to Trump. Now, the DOJ and losing Republican candidates have a legal record to pull on to claim fraud and challenge state election results.
Rick Hasen, law professor at UCLA and director of the Safeguarding Democracy Project, described this approach in a recent post on his Election Law Blog. Though Hasen expects the DOJ's lawsuit against California “to go nowhere” in a court of law, he believes “this is a political document, potentially laying the groundwork for Trump to claim that the election results are illegitimate because California has not done enough to deal with noncitizen voting.”
To put a finer point on this, the DOJ this week announced a second lawsuit against 28 Californians for election crimes. They’re each being accused of making false statements in their naturalization applications—those applications ask whether applicants previously registered to vote or claimed U.S. citizenship. A number of these folks, though, do not appear to , and some registered to vote more than 20 years ago, likely by accident. “Twenty-eight out of 23 million registered voters in California is just … a drop in the bucket numerically,” California Attorney General Rob Bonta said. “It’s 0.0001% of all the registered voters, and it makes the point that there is no widespread voter fraud.”
Research backs this up, with one study finding that when noncitizen voting and registration does happen, it’s usually due to bureaucratic error and not intentional. For instance, just this year New Jersey revealed that its Motor Vehicle Commission improperly registered about 6,600 noncitizens to vote back in 2023, but fewer than 400 of them actually cast ballots between 2023 and 2024.
The Supreme Court has a hand in all of this, after it effectively emboldened the administration to pursue these types of lawsuits through an opinion issued just a month ago in DHS v. League of Women Voters. In a 6–3 decision, the justices have allowed the federal government to use an expanded federal database, known as the Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements, to identify noncitizen voting in states’ voter rolls.
What can be done now? Well, Americans are the only ones who carry the power of the vote, and right now they can control when they cast their ballots. As Joyce Vance, former U.S. attorney for the Northern District of Alabama, emphasized, “this is the time to vote early.” It will be far more difficult for the Trump administration to challenge election results with ballots submitted weeks ahead of Election Day, especially when races have a large margin of victory. And that’s only possible with strong voter turnout.

item.title: New Developments in the Expanding “Wedgewood” Polling Scandal!
item.author: Josh Marshall
item.source: Josh Marshall – TPM – Talking Points Memo
item.content:encoded: I’m not sure where to start with this. The latest news is some mix of Webistics, Jukt Micronics and Animal House. But here goes. Yesterday we noted that a FiftyPlusOne investigation had led to the outing of “Wedgewood Polls” as a publisher of entirely fake polls. It’s still unclear the precise motives, but some political narrative setting aim and gaming betting markets seem like good bets. The details are wild. (But see the earlier post or FiftyPlusOne’s write-up for more.) Early this morning I woke to a short item in The Washington Post noting another pollster, SoCal Strategies, had straight up disappeared. By disappeared it meant that overnight its website, Substack and Twitter account had all vanished. In the earlier write-up of the investigation of Wedgewood, FiftyPlusOne had noted that one of the ways it had initially vetted Wedgewood was speaking to people at another polling firm where one or more of the Wedgewood guys had worked. I can’t remember if I’d already heard SoCal’s name come up in this story. But when I saw the Post item I immediately knew it had to be them. Yes, fake polls are a problem. But stuff like we’re seeing here is super rare. They had to be connected.

item.content:encoded: Here is one of those things we can see on the horizon and it will be important to be ready for. It will become especially important if Democrats take both the House and the Senate. It’s a given that even with only the House under Democratic control, we’re in for a period of pretty intense inter-branch conflict. Just how intense, whether Democrats will fight as much as their partisans demand … those things we can’t know. But this basic feature of the next Congress is pretty clear. What I’d like to discuss here is a wrinkle in that fabric that hasn’t gotten enough attention.

item.title: Donating Agent Skills to the Agentic AI Foundation
item.author: Simon Willison
item.content:encoded: News today from Anthropic:We’re committed to keeping Agent Skills open, community-driven, and vendor-neutral. Today, we are donating the standard to the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF) under the Linux Foundation, which we co-founded with Block and OpenAI last year, and to which we donated the Model Context Protocol (MCP).I'm pleased to note I called this one last December, when Anthropic first declared skills to be an "open standard":I wouldn't be surprised to see this end up in the AAIF, recently the new home of the MCP specification.Fun side note: since my blog content is available to Claude via the datasette-mcp plugin I found that post by prompting Claude to "Use simonwillison.net MCP to find if I ever talked about how I want skills to be donated to a standards body".

item.title: Your Election Interference Fears Were 100% Justified
item.author: David Kurtz
item.content:encoded: This Is Not a Drill … Repeat … NOT a DrillThe Trump administration has launched a full-blown attack on the midterm elections in California. It’s the very thing that everyone has been worrying that Trump would do for more than a year and yet … it doesn’t feel like the totality of what’s happening has really sunk in or embedded itself in the national political conversation as we sit here 12 days out from the end of voting.To recap for those just joining us, the Trump administration has used the false pretext of rampant noncitizen voting to:gin up criminal prosecutions nationwide against noncitizens for alleged voting-related crimes, with a special focus on California, where it rolled out a bunch of dubious new charges with high-profile arrests and official press conferences two weeks before the election;sue California to force it to segregate and mail-in ballots from alleged noncitizen voters until it undertakes some new, uncertain, and open-ended investigation into whether the voters are citizens;send federal agents door-to-door looking for noncitizen voters in what is at best a fishing expedition and at worst a campaign to terrorize and instill fear in potential voters in minority communities.All of this happening — and I cannot emphasize it enough — universal mail-in voting is already underway in California.The various ways in which the Trump administration spent the past several months trying to monkey with the midterms — asserting unprecedented federal control over state-run federal elections, attempting to use the Postal Service to throttle mail-in ballot delivery, demanding access to voter rolls and individual voter information; marshaling federal databases in a purported effort to ferret out noncitizen voters; among other things — was merely a prelude to its open attack on the midterms now ongoing in California.The breadth and persistence of those earlier efforts by the administration has probably dulled the senses a bit and made it harder to distinguish what it happening now as a more serious and immediate threat to free and fair elections. The other complicating factor is that the fight to fend off the administration’s attack in California stretches from coast to coast, making it harder for reporters to cover it as a single unified story and for the public to grasp the various tendrils.There’s a major civil lawsuit underway in California and two separate important lawsuits in D.C. Plus the myriad criminal cases in California, which won’t be decided until after the election. At the same time, federal grand jury subpoenas are still outstanding that demand voter information from California election officials. And amidst all of that the Trump DOJ continues to actively threaten California election officials with prosecution if they don’t capitulate to administration demands.None of this is how the Justice Department behaved in the run up to past elections — quite the opposite.None of this is how to run an election.Drilling Down Into the DetailsI hope you’re still with me!Above is the high level view of the battlefield. If you only take away that broad impression, it’s all good.But of course, I want to dig down into all the specifics and give you updates on each front in this battle so you know exactly what you need to follow this closely. I’ll still try to keep it manageable in these next few items.More Threats From the Trump DOJI hadn’t zeroed in on this until yesterday, but in the litigation between the Trump DOJ and California, it emerged that acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter, the No. 2 official, sent another letter last Friday containing an array of new threats against California election officials:The legal consequences for either facilitating or ignoring a federal crime are significant. Noncitizen voting in a federal election is a federal crime—and knowingly facilitating such conduct is equally unlawful. Under 18 U.S.C. § 611(a), noncitizens are prohibited from voting in any election involving federal offices. Under 18 USC. § 2, anyone who aids, abets, ‘counsels, induces, or procures the commission of a federal offense is equally liable. If persons: knowingly tabulate ballots cast by individuals identified by federal agencies as noncitizens, they risk becoming aiders and abettors: to a federal crime.Administrative difficulty is not a defense to violating federal law or aiding or abetting a federal offense.The Department strongly urges the County and the SOS to reconsider their positions before taking actions that risk significant federal scrutiny and legal exposure.As California subsequently told a court, election officials are being asked to conduct the midterm elections under the threat of criminal prosecution from the federal government.DOJ Is Running Out of TimeIn the main case in California, where the Trump DOJ is suing to force California to segregate and not count mail-in ballots from alleged noncitizen voters, both sides are seeking quick rulings.The Trump DOJ wants a TRO issued by noon PT .For now, the federal judge has set a hearing on the Trump DOJ’s TRO request for next Tuesday, Oct. 27. (The judge set this hearing before the Trump DOJ asked for a ruling by noon today.)With voting ending in 12 days, the timeframes are tight under every scenario. But they’re slightly tighter for the Trump DOJ, assuming it wants to get this case to the Supreme Court in an emergency posture before Election Day, a fair assumption.Meanwhile, in D.C. Federal Court …U.S. District Judge James Boasberg is overseeing two separate but related cases that are challenging more broadly aspects of the Trump administration’s attack on the midterm elections. As of yesterday, Judge Boasberg put one of those cases on an expedited pre-election timeline similar to the California case. The other case, just filed on Tuesday, isn’t moving as quickly yet, but it may.I’m sparing you details on these cases until they ripen a bit more.Judge Halts DHS Voter Fraud OpsIn yet another case, a federal judge in California blocked DHS from carrying out field operations focused on uncovering voter fraud in California, Connecticut, Georgia, Missouri, Nevada, New York, Pennsylvania, Washington and Wisconsin. The order is to remain in place until the polls close on Nov. 3.The judge was most concerned with U.S. citizens getting swept up in and being intimidated by the DHS field ops, so she blocked ops when they are “likely to involve” people who DHS agents “know, suspect, or should reasonably know or suspect are U.S. citizens.”That leaves some wiggle room for DHS to exploit.The judge’s ruling came the same day that CBS News reported that armed and uniformed DHS agents have have been knocking on doors in several states to ask residents about their immigration status, in an operation that ramped up beginning in September.“[T]he public’s interest in safe elections, free from interference or intimidation, far exceed Defendants’ purported interest in combating unlawful voting by non-U.S. citizens,” U.S. District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguin wrote.While the California battlefront is the most urgent and pressing threat to the midterms, I would still assess as low the Trump administration’s chances of ultimately prevailing in court. But that doesn’t mean it can’t win. And even more importantly, the fight itself is part of the point and is doing real damage right now by actually interfering in an ongoing election.Third Country Removal UpdateUpdates on a couple of the most egregious third country removals that I’ve mentioned over the last couple of months:: A federal judge in California has confirmed that a wrongfully deported Nigerian national is back in the United States after she ordered the Trump administration to facilitate his return. Etinosa Osahon — who was legally barred from being deported to Nigeria because he had already been tortured twice there and was at risk of future torture — was wrongfully deported in May to Ghana, which promptly attempted to transfer him to Nigeria. He refused to continue on the overland journey and was dumped en route in Togo, where he had remained in hiding.: A federal judge in Arizona who ordered the Trump administration on Oct. 6 to facilitate the return of an Egyptian national who had been deported to Equatorial Guinea ratcheted up the pressure on the administration to act more quickly to abide by his original order. The new order comes after Gillian Brockell reported that an ICE deportation flight was scheduled to arrive in Equatorial Guinea today but still not retrieve Ahmed Soliman, whose health is reportedly rapidly deteriorating.The Retribution: Free Press EditionIn a retaliatory move, the Trump White House removed Andrew Feinberg, the reporter whom it derided earlier this week as a “Mongoloid moron,” from the out-of-town print pool for President Trump’s trip to Iowa today.In an extraordinary letter, a White House lawyer demanded that Politico retract a series of palace intrigue stories on Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, concluding his letter with this not-at-all-veiled retaliatory threat:I therefore demand that Politico immediately correct or retract these publications, issue a prominent and public apology to the President of the United States and to Ms. Wiles, and remove the false reporting from your digital archives. Failure to do so or otherwise respond justifying Politico’s publications within 48 hours will prompt an immediate review of Politico’s relationship with the White House, and, of course, consideration of all other appropriate and available legal remedies.Hegseth Broke Eisenhower’s GlobeThe WaPo, with a metaphor for our time: Hegseth wanted Eisenhower’s globe for his office. His staff broke it.
